chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 1
paragraphs: The learned among the Persians say the Phoenicians were the ones who started the quarrel. They came, so the story goes, from what is called the Erythraean Sea to the Mediterranean, and once they had settled in the land where they still live today, they immediately began making long sea voyages. Carrying Egyptian and Assyrian merchandise, they traded in many places, and eventually reached Argos — which at that time was the leading state in what is now called Hellas. When the Phoenicians arrived at Argos, they began selling their cargo. On the fifth or sixth day, when nearly all their goods had been sold, a great crowd of women came down to the shore, and among them was the king's daughter, whose name, as the Hellenes also agree, was Io, daughter of Inachus. The women were standing near the ship's stern, buying whatever pleased them most, when the Phoenicians, passing the word among themselves, suddenly rushed at them. Most of the women escaped by running, but Io and a few others were seized, thrown aboard the ship, and carried off at once to Egypt.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 2
paragraphs: This, the Persians say, is how Io came to Egypt — though the Hellenes tell it differently — and this, according to them, was the first injury. Afterwards, they say, some Hellenes (whose nationality they cannot name) put in at the Phoenician city of Tyre and carried off the king's daughter Europa. These must have been Cretans, and so the two sides were even. But after this, they say, the Hellenes committed the second wrong. They sailed in a warship to Aia in Colchis and up the river Phasis, and after completing the other business that had brought them there, they carried off the king's daughter Medea. The king of Colchis sent a herald to Hellas demanding satisfaction for the abduction and the return of his daughter. The Hellenes replied that since the barbarians had given no satisfaction for the abduction of Io the Argive, they would give none for Medea either.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 3
paragraphs: In the next generation, the Persians say, Alexander, the son of Priam, heard of these events and wanted to get a wife for himself out of Hellas by force, certain that he would never be required to give satisfaction, since the Hellenes had given none themselves. So he carried off Helen. The Hellenes decided first to send messengers demanding her back along with compensation for the abduction. When they pressed this demand, the Trojans threw the abduction of Medea back at them, pointing out that the Hellenes were now demanding from others what they themselves had refused to give, and had not surrendered the woman when she was demanded of them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Up to this point, the Persians say, only women had been carried off on both sides, but now the Hellenes were very greatly to blame, because they were the first to make war, launching an expedition into Asia before the barbarians had launched any into Europe. In their view, it is wrong to carry off women by force, but foolish to take it so much to heart as to seek revenge for the abduction — the sensible thing is to ignore it, since obviously no woman is ever carried off unless she is willing to go. The Persians say that they, the peoples of Asia, paid no attention at all when their own women were taken, while the Hellenes, on account of a single woman from Lacedaemon, gathered a great army, crossed into Asia, and destroyed the kingdom of Priam. From that time on, they have always regarded the Hellenic race as their enemy. For the Persians claim Asia and the barbarian peoples who live there as their own, while Europe and the Hellenes they consider a thing apart.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 5
paragraphs: This, then, is the Persian account, and they trace the beginning of their quarrel with the Hellenes to the capture of Ilion. As for Io, the Phoenicians do not tell the story the way the Persians do. They deny that they carried her off to Egypt by force, and say instead that while she was at Argos she became intimate with the captain of their ship, and when she discovered that she was pregnant and was too ashamed to confess it to her parents, she sailed off with the Phoenicians of her own accord, for fear of being found out. So much for the tales told by the Persians and Phoenicians respectively. As for myself, I am not going to say whether things happened this way or that — but once I have pointed out the man who, within my own knowledge, first began to do wrong to the Hellenes, I shall move forward with my account, describing the cities of men, small as well as great. For those that were once great have for the most part become small, while those that are great in my own time were small in earlier days. Knowing that human prosperity never stays long in the same place, I shall treat both alike.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Croesus was a Lydian by race, the son of Alyattes, and ruler of the nations that live this side of the river Halys — the river that flows from the south between the Syrians and the Paphlagonians and runs out northward into the sea called the Euxine. This Croesus was the first of the barbarians we know of to subdue certain Hellenes and force them to pay tribute, while others he won over as friends. Those he subdued were the Ionians, Aeolians, and Dorians who live in Asia; those he made his friends were the Lacedaemonians. Before the reign of Croesus, all the Hellenes had been free, for the Cimmerian invasion of Ionia, which came before his time, had not been a conquest of the cities but only a raid for plunder.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 7
paragraphs: The sovereignty that had belonged to the Heraclids passed to the family of Croesus, called the Mermnadae, in the following way. Candaules — whom the Hellenes call Myrsilus — was the ruler of Sardis and a descendant of Alcaeus, son of Heracles. For Agron, the son of Ninus, son of Belus, son of Alcaeus, was the first of the Heraclids to become king of Sardis, and Candaules, the son of Myrsus, was the last. The kings of this land before Agron were descended from Lydus the son of Atys, from whom the whole people took the name Lydian, having earlier been called Meonian. From these kings the Heraclids — descended from Heracles and the slave-girl of Iardanus — inherited the throne in obedience to an oracle, and they reigned for twenty-two generations, five hundred and five years, passing the power from father to son down to Candaules, the son of Myrsus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 8
paragraphs: This Candaules had fallen passionately in love with his own wife, and being in love, he came to believe that she was far more beautiful than any other woman. With this conviction, he began to confide in Gyges, the son of Dascylus — for Gyges was his favorite among the royal guards — speaking to him of the most important matters of state, and above all praising his wife's beauty beyond measure. And after no great time, since misfortune was destined to befall Candaules, he spoke to Gyges as follows: “Gyges, I don't think you believe me when I describe my wife's beauty — people's ears are less trusting than their eyes. So you must find some way to see her naked.” Gyges cried out and said, “Master, what an unwise thing to say! You are telling me to look upon my mistress naked? When a woman takes off her tunic, she takes off her modesty with it. There are fine old sayings handed down from long ago by which we should learn wisdom — and among them is this: let each man look upon his own. I do indeed believe that she is the most beautiful of all women, and I beg you not to ask of me what I am not permitted to do.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 9
paragraphs: With such words Gyges resisted, afraid that some evil might come of it, but the king answered, “Take heart, Gyges, and do not be afraid — not of me, as though I were saying this only to test you, and not of my wife, as though any harm might come to you from her. I will arrange it from the start so that she does not even realize she has been seen by you. I will place you in the room where we sleep, behind the open door. After I have gone in, my wife will come in to lie down. There is a chair near the entrance of the room, and on it she will lay her garments one by one as she takes them off, so you will be able to look at her at your leisure. Then when she goes from the chair to the bed and her back is turned to you, take care that she does not see you as you slip out through the door.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Gyges, since he could not avoid it, consented. When Candaules judged it time to rest, he led Gyges into the chamber, and the queen soon followed. Gyges watched her as she came in and laid aside her garments, and when her back was turned as she walked toward the bed, he slipped out from his hiding place and made for the door. But as he went out, she caught sight of him, and understanding what her husband had done, she did not cry out, though she was struck with shame, but pretended she had noticed nothing, intending to take her revenge on Candaules. For among the Lydians, as among most other barbarians, it is a disgrace even for a man to be seen naked.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 11
paragraphs: For the moment, then, she kept silent and gave no sign. But as soon as day had dawned, she made ready those of her servants whom she knew to be most devoted to her, and sent for Gyges. He, not supposing that she knew anything of what had happened, came at her summons, for he had always been accustomed to come whenever the queen called for him. When Gyges had arrived, she said to him, “Two paths now lie open before you, Gyges, and I leave you the choice. Either kill Candaules and possess me and the kingdom of Lydia, or die here on the spot yourself, so that you shall not in future, by obeying Candaules in everything, see what you should not. One of you must die — either the man who devised this scheme, or you, who looked on me naked and did what is not permitted.” For a moment Gyges stood astonished at her words, and then began to beg her not to force such a choice on him. But when he could not move her and saw that he really had no choice but to kill his master or be killed himself, he chose to live, and asked her this: “Since you are forcing me to kill my master against my will, tell me how we are to lay hands on him.” She answered, “The attack will be made from the very same place where he displayed me naked, and we will strike him while he sleeps.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 12
paragraphs: So they prepared their plot, and when night came — for Gyges was not allowed to leave, and there was no way out for him but to kill or be killed — he followed the woman into the bedchamber. She gave him a dagger and hid him behind that same door. Then, while Candaules was sleeping, Gyges came on him secretly, killed him, and took both the woman and the kingdom. The Parian poet Archilochus, who lived about that time, mentioned him in an iambic trimeter verse.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 13
paragraphs: He took possession of the kingdom, and the oracle at Delphi confirmed his rule. For when the Lydians, angry over the death of Candaules, had risen in arms, an agreement was reached between Gyges's supporters and the rest of the Lydians: that if the oracle answered that he was to be king of the Lydians, he should be king, and if not, he should hand the power back to the descendants of Heracles. The oracle gave its answer, and Gyges became king. But the Pythian prophetess added this: that vengeance for the Heraclids would fall upon the fifth descendant of Gyges. Of this oracle the Lydians and their kings took no account — until it was in fact fulfilled.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 14
paragraphs: In this way the Mermnadae gained the throne, ousting the Heraclids. When Gyges became ruler, he sent a good many votive offerings to Delphi — among all the silver offerings there, his are more numerous than any other man's, and besides the silver he dedicated a vast quantity of gold, and in particular one offering worth mentioning above the rest: six golden mixing-bowls, dedicated there as his gift. Their weight is thirty talents, and they stand in the treasury of the Corinthians — though in truth this treasury does not belong to the Corinthian state, but to Cypselus, the son of Eëtion. This Gyges was the first of the barbarians known to us to dedicate votive offerings at Delphi, except for Midas, son of Gordias, king of Phrygia, who dedicated the royal throne on which he sat in judgment — a throne well worth seeing, and it stands in the same place as the bowls of Gyges. The gold and silver Gyges dedicated is called Gygian by the Delphians, after the name of the giver.

Now Gyges, as soon as he became king, led an army against Miletus and Smyrna, and took the lower town of Colophon. But no other great deed did he accomplish in his reign, which lasted thirty-eight years, so we will say no more of him than has already been said,

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 15
paragraphs: and turn instead to Ardys, the son of Gyges, who became king after him. He took Priene and launched an invasion against Miletus, and while he was ruling at Sardis, the Cimmerians — driven from their homes by the nomad Scythians — came to Asia and captured Sardis, except for the citadel.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 16
paragraphs: After Ardys had reigned forty-nine years, his son Sadyattes succeeded him and reigned twelve years; and after him came Alyattes. This last made war on Cyaxares, the descendant of Deioces, and on the Medes, drove the Cimmerians out of Asia, captured Smyrna — which had been founded from Colophon — and launched an invasion against Clazomenae. From Clazomenae he returned not as he wished, but with heavy losses. During his reign, however, he accomplished other deeds very much worth recording, as follows:

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 17
paragraphs: He carried on the war with the Milesians, having inherited it from his father. He would invade their territory and besiege Miletus in this fashion: whenever the crops were ripe in the fields, he marched his army into their country to the sound of pipes, harps, and flutes of both male and female tone. When he reached Milesian land, he did not tear down the farmhouses, burn them, or rip off their doors — he let them stand just as they were. But the trees and the crops on the land he destroyed, and then retreated the way he had come. Since the Milesians controlled the sea, it was useless for his army to lay siege. He spared the houses so that the Milesians would have places to live while they sowed and tilled their fields, and so that through their labor he would have something to destroy the next time he invaded.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 18
paragraphs: He kept up this war for eleven years, in the course of which the Milesians suffered two great defeats — once when they fought a battle in their own territory in the district of Limeneium, and again on the plain of the Maeander. For six of those eleven years, Sadyattes the son of Ardys was still ruler of the Lydians and was the one who kept invading Milesian territory at those seasons, for he was the one who had first begun the war. But for the last five of the eleven years, the war was carried on by Alyattes, the son of Sadyattes, who inherited it from his father (as I have already said) and took it up in earnest. None of the Ionians helped the Milesians bear the burden of this war except the people of Chios. They came to their aid to repay them in kind, for the Milesians had earlier helped the Chians all the way through their war against the people of Erythrae.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 19
paragraphs: In the twelfth year of the war, while the standing corn was being burned by the Lydian army, this happened. As soon as the corn was set ablaze, the fire was carried by a strong wind and set fire to the temple of Athena called Athena of Assesos, and the temple burned to the ground. At the time no account was taken of it, but afterwards, when the army had returned to Sardis, Alyattes fell sick, and as the sickness went on long, he sent messengers to consult the oracle at Delphi — either advised by someone to do so, or because he himself thought it best to send and ask the god about his illness. But when the messengers arrived at Delphi, the Pythian prophetess refused to give them any answer until they had rebuilt the temple of Athena which they had burned at Assesos in Milesian territory.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 20
paragraphs: This much I know from the account of the Delphians; but the Milesians add that Periander the son of Cypselus, who was a close guest-friend of Thrasybulus, at that time tyrant of Miletus, heard of the oracle that had been given to Alyattes and sent a messenger to tell Thrasybulus, so that he might know in advance and take whatever counsel the situation required. This is the Milesian version of the story.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 21
paragraphs: When Alyattes received the oracle's answer, he at once sent a herald to Miletus, proposing a truce with Thrasybulus and the Milesians for as long as it would take to rebuild the temple. The man was sent off as envoy to Miletus; and Thrasybulus, informed of the whole matter in advance and knowing what Alyattes intended to do, devised this stratagem: he had all the supplies of provisions in the city — his own and those belonging to private citizens — gathered together in the marketplace, and he proclaimed to the Milesians that when he gave the signal they should all start drinking and making merry together.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Thrasybulus did this and made this proclamation so that the herald from Sardis would see a vast quantity of provisions carelessly piled up and the people feasting, and would report it to Alyattes. And in fact that is what happened. The herald saw it, delivered the king of Lydia's message to Thrasybulus, and returned to Sardis; and, as I am informed, the peace that was made came about simply because of this. Alyattes, who had imagined there was a severe famine in Miletus and that the people had been ground down to the extreme of misery, heard from the herald when he returned from Miletus the exact opposite of what he had supposed. Afterwards peace was made between them on terms of mutual guest-friendship and alliance, and Alyattes built two temples to Athena at Assesos in place of the one, and himself recovered from his sickness. So much, then, for the war waged by Alyattes against the Milesians and Thrasybulus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 23
paragraphs: As for Periander, the man who passed word of the oracle to Thrasybulus, he was the son of Cypselus and tyrant of Corinth. During his lifetime, say the Corinthians (and the Lesbians agree with them), there happened to him an extraordinary marvel — namely, that Arion of Methymna was carried ashore at Taenarum on the back of a dolphin. Arion was a harper second to none of his day, and the first, so far as we know, to compose a dithyramb, to give it that name, and to teach it to a chorus at Corinth.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 24
paragraphs: This Arion, they say, who spent most of his time with Periander, conceived a desire to sail to Italy and Sicily, and after making a great deal of money there, he wished to return to Corinth. He set sail from Tarentum, and because he trusted Corinthians more than any other men, he hired a ship with a Corinthian crew. These men, out in the open sea, so the story goes, plotted to throw Arion overboard and seize his wealth. When he learned of it, he begged for his life, offering them his money in exchange. But he could not move them — the men conveying him told him either to kill himself on board, so that he might be buried on land, or to jump into the sea at once. Arion, driven to extremity, asked them, since they were of that mind, to let him stand on the deck in his full minstrel's costume and sing, promising to kill himself afterwards. Pleased at the thought of hearing the finest musician alive, they withdrew from the stern toward the middle of the ship. Arion put on his full minstrel's garb, took up his lyre, stood on the deck, and performed the Orthian strain; and when the song ended, he threw himself into the sea just as he was, in full costume. They went on sailing to Corinth — but a dolphin, they say, took him on its back and brought him safely to shore at Taenarum. Once on land he made his way to Corinth in his minstrel's dress, and there told the whole story. Periander, not believing him, kept Arion under guard and would not let him go anywhere, while he kept a close watch for the men who had carried him. When they arrived, he called them in and asked whether they had any news of Arion; and when they said he was safe in Italy and they had left him prospering at Tarentum, Arion suddenly appeared before them, just as he was when he jumped from the ship. Astonished, they could no longer deny anything when questioned. This is the tale told by the Corinthians and the Lesbians alike, and at Taenarum there is a small votive offering of Arion's — a bronze figure of a man on a dolphin's back.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 25
paragraphs: Alyattes the Lydian, after waging war against the Milesians as described, died, having reigned fifty-seven years. When he had recovered from his sickness, he dedicated a votive offering at Delphi — the second of his house to do so — a great silver mixing-bowl with an iron stand welded together, the latter being, above all the offerings at Delphi, a sight well worth seeing. It was the work of Glaucus of Chios, who was the first of all men to discover the art of welding iron.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 26
paragraphs: After Alyattes's death, Croesus, his son, succeeded to the kingdom at the age of thirty-five. He (as I said) waged war against the Hellenes, and the first he attacked were the Ephesians. When the Ephesians were besieged by him, they dedicated their city to Artemis and tied a rope from the temple to the wall of the city — the distance between the old city, then under siege, and the temple being seven furlongs. They, then, were the first on whom Croesus laid hands, but afterwards he did the same to the other Ionian and Aeolian cities one by one, making various complaints against them — serious charges where he could find serious grounds, and trifling ones against others.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 27
paragraphs: When the Hellenes of Asia had been conquered and forced to pay tribute, he intended next to build ships and attack those who lived on the islands. All was ready for shipbuilding when — so they say — Bias of Priene (or, according to another version, Pittacus of Mytilene) came to Sardis. Asked by Croesus whether there was any news from Hellas, he stopped the shipbuilding with this reply. “O king,” he said, “the men of the islands are hiring a force of ten thousand horsemen, and with them they mean to march on Sardis and fight against you.” Croesus, supposing the report to be true, said, “May the gods put it into the minds of the islanders to come on horseback against the sons of the Lydians!” The other answered, “O king, I see that you greatly desire to catch the men of the islands riding on horses on the mainland, and there is nothing unreasonable in that wish. But what do you think the islanders have been wishing and praying for ever since they heard that you were going to build ships against them, except to catch the Lydians at sea, so that they might take vengeance on you for the Hellenes on the mainland, whom you hold enslaved?” Croesus, they say, was greatly pleased with this reply, and, thinking the man had spoken well, he obeyed his suggestion and put a stop to the shipbuilding; and on that basis he formed a friendship with the Ionians who lived on the islands.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 28
paragraphs: As time went on, nearly all the peoples on this side of the river Halys had been subdued — for except the Cilicians and Lycians, Croesus had reduced and kept under his rule all the nations, that is to say the Lydians, Phrygians, Mysians, Mariandynians, Chalybes, Paphlagonians, Thynian and Bithynian Thracians, Carians, Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians, and Pamphylians —

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 29
paragraphs: when these, I say, had been subdued and while he was still extending his Lydian dominion, there came to Sardis — which was then at the height of its wealth — all the wise men of Hellas who happened to be alive at the time, each brought there for his own reason. Among them was Solon the Athenian, who, after making laws for the Athenians at their request, had left his native country for ten years and sailed away, saying that he wanted to see various lands, so that he would not be forced to repeal any of the laws he had proposed. For the Athenians on their own could not do so, since they had bound themselves with solemn oaths to live for ten years under the laws Solon had made for them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 30
paragraphs: So Solon, having left his native country for that reason and for the sake of seeing the world, came to Amasis in Egypt and also to Croesus at Sardis. There he was entertained as a guest by Croesus in the king's palace; and afterwards, on the third or fourth day, at Croesus's order, the servants led Solon around to see the royal treasuries, and they showed him everything — how great and magnificent it all was. After Solon had looked at it all and examined it at leisure, Croesus asked him, “My Athenian guest, much report of you has come to us, both of your wisdom and of your travels — how, in search of wisdom, you have visited many lands to see them. Now, then, a desire has come upon me to ask whether you have seen any man whom you consider the happiest of all men.” He asked this supposing that he himself was the happiest, but Solon, using no flattery and speaking only the truth, said, “Yes, O king — Tellus the Athenian.” Croesus, astonished at this, asked him earnestly, “In what way do you judge Tellus to be the happiest?” Solon replied, “Tellus, in the first place, lived when his native state was prospering, and he had sons who were fine and good, and saw children born to each of them and all of them growing up. And secondly, he had what with us passes for wealth, and he met with the most glorious end of his life: for when the Athenians fought a battle against their neighbors at Eleusis, he came up in support, routed the enemy, and there died a most noble death. The Athenians buried him publicly on the spot where he fell and honored him greatly.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 31
paragraphs: After Solon had moved Croesus to ask further with his story about Tellus—recounting how many marks of happiness the man possessed—the king asked again whom he had judged worthy to be placed next after him, supposing that he himself would certainly win at least the second place. But Solon replied: “Cleobis and Biton. These men, Argives by birth, had wealth enough to live on and, in addition, bodily strength such as I shall describe. Both had equally won prizes in the games, and the following tale is also told of them. There was a festival of Hera among the Argives, and it was absolutely necessary that their mother should be carried in a cart to the temple. But the oxen were not brought up from the field in time. Barred by the shortage of time from any other solution, the young men put themselves under the yoke and drew the wagon, their mother riding upon it. So they pulled it for forty-five stades and arrived at the temple. After they had accomplished this and had been seen by the gathered crowd, a most excellent ending was given to their lives, and in this matter the deity showed that it is better for a man to die than to continue living. For the Argive men stood around praising the strength of the young men, and the Argive women praised the mother for having been lucky enough to bear such sons. The mother, overjoyed both by the deed itself and by the reports of it, took her stand before the image of the goddess and prayed that she would grant to her sons Cleobis and Biton, who had so greatly honored her, the gift that is best for a man to receive. After this prayer, once the young men had sacrificed and feasted, they lay down to sleep inside the temple itself and never rose again, but were held fast in that final ending. The Argives had statues made in their likeness and dedicated them as offerings at Delphi, believing that they had proved themselves most excellent men.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 32
paragraphs: So Solon assigned the second place in happiness to these men, and Croesus, provoked to anger, said: “Athenian guest, have you then cast aside our prosperity as worth nothing, so that you prefer even private citizens to us?” And Solon said: “Croesus, you are questioning about human fortunes a man who knows well that the deity is altogether envious and given to disturbing our lot. For in the course of a long life a man is bound to see many things he would not wish to see, and to suffer many things he would not wish to suffer. I set the limit of a man’s life at seventy years. These seventy years give twenty-five thousand two hundred days, without counting any intercalary month. And if every second year is lengthened by a month so that the seasons may come round at their due time, the intercalated months over the seventy years will number thirty-five, and the days in those months will be one thousand and fifty. So of all these days in the seventy years—twenty-six thousand two hundred and fifty in total—no single day produces anything at all like what another brings with it. Thus, Croesus, man is altogether a creature of chance. As for you, I see that you are both great in wealth and king over many men; but what you asked me I cannot yet call you, until I learn that you have brought your life to a fair ending. For the very rich man is no happier than the man who has only his daily subsistence, unless good fortune also attends him so that he ends his life well while still in possession of all fair things. For many very wealthy men are not happy, while many who have only a moderate living are fortunate. In truth the rich man who is not happy has only two advantages over the poor man who is fortunate, whereas the poor fortunate man has many advantages over him. The rich man is better able to fulfill his desires, and to endure a great calamity if it falls upon him; but the other surpasses him in these ways: he is not indeed able to endure calamity or fulfill desire as well as the rich man, yet his good fortune keeps such things away from him, while he is sound of limb, free from disease, untouched by suffering, father of fair children, and himself of comely form. And if in addition he ends his life well, he is worthy to be called that which you are seeking—a happy man. But before he comes to his end, it is well to hold back and not yet call him happy, but only fortunate. Now to possess all these things together is impossible for any mere mortal, just as no single land suffices to supply everything for itself, but has one thing and lacks another, and the land that has the greatest number is the best. So too in the case of a man: no single person is complete in himself; he has one thing and lacks another. But whoever continues to the end in possession of the greatest number of these things and then comes to a gracious ending of his life—this man, O king, I judge worthy to receive this name. In every matter we must examine the end and how it will turn out at last, for to many men God has shown a glimpse of happiness and then uprooted and overturned them.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 33
paragraphs: Saying this, Solon refused to gratify Croesus, who dismissed him from his presence holding him of no account, and thinking him utterly senseless for passing over present good things and telling men to look to the end of every matter.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 34
paragraphs: After Solon had departed, a great retribution from God came upon Croesus, probably because he had judged himself to be the happiest of all men. First there came and stood beside him in sleep a dream, which revealed to him the truth of the evils that were about to come to pass concerning his son. For Croesus had two sons, of whom one was afflicted, being deaf and dumb, while the other far surpassed his peers of the same age in every way; and the name of this second son was Atys. Concerning this Atys, then, the dream signified to Croesus that he would lose him by the blow of an iron spear-point. When Croesus rose from sleep and turned the matter over in his mind, he was struck with fear on account of the dream. First he took a wife for his son, and whereas Atys had been accustomed to lead the armies of the Lydians, Croesus now no longer sent him forth on any such business. The javelins, lances, and all such weapons that men use in fighting he had removed from the men’s apartments and piled up in the inner bedchambers, for fear that something hanging on the walls might fall down upon his son.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 35
paragraphs: While Croesus was busy with his son’s marriage, there came to Sardis a man under a misfortune, with unclean hands—a Phrygian by birth and of the royal house. This man came to the house of Croesus and, according to the customs that prevail in that land, asked that he might be purified. Croesus granted him the purification, for the manner of purification among the Lydians is almost the same as what the Greeks use. So when Croesus had performed what was customary, he asked the stranger where he came from and who he was, saying: “Man, who are you, and from what part of Phrygia have you come to sit upon my hearth? And what man or woman have you killed?” He answered: “O king, I am the son of Gordias, son of Midas, and I am called Adrastus. I killed my own brother against my will, and for this reason I am here, having been driven out by my father and stripped of all that I had.” Croesus answered him: “You are, as it happens, the offshoot of men who are our friends, and you have come among friends, where you shall want for nothing as long as you remain in our land. And you will find it most to your profit to bear this misfortune as lightly as you can.” So the man made his home with Croesus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 36
paragraphs: During this same time there appeared on Mysian Olympus a boar of monstrous size. Coming down from that mountain, it ravaged the fields of the Mysians, and though the Mysians went out against it often, they could do it no harm but rather suffered harm from it themselves. At length messengers came from the Mysians to Croesus and said: “O king, a boar of monstrous size has appeared in our land and is laying waste our fields. Though we eagerly wish to take it, we are unable. We therefore ask you to send with us your son along with a chosen band of young men and dogs, so that we may drive this creature out of our land.” So they made their request, and Croesus, calling to mind the words of the dream, spoke to them as follows: “As for my son, make no further mention of him in this matter, for I will not send him with you. He is newly married and is occupied now with the business of his marriage. But I will send with you chosen Lydian men and the whole of my pack of hunting dogs, and I will order those who go to be as zealous as possible in helping you drive the wild beast out of your land.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Thus he replied, and while the Mysians were content with this answer, Croesus’s son came in, having heard of the request made by the Mysians. When Croesus said he would not send his son with them, the young man spoke as follows: “Father, in former times the fairest and noblest lot was allotted to us: to go out continually to war and to the hunt, and so to gain good repute. But now you have barred me from both of these, even though you have never observed in me any cowardly or faint-hearted spirit. With what face must I now appear as I come to and from the market-place of the city? What kind of a man shall I be thought by the citizens, and what kind of a man shall I be thought by my newly-married wife? With what sort of husband will she think herself matched? Therefore either let me go to the hunt, or persuade me with reason that things are better for me as they now stand.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Croesus answered him: “My son, it is not because I have observed in you any spirit of cowardice or any other ungracious thing that I act as I do. But a vision in a dream came and stood beside me in my sleep, and told me that you would be short-lived and that you would perish by an iron spear-point. With this vision in mind I both hastened your marriage, and now I refuse to send you on the undertaking at hand, taking care of you so that I may steal you from your fate—at least for the span of my own life, if by any means possible. For you are, as it happens, my only son: the other I do not reckon as one, since he is deficient in hearing.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 39
paragraphs: The young man answered: “Father, it is understandable that you should take care of me after having seen such a vision. But there is a point you do not grasp, and in which the meaning of the dream has escaped you, and it is right that I should explain it to you. You say the dream declared that I would end my life by an iron spear-point. But what hands has a boar, or what iron spear-point, of which you are afraid? If the dream had told you that I would end my life by a tusk, or by some other thing resembling one, then it would indeed be right for you to do as you are doing. But it said ‘by a spear-point.’ Since, therefore, our fight will not be with men, let me now go.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 40
paragraphs: Croesus answered: “My son, you have in part prevailed upon me by declaring your judgment about the dream. Having been prevailed upon by you, I change my resolution and allow you to go to the hunt.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 41
paragraphs: Having said this, Croesus went to summon Adrastus the Phrygian, and when he came, addressed him thus: “Adrastus, when you were struck by a grievous misfortune—with which I do not reproach you—I purified you, and I have received you into my house and supplied all your expenses. Now, therefore, since you have first received kindness from me and are bound to repay me with kindness, I ask you to be the protector of my son, who is going out to the hunt, lest any evil robbers set upon you along the way to do you harm. And besides this, you yourself ought to go where you may become famous by your deeds, for this belongs to you as an inheritance from your fathers, and moreover you have the strength for it.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 42
paragraphs: Adrastus answered: “O king, otherwise I would not have been going out to any such contest of valor. For one thing, it is not fitting that a man suffering such great misfortune as mine should seek the company of prosperous companions, and for another I have no desire for it, and for many reasons I would have kept myself away. But now, since you are pressing me, and I ought to gratify you—for I am bound to repay you with kindness—I am ready to do this. Expect, therefore, that your son, whom you command me to protect, will return to you unhurt, so far as his protector may be able to keep him safe.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 43
paragraphs: When Adrastus had answered Croesus with words like these, they afterward set out, provided with chosen young men and with dogs. When they had come to Mount Olympus, they tracked the beast, and having found it and taken their stand in a circle around it, they began hurling their spears at it. Then the guest—the one who had been purified of manslaughter, whose name was Adrastus—hurling a spear at the boar, missed it and struck the son of Croesus instead. So, being struck by the spear-point, the young man fulfilled the saying of the dream. Someone ran to report what had happened to Croesus, and having come to Sardis, he made known to him the combat and the fate of his son. Croesus was overwhelmed with grief at the death of his son, and he was moved all the more to lamentation by this fact: that his son had been slain by the very man whom he himself had purified of manslaughter. Grievously troubled by the misfortune, he called upon Zeus the Purifier, protesting to him what he had suffered at his guest’s hands, and he called moreover upon the Protector of Suppliants and the Guardian of Friendship—naming the same god each time—calling upon him as Protector of Suppliants because, when he had received the guest into his house, he had been unknowingly nourishing the slayer of his son, and as Guardian of Friendship because, having sent him as a protector, he had found him to be the worst of foes.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 44
paragraphs: After this, the Lydians came bearing the corpse, and the slayer followed behind it. Taking his stand before the corpse, he gave himself up to Croesus, holding out his hands and bidding the king slay him over the corpse, speaking of his former misfortune and saying that in addition to it he had now become the destroyer of the man who had purified him of it, and that for him life was no longer worth living. But Croesus, hearing this, pitied Adrastus, although he was himself suffering so great a calamity of his own, and said to him: “Guest, I have already received from you all the satisfaction that is due, seeing that you condemn yourself to death. Nor are you alone the cause of this evil—except insofar as you were its unwilling instrument—but someone among the gods, as I suppose, who long ago signified to me what was about to happen.” So Croesus buried his son in fitting fashion. But Adrastus, son of Gordias, son of Midas—he who had been the slayer of his own brother and the slayer also of the man who had purified him—when a hush fell upon all the people around the tomb, recognizing that he was more grievously burdened by misfortune than any man he knew of, killed himself upon the grave.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 45
paragraphs: For two years Croesus remained quiet in his mourning, deprived of his son. But after this period of time, the overthrow of the rule of Astyages, son of Cyaxares, by Cyrus, son of Cambyses, and the growing greatness of the Persians, caused Croesus to leave off his mourning and turned his attention to cutting short the power of the Persians, if by any means he might, while it was still growing and before they should have become great.

Having formed this design, he began at once to test the Oracles—both those of the Greeks and the one in Libya—sending messengers, some to one place and some to another: some to go to Delphi, others to Abae of the Phocians, and others to Dodona; and some were sent to the shrine of Amphiaraus and to that of Trophonius, while others went to Branchidae in the land of Miletus. These are the Oracles of the Greeks to which Croesus sent messengers to seek divination. And others he sent to the shrine of Ammon in Libya to inquire there. Now he was sending these messengers abroad in order to test the Oracles and find out what knowledge they had, so that if they should be found to possess knowledge of the truth, he might send a second time and ask them whether he should attempt to march against the Persians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 46
paragraphs: To the Lydians whom he sent to test the Oracles he gave the following charge: from the day they set out from Sardis they were to count the days, and on the hundredth day they were to consult the Oracles, asking what Croesus, son of Alyattes, king of the Lydians, happened to be doing at that moment. Whatever each Oracle prophesied, they were to have written down and bring back to him. Now what the other Oracles prophesied is not reported by anyone; but at Delphi, as soon as the Lydians entered the sanctuary of the temple to consult the god and asked what they had been commanded to ask, the Pythian prophetess spoke thus in hexameter measure:

“I know the number of the sand and the measure of the ocean; I understand the dumb man, and I hear the speech of the speechless. There has come to my soul the smell of a hard-shelled tortoise boiling in a cauldron of bronze, with the flesh of a lamb mingled with it; bronze is laid beneath it, and bronze is cast over it as a covering.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 47
paragraphs: When the Pythian prophetess had uttered this oracle, the Lydians had the prophecy written down and went away at once to Sardis. And when the others also who had been sent to the various shrines had returned with the answers of the Oracles, Croesus then unrolled the writings one by one and looked them over. At first none of them pleased him, but when he heard the answer from Delphi, he at once worshipped the god and accepted it, judging that the Oracle at Delphi was the only true one, because it had discovered what he himself had been doing. For when he had sent to the several Oracles his messengers to consult the gods, keeping the appointed day firmly in mind, he had contrived the following device: he thought of something that would be impossible to discover or even to imagine, and cutting up a tortoise and a lamb, he boiled them together himself in a cauldron of bronze, laying a cover of bronze over them.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 48
paragraphs: Such, then, was the answer given to Croesus from Delphi. As for the answer of Amphiaraus, I cannot tell what he replied to the Lydians after they had performed the customary rites in his temple, for there is no record of this any more than of the others—except only that Croesus thought that he too possessed a true Oracle.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 49
paragraphs: After this, with great sacrifices he sought to win the favor of the god at Delphi: for of every kind of animal fit for sacrifice he offered three thousand, and he heaped up couches overlaid with gold and with silver, and cups of gold, and robes of purple, and tunics, making of them a great pyre, and he burnt all this up, hoping by these means to win the god all the more to the side of the Lydians. He also proclaimed to all the Lydians that every one of them should make sacrifice with whatever he had. And when he had finished the sacrifice, he melted down a vast quantity of gold, and from it he wrought half-plinths, making them six palms in length, three in breadth, and one in height. Their number was one hundred and seventeen. Of these, four were of pure gold, weighing two and a half talents each; the others were of gold alloyed with silver, weighing two talents each. He also had made an image of a lion of pure gold, weighing ten talents. This lion, when the temple at Delphi was being burned down, fell from off the half-plinths, for it had been set upon them, and is now placed in the treasury of the Corinthians, weighing six and a half talents, since three and a half talents had been melted away from it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Croesus sent all of this to Delphi, along with much more: two enormous mixing bowls, one gold and one silver. The gold one was placed to the right as you enter the temple, the silver one to the left. Both were moved after the temple fire. The gold bowl now sits in the treasury of the people of Clazomenai, weighing eight and a half talents plus twelve extra pounds. The silver one stands in the corner of the vestibule and holds six hundred amphors—the Delphians fill it with wine for the festival of the Theophania. The Delphians say it is the work of Theodoros the Samian, and I believe them. The craftsmanship is clearly exceptional. Croesus also sent four silver wine jars, now in the Corinthian treasury, and two vessels for holy water—one gold, one silver. The gold one bears the inscription "from the Spartans," who claim it as their offering. But they are wrong. This too came from Croesus. A man of Delphi wrote the inscription to please the Spartans. I know his name but will not mention it. The bronze boy through whose hands the water flows is indeed a Spartan gift, but neither of the water vessels came from them. Along with these, Croesus sent many other offerings not specially distinguished, including round silver castings and a golden statue of a woman three cubits tall, which the Delphians say represents Croesus' baker. He also dedicated the jewelry from his wife's neck and her girdles.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 51
paragraphs: Those were the gifts Croesus sent to Delphi. To Amphiaraos, having heard of his courage and his tragic fate, he dedicated a shield made entirely of gold and a spear of solid gold—shaft, blade, and both points. Both offerings were still at Thebes in the temple of Ismenian Apollo in my own time.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 52
paragraphs: To the Lydians who were to carry these gifts to the temples, Croesus gave the charge that they should also ask the Oracles this question: whether Croesus should march against the Persians, and, if so, whether he should join any army of men with himself as allies. When the Lydians had arrived at the places to which they had been sent and had dedicated the votive offerings, they consulted the Oracles, saying: “Croesus, king of the Lydians and of other nations, considering that these are the only true Oracles among men, presents to you gifts such as your revelations deserve, and asks you once again whether he should march against the Persians, and if so, whether he should join any army of men with himself as allies.” Thus they inquired, and the answers of both Oracles agreed as one, declaring to Croesus that if he should march against the Persians he would destroy a great empire. And they counseled him to find out which of the Greeks was most powerful and to join these to himself as friends.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 53
paragraphs: So when the answers were brought back and Croesus heard them, he was delighted with the oracles, and expecting that he would certainly destroy the kingdom of Cyrus, he sent again to Pytho and presented the men of Delphi—having first ascertained their number—with two staters of gold for each man. In return, the Delphians granted to Croesus and to the Lydians precedence in consulting the Oracle, exemption from all payments, and the right to front seats at the games, together with this privilege in perpetuity: that any of them who wished might become a citizen of Delphi.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 54
paragraphs: After making these presents to the men of Delphi, Croesus consulted the Oracle a third time, for from the moment he had learned the truth of the Oracle he made abundant use of it. And consulting the Oracle, he inquired whether his monarchy would endure for a long time. The Pythian prophetess answered him thus:
“But when it comes to pass that a mule shall be king of the Medes, then, by the pebbly Hermus, O delicate-footed Lydian, flee and do not stay, and be not ashamed to be called a coward.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 55
paragraphs: These lines, when they reached him, pleased Croesus more than all the rest, for he supposed that a mule would never be ruler of the Medes in place of a man, and that consequently he himself and his heirs would never cease from their rule. After this he turned his thoughts to inquiring which of the Greek peoples he should esteem the most powerful and win over to himself as friends. On inquiring he found that the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians had the pre-eminence, the first among the Dorian and the others among the Ionian race. For these were the most eminent peoples in ancient times, the second being a Pelasgian and the first a Hellenic race. The one never migrated from its original seat in any direction, while the other was exceedingly given to wanderings. For in the reign of Deucalion this race dwelt in Phthiotis, and in the time of Dorus, son of Hellen, in the land lying below Ossa and Olympus, which is called Histiaeotis. When it was driven out of Histiaeotis by the sons of Cadmus, it dwelt in Pindus and was called Macednian; from there it moved afterward to Dryopis, and from Dryopis it came finally to the Peloponnesus, where it began to be called Dorian.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 56
paragraphs: What language the Pelasgians used to speak I am not able to say with certainty. But if one must pronounce judging by those Pelasgians who still remain—those who dwelt in the city of Creston above the Tyrsenians, and who were once neighbors of the race now called Dorian, dwelling then in the land now called Thessaliotis, and also by those Pelasgians who remain from the settlers at Placia and Scylace in the region of the Hellespont, who before that had been fellow-settlers with the Athenians, and by the natives of the various other towns which are really Pelasgian, though they have lost the name—if one must judge by these, then the Pelasgians used to speak a barbarian language. If, therefore, the whole Pelasgian race was like these, then the Attic race, being Pelasgian, must at the same time that it changed and became Hellenic have unlearned its language as well. For the people of Creston do not speak the same language as any of those who dwell around them, nor do the people of Placia; but they speak the same language as one another. And by this it is proved that they still preserve unchanged the form of speech which they brought with them when they migrated to these places.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 57
paragraphs: As for the Hellenic race, it has always used the same language, as I clearly perceive, ever since it first took its rise. But since the time when it branched off—feeble at first—from the Pelasgian race, starting from a small beginning it has grown into the great number of peoples that we now see, chiefly because many barbarian peoples have been added to it besides. Moreover it is true, I think, of the Pelasgian race as well, that insofar as it remained barbarian, it never made any great increase.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Of these two peoples, then, Croesus was informed that the Athenian was held in subjection and torn by faction under Peisistratus, son of Hippocrates, who was at that time tyrant of the Athenians. For to Hippocrates, while he was still a private citizen and had gone to view the Olympic games, a great marvel had occurred. After he had offered the sacrifice, the cauldrons standing upon the hearth, full of pieces of flesh and of water, boiled over without fire beneath them and ran over. Chilon the Lacedaemonian, who happened to be present and to have seen the marvel, advised Hippocrates first not to bring into his house a wife to bear him children, and secondly, if he already had one, to dismiss her, and, if he happened to have a son, to disown him. But Hippocrates, they say, was not willing to be persuaded by Chilon’s advice. And so afterward this Peisistratus was born to him. When the Athenians of the shore were at feud with those of the plain—Megacles, son of Alcmaeon, being leader of the first faction, and Lycurgus, son of Aristolaidas, leader of that of the plain—Peisistratus aimed at the tyranny for himself and gathered a third party. After he had collected supporters and proclaimed himself leader of the men of the mountain-lands, he contrived the following device: he inflicted wounds upon himself and upon his mules, and then drove his chariot into the market-place as if he had just escaped from his enemies, who, he alleged, had tried to kill him as he was driving into the country. He then begged of the commons that he might obtain some protection from them, for before this he had gained a reputation in his command against the Megarians, during which he took Nisaea and performed other signal services. The commons of the Athenians, being deceived, gave him a body of men chosen from among the dwellers in the city—men who became not the spearmen of Peisistratus but his club-men, for they followed behind him bearing wooden clubs. These rose up with Peisistratus and seized the Acropolis. Then Peisistratus became ruler of the Athenians, without disturbing the existing magistrates or changing the ancient laws; but he administered the State under that constitution which was already established, ordering it fairly and well.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 59
paragraphs: However, not long after this, the followers of Megacles and those of Lycurgus joined together and drove him out. Thus Peisistratus had obtained possession of Athens for the first time, and thus he lost the power before he had it firmly rooted. But those who had driven Peisistratus out afterwards became embroiled in feud with one another again. And Megacles, harassed by the party strife, sent a message to Peisistratus asking whether he was willing to take his daughter to wife on condition of becoming tyrant. Peisistratus accepted the proposal, and when they had made an agreement on these terms, they contrived with a view to his return a device the most naive by far, as I think, that ever was practiced—especially considering that it was devised at a time when the Hellenic race had long been set apart from the barbarian as more clever and further removed from foolish simplicity, and devised among the Athenians, who are accounted the first of the Greeks in ability. In the deme of Paeania there was a woman named Phya, four cubits high all but three fingers, and also fair of form. This woman they dressed in full armor and set upon a chariot, and showed her the bearing in which she would best look the part, and so they drove to the city, having sent on heralds to run before them. When these heralds arrived at the city, they said what they had been commanded to say, speaking as follows: “Athenians, receive with favor Peisistratus, whom Athena herself, honoring him above all men, is bringing back to her Acropolis.” So the heralds went around everywhere saying this, and a report immediately reached the demes in the country round about that Athena was bringing Peisistratus back. At the same time the men of the city, convinced that the woman was the goddess herself, were paying worship to a human creature and receiving Peisistratus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 60
paragraphs: Having thus recovered the tyranny in the manner described, Peisistratus, in accordance with the agreement he had made with Megacles, married the daughter of Megacles. But as he already had young sons, and as the descendants of Alcmaeon were said to be under a curse, he did not wish children to be born to him from his newly married wife, and so had intercourse with her in an unaccustomed manner. At first the woman kept this secret, but afterwards she told her mother—whether in answer to her inquiry or not I cannot say—and the mother told her husband Megacles. He then was deeply indignant at being dishonored by Peisistratus, and in his anger immediately moved to compose his quarrel with the men of his faction. When Peisistratus heard what was being done against him, he departed entirely from the land and came to Eretria, where he took counsel together with his sons. When the advice of Hippias prevailed—that they should try to win back the tyranny—they began to gather gifts of money from those states that owed them obligations for favors received. Many contributed great sums, but the Thebans surpassed the rest in the giving of money. Then, not to make the story long, time passed and at last everything was prepared for their return. For certain Argives came as mercenaries from the Peloponnesus, and a man of Naxos called Lygdamis had come to them of his own accord, showing very great zeal in providing both money and men.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 61
paragraphs: So, starting from Eretria after a lapse of ten years, they returned. In Attica the first place of which they took possession was Marathon. While they were encamped there, their partisans from the city came out to them, and others also flowed in from the various demes—men to whom tyrannical rule was more welcome than freedom. So these were gathering themselves together, but the Athenians in the city, so long as Peisistratus was collecting the money, and afterwards when he took possession of Marathon, made no account of it. But when they heard that he was marching from Marathon toward the city, then they went out to the rescue against him. So these were going in full force to fight against the returning exiles, and the forces of Peisistratus, as they went toward the city starting from Marathon, met them just as they came to the temple of Athena Pallenis, where they encamped opposite. Then, moved by divine guidance, there came into the presence of Peisistratus one Amphilytus of Acarnania, a soothsayer, who approaching him uttered an oracle in hexameter verse, speaking thus:
“The cast has been made, and the net has been widely spread; in the night the tunnies will dart through the moon-lit waters.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 62
paragraphs: This oracle he uttered to him, being divinely inspired, and Peisistratus, understanding the oracle and declaring that he accepted the prophecy which had been spoken, led his army against the enemy. Now at that very moment the Athenians from the city happened to be occupied with the morning meal, and some of them after their meal with games of dice or with sleep. Then the forces of Peisistratus fell upon the Athenians and put them to flight. As they fled, Peisistratus devised a very skilful stratagem, so that the Athenians would not gather together again into one body but would remain scattered abroad. He mounted his sons on horseback and sent them before him, and overtaking the fugitives they said what Peisistratus had commanded: they bade the Athenians be of good cheer and that each man should depart to his own home.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 63
paragraphs: The Athenians did as they were told, and so Peisistratus for the third time gained possession of Athens, and he firmly rooted his tyranny by means of many foreign mercenaries and much revenue of money, coming partly from the land itself and partly from the region of the river Strymon. He also took as hostages the sons of those Athenians who had remained in the land and had not at once fled, and placed them in the hands of Naxos; for Peisistratus had also conquered this island by war and had handed it over to the charge of Lygdamis. Moreover, besides this, he purified the island of Delos in obedience to the oracles, and his purification was of this kind: so far as the view from the temple extended, he dug up all the dead bodies that were buried in that part and removed them to another part of Delos. So Peisistratus was tyrant of the Athenians; but of the Athenians some had fallen in the battle, while others, along with the sons of Alcmaeon, were exiles from their native land.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 64
paragraphs: Such was the condition of things that Croesus heard was prevailing among the Athenians during this time. As for the Lacedaemonians, he heard that they had escaped from great troubles and had now got the better of the Tegeans in the war. For while Leon and Hegesicles were kings of Sparta, the Lacedaemonians, who had been successful in all their other wars, suffered disaster only in the one they waged against the men of Tegea. Moreover, in earlier times they had had almost the worst laws of any Greeks, both in matters that concerned themselves alone and also in that they had no dealings with strangers. And they made their change to a good constitution of laws in this way: Lycurgus, a man of the Spartans who was held in high repute, came to the Oracle at Delphi, and as he entered the sanctuary of the temple the Pythian prophetess at once spoke as follows:

“See, you are come, O Lycurgus, to this rich shrine of my temple, loved by Zeus and by all who possess the abodes of Olympus. Whether to call you a god, I doubt in my prophetic voices—god or man—but rather a god, I think, O Lycurgus.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Some say in addition that the Pythian prophetess also set forth to him the order of things that is now established for the Spartans; but the Lacedaemonians themselves say that Lycurgus, having become guardian of Leobotes, his brother’s son, who was king of the Spartans, brought in these things from Crete. For as soon as he became guardian he changed all the prevailing laws and took measures that they should not transgress his institutions. After this Lycurgus established what pertains to war—namely the Enomoties and the Triecades and the Common Meals—and, in addition, the Ephors and the Senate. Having made these changes, the Spartans had good laws; and to Lycurgus, after he was dead, they erected a temple, and they pay him great honor. As might be expected, with a fertile land and no small number of men dwelling in it, they quickly shot up and became prosperous, and it was no longer enough for them to keep still. Presuming that they were superior in strength to the Arcadians, they consulted the Oracle at Delphi about the conquest of the whole of Arcadia. The Pythian prophetess answered them thus:

“You ask me for Arcadia; you ask much—I refuse it. Many are the stout men in Arcadia, eating acorns; these will prevent you. But I am not grudging toward you: Tegea, beaten with sounding feet, I will give you to dance in, and a fair plain I will give you to measure with line and divide.”

When the Lacedaemonians heard report of this, they held off from the other Arcadians and marched against the Tegeans with fetters in their hands, trusting in a deceitful oracle and expecting to make slaves of the men of Tegea. But having been worsted in the encounter, those of them who were taken alive worked wearing the very fetters they had brought with them, having “measured with line and divided” the plain of the Tegeans. And these fetters with which they had been bound were preserved even to my own time at Tegea, hanging about the temple of Athena Alea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 66
paragraphs: In the earlier war, then, as I said, they struggled against the Tegeans continually with ill success; but in the time of Croesus, and in the reigns of Anaxandrides and Ariston at Lacedaemon, the Spartans had at last become victors in the war. And they became victors in the following manner: since they kept being defeated by the men of Tegea, they sent messengers to consult the Oracle at Delphi and asked what god they should propitiate in order to prevail over the men of Tegea in the war. The Pythian prophetess answered them that they should bring into their land the bones of Orestes, son of Agamemnon. But as they were not able to find the grave of Orestes, they sent men again to go to the god and ask about the place where Orestes lay. When the messengers who were sent asked this, the prophetess said as follows:

“There is a place, Tegea, in Arcadian land, founded on a smooth plain, where two blasts blow by strong compulsion together; there is stroke and counter-stroke, and trouble upon trouble. There Agamemnon’s son lies resting in the life-giving earth; bring him home with you and you shall be master of Tegea.”

When the Lacedaemonians had heard this, they were no nearer finding it out, though they searched everywhere, until the time when Lichas, one of those Spartans called “Well-doers,” discovered it. Now the “Well-doers” are the oldest of the citizens who are passing out of the ranks of the “Horsemen,” five in each year; and these men are bound, during the year in which they leave the “Horsemen,” to allow themselves to be sent without ceasing to various places by the Spartan State.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 67
paragraphs: Lichas, being one of these, discovered it in Tegea by means both of luck and skill. For at that time there were dealings under a truce with the men of Tegea, and he had come to a forge there and was watching iron being worked, and he stood marveling at what was being done. The smith, perceiving that he was astonished, ceased from his work and said: “Surely, stranger of Lacedaemon, if you had seen what I once saw, you would have marveled much more—since now it happens that you marvel so greatly at the working of this iron. For I, wishing to dig a well in this enclosure, in my digging came upon a coffin seven cubits long; and not believing that there had ever been men larger than those of the present day, I opened it, and I saw that the dead body was equal in length to the coffin. Then, after I had measured it, I filled in the earth over it again.” So the smith told him what he had seen; and the other, reflecting on what he had been told, conjectured that this was Orestes according to the saying of the Oracle, forming his conjecture in the following way: seeing that the smith had two pairs of bellows, he concluded that these were the “blasts” spoken of, and that the anvil and the hammer were the stroke and the counter-stroke, and that the iron which was being worked was the “trouble laid upon trouble,” reasoning that iron has been discovered for the harm of mankind. Having thus conjectured, he returned to Sparta and declared the whole matter to the Lacedaemonians. They, however, brought a charge against him on a fictitious pretext and drove him out into exile. So having come to Tegea, he told the smith of his misfortune and tried to rent the enclosure from him. At first the smith would not allow him to have it, but at last Lichas persuaded him and took up his abode there. Then he dug up the grave, gathered together the bones, and went away with them to Sparta. From that time on, whenever they made trial of one another, the Lacedaemonians had much the advantage in war, and by now they had subdued to themselves the greater part of the Peloponnesus besides.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 68
paragraphs: Croesus, then, being informed of all these things, was sending messengers to Sparta with gifts in their hands to ask for an alliance, having instructed them what they should say. When they arrived they said: “Croesus, king of the Lydians and of other nations as well, has sent us here and says as follows: O Lacedaemonians, whereas the god by an oracle bade me join with myself the Greek as a friend, therefore, since I am informed that you are the chief men of Greece, I invite you in accordance with the oracle, desiring to be your friend and ally, apart from all guile and deceit.” Thus did Croesus announce to the Lacedaemonians through his messengers; and the Lacedaemonians, who themselves had also heard of the oracle given to Croesus, were pleased at the arrival of the Lydians and exchanged oaths of friendship and alliance. They were bound to Croesus as well by some services rendered to them even before this time, for the Lacedaemonians had sent to Sardis and were buying gold there with the intent of using it for the image of Apollo which is now set up on Mount Thornax in the Lacedaemonian land; and Croesus, when they wished to buy it, had given it to them as a gift.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 69
paragraphs: For this reason, then, the Lacedaemonians accepted the alliance, and also because he had chosen them as his friends, preferring them to all the other Greeks. Not only were they ready themselves when he made his offer, but they had a mixing-bowl made of bronze, covered on the outside with figures around the rim and of such a size as to hold three hundred amphorae, and this they conveyed intending to give it as a gift in return to Croesus. But this bowl never came to Sardis, for reasons of which two accounts are given, as follows. The Lacedaemonians say that when the bowl was on its way to Sardis and came opposite the land of Samos, the men of Samos, having heard of it, sailed out with ships of war and took it away. But the Samians themselves say that the Lacedaemonians who were conveying the bowl, finding that they were too late and hearing that Sardis had been taken and Croesus was a prisoner, sold the bowl in Samos, where certain private persons bought it and dedicated it as a votive offering in the temple of Hera; and probably those who had sold it would say, when they returned to Sparta, that it had been taken from them by the Samians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Such, then, was what happened concerning the mixing-bowl. Meanwhile Croesus, mistaking the meaning of the oracle, was making a march into Cappadocia, expecting to overthrow Cyrus and the power of the Persians. While Croesus was preparing to march against the Persians, one of the Lydians—who even before this time was thought to be a wise man, and as a result of this opinion gained a very great name for wisdom among the Lydians—had advised Croesus as follows (the man’s name was Sandanis): “O king, you are preparing to march against men who wear breeches of leather, and the rest of their clothing is leather as well. They eat not such food as they desire but such as they can obtain, dwelling in a rugged land. Moreover they make no use of wine but drink water, and they have no figs for dessert, nor any other good thing. On the one hand, if you conquer them, what will you take from them, seeing they have nothing? And on the other hand, if you are conquered, consider how many good things you will lose. For once having tasted our good things, they will cling to them fast, and it will not be possible to drive them away. For my own part, I feel gratitude to the gods that they do not put it into the minds of the Persians to march against the Lydians.” Thus he spoke, but he did not persuade Croesus. For it is true that the Persians, before they subdued the Lydians, had no luxury nor any good thing.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 71
paragraphs: Now the Cappadocians are called Syrians by the Greeks, and these Syrians, before the Persians came to power, were subjects of the Medes, but at this time they were subjects of Cyrus. For the boundary between the Median empire and the Lydian was the river Halys, which flows from the mountain-land of Armenia through Cilicia, and afterwards, as it flows, has the Matieni on the right hand and the Phrygians on the other side. Then, passing by these and flowing up toward the North, it bounds on the one side the Cappadocian Syrians and on the left the Paphlagonians. Thus the river Halys cuts off from the rest almost all the lower parts of Asia by a line extending from the sea opposite Cyprus to the Euxine. This tract is the neck of the whole peninsula, the distance of the journey being such that five days are spent on the way by a man without baggage.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Now for the following reasons Croesus was marching into Cappadocia: first, because he wished to add its land to his own possessions, and then especially because he had confidence in the oracle and wished to take vengeance on Cyrus on behalf of Astyages. For Cyrus, son of Cambyses, had conquered Astyages and was keeping him in captivity; Astyages, who was king of the Medes, was Croesus’s brother-in-law, and he had become Croesus’s brother-in-law in this way. A horde of nomad Scythians, at feud with the rest of their people, withdrew and sought refuge in the land of the Medes. At this time the ruler of the Medes was Cyaxares, son of Phraortes, son of Deioces, who at first dealt kindly with these Scythians, as they were suppliants for his protection. Esteeming them highly, he handed over boys to them to learn their speech and the art of shooting with the bow. Time went by, and the Scythians used to go out continually to hunt and always brought back something, until on one occasion they took nothing, and when they returned with empty hands Cyaxares—who, as he showed on this occasion, was not of an eminently good disposition—treated them very harshly and insulted them. The Scythians, having received such treatment from Cyaxares, considered that they had suffered indignity, and planned to kill and cut up one of the boys who were being instructed among them, and, dressing his flesh as they had been accustomed to dress the flesh of wild animals, to carry it to Cyaxares and give it to him, pretending that it was game taken in hunting. Once they had done so, their plan was to make their way as quickly as possible to Alyattes, son of Sadyattes, at Sardis. This was accordingly done, and Cyaxares together with the guests who ate at his table tasted of that meat. The Scythians, having done this, became suppliants for the protection of Alyattes.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 73
paragraphs: After this, since Alyattes would not give up the Scythians when Cyaxares demanded them, war arose between the Lydians and the Medes that lasted five years. In those years the Medes often defeated the Lydians and the Lydians often defeated the Medes, and they fought, among other engagements, a battle by night. And as they still carried on the war with equally balanced fortune, in the sixth year a battle took place in which, when the fight had begun, it happened that day suddenly turned to night. This change of day Thales of Miletus had foretold to the Ionians, setting as its limit this very year in which the change took place. The Lydians and Medes, when they saw that night had come in place of day, ceased fighting and both became much more eager that peace should be made between them. Those who brought about the peace between them were Syennesis the Cilician and Labynetus the Babylonian. These were the men who urged them to take the oaths, and they also arranged an exchange of marriages: they determined that Alyattes should give his daughter Aryenis to Astyages, son of Cyaxares, since without the compulsion of a strong tie agreements tend not to hold firmly together. Now these nations observe the same ceremonies in the taking of oaths as the Greeks do, and in addition they make an incision in the skin of their arms and then lick up the blood, each from the other.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 74
paragraphs: This Astyages, then, who was Cyrus’s mother’s father, Cyrus had conquered and made a prisoner, for a reason I shall declare in the history that follows. This, then, was the complaint Croesus had against Cyrus when he sent to the Oracles to ask whether he should march against the Persians; and when a deceitful answer had come back to him, he marched into the dominion of the Persians, supposing that the answer was favorable to himself. When Croesus came to the river Halys, then, according to my account, he passed his army across by the bridges that were there. But according to the account prevailing among the Greeks, Thales of Miletus enabled him to pass his army across.
