For they say that when Croesus was at a loss how his army should cross over the river—since, they add, at that time the bridges that now exist did not yet exist—Thales, who was present in the army, caused the river, which was then flowing on the left side of the army, to flow partly on the right as well. He did it in this way: beginning above the camp, he proceeded to dig a deep channel, directing it in the form of a crescent moon, so that the river, turned aside from its ancient course along this channel, would take the camp, which was pitched there, in the rear, and then, passing by the camp, would fall back into its ancient course. So as soon as the river was divided in two, it became fordable in both its branches. And some even say that the ancient course of the river was altogether dried up. But this tale I do not admit as true, for how then would they have crossed the river on their way back?

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 75
paragraphs: Croesus, when he had passed over with his army, came to that place in Cappadocia called Pteria. Pteria is the strongest position in this region, and is situated somewhere about in a line with the city of Sinope on the Euxine. Here he encamped and ravaged the fields of the Syrians. Moreover he took the city of the Pterians, sold its people into slavery, and took all the towns that lay about it as well; and the Syrians, who had done him no wrong, he forced to leave their homes. Meanwhile Cyrus, having gathered his own forces and added to them all who dwelt in the region in between, was coming to meet Croesus. Before he began to lead forth his army, however, he had sent heralds to the Ionians and tried to persuade them to revolt from Croesus. But the Ionians would not do as he said. Then when Cyrus had arrived and had encamped opposite Croesus, the two armies made trial of one another by force of arms in the land of Pteria. After hard fighting, when many had fallen on both sides, at last, night having come on, they parted from one another with no victory on either side.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 76
paragraphs: Thus the two armies contended with one another; and Croesus, being dissatisfied with his own army as regards numbers—for the army with which he had fought was far smaller than that of Cyrus—being dissatisfied, I say, on this account, when Cyrus did not try to advance against him on the following day, marched back to Sardis. He had in mind to call upon the Egyptians for help according to the oath they had sworn (for he had made an alliance with Amasis, king of Egypt, before making the alliance with the Lacedaemonians); and to summon the Babylonians as well, for with them too an alliance had been concluded by him, Labynetus being at that time ruler of the Babylonians; and moreover to send a message to the Lacedaemonians bidding them appear at a fixed time. Then, after he had gathered all these together and had assembled his own army, his plan was to let the winter pass and at the coming of spring march against the Persians. With these thoughts in mind, as soon as he reached Sardis he proceeded to send heralds to his several allies, giving them notice that by the fifth month from that time they should assemble at Sardis. But the army he had with him, which had fought with the Persians—an army consisting of mercenary troops—he let go and disbanded altogether, never expecting that Cyrus, after having contended against him with such evenly balanced fortune, would after all march upon Sardis.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 77
paragraphs: While Croesus had these plans in mind, the suburb of the city suddenly became full of serpents; and when they had appeared, the horses, leaving off feeding in their pastures, kept coming there and devouring them. When Croesus saw this he deemed it a portent, as indeed it was, and at once dispatched messengers to the dwelling of the Telmessians, who interpret omens. The messengers who were sent to consult arrived there and learned from the Telmessians what the portent meant to signify, but they did not succeed in reporting the answer back to Croesus, for before they could sail back to Sardis, Croesus had been taken prisoner. The Telmessians, however, gave their judgment thus: that an army speaking a foreign tongue was to be expected to invade Croesus’s land, and that when it came it would subdue the native inhabitants. For they said that the serpent was a child of the soil, while the horse was an enemy and a stranger. The men of Telmessus thus made their answer to Croesus after he had already been taken prisoner, not knowing as yet anything of what had happened to Sardis or to Croesus himself.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 78
paragraphs: Cyrus, however, as soon as Croesus marched away after the battle that had been fought in Pteria, having learned that Croesus intended to disband his army once he had marched off, took counsel with himself and concluded that it was best for him to march to Sardis as quickly as possible, before the power of the Lydians could again be gathered together. So once he had resolved on this, he carried it out without delay, for he marched his army into Lydia with such speed that he was himself the first to announce his coming to Croesus. Then Croesus, although he had come to a great strait—since his affairs had fallen out altogether contrary to his own expectation—still proceeded to lead the Lydians out into battle. At this time there was no nation in Asia more courageous or stouter in battle than the Lydian; they fought on horseback carrying long spears, and the men were excellent horsemen.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 79
paragraphs: So when the armies had met in that plain in front of the city of Sardis—a plain wide and open, through which flow rivers (and especially the river Hyllus), all rushing down to join the largest, called the Hermus, which flows from the mountain sacred to the Mother surnamed “of Dindymus” and runs out into the sea by the city of Phocaea—then Cyrus, when he saw the Lydians being arrayed for battle, fearing their horsemen, did as Harpagus the Mede suggested. He gathered all the camels in the train of his army that were carrying provisions and baggage, took off their burdens, and set men upon them equipped like cavalry. Having thus furnished them, he ordered them to go in front of the rest of the army toward the horsemen of Croesus; and after the camel-troop he commanded the infantry to follow; and behind the infantry he placed his whole force of cavalry. When all his men had been placed in their several positions, he charged them to spare none of the rest of the Lydians, slaying all who came in their way, but they were not to kill Croesus himself, not even if he should resist when he was captured. Such was his charge. He had set the camels opposite the horsemen for this reason: because the horse is afraid of the camel and cannot endure either to see its shape or to scent its smell. For this reason, then, the trick had been devised, in order that the cavalry of Croesus might be useless—the very force with which the Lydian king expected most to shine. And as they were coming together to battle, as soon as the horses scented the camels and saw them, they turned back, and the hopes of Croesus were at once brought to nothing. The Lydians, however, did not behave as cowards on that account, but when they perceived what was happening, they leapt from their horses and fought the Persians on foot. At length, however, when many had fallen on either side, the Lydians turned to flight; and having been driven within the wall of their fortress, they were besieged by the Persians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 80
paragraphs: So the Persians had established a siege. But Croesus, supposing that the siege would last a long time, proceeded to send from the fortress further messengers to his allies. For the earlier messengers had been sent round to give notice that they should assemble at Sardis by the fifth month, but these now he was sending out to ask them to come to his assistance as quickly as possible, since Croesus was now being besieged.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 81
paragraphs: So in sending to his other allies, he sent also to Lacedaemon. But these—the Spartans, I mean—had at this very time (as it happened) a quarrel of their own in hand with the Argives about the district called Thyrea. For the Lacedaemonians had cut off this Thyrea, which was part of the Argive territory, and had taken it for themselves. At that time the Argives possessed the whole region toward the west extending as far down as Malea, both the parts on the mainland and also the island of Cythera with the other islands. When the Argives had come to the rescue to save their territory from being cut off, the two sides came to a parley and agreed that three hundred men should fight on each side, and whichever side had the better in the fight, that nation should possess the disputed land. They also agreed that the main body of each army should withdraw to its own country and not stand by while the contest was fought, for fear that, if the armies were present, one side, seeing their countrymen suffering defeat, would come up to their support. Having made this agreement, they withdrew, and chosen men of both sides were left behind and engaged in combat with one another. They fought and proved themselves evenly matched, and at last, of six hundred men, only three were left alive—on the Argive side Alcenor and Chromius, and on the Lacedaemonian side Othryades. These were left alive when night came on. The two Argives, supposing that they were the victors, set off to run back to Argos; but the Lacedaemonian Othryades, after stripping the corpses of the Argives and carrying their arms to his own camp, remained in his place. On the next day both sides came to the spot to inquire about the result, and for some time both claimed the victory for themselves: the one side saying that more of them had survived, the others declaring that those men had fled whereas their own man had stood his ground and had stripped the corpses of the other party. At length, because of this dispute, they fell upon one another and began to fight again, and after many had fallen on both sides, the Lacedaemonians were victorious. The Argives then cut their hair short, whereas formerly they were required by law to wear it long, and they made a law with a curse attached: that from that time forth no Argive man should grow his hair long nor their women wear ornaments of gold until they had won back Thyrea. The Lacedaemonians, on the contrary, laid down for themselves the opposite law: that they should wear long hair from that time forward, whereas before that time they had not worn it long. And they say that the one man left alive of the three hundred, Othryades, being ashamed to return to Sparta when all his comrades had been slain, killed himself there in Thyrea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 82
paragraphs: Such was the condition of things at Sparta when the herald from Sardis arrived asking them to come to the assistance of Croesus, who was being besieged. And despite their own difficulties, as soon as they heard the news from the herald, they were eager to go to his aid. But when they had completed their preparations and their ships were ready, there came another message reporting that the fortress of the Lydians had been taken and that Croesus had been made a prisoner. Then, and not before, they ceased their efforts, being grieved at the event as at a great calamity.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 83
paragraphs: Now the taking of Sardis came about as follows. When the fourteenth day came after Croesus had begun to be besieged, Cyrus made proclamation to his army, sending horsemen round to the several parts of it, that he would give gifts to the man who first scaled the wall. After this the army made an attempt; and when it failed, then after all the rest had ceased from the attack, a certain Mardian named Hyroeades attempted to approach on that side of the citadel where no guard had been set. For they had no fear that it would ever be taken from that side, seeing that the citadel there is precipitous and unassailable. To this part of the wall alone Meles, who was formerly king of Sardis, did not carry round the lion which his concubine bore to him, the Telmessians having decreed that if the lion were carried round the wall Sardis would be safe from capture. Meles carried it round the rest of the wall—those parts of the citadel where the fortress was open to attack—but passed over this part as unassailable and precipitous; it is the part of the city that faces toward Tmolus. So this Mardian Hyroeades, having on the day before seen one of the Lydians descend on that side of the citadel to recover his helmet, which had rolled down from above, and seen him pick it up and come back, took thought and turned the matter over in his mind. Then he himself climbed up first, and after him others of the Persians came up, and many having thus made their approach, Sardis was finally taken and the whole city was given up to plunder.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 84
paragraphs: Meanwhile, to Croesus himself it happened thus. He had a son, of whom I made mention before, who was of good disposition enough but deprived of speech. In his former time of prosperity Croesus had done everything that was possible for him, and among the other things which he devised, he had sent messengers to Delphi to inquire concerning him. The Pythian prophetess spoke to him thus:

“Lydian, master of many, much blind to destiny, Croesus, do not desire to hear in your halls that voice which is prayed for—the voice of your son. Much better if this were removed from you, since he shall first utter speech on an evil day of misfortune.”

Now when the fortress was being taken, one of the Persians was about to slay Croesus, taking him for someone else. Croesus, for his part, seeing the man coming on, cared nothing for it because of the misfortune which was upon him, and to him it was a matter of indifference that he should be slain by the blow. But this voiceless son, when he saw the Persian coming on, through terror and anguish burst the bonds of his utterance and cried out: “Man, do not kill Croesus.” This son, I say, spoke then for the first time of all, but after this he continued to use speech for the whole rest of his life.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 85
paragraphs: The Persians, then, had obtained possession of Sardis and had taken Croesus himself prisoner, after he had reigned fourteen years and had been besieged fourteen days, having fulfilled the oracle in that he had brought to an end his own great empire. The Persians then, having captured him, brought him into the presence of Cyrus. And Cyrus piled up a great pyre and made Croesus go up onto it bound in fetters, and with him twice seven sons of Lydians, whether it was that he meant to dedicate this offering as first-fruits of his victory to some god, or whether he wished to fulfill a vow, or else had heard that Croesus was a god-fearing man and so caused him to go up on the pyre because he wished to know if one of the divine powers would save him from being burned alive. This, they say, is what Cyrus did. But to Croesus, as he stood upon the pyre, there came, even in such evil plight, a memory of the saying of Solon, how he had declared with divine inspiration that no one of the living might be called happy. And when this thought came into his mind, they say that he sighed deeply and groaned aloud, having been long silent, and three times he uttered the name of Solon. Hearing this, Cyrus bade the interpreters ask Croesus who this person was on whom he called, and they came near and asked. Croesus for a time, it is said, kept silent when asked this, but afterwards, being pressed, he said: “One whom—more than much wealth—I should have wished all monarchs to have speech with.” Then, since his words were of doubtful meaning, they asked again what he meant; and as they were urgent with him and gave him no peace, he told how once Solon an Athenian had come, and having inspected all his wealth had made light of it with such and such words, and how it had all turned out for him according to what Solon had said, and that Solon had been speaking not at all with a view to Croesus in particular, but with a view to the whole human race and especially those who seem to themselves to be happy men. And while Croesus related these things, already the pyre was lighted and the edges of it all around were burning. Then they say that Cyrus, hearing from the interpreters what Croesus had said, changed his purpose and considered that he himself also was but a man, and that he was delivering another man—one who had been not inferior to himself in felicity—alive to the fire. Moreover he feared retribution, and reflected that nothing of what men possess is secure. Therefore, they say, he ordered his men to extinguish as quickly as possible the fire that was burning and to bring down Croesus and those who were with him from the pyre. But they, despite their efforts, were no longer able to master the flames.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 86
paragraphs: Then it is related by the Lydians that Croesus, having learned how Cyrus had changed his mind, and seeing that everyone was trying to put out the fire but that they were no longer able to check it, cried aloud, entreating Apollo that if any gift had ever been given by him that had been acceptable to the god, he would come to his aid and rescue him from the evil which was now upon him. So with tears he entreated the god, and suddenly, they say, after clear sky and calm weather, clouds gathered and a storm burst, and it rained with a very violent shower, and the pyre was extinguished. Then Cyrus, having perceived that Croesus was a lover of the gods and a good man, caused him to be brought down from the pyre and asked him as follows: “Croesus, tell me: who of all men was it who persuaded you to march upon my land and so to become an enemy to me instead of a friend?” And he said: “O king, I did this to your felicity and to my own misfortune, and the one who caused it was the god of the Greeks, who incited me to march out with my army. For no one is so senseless as to choose war over peace of his own free will, since in peace sons bury their fathers, but in war fathers bury their sons. But it was pleasing, I suppose, to the divine powers that these things should come to pass thus.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 87
paragraphs: So he spoke, and Cyrus loosed his bonds and caused him to sit near himself, and paid him much regard; and Cyrus himself and all those around him marveled at the sight of Croesus. Croesus, wrapped in thought, was silent; but after a time, turning round and seeing the Persians plundering the city of the Lydians, he said: “O king, must I say to you what I happen to have in my thought, or must I keep silent in my present fortune?” Cyrus bade him say boldly whatever he wished, and Croesus asked: “What is it that this great multitude of men is doing with such eagerness?” And Cyrus said: “They are plundering your city and carrying away your wealth.” Croesus answered: “It is not my city they are plundering, nor my wealth they are carrying away, for I no longer have any property in these things. It is your wealth they are carrying and driving away.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 88
paragraphs: Cyrus was concerned by what Croesus had said, and he caused all the rest to withdraw and asked Croesus what he discerned for his advantage as regards what was being done. Croesus said: “Since the gods have given me to you as a slave, I think it right, if I discern anything more than others, to signify it to you. The Persians, who are by nature unruly, are without wealth. If, therefore, you allow them to carry off great wealth in plunder and to take possession of it, you must expect this result: whoever gets the largest share will rise up in rebellion against you. Now therefore, if what I say pleases you, do this: set spearmen of your guard to watch at all the gates, and let them take the things away from the men who are carrying them out of the city, telling them that the goods must first be tithed for Zeus. Thus on the one hand you will not be hated by them for taking away the things by force, and they on the other will willingly let the things go, acknowledging within themselves that you are doing what is just.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 89
paragraphs: Hearing this, Cyrus was beyond measure pleased, because he thought that Croesus gave good counsel. He praised him highly and enjoined the spearmen of his guard to carry out what Croesus had advised. After that, he spoke to Croesus thus: “Croesus, since you are prepared, like the king you are, to do good deeds and speak good words, therefore ask me for a gift, whatever you wish to be given you forthwith.” And Croesus said: “Master, you will most of all do me a pleasure if you permit me to send to the god of the Greeks, whom I honored most of all the gods, these fetters, and to ask him whether it is reckoned right by him to deceive those who do well by him.” Then Cyrus asked him what accusation he was making against the god, that he should make such a request; and Croesus repeated to him everything that had been in his mind, and the answers of the Oracles, and especially the votive offerings, and how he had been incited by the prophecy to march against the Persians; and thus speaking, he came back again to the request that he might be permitted to make this reproach against the god. And Cyrus laughed and said: “Not only this shall you obtain from me, Croesus, but also whatever you may at any time desire of me.” Hearing this, Croesus sent certain of the Lydians to Delphi, enjoining them to lay the fetters upon the threshold of the temple and to ask the god whether he felt no shame at having incited Croesus by his prophecies to march against the Persians, persuading him that he would bring an end to the empire of Cyrus—seeing that these fetters were the first-fruits of the spoil he had won from it—at the same time displaying the fetters. This they were to ask, and moreover whether it was considered right by the gods of the Greeks to practice ingratitude.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 90
paragraphs: When the Lydians came and repeated what they had been enjoined to say, it is related that the Pythian prophetess spoke as follows: “The fated destiny it is impossible even for a god to escape. And Croesus has paid the debt owed for the sin of his fifth ancestor, who, being one of the spearmen of the Heraclidae, followed the treacherous device of a woman, and having slain his master, took possession of his royal dignity, which did not belong to him by right. And although Loxias eagerly desired that the calamity of Sardis might come upon the sons of Croesus and not upon Croesus himself, it was not possible for him to turn the Destinies aside from their course. Yet so much as they granted, he brought to pass and gave as a gift to Croesus: for he put off the taking of Sardis by three years; and let Croesus be assured that he was taken prisoner later by these years than the fated time. And moreover, secondly, he assisted him when he was about to be burned. As to the oracle that was given, Croesus finds fault on good grounds: for Loxias told him beforehand that if he marched against the Persians he would destroy a great empire. And he, on hearing this, if he wished to take counsel well, ought to have sent and asked further whether the god meant his own empire or that of Cyrus. But since he did not comprehend what was said and did not ask again, let him pronounce himself to be the cause of what followed. To him also, when he consulted the Oracle for the last time, Loxias said what he said concerning a mule; but this too he failed to comprehend. For Cyrus was in fact this mule, seeing that he was born of parents of two different races, his mother being of nobler descent and his father of less noble: for she was a Median woman, daughter of Astyages, king of the Medes, while he was a Persian, one of a race subject to the Medes, and being inferior in every respect he was the husband of a woman who was his royal mistress.” Thus the Pythian prophetess replied to the Lydians, and they brought the answer back to Sardis and repeated it to Croesus; and he, when he heard it, acknowledged that the fault was his own and not the god’s. With regard, then, to the empire of Croesus and the first conquest of Ionia, it happened thus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 91
paragraphs: There are many other offerings by Croesus in Greece beyond those I have already mentioned. At Thebes in Boeotia, he dedicated a golden tripod to Ismenian Apollo. At Ephesus, there are the golden cows and most of the temple pillars. In the temple of Athena Pronaia at Delphi, there is a large golden shield. These were still in place in my own time. Other offerings have been lost. His offerings at Branchidai in Milesian territory were, I am told, equal in weight and similar in kind to those at Delphi. The gifts he sent to Delphi and to the shrine of Amphiaraos came from his own wealth, the first-fruits of his inheritance. But the other offerings were made from the property of an enemy—a man who had conspired against Croesus before he became king, trying to make Pantaleon ruler of Lydia instead. Pantaleon was a son of Alyattes and half-brother to Croesus, but by a different mother: Croesus was born to a Carian woman, Pantaleon to an Ionian. When Croesus won the kingdom by his father's choice, he executed his rival by drawing him across a carding comb. The man's property, which Croesus had earlier vowed to dedicate, he offered to the shrines I have named. That is enough about his offerings.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 92
paragraphs: As regards marvels worth recording, the land of Lydia has no great store of them compared with other lands, apart from the gold-dust that is carried down from Tmolus; but one work it has to show that is larger by far than any other, except only those in Egypt and Babylon. For there stands there the sepulchral monument of Alyattes, father of Croesus, of which the base is made of larger stones and the rest of the monument is of earth piled up. This was built by contributions of those who practiced trade, of the artisans, and of the girls who plied their traffic there. And even in my own time there still existed upon the monument above five boundary-stones, on which were carved inscriptions telling how much of the work had been done by each class; and upon measurement it was found that the work of the girls was the greatest in amount. For the daughters of the common people in Lydia all practice prostitution to gather dowries for themselves, continuing this until the time when they marry, and the girls give themselves away in marriage. Now the circuit of the monument is six stades and two hundred feet, and the breadth is thirteen hundred feet. Adjoining the monument is a great lake, which the Lydians say has a never-failing supply of water, and it is called the lake of Gyges. Such is the nature of this monument.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Lydians have very nearly the same customs as the Greeks, with the exception that they prostitute their female children. They were the first of men, so far as we know, who struck and used coin of gold or silver, and also the first retailers. The Lydians themselves claim that the games now in use both among them and among the Greeks were their own invention. These games, they say, were invented among them at the same time that they colonized Tyrsenia, and this is the account they give. In the reign of Atys, son of Manes, their king, there came a grievous dearth over the whole of Lydia. The Lydians for a time continued to endure it, but afterwards, since it did not cease, they sought for remedies, and one man devised one thing and another another. Then, they say, were invented the ways of playing with dice and with knucklebones and with the ball, and all the other games except draughts, for the discovery of this last is not claimed by the Lydians. These games they invented as a resource against the famine, and this was what they would do: on one day they would play games all day in order not to feel the want of food, and on the next day they would leave off their games and eat. Thus they went on for eighteen years. Since, however, the evil did not slacken but pressed upon them ever more and more, the king divided the whole Lydian people into two parts and assigned by lot one part to remain and the other to go forth from the land. The king appointed himself to be over that part which had drawn the lot to stay in the land, and his son to be over the part that was departing, and the name of his son was Tyrsenus. So the party that had drawn the lot to leave went down to the sea at Smyrna, built ships for themselves in which they placed all the movable goods they had, and sailed away to seek means of living and a land to dwell in. After passing by many nations, they came at last to the land of the Umbrians, and there they founded cities and dwell up to the present time. And changing their name, they were called, after the king’s son who had led them out from home, not Lydians but Tyrsenians, taking the name from him.
The Lydians, then, had been made subject to the Persians, as I have said.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 94
paragraphs: After this our history proceeds to inquire about Cyrus, who he was that destroyed the empire of Croesus, and about the Persians, in what manner they obtained the lead of Asia. Following, then, the report of certain of the Persians—I mean those who do not desire to glorify the history of Cyrus but to speak what is in fact true—according to their report, I say, I shall write; though I could also set forth the other forms of the story in three different ways.

The Assyrians ruled Upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years, and from them the Medes were the first to revolt. These, having fought for their freedom against the Assyrians, proved themselves brave men, and so they pushed off the yoke of slavery from themselves and were set free. After them the other nations also did the same as the Medes; and when all on the continent were thus independent, they returned again to despotic rule as follows.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 95
paragraphs: There appeared among the Medes a man of great ability whose name was Deioces, and this man was the son of Phraortes. This Deioces, having formed a desire for despotic power, did this: whereas the Medes dwelt in separate villages, he, being even before this time of great repute in his own village, set himself to practice just dealing much more and with greater zeal than before. And this he did although there was much lawlessness throughout the whole of Media, and although he knew that injustice is ever at feud with justice. The Medes of his own village, seeing his ways, chose him for their judge. So Deioces, since he was aiming at power, was upright and just; and doing thus he received no small praise from his fellow citizens, so that those of the other villages, learning that Deioces was a man who, more than any other, gave decisions rightly—whereas before this they had been accustomed to suffer from unjust judgments—they too, when they heard it, came gladly to Deioces to have their causes determined. At last they entrusted the business to no one else.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 96
paragraphs: Then, as more and more kept continually coming to him—because men learned that his decisions proved to be in accordance with the truth—Deioces, perceiving that everything was being referred to himself, would no longer sit in the place where he had formerly sat in public to judge cases, and said that he would judge cases no more, for it was not profitable for him to neglect his own affairs and to determine cases for his neighbors all day long. So then, since robbery and lawlessness prevailed in the villages even more than they did before, the Medes assembled together in one place and consulted with one another and discussed the state in which they were. And I suppose the friends of Deioces spoke much to this effect: “Seeing that we are not able to dwell in the land under the present order of things, let us set up a king from among ourselves; thus the land will be well governed and we ourselves shall be able to turn to our work, and not be ruined by lawlessness.” With words like these they persuaded themselves to have a king.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 97
paragraphs: When they straightway proposed the question whom they should set up to be king, Deioces was much put forward and commended by everyone, until at last they agreed that he should be their king. He bade them build for him a palace worthy of the royal dignity and strengthen him with a guard of spearmen. The Medes did so: they built him a large and strong palace in that part of the land which he indicated, and they allowed him to select spearmen from all the Medes. When he had obtained the rule over them, he compelled the Medes to make one fortified city and to pay chief attention to it, having less regard for the other cities. And as the Medes obeyed him in this also, he built large and strong walls—those which are now called Ecbatana—standing in circles one within the other. This wall is so contrived that one circle is higher than the next by the height of its battlements alone. To some extent, I suppose, the nature of the ground, since it is on a hill, assists toward this end; but much more was it produced by art, since the circles are seven in number altogether. Within the last circle are the royal palace and the treasure-houses. The largest of these walls is in size about equal to the circuit of the wall around Athens. And of the first circle the battlements are white, of the second black, of the third crimson, of the fourth blue, of the fifth red—thus the battlements of all the circles are colored with various tints; and the two innermost have their battlements, one of them overlaid with silver and the other with gold.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Deïokes built these walls around his palace. The rest of the people were ordered to live outside the walls. When the building was complete, he established a protocol—the first of its kind. No one was permitted to enter the king's presence. All business was conducted through messengers. No one could see the king. Laughing or spitting in his presence was forbidden for everyone without exception. He wrapped himself in this ceremony so that his former companions—men raised alongside him, of equally good families and no less courageous—would not grow resentful at seeing him and plot against him. If they could not see him, they might come to think of him as a different kind of being.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Having set these things in order and strengthened himself in his despotism, he was strict in preserving justice. The people used to write down their cases and send them in to his presence, and he determined the questions that were brought in to him and sent them out again. Such was his manner with the judgment of cases. He also took order for this, namely, that if he heard that anyone was behaving in an unruly manner, he would send for him and punish him as each act of wrong deserved. And he had watchers and listeners throughout all the land over which he ruled.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 100
paragraphs: Deïokes united the Median nation under his sole rule. The Median tribes are as follows: the Busai, Paretakenians, Struchates, Arizantians, Budians, and Magians. Those are all the tribes of the Medes.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 101
paragraphs: Now the son of Deioces was Phraortes, who, when Deioces was dead after having reigned fifty-three years, succeeded him in power. Having received it, he was not satisfied to be ruler of the Medes alone but marched against the Persians; and attacking them first before any others, he made these the first to be made subject to the Medes. After this, being ruler of these two nations and both of them strong, he proceeded to subdue Asia, going from one nation to another, until at last he marched against the Assyrians—those Assyrians, I mean, who dwelt at Nineveh, and who formerly had been rulers of the whole, but at that time were left without support, since their allies had revolted from them, though at home they were prosperous enough. Phraortes marched, I say, against these, and was both himself slain, after he had reigned twenty-two years, and the greater part of his army was destroyed.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 102
paragraphs: When Phraortes had brought his life to an end, Cyaxares, son of Phraortes, son of Deioces, received the power. This king is said to have been still much more warlike than his forefathers; and he first banded the men of Asia into separate divisions—that is, he first arrayed apart from one another the spearmen, the archers, and the horsemen, for before that time they had all been mingled together without distinction. This was the man who fought with the Lydians when day became night as they fought, and who also united under his rule the whole of Asia above the river Halys. And having gathered together all his subjects, he marched upon Nineveh to avenge his father, and also because he wished to take the city. After he had fought a battle with the Assyrians and defeated them, while he was sitting in siege before Nineveh, there came upon him a great army of Scythians, whose leader was Madyes, son of Protothyes, king of the Scythians. These had invaded Asia after driving the Cimmerians out of Europe, and in pursuit of them as they fled they had come into the land of Media.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Now from the Maeotian lake to the river Phasis and the land of the Colchians is a journey of thirty days for one without baggage; and from Colchis it is not far to cross over into Media, for there is only one nation between them, the Saspeirians, and passing by this nation you are in Media. The Scythians, however, did not make their invasion by this route, but turned aside from it to take the upper road, which is much longer, keeping Mount Caucasus on their right hand. Then the Medes fought with the Scythians, and having been defeated in the battle they lost their power, and the Scythians obtained rule over all Asia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 104
paragraphs: From there they went on to invade Egypt; and when they were in Syria, which is called Palestine, Psammetichus, king of Egypt, met them, and by gifts and entreaties he turned them from their purpose so that they should advance no further. As they retreated, when they came to the city of Ascalon in Syria, most of the Scythians passed through without doing any damage, but a few of them who had stayed behind plundered the temple of Aphrodite Urania. This temple, as I find by inquiry, is the most ancient of all the temples that belong to this goddess; for the temple in Cyprus was founded from this one, as the people of Cyprus themselves report, and it was the Phoenicians who founded the temple in Cythera, coming from this land of Syria. So these Scythians who had plundered the temple at Ascalon, and their descendants forever after, were smitten by the divinity with a disease that made them women instead of men. The Scythians say that for this reason they were diseased, and that for this reason travelers who visit Scythia today see among them the affliction of those whom the Scythians call Enareis.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 105
paragraphs: For twenty-eight years, then, the Scythians were rulers of Asia, and by their unruliness and reckless behavior everything was ruined. For on the one hand they exacted as tribute from each people whatever sum they laid upon them, and apart from the tribute they rode about and carried off by force the possessions of each tribe. Then Cyaxares with the Medes, having invited the greater number of them to a banquet, made them drunk and slew them; and thus the Medes recovered their power and ruled over the same nations as before. They also took Nineveh—the manner in which it was taken I shall set forth in another history—and made the Assyrians subject to them, except only the land of Babylon.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 106
paragraphs: After this Cyaxares died, having reigned forty years, including those years during which the Scythians had ruled, and Astyages, son of Cyaxares, received the kingdom from him. To him was born a daughter whom he named Mandane; and in his sleep it seemed to him that there passed from her so much water as to fill his city and even to flood the whole of Asia. This dream he handed over to the Magian interpreters of dreams, and when he heard from them the truth of each detail, he became afraid. And afterwards, when this Mandane was of an age to have a husband, he did not give her in marriage to any of the Medes who were his peers, because he feared the vision; but he gave her to a Persian named Cambyses, whom he found to be of good descent and of a quiet disposition, counting him in station much below a Mede of middle rank.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 107
paragraphs: When Mandane had been married to Cambyses, in the first year Astyages saw another vision. It seemed to him that from the womb of this daughter a vine grew, and this vine overspread the whole of Asia. Having seen this vision and delivered it to the interpreters of dreams, he sent for his daughter, then with child, to come from the land of the Persians. When she had come, he kept watch over her, intending to destroy whatever should be born of her, for the Magian interpreters of dreams had signified to him that the offspring of his daughter would be king in his place. Astyages, then, wishing to guard against this, when Cyrus was born, called Harpagus, a man who was of close kin to him and whom he trusted above all the other Medes, and had made him manager of all his affairs; and to him he said as follows: “By no means neglect, Harpagus, the matter that I shall lay upon you to do, and beware lest you set me aside and, choosing the advantage of others instead, bring yourself afterwards to destruction. Take the child whom Mandane has borne, and carry it to your house and slay it; and afterwards bury it in whatever manner you yourself wish.” To this he answered: “O king, never yet at any past time have you discerned in me an offence against you, and I keep watch over myself also with a view to the time that is to come, that I may commit no error toward you. If, then, it is indeed your pleasure that this should be done, my service at least must be fittingly rendered.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 108
paragraphs: When the child was handed over to him, dressed for death, Harpagos went home weeping and told his wife everything Astyages had said. She asked: "What do you intend to do?" He answered: "Not what Astyages commanded. Even if he grows more deranged than he already is, I will not do his bidding or serve him in such a murder. I will not kill this child, for many reasons: the child is my own kin, and Astyages is old and has no male heir. If the throne passes to Mandane after his death—the very woman whose son he now orders me to kill—what is left for me but the greatest danger? For my own safety, the child must die. But one of Astyages' own servants must do the killing, not one of mine."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 109
paragraphs: He immediately sent a messenger to one of Astyages' herdsmen who, he knew, grazed his cattle on the most suitable pastures in mountains full of wild beasts. The herdsman's name was Mitradates, and he lived with a woman who was also a slave of Astyages. Her Greek name would be Kyno (meaning "dog"), since her Median name, Spako, translates to the same thing—the Median word for dog being "spaka." The foothills where this herdsman kept his cattle lie north of Agbatana, toward the Euxine Sea. That part of Media, bordering Saspeiran territory, is very mountainous, heavily forested, and high, while the rest of Media is entirely flat. When the herdsman came with great speed at the summons, Harpagos said: "Astyages commands you to take this child and leave it in the wildest part of the mountains, so that it dies as quickly as possible. He told me to say this: if you do not kill the child and try to save it by any means, you will die by the most terrible death. I have been ordered to verify that it is exposed."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 110
paragraphs: After hearing this and taking up the child, the herdsman went back by the way he had come and arrived at his dwelling. Now his own wife, who had been on the point of giving birth every day, by a providential chance delivered her child at just this time, while her husband was away in the city. Both were in anxiety, each for the other: the man afraid about his wife's labor, the woman about why Harpagos had summoned her husband so urgently, which he had never done before. So as soon as he came back and stood before her, his wife, seeing him again beyond her hopes, was the first to speak, and asked him for what purpose Harpagos had sent for him. He answered: “Wife, when I came to the city I saw and heard things I wish I had never seen, and which I wish had never befallen those whom we serve. The whole house of Harpagos was full of mourning, and in my astonishment I went inside. As soon as I entered I saw laid out to view an infant child gasping for breath and screaming, which was adorned with gold ornaments and embroidered clothing. When Harpagos saw me he ordered me at once to take up the child and carry it away and lay it on that part of the mountains most haunted by wild beasts, saying that Astyages had laid this task upon me, and threatening me with many punishments if I failed. I took the child and carried it off, supposing it was the son of one of the servants of the house, for I could never have guessed whose child it really was. But I marveled to see it adorned with gold and fine raiment, and I marveled too that mourning was made for it openly in the house of Harpagos. And straightaway on the road I learned the whole matter from the servant who came with me out of the city and placed the babe in my hands: namely that it was in truth the son of Mandane, the daughter of Astyages, and of Cambyses the son of Cyrus, and that Astyages orders it to be killed. And now here it is.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 111
paragraphs: And as he said this, the herdsman uncovered the child and showed it to her. When she saw that it was large and of fair form, she wept and clung to her husband's knees, begging him by no means to expose it. But he said he could do nothing else, for watchers sent by Harpagos would come back and forth to see that it was done, and he would perish by a miserable death if he failed. When she could not persuade her husband, the wife next spoke thus: “Since I cannot persuade you not to expose it, do this which I shall tell you, if indeed the child must be seen laid forth. I too have borne a child, but I have borne it dead. Take that one and expose it, and let us rear the daughter of Astyages' grandson as if it were our own. In this way you will not be found doing a wrong to those whom we serve, nor shall we have taken ill counsel for ourselves: for the dead child will receive a royal burial, and the surviving one will not lose his life.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 112
paragraphs: To the herdsman it seemed, the case standing thus, that his wife spoke well, and at once he did so. The child he was carrying to put to death he handed over to his wife, and his own dead child he took and placed in the chest in which he had been carrying the other. Having adorned it with all the ornaments of the other child, he bore it to the most desolate part of the mountains and left it there. And when the third day came after the child had been exposed, the herdsman went to the city, leaving one of his under-herdsmen to keep watch there, and when he came to the house of Harpagos he said that he was ready to display the dead body of the child. Harpagos sent the most trusted of his spearmen, and through them saw and buried the herdsman's child. This child then had its burial; but the one who was afterwards called Cyrus the herdsman's wife had received, and was bringing him up, giving him no doubt some other name, not Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 113
paragraphs: When the boy was ten years old, something happened to him which made his true identity known. He was playing in the village where the stalls for oxen stood, playing in the road with other boys of his age. And the boys in their game chose as their king this one who was called the son of the herdsman. He assigned some of them to build palaces, others to be spearmen of his guard, one to be the eye of the king, and one to bear messages — appointing a duty to each one. Now one of these boys who was playing with the rest, the son of Artembares, a man of repute among the Medes, did not do what Cyrus had appointed him to do. So Cyrus ordered the other boys to seize him by hand and foot, and when they obeyed his command he dealt with the boy very roughly, scourging him. As soon as he was let go, being all the more angry because he considered he had been treated with indignity, he went down to the city and complained to his father of the treatment he had received from Cyrus — calling him not Cyrus, for this was not yet his name, but the son of the herdsman of Astyages. And Artembares, in the anger of the moment, went at once to Astyages, taking the boy with him, and declared that he had suffered treatment that was unfitting, saying: “O king, by your slave, the son of a herdsman, we have been thus outraged” — and he showed him the shoulders of his son.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 114
paragraphs: When Astyages heard and saw this, he wanted to punish the boy to avenge Artembares' honor. He summoned both the herdsman and his son. When both stood before him, Astyages looked at Cyrus and said: "You—the son of this nobody—dared to treat the son of a man I hold in the highest honor like this?" The boy replied: "Master, I treated him as he deserved. The boys of the village chose me as their king in a game, because they thought I was the best suited for it. All the other boys did what I told them. But this one disobeyed and ignored my orders, so he was punished. If I deserve to suffer for that, here I am."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 115
paragraphs: While the boy thus spoke, a sense of recognition came over Astyages. The features of his face seemed to resemble his own, his answer appeared to be somewhat too free for his station, and the time of the exposure seemed to agree with the age of the boy. Struck with amazement by these things, he was for a while speechless. Having at length with difficulty recovered himself, he said, wishing to dismiss Artembares so that he might get the herdsman alone and examine him: “Artembares, I will so order these things that you and your son shall have no cause to find fault.” So he dismissed Artembares, and the servants, upon the command of Astyages, led Cyrus within. When the herdsman was left alone with the king, Astyages asked him where he had got the boy from and who had delivered him. The herdsman said that he was his own son, and that the boy's mother was living with him still as his wife. But Astyages said he was not well advised in wishing to be brought to extreme necessity, and as he said this he signaled to the spearmen of his guard to seize him. So as he was being led away to torture, the herdsman declared the story as it really was, and beginning from the beginning he went through the whole, telling the truth about it, and finally ended with entreaties, asking to be pardoned.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 116
paragraphs: So when the herdsman had made the truth known, Astyages now cared less about him, but with Harpagos he was greatly displeased and ordered his spearmen to summon him. When Harpagos came, Astyages asked him thus: “By what death, Harpagos, did you destroy the child whom I delivered to you, born of my daughter?” Harpagos, seeing that the herdsman was in the king's palace, did not turn to any false way of speech, lest he be convicted and found out, but said as follows: “O king, as soon as I received the child, I took counsel and considered how I should act according to your wishes, and how, without offending your command, I might not be guilty of murder against your daughter and yourself. I therefore did this: I called this herdsman and delivered the child to him, telling him first that you were the one who ordered it to be killed — and in this at least I did not lie, for you did so command. I gave it to this man with instructions to place it on a desolate mountain, and to stay beside it and watch until it died, threatening him with every kind of punishment if he failed. And when he had done what was ordered and the child was dead, I sent the most trusted of my eunuchs and through them saw it and buried it. Thus, O king, it happened in this matter, and the child had the death I have described.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 117
paragraphs: So Harpagos declared the truth, and Astyages, concealing the anger he held against him for what had come to pass, first related the matter over again to Harpagos just as he had been told it by the herdsman. Then, when it had been thus repeated, he ended by saying that the child was alive and that what had come to pass was well. “For,” he continued, “I was greatly troubled by what had been done to this child, and I thought it no light thing that I had been at variance with my daughter. Therefore, consider this a happy change of fortune. First send your son to be with the boy who is newly come, and then, since I intend to make a sacrifice of thanksgiving for the preservation of the boy to those gods to whom that honor belongs, be here yourself to dine with me.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 118
paragraphs: When Harpagos heard this, he made obeisance and thought it a great matter that his offense had turned out for his profit, and moreover that he had been invited to dinner with such a happy omen. So he went to his house. Having entered, he at once sent forth his son — for he had one only son, about thirteen years old — bidding him go to the palace of Astyages and do whatever the king commanded, and overjoyed he told his wife what had befallen him. But Astyages, when the son of Harpagos arrived, cut his throat and divided him limb from limb, and having roasted some pieces of the flesh and boiled others, he had them dressed for eating and kept them ready. When the time came for dinner and the other guests were present, including Harpagos, then before the other guests and before Astyages himself were placed tables covered with mutton; but before Harpagos was placed the flesh of his own son — all but the head, hands, and feet, which were laid aside, covered up, in a basket. When it seemed that Harpagos had had enough food, Astyages asked him whether he had been pleased with the banquet. When Harpagos said he had been very greatly pleased, those who had been commanded to do so brought to him the head of his son, covered up, together with the hands and the feet. Standing near, they bade Harpagos uncover and take whichever of them he desired. When Harpagos obeyed and uncovered them, he saw the remains of his son. Seeing them, he was not overcome with amazement but contained himself. Astyages asked him whether he knew of what animal he had been eating the flesh, and he said that he knew, and that whatever the king might do was well pleasing to him. Having made this reply and taking up the parts of the flesh that remained, he went to his house; and afterwards, I suppose, he would gather all the parts together and bury them.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 119
paragraphs: This was the penalty Astyages laid upon Harpagos. And about Cyrus he took thought, and summoned the same Magians who had given judgment about his dream in the manner already described. When they came, Astyages asked them how they had judged his vision, and they spoke according to the same manner, saying that the child must have become king if he had lived on and had not died before. Astyages answered them thus: “The child is alive and not dead. And while he was living in the country, the boys of the village appointed him king, and he performed completely all those things which real kings do — for he exercised rule, appointed spearmen of the guard and doorkeepers and message-bearers, and everything else. Now then, to what do these things seem to you to tend?” The Magians said: “If the child is still alive and became king without any arrangement, then concerning him be confident and of good courage, for he shall not rule again a second time. Some even of our oracles have had but small fulfillment, and that at least which has to do with dreams often comes in the end to a feeble accomplishment.” Astyages answered in these words: “I too, O Magians, am most disposed to believe that this is so, namely that since the boy was named king, the dream has had its fulfillment, and this boy is no longer a source of danger to me. Nevertheless, give me counsel, having well considered what is likely to be safest both for my house and for you.” In reply the Magians said: “To us also, O king, it is of great consequence that your rule should stand firm; for in the other case it is transferred to strangers, coming round to this boy who is a Persian, and we, being Medes, are made slaves and become of no account in the eyes of the Persians, since we are of a different race. But while you, who are one of our own nation, are established as our king, we both share in the rule and receive great honors from you. Therefore we must by all means take care of you and of your rule. And now, if we saw in this anything to cause fear, we would declare everything to you beforehand; but since the dream has had its issue in a trifling matter, we ourselves are of good cheer and exhort you to be so likewise. As for this boy, send him away from before your eyes to the Persians and to his parents.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 120
paragraphs: When Astyages heard this he rejoiced, and calling Cyrus spoke to him thus: “My son, I wronged you on account of a vision in a dream which has not come to pass, but you are still alive by your own destiny. Now therefore go in peace to the land of the Persians, and I will send men with you to conduct you. And when you arrive there, you shall find a father and mother not after the fashion of Mitradates the herdsman and his wife.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 121
paragraphs: Having spoken thus, Astyages sent Cyrus away. When he arrived at the house of Cambyses, his parents received him, and afterwards, when they learned who he was, they welcomed him with great joy, for they had supposed without doubt that their son had perished straightway after his birth. They asked how he had survived. He told them, saying that before this he had not known but had been utterly mistaken; on the way, however, he had learned all his own fortunes. For he had supposed without doubt that he was the son of the herdsman of Astyages, but since his journey from the city began he had learned the whole story from those who were conducting him. And he said that he had been brought up by the wife of the herdsman, and he continued to praise her throughout, so that Kyno was the chief figure in his tale. And his parents took up this name from him, and in order that their son might be thought by the Persians to have been preserved in a more supernatural manner, they set on foot a report that Cyrus, when he was exposed, had been reared by a bitch (“kyno” in Greek means bitch). And from this source has come that report.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 122
paragraphs: As Cyrus grew to be a man, being of all those of his age the most courageous and the best beloved, Harpagos sought to become his friend and sent him gifts, because he desired to take vengeance on Astyages. For he could not see how, from his own private station, punishment should come upon Astyages; but when he saw Cyrus growing up, he tried to make him an ally, finding a likeness between Cyrus's fortunes and his own. Even before this he had done something: for since Astyages was harsh to the Medes, Harpagos communicated separately with the chief men of the Medes and persuaded them that they ought to make Cyrus their leader and cause Astyages to cease being king. When he had achieved this and all was ready, Harpagos, wishing to make his design known to Cyrus, who lived among the Persians, could do it no other way, since the roads were watched, and so devised this scheme: he prepared a hare, and having cut open its belly but without pulling off any of the fur, he placed inside it, just as it was, a piece of paper on which he had written what he thought good. Then he sewed up the belly of the hare again, and giving nets to the most trusted of his servants as if he were a hunter, he sent him to the land of the Persians, enjoining him by word of mouth to give the hare to Cyrus, and to tell him to open it with his own hands and let no one else be present when he did so.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 123
paragraphs: This was accomplished, and Cyrus, having received the hare from him, cut it open. Finding the paper within, he took it out and read it over. The writing said this: “Son of Cambyses, the gods watch over you, for otherwise you would never have come to so much good fortune. Take vengeance, then, on Astyages who is your murderer — for so far as his will is concerned, you are dead; but by the care of the gods and of me you are still alive. And this I think you have long ago learned from first to last, both how it happened concerning yourself and what I have suffered from Astyages, because I did not slay you but gave you to the herdsman. If, therefore, you will be guided by me, you shall be ruler of all the land over which Astyages now rules. Persuade the Persians to revolt, and march an army against the Medes. Whether I am appointed leader of the army against you, or whoever else of the Medes is in repute, you have what you desire; for these will be the first to attempt to destroy Astyages, revolting from him and coming over to your party. Consider, then, that here at least all is ready, and therefore do this, and do it with speed.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 124
paragraphs: When Cyrus heard this, he began to consider in what manner he might most skillfully persuade the Persians to revolt. On consideration he found that this was the most convenient way, and so in fact he did it: he wrote first on a paper what he wished to write, and he called an assembly of the Persians. Then he unfolded the paper and, reading from it, said that Astyages had appointed him commander of the Persians. “And now, O Persians,” he continued, “I give you command to come to me, each one with a reaping-hook.” This was Cyrus's proclamation. (Now there are many tribes of the Persians, and some of them Cyrus gathered together and persuaded to revolt from the Medes, namely those on whom all the other Persians depend: the Pasargadai, the Maraphians, and the Maspians; of these the Pasargadai are the most noble, and the Achaimenidai are a clan of them, from whom are sprung the Perseid kings. There are other Persian tribes as follows: the Panthaliaians, the Derusiaians, and the Germanians, all of whom are tillers of the soil; and the rest are nomad tribes, namely the Daoi, Mardians, Dropicans, and Sagartians.)

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 125
paragraphs: Now there was a certain region of the Persian land overgrown with thorns, extending some eighteen or twenty furlongs in each direction. When all had come with what they had been commanded to bring, Cyrus ordered them to clear this region for cultivation within one day. When the Persians had achieved the task set before them, he ordered them to come to him on the next day bathed and clean. Meanwhile Cyrus, having gathered in one place all the flocks of goats and sheep and herds of cattle belonging to his father, slaughtered them and prepared with them to entertain the host of the Persians, and moreover with wine and other provisions of the most agreeable kind. So when the Persians came the next day, he made them recline in a meadow and feasted them. When they had finished dinner, Cyrus asked them whether what they had on the former day or what they had now seemed preferable to them. They said the difference was great, for the former day had for them nothing but evil, and the present day nothing but good. Taking up this saying, Cyrus proceeded to lay bare his whole design, saying: “Men of the Persians, thus it is with you. If you will do as I say, you shall have these and ten thousand other good things, with no servile labor; but if you will not, you shall have labors like that of yesterday, innumerable. Now therefore do as I say and make yourselves free: for I seem to myself to have been born by providential fortune to take these matters in hand, and I think you are not worse men than the Medes, either in other matters or in those which have to do with war. Consider, then, that this is so, and revolt from Astyages at once.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 126
paragraphs: The Persians, who had long resented Median rule, now had a leader. They eagerly set about winning their freedom. When Astyages heard what Cyrus was doing, he sent a messenger to summon him. Cyrus told the messenger to report back that he would be with Astyages sooner than Astyages wished. When Astyages heard this, he armed the entire Median nation. As if heaven had robbed him of his senses, he appointed Harpagos as their general—forgetting what he had done to the man. When Harpagos took the field with the Median army and engaged the Persians, some of the Medes fought, but those in the conspiracy deserted to the Persians. Most of the rest, seeing what was happening, deliberately fought badly and fled.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 127
paragraphs: So when the Median army had been shamefully dispersed, as soon as Astyages heard of it he said, threatening Cyrus: “Even so, Cyrus shall not escape punishment.” Having spoken thus, he first impaled the Magian interpreters of dreams who had persuaded him to let Cyrus go, and then he armed those Medes, youths and old men, who had been left behind in the city. These he led out, and having engaged in battle with the Persians, he was defeated, and Astyages himself was taken alive, and he also lost the Medes whom he had led forth.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 128
paragraphs: When Astyages had been made prisoner, Harpagos came and stood near him and exulted over him and mocked him. Among other things he said to grieve him, he asked in particular how it pleased him to be a slave instead of a king, making reference to that dinner at which Astyages had feasted him on the flesh of his own son. Astyages, looking at him, asked in return whether he claimed the work of Cyrus as his own deed. Harpagos said that since he had written the letter, the deed was justly his. Then Astyages declared him to be at the same time the most unskillful and the most unjust of men: the most unskillful because, when it was in his power to become king himself (as it was, if the thing now done had really been brought about by him), he had conferred the chief power on another; and the most unjust, because on account of that dinner he had reduced the Medes to slavery. For if he had to confer the kingdom on some other and not keep it himself, it was more just to give this good thing to one of the Medes rather than to one of the Persians. But as things stood, the Medes, who were guiltless in this matter, had become slaves instead of masters, and the Persians, who formerly were slaves of the Medes, had now become their masters.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 129
paragraphs: So Astyages was deposed after ruling thirty-five years. The Medes bowed under Persian rule because of his cruelty, having themselves ruled Asia above the river Halys for one hundred and twenty-eight years, not counting the Scythian period. Later they would rebel against the Persians and regain independence, but they were defeated again by Darius' forces. But at this point in time, the Persians under Cyrus rose against the Medes and from then on ruled Asia. As for Astyages, Cyrus kept him at his court and did him no further harm for the rest of his life. That is how Cyrus was born, raised, and became king. And afterward, as I have already described, he conquered Croesus, who had attacked him first. With that victory, he became master of all Asia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 130
paragraphs: These are the customs, as far as I know, that the Persians follow. They consider it unlawful to set up statues, temples, and altars, and they criticize those who do so. This, I believe, is because they do not think of the gods as having human form, as the Greeks do. Their practice is to climb to the tops of the highest mountains and offer sacrifice to Zeus, which is the name they give to the whole vault of the sky. They also sacrifice to the sun, the moon, the earth, fire, water, and the winds. These are the only gods to whom they have sacrificed from the beginning. They later adopted the worship of Aphrodite Ourania from the Assyrians and Arabians. The Assyrians call Aphrodite Mylitta, the Arabians call her Alilat, and the Persians call her Mitra.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 131
paragraphs: The manner of sacrifice for the gods mentioned is established among the Persians as follows: they make no altars, nor do they kindle fire; and when they intend to sacrifice, they use no libation, no music of the pipe, no garlands, no barley-meal for sprinkling. When a man wishes to sacrifice to any one of the gods, he leads the animal for sacrifice to an unpolluted place and calls upon the god, having his tiara usually wreathed with a branch of myrtle. The man who sacrifices may not pray for good things for himself alone; instead he prays that it may be well with all the Persians and with the king, for he himself is of course included in the whole body of Persians. When he has cut up the victim into pieces and boiled the flesh, he spreads a layer of the freshest grass, especially clover, upon which he at once places all the pieces of flesh. When he has arranged them in order, a Magian stands by them and chants over them a theogony (for of such a nature, they say, is their incantation), since without a Magian it is not lawful for them to make sacrifices. Then, after waiting a short time, the sacrificer carries away the flesh and uses it for whatever purpose he pleases.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 132
paragraphs: Of all days, their custom is to honor most the day on which each one was born: on this day they think it right to set out a more lavish feast than on other days. At this feast, the wealthier among them set upon the table an ox, a horse, a camel, or an ass, roasted whole in an oven; the poor set out small animals in the same way. They have few solid dishes, but many served afterwards as dessert, and these not in a single course. For this reason the Persians say that the Hellenes leave off dinner hungry, because after dinner they have nothing worth mentioning served as dessert; whereas, if any good dessert were served up, they would not stop eating so soon. They are very much given to wine-drinking, and it is not permitted for a man to vomit or to make water in the presence of another. So they guard against these things. They are also accustomed to deliberate over matters of the greatest importance when they are drinking hard, and whatever conclusion has pleased them in their deliberation, this on the next day, when they are sober, the master of the house in which they happen to be when deliberating lays before them again for discussion. If it pleases them when sober as well, they adopt it; but if it does not please them, they let it go. And whatever they have first deliberated on when sober, they reconsider when they are drinking.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 133
paragraphs: When they meet one another in the roads, you can tell by this whether those who meet are of equal rank: for instead of greeting by words, they kiss one another on the mouth; but if one is a little inferior to the other, they kiss one another on the cheeks; and if one is of much less noble rank, he falls down before him and does him obeisance. They honor most, after themselves, those nations which dwell nearest to them, and next those which dwell next nearest, and so they go on giving honor in proportion to distance. They hold in least honor those who dwell furthest from themselves, esteeming themselves to be by far the best of all the human race in every respect, and thinking that others possess merit according to this proportion, so that those who dwell furthest from themselves are the worst. Under the supremacy of the Medes, the various nations also used to govern one another according to the same rule the Persians observe in giving honor: the Medes governed the whole, and in particular those who dwelt nearest to themselves; these, in turn, ruled over those who bordered upon them; and those again over the nations next to them. For the race proceeded thus, always from government by themselves to government through others.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 134
paragraphs: The Persians are more open than any people to adopting foreign customs. They wear Median dress because they think it looks better than their own, and they use Egyptian body armor for war. They eagerly take up every kind of luxury they hear about, including Greek ones. Each Persian man has many wives and even more concubines.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 135
paragraphs: It is established as a sign of manly excellence, next after excellence in fighting, to be able to show many sons; and to the men who have most, the king sends gifts every year, for they consider number to be a source of strength. They educate their children, from the age of five to twenty, in three things only: riding, shooting with the bow, and speaking the truth. But before the boy is five years old, he does not come into the presence of his father, but lives with the women. This is done for the following reason: if the child should die while he is being brought up, he may not be the cause of any grief to his father.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 136
paragraphs: I commend this custom of theirs, and also the one next to be mentioned: namely that neither the king himself shall put anyone to death for a single cause, nor any of the other Persians for a single cause shall do irremediable harm to any of his own servants. Only if, after reckoning, he finds that the wrongs done are more in number and greater than the services rendered, does he then give vent to his anger. Moreover, they say that no one has ever killed his own father or mother, and whatever deeds have been done that seemed to be of this nature must necessarily, if examined, be found to be due either to changelings or to children of adulterous birth. For, they say, it is not reasonable to suppose that the true parent would be killed by his own son.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 137
paragraphs: Whatever it is unlawful for them to do, it is also unlawful for them to speak of. The most disgraceful thing in their view is to tell a lie. The next most disgraceful is to owe a debt—for many reasons, but especially because they say a debtor is bound to tell lies. Any citizen with leprosy or a similar skin disease is not allowed to enter the city or mix with other Persians. They say such a person has sinned against the sun. Many Persians drive any foreigner with such a disease out of the country. They apply the same rule to white doves, for the same reason. They do not urinate or spit into rivers, nor do they wash their hands in them. They do not allow anyone else to do so either. They hold rivers in great reverence.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 138
paragraphs: This moreover has also been the case with them, which the Persians themselves have failed to notice but I have not: their names, which are formed to correspond with their bodily shapes or the magnificence of their station, all end with the same letter — the letter which the Dorians call “san” and the Ionians “sigma.” If you examine the matter, you will find that all the Persian names end with this letter, not some with this and others with other letters, but all alike.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 139
paragraphs: This much I can say with certainty from my own knowledge. What follows is reported as a secret matter and not openly discussed: the body of a Persian man is not buried until it has been torn by a bird or a dog. I know for certain that the Magians do this, since they practice it openly. The Persians coat the body in wax before putting it in the ground. The Magians are very different from other men and from the Egyptian priests. The Egyptian priests scrupulously avoid killing any living creature except those they sacrifice. The Magians, however, kill everything with their own hands except dogs and humans. They kill ants, snakes, flying creatures, crawling creatures—everything—and regard it as a great achievement. Let this custom remain as it has always been, and I will return to my earlier narrative.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 140
paragraphs: The Ionians and Aiolians, as soon as the Lydians had been subdued by the Persians, sent messengers to Cyrus at Sardis, asking to be his subjects on the same terms as they had been subjects of Croesus. When he heard what they proposed to him, he spoke to them a fable, saying that a certain piper saw fishes in the sea and played on his pipe, supposing they would come out onto land; but being deceived in his expectation, he took a casting-net and enclosed a great multitude of fishes and drew them out of the water. When he saw them leaping about, he said to the fishes: “Stop your dancing now, I pray you, since you would not come out and dance before when I piped.” Cyrus spoke this fable to the Ionians and Aiolians for this reason: because the Ionians had refused to comply earlier, when Cyrus himself by a messenger had requested them to revolt from Croesus, while now, after the conquest had been made, they were ready to submit to Cyrus. He said this to them in anger. When the Ionians heard this answer brought back to their cities, they each put walls around them and gathered together at the Panionion, all except the Milesians, for with these alone Cyrus had sworn an agreement on the same terms the Lydians had granted. The rest of the Ionians resolved by common consent to send messengers to Sparta, to ask the Spartans to help the Ionians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 141
