paragraphs: These Ionians, to whom the Panionion belongs, happened to build their cities in the most favorable position for climate and seasons of any men we know. For neither the regions above Ionia nor those below, neither those toward the East nor those toward the West, produce the same results as Ionia itself; the regions in one direction are oppressed by cold and moisture, and those in the other by heat and drought. These Ionians do not all use the same speech, but have four different variations of language. First of their cities on the southern side lies Miletos, and next to it Myus and Priene. These are settlements made in Caria and speak the same language with one another. The following are in Lydia: Ephesos, Colophon, Lebedos, Teos, Clazomenai, Phocaia. These cities resemble not at all those mentioned before in the speech they use, but they agree among themselves. There remain besides three Ionian cities, of which two are established in the islands of Samos and Chios, and one is built upon the mainland, namely Erythrai. Now the men of Chios and of Erythrai use the same form of language, but the Samians have one for themselves alone. Thus there result four separate forms of language.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 142
paragraphs: Of these Ionians, the Milesians were safe from danger because of their treaty. The islanders also had nothing to fear, since the Phoenicians were not yet Persian subjects, and the Persians themselves were not a seafaring people. The Ionians of the mainland had split from the others for one reason only: the Greek race as a whole was weak at that time, and the Ionians were by far the weakest and least significant part of it. Apart from Athens, no Ionian city of any importance existed. The Athenians and most other Ionians were ashamed of the name and did not want to be called Ionian. Even now, most of them seem to regard the name as a reproach. But the twelve Asiatic cities were proud of the name. They established a sanctuary called the Panionion exclusively for themselves and voted to exclude all other Ionians from it—though no one else actually asked to be admitted, except the people of Smyrna.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 143
paragraphs: just as the Dorians of that district now called the Five Cities, but formerly called the Six Cities, take care not to admit any of the neighboring Dorians to the temple of Triopion, and even exclude from sharing in it those of their own body who commit any offense concerning the temple. For example, in the games of the Triopian Apollo they used formerly to set bronze tripods as prizes for the victors, and the rule was that those who received them should not carry them out of the temple but dedicate them then and there to the god. There was a man of Halicarnassos, named Agasicles, who, being a victor, paid no regard to this rule but carried away the tripod to his own house and hung it up on a nail. On this ground the other five cities — Lindos, Ialysos and Cameiros, Cos and Cnidos — excluded the sixth city, Halicarnassos, from sharing in the temple.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 144
paragraphs: The reason the Ionians established exactly twelve cities, refusing to admit any more, was that when they lived in the Peloponnese they had been divided into twelve parts—just as the Achaeans who drove them out are divided into twelve parts today. First is Pellene, nearest to Sicyon, then Aigeira and Aigai (where the ever-flowing river Crathis rises, from which the river of the same name in Italy takes its name), then Bura, Helike (where the Ionians fled after being defeated by the Achaeans), Aigion, Rhypes, Patrae, Pharae, Olenos (where the great river Peiros flows), Dyme, and Tritaeae—the only inland city of the twelve. These formed the twelve divisions of the Ionians in old times, and these are the twelve divisions of the Achaeans now.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 145
paragraphs: For this reason, then, the Ionians also made twelve cities for themselves; for to say that these are in any way more Ionian than the other Ionians, or have a nobler descent, is mere folly. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have no share even in the name of Ionia; Minyai of Orchomenos have been mingled with them; also Cadmeians, Dryopians, Phokians who seceded from their native state, Molossians, Pelasgians of Arcadia, Dorians of Epidauros, and many other races have been mingled with them. And those of them who set forth to their settlements from the City Hall of Athens, and who consider themselves the most nobly born of the Ionians — these, I say, brought no women with them to their settlement, but took Carian women, whose parents they slew. On account of this slaughter, these women laid down a rule for themselves, imposing oaths on one another and handing it down to their daughters, that they should never eat with their husbands, nor should a wife call her own husband by name. This was because the Ionians had slain their fathers and husbands and children, and then, having done this, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 146
paragraphs: Some of these Ionians appointed Lycian kings over them, descended from Glaucos and Hippolochos. Others chose Cauconian rulers from Pylos, descended from Codros son of Melanthos. Others were ruled by princes of both lines combined. Since they cling to the Ionian name more than the rest, let them be called the pure-blooded Ionians. In truth, all who trace their origin to Athens and celebrate the festival of the Apaturia are Ionian. Everyone celebrates it except the people of Ephesus and Colophon, who were excluded because of a blood-guilt.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 147
paragraphs: Now the Panionion is a sacred place on the north side of Mycale, set apart by common agreement of the Ionians for Poseidon of Helike. This Mycale is a promontory of the mainland running out westwards toward Samos, where the Ionians, gathering together from their cities, used to hold a festival which they called the Panionia. (And not only the feasts of the Ionians but also those of all the Hellenes equally are subject to this rule, that their names all end in the same letter, just like the names of the Persians.)
These, then, are the Ionian cities:

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 148
paragraphs: And those of Aiolia are as follows: Kyme (which is called Phriconis), Larisai, Neon-teichos, Temnos, Killa, Notion, Aigiroessa, Pitane, Aigaiai, Myrina, Gryneia. These are the ancient cities of the Aiolians, eleven in number, since one, Smyrna, was severed from them by the Ionians; for these cities — that is, those on the mainland — used also formerly to be twelve in number. And these Aiolians happened to settle in a land which is more fertile than that of the Ionians, but in respect of climate less favored.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 149
paragraphs: The Aeolians lost Smyrna this way. Certain men from Colophon, defeated in a civil war and driven from their city, had taken refuge in Smyrna. Later, the Colophonian exiles watched for a time when the Smyrnaeans were celebrating a festival outside the walls in honor of Dionysus. They shut the gates, seized the city, and held it. The Aeolians came to the rescue, and terms were negotiated: the Ionians would return all movable property, and the Aeolians would give up the city. The Smyrnaeans agreed. They were then distributed among the other eleven Aeolian cities and made citizens.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 150
paragraphs: These, then, are the Aiolian cities upon the mainland, with the exception of those situated on Mount Ida, for these are separate from the rest. As for those in the islands, there are five in Lesbos — for the sixth which was situated in Lesbos, namely Arisba, was enslaved by the men of Methymna, though its citizens were of the same race as they. In Tenedos there is one city, and another in what are called the “Hundred Isles.” Now the Lesbians and the men of Tenedos, like those Ionians who dwelt in the islands, had no cause for fear; but the remaining cities came to a common agreement to follow the Ionians wherever they should lead.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 151
paragraphs: Now when the messengers from the Ionians and Aiolians came to Sparta (for this business was carried out with speed), they chose, before all others, as their spokesman the Phocaian named Pythermos. He put on a purple cloak, so that as many of the Spartans as possible might hear of it and come together, and having been introduced before the assembly, he spoke at length, asking the Spartans to help them. The Lacedemonians, however, would not listen to him, but on the contrary resolved not to help the Ionians. So the messengers departed. The Lacedemonians, having dismissed the messengers of the Ionians, nevertheless sent men in a fifty-oared ship, to find out, as I imagine, about the affairs of Cyrus and about Ionia. When these men came to Phocaia, they sent to Sardis the man of most repute among them, whose name was Lacrines, to report to Cyrus the saying of the Lacedemonians, bidding him do harm to no city of Hellas, since they would not permit it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 152
paragraphs: When the herald had spoken, Cyrus reportedly asked the Greeks in his company who the Spartans were and how many. On hearing the answer, he told the Spartan herald: "I have never yet feared the kind of men who have a special place in the center of their city where they gather to cheat each other with oaths." This was a jab at the Greeks for having marketplaces, something the Persians do not use—they never buy or sell in markets. He added: "If I stay healthy, it will be their own misfortunes they discuss, not those of the Ionians." Cyrus aimed this threat at all the Greeks, since they had marketplaces. He then appointed a Persian named Tabalos as governor of Sardis and gave a Lydian named Pactyas the task of transporting Croesus' gold. Cyrus himself marched back toward Agbatana, taking Croesus with him. He considered the Ionians too unimportant to deal with personally. Babylon, the Bactrians, the Sacae, and the Egyptians—those were his primary concerns. He intended to lead campaigns against them himself and send a subordinate to handle the Ionians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 153
paragraphs: But as soon as Cyrus had left Sardis, Pactyas persuaded the Lydians to revolt against Tabalos and against Cyrus. He went down to the coast and, since he had all the gold from Sardis, he hired mercenaries and convinced the coastal peoples to join him. Then he marched on Sardis and besieged Tabalos in the citadel.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 154
paragraphs: Hearing this on his way, Cyrus said to Croesus as follows: “Croesus, what end shall I find of these things which are coming to pass? The Lydians, it seems, will not cease from giving me trouble and having trouble themselves. I wonder whether it were not best to sell them all as slaves; for I see that I have acted as if someone should slay the father and then spare his sons: just so I took you prisoner and am carrying you off, you who were much more than the father of the Lydians, while to the Lydians themselves I delivered up their city. And can I feel surprise, after this, that they have revolted from me?” Thus he said what was in his mind, but Croesus answered him as follows, fearing lest he destroy Sardis: “O king, what you have said is not without reason; but do not altogether give vent to your wrath, nor destroy an ancient city which is guiltless both of the former things and of those which have come to pass now. The former things I did, and I bear the consequences heaped upon my head; and as for what is now being done, since the wrongdoer is Pactyas, to whom you entrusted the charge of Sardis, let him pay the penalty. But pardon the Lydians, and lay upon them commands as follows, so that they may not revolt nor be a cause of danger to you: send to them and forbid them to possess weapons of war; bid them instead put on tunics under their outer garments and be shod with buskins; and proclaim to them that they are to train their sons to play the lyre and the harp and to be retail-dealers. Soon, O king, you shall see them become women instead of men, so that there will be no fear they will revolt from you.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 155
paragraphs: Croesus proposed this because he thought it was better for the Lydians than being sold into slavery. He knew that without a strong argument, he could not change Cyrus' mind. He also feared that even if the Lydians escaped this time, they might revolt again and be destroyed. Cyrus was pleased with the advice. He calmed his anger and said he would follow Croesus' suggestion. He summoned a Mede named Mazares and ordered him to tell the Lydians exactly what Croesus had recommended. He also ordered Mazares to sell into slavery everyone who had joined the Lydians in besieging Sardis—and above all, to bring Pactyas back alive.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 156
paragraphs: Having given this charge upon the road, Cyrus continued his march to the native land of the Persians; but Pactyas, hearing that an army was approaching to fight against him, was struck with fear and at once fled to Kyme. Then Mazares the Mede marched upon Sardis with a certain portion of the army of Cyrus, and as he no longer found Pactyas or his followers at Sardis, he first compelled the Lydians to perform the commands of Cyrus. By his commands the Lydians changed the whole manner of their life. After this, Mazares sent messengers to Kyme bidding them give up Pactyas. The men of Kyme resolved to refer the question to the god at Branchidai, asking what counsel they should follow. For there was there an Oracle established of old, which all the Ionians and Aiolians were accustomed to consult, and this place lies in the territory of Miletos above the port of Panormos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 157
paragraphs: So the men of Kyme sent messengers to the Branchidai to inquire of the god, and asked what course they should take concerning Pactyas so as to do what was pleasing to the gods. When they thus inquired, the answer was given that they should deliver up Pactyas to the Persians. The men of Kyme, having heard this answer reported, were disposed to give him up. But when the mass of the people were thus disposed, Aristodicos the son of Heracleides, a man of repute among the citizens, stopped the men of Kyme from doing so, distrusting the answer and thinking that those sent to inquire were not speaking the truth. At last other messengers were sent to the Oracle to ask a second time about Pactyas, and among them was Aristodicos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 158
paragraphs: When these came to Branchidai, Aristodicos stood forth from the rest and consulted the Oracle, asking as follows: “Lord, there came to us a suppliant for protection, Pactyas the Lydian, fleeing a violent death at the hands of the Persians. They demand him from us, bidding the men of Kyme give him up. But we, though we fear the power of the Persians, have not yet ventured up to this time to deliver to them the suppliant, until your counsel shall be clearly manifested to us, telling which of the two things we ought to do.” He thus inquired, but the god again declared to them the same answer, bidding them deliver up Pactyas to the Persians. Upon this, Aristodicos with deliberate purpose did as follows: he went all round the temple, destroying the nests of sparrows and of all the other kinds of birds which had been hatched on the temple. While he was doing this, it is said that a voice came from the inner shrine directed to Aristodicos, speaking thus: “Most impious of men, why do you dare to do this? Do you carry off by force from my temple the suppliants for my protection?” And Aristodicos, not at all at a loss, replied: “Lord, do you thus come to the assistance of your suppliants, and yet bid the men of Kyme deliver up theirs?” The god answered him again thus: “Yes, I bid you do so, that you may perish the more quickly for your impiety, so that you may not at any future time come to the Oracle to ask about the delivering up of suppliants.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 159
paragraphs: When the Cymeans heard this, they did not want to be destroyed for surrendering Pactyas or besieged for sheltering him. So they sent him to Mytilene. But when Mazares demanded his surrender from Mytilene, the Mytilenaeans were preparing to hand him over for a price. (I cannot say the exact amount because the deal was never completed.) When the Cymeans learned this, they sent a boat to Lesbos and took Pactyas to Chios instead. But he was dragged from the sanctuary of Athena Poliouchos by the Chians, who surrendered him. The price for handing him over was the district of Atarneus on the Mysian mainland, opposite Lesbos. The Persians received Pactyas and kept him under guard to present to Cyrus. For a long time after this, no Chian would use barley meal from Atarneus in any offering to any god, and nothing grown there was used in any sacred rite. Everything from that district was excluded from all their temples.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 160
paragraphs: So the Chians handed Pactyas over. After this, Mazares campaigned against all who had helped besiege Tabalos. He enslaved the people of Priene and overran the entire plain of the Maeander, giving it to his army to plunder. He did the same to Magnesia. Then he fell ill and died.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 161
paragraphs: After he was dead, Harpagos came down to take his place in command, being also a Mede by race — this was the man whom the king of the Medes, Astyages, had feasted with the unlawful banquet, and who had helped to give the kingdom to Cyrus. This man, appointed commander by Cyrus, came to Ionia and proceeded to take the cities by throwing up mounds against them: for whenever he had enclosed any people within their walls, he then threw up mounds against the walls and took their city by storm. The first city of Ionia upon which he made an attempt was Phocaia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 162
paragraphs: Now these Phocaians were the first of the Hellenes to make long voyages, and it was they who discovered the Adriatic, Tyrsenia, Iberia, and Tartessos. They made these voyages not in round ships, but in vessels of fifty oars. When they came to Tartessos, they became friends with the king of the Tartessians, whose name was Arganthonios: he ruled over the Tartessians for eighty years and lived altogether one hundred and twenty. With this man the Phocaians became so exceedingly friendly that at first he bade them leave Ionia and dwell wherever they desired in his own land. When he did not persuade the Phocaians to do this, afterwards, hearing from them of the Mede and how his power was increasing, he gave them money to build a wall around their city. He did this without stinting, for the circuit of the wall is many furlongs in extent, and it is built entirely of large stones closely fitted together.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 163
paragraphs: The wall of the Phocaians was made in this manner. Harpagos, having marched his army against them, began to besiege them, at the same time holding forth proposals, saying that it would be enough to satisfy him if the Phocaians were willing to throw down one battlement of their wall and dedicate one single house. But the Phocaians, greatly grieved at the thought of subjection, said that they wished to deliberate about the matter for one day, and after that they would give their answer; and they asked him to withdraw his army from the wall while they were deliberating. Harpagos said that he knew very well what they were intending to do, but nevertheless he was willing to allow them to deliberate. So in the time that followed, when Harpagos had withdrawn his army from the wall, the Phocaians drew down their fifty-oared galleys to the sea, put into them their children and women and all their movable goods, and besides these the images from the temples and the other votive offerings — except such as were made of bronze or stone or consisted of paintings. All the rest, I say, they put into the ships, and having embarked themselves, they sailed toward Chios; and the Persians obtained possession of Phocaia, the city being deserted by its inhabitants.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 164
paragraphs: As for the Phocaians, since the men of Chios would not sell them, at their request, the islands called Oinussai — fearing lest these islands might be made a seat of trade and their island might be shut out of it — they set out for Kyrnos. For in Kyrnos, twenty years before this, they had established a city named Alalia, in accordance with an oracle (Arganthonios was by then dead). When they were setting out for Kyrnos, they first sailed to Phocaia and slaughtered the Persian garrison, to whose charge Harpagos had delivered the city. After they had achieved this, they made solemn imprecations on any of their number who should stay behind from their voyage, and moreover they sank a mass of iron in the sea, swearing that not until that mass should appear again on the surface would they return to Phocaia. However, as they were setting forth to Kyrnos, more than half the citizens were seized with yearning and regret for their city and for their native land, and they proved false to their oath and sailed back to Phocaia. But those of them who kept the oath still weighed anchor from the islands of Oinussai and sailed on.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 165
paragraphs: When these Phocaeans reached Corsica, they lived for five years alongside the earlier settlers and founded temples. But they plundered all their neighbors, so the Etruscans and Carthaginians joined forces against them. Each brought sixty ships, making a total of one hundred and twenty against the Phocaeans' sixty. They fought a sea battle off the Sardinian coast. The Phocaeans won, but it was a hollow victory: they lost forty ships, and the remaining twenty had their rams bent and were useless. They sailed back to Alalia, picked up their women, children, and whatever possessions they could carry, abandoned Corsica, and sailed to the Italian mainland, where they founded the city of Velia.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 166
paragraphs: As for the crews of the ships that were destroyed, the Carthaginians and Tyrsenians obtained much the greater number of them, and these they brought to land and killed by stoning. After this, the men of Agylla found that everything which passed by the spot where the Phocaians were laid after being stoned became either distorted, crippled, or paralyzed — whether small cattle, beasts of burden, or human beings. So the men of Agylla sent to Delphi, desiring to purge themselves of the offense; and the Pythian prophetess bade them do what the men of Agylla still continue to perform to this day: they make great sacrifices in honor of the dead, and hold at the place a contest of athletics and horse-racing. Such, then, was the fate of these Phocaians. But those of them who took refuge at Rhegion set out from there and took possession of that city in the land of Oinotria which is now called Hyele. This they founded, having learned from a man of Poseidonia that the Pythian prophetess by her answer meant them to found a temple to Kyrnos, who was a hero, and not to found a settlement on the island of Kyrnos.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 167
paragraphs: That is the story of Phocaea in Ionia. The people of Teos did much the same thing. As soon as Harpagos captured their wall with a siege ramp, they boarded their ships and sailed to Thrace. There they founded the city of Abdera. (A man from Clazomenai named Timesios had actually founded Abdera before them, but the Thracians drove him out. He is now honored as a hero by the Teans in Abdera.)

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 168
paragraphs: These alone of all the Ionians left their native cities because they would not endure subjection; but the other Ionians, except the Milesians, did indeed contend in arms with Harpagos like those who left their homes, and proved themselves brave men, each fighting for his own native city. But when they were defeated and captured, they all remained in their own places and performed what was laid upon them. The Milesians, as I have also said before, had made a sworn agreement with Cyrus himself and kept still. Thus for the second time Ionia had been reduced to subjection. And when Harpagos had conquered the Ionians on the mainland, then the Ionians who dwelt in the islands, struck with fear by these things, gave themselves over to Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 169
paragraphs: When the Ionians had been thus ill-treated but were continuing still to hold their gatherings as before at the Panionion, Bias, a man of Priene, set forth to the Ionians, as I am informed, a most profitable counsel, by following which they might have become the most prosperous of all the Hellenes. He urged that the Ionians should set forth in one common expedition and sail to Sardinia, and after that found a single city for all the Ionians; and thus they would escape subjection and be prosperous, inhabiting the largest of all islands and being rulers over others. Whereas, if they remained in Ionia, he said, he did not see that freedom would any longer exist for them. This was the counsel given by Bias of Priene after the Ionians had been ruined. But a good counsel too was given before the ruin of Ionia by Thales, a man of Miletos, who was by descent of Phoenician race. He advised the Ionians to have one single seat of government, and that this should be at Teos (for Teos, he said, was in the center of Ionia), and that the other cities should be inhabited as before, but accounted just as if they were demes.
These men set forth to them counsels of the kind I have described:

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 170
paragraphs: But Harpagos, after subduing Ionia, proceeded to march against the Carians and Caunians and Lykians, taking Ionians and Aiolians with him to help. Of these, the Carians came to the mainland from the islands; for being in olden times subjects of Minos and called Leleges, they used to dwell in the islands, paying no tribute — so far back as I am able to reach by hearsay — but whenever Minos required it, they used to supply his ships with seamen. And since Minos subdued much land and was fortunate in his fighting, the Carian nation was at that time by much the most famous of all nations, together with him. They produced three inventions of which the Hellenes adopted the use: the Carians were the first to set the fashion of fastening crests on helmets, and of making the devices that are put on shields, and these also were the first to make handles for their shields — whereas up to that time all who were accustomed to use shields carried them without handles and with leathern straps to guide them, having them slung about their necks and left shoulders. Then after a long time, the Dorians and Ionians drove the Carians out of the islands, and so they came to the mainland. With respect to the Carians, the Cretans relate that it happened thus; but the Carians themselves do not agree with this account and suppose that they are dwellers on the mainland from the beginning, and that they always went by the same name they have now. As evidence of this, they point to an ancient temple of Carian Zeus at Mylasa, in which the Mysians and Lydians share as brother races of the Carians, for they say that Lydos and Mysos were brothers of Car. These share in it; but those who, being of another race, have come to speak the same language as the Carians, have no share in it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 171
paragraphs: It seems to me, however, that the Caunians are dwellers there from the beginning, although they say themselves that they came from Crete. But they have been assimilated to the Carian race in language, or else the Carians have been assimilated to the Caunian race in language — which of the two, I cannot with certainty determine. They have customs, however, in which they differ very much from all other men, as well as from the Carians. For example, the fairest thing in their estimation is to meet together in numbers for drinking, according to equality of age or friendship, both men, women, and children. And again, when they had founded temples for foreign deities, they afterwards changed their purpose and resolved to worship only their own native gods, and the whole body of Caunian young men put on their armor and made pursuit as far as the borders of the Calyndians, beating the air with their spears, saying that they were casting the foreign gods out of the land. Such are the customs which these people have.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 172
paragraphs: The Lykians, however, have sprung originally from Crete (for in olden times the whole of Crete was possessed by barbarians). When the sons of Europa, Sarpedon and Minos, came to be at variance in Crete about the kingdom, Minos, having got the better in the strife of parties, drove out both Sarpedon himself and those of his party. They, having been expelled, came to the land of Milyas in Asia, for the land which the Lykians now inhabit was anciently called Milyas, and the Milyans were then called Solymoi. While Sarpedon reigned over them, they were called by the name they had when they came there, by which the Lykians are even now called by the neighboring tribes, namely Termilai. But when Lycos the son of Pandion came from Athens to the land of the Termilai and to Sarpedon — having himself been driven out by his brother Aigeus — then by the name taken from Lycos they were after a time called Lykians. The customs they have are partly Cretan and partly Carian; but one custom they have which is peculiar to them and in which they agree with no other people: they call themselves by their mothers and not by their fathers. If one asks his neighbor who he is, he will state his parentage on the mother's side and enumerate his mother's female ancestors. And if a woman who is a citizen marries a slave, the children are accounted of gentle birth; but if a man who is a citizen, though he were the first among them, has a slave for wife or concubine, the children are without civil rights.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 173
paragraphs: Now the Carians were reduced to subjection by Harpagos without any brilliant deed displayed either by the Carians themselves or by those of the Hellenes who dwell in this land. Among these last are, besides others, the men of Cnidos, settlers from Lacedemon, whose land runs out into the sea, being in fact the region called Triopion, beginning from the peninsula of Bybassos. Since all the land of Cnidos except a small part is washed by the sea (for the part looking toward the North is bounded by the Gulf of Keramos, and that looking to the South by the sea off Syme and Rhodes), the men of Cnidos began to dig through this small part, which is about five furlongs across, while Harpagos was subduing Ionia, desiring to make their land an island. Within the isthmus, all was theirs; for where the territory of Cnidos ends in the direction of the mainland, there is the isthmus which they were digging across. While the Cnidians were working at it with a great number of men, it was observed that the men who worked suffered injury much more than might have been expected, and in a more supernatural manner — both in other parts of their bodies and especially in their eyes, when the rock was being broken up. So they sent men to ask the Oracle at Delphi what the cause of the difficulty was. And the Pythian prophetess, as the men of Cnidos themselves report, gave them this reply in trimeter verse:
“Fence not the place with towers, nor dig the isthmus through; for Zeus would have made your land an island, had he willed it so.”

When the Pythian prophetess had given this oracle, the men of Cnidos not only ceased from their digging, but when Harpagos came against them with his army, they delivered themselves to him without resistance.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 174
paragraphs: There were also the Pedasians, who lived in the interior above Halicarnassos. Among them, whenever disaster was about to strike either themselves or their neighbors, the priestess of Athena would grow a great beard. This happened to them three times. They were the only people in all of Caria who held out against Harpagos for any length of time. They caused him considerable trouble by fortifying a hill called Lide.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 175
paragraphs: After a time the Pedasians were conquered; and the Lykians, when Harpagos marched his army into the plain of Xanthos, came out against him and fought, few against many, and displayed proofs of valor. But being defeated and confined within their city, they gathered together into the citadel their wives, their children, their property, and their servants, and after that they set fire to this citadel, so that it was all in flames. Having done this and sworn terrible oaths with one another, they went forth against the enemy and were slain in battle — that is to say, all the men of Xanthos. Of the Xanthians who now claim to be Lykians, the greater number have come in from abroad, except only eighty households; but these eighty households happened at that time to be away from their native place, and so escaped destruction. Thus Harpagos obtained possession of Xanthos; and he obtained Caunos in like manner, for the men of Caunos imitated in most respects the behavior of the Lykians.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 176
paragraphs: So Harpagos was conquering the coast regions of Asia, and Cyrus himself meanwhile was doing the same in the upper parts of it, subduing every nation and passing over none. Now most of these actions I shall pass over in silence; but the undertakings which gave him trouble more than the rest and which are the most worthy of note, of these I shall make mention.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 177
paragraphs: Cyrus, as soon as he had made subject to himself all the other parts of the mainland, proceeded to attack the Assyrians. Now Assyria has no doubt many other great cities, but the most famous and the strongest, and the place where the seat of their monarchy had been established after Nineveh was destroyed, was Babylon, which was a city such as I shall now describe. It lies in a great plain, and in size it is such that each face measures a hundred and twenty furlongs, the shape of the whole being square; thus the furlongs of the circuit of the city amount in all to four hundred and eighty. Such is the size of the city of Babylon, and it had a magnificence greater than all other cities of which we have knowledge. First there runs round it a trench, deep and broad and full of water; then a wall fifty royal cubits in thickness and two hundred cubits in height — now the royal cubit is larger by three fingers than the common cubit.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 178
paragraphs: I must also tell, in addition to this, for what purpose the earth was used that was taken out of the trench, and in what manner the wall was made. As they dug the trench, they made the earth carried out of the excavation into bricks, and having moulded enough bricks they baked them in kilns; and then afterwards, using hot asphalt for mortar and inserting reed mats at every thirty courses of brickwork, they built up first the edges of the trench and then the wall itself in the same manner. At the top of the wall, along the edges, they built chambers of one story facing one another; and between the rows of chambers they left space to drive a four-horse chariot. In the circuit of the wall there are set a hundred gates made of bronze throughout, and the gate-posts and lintels likewise. Now there is another city, distant from Babylon a space of eight days' journey, of which the name is Is. There is a river there of no great size, and the name of the river is also Is, and it sends its stream into the river Euphrates. This river Is throws up together with its water lumps of asphalt in great abundance, and from there was brought the asphalt for the wall of Babylon.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 179
paragraphs: Babylon, then, was walled in this manner; and there are two divisions of the city, for a river whose name is Euphrates parts it in the middle. This river flows from the land of the Armenians and is large, deep, and swift, and it flows out into the Erythraian sea. The wall on each side has its bends carried down to the river, and from this point the walls stretch along each bank of the stream in the form of a rampart of baked bricks. The city itself is full of houses of three and four stories, and the roads by which it is cut up run in straight lines, including the cross roads which lead to the river. Opposite to each road there were set gates in the rampart which ran along the river, equal in number to the ways, and these also were of bronze, leading like the ways to the river itself.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 180
paragraphs: This wall, then, which I have mentioned, is as it were a breastplate for the town, and another wall runs round within it, not much weaker for defense than the first, but enclosing a smaller space. In each division of the city there was a building in the midst: in the one, the king's palace of great extent and strongly fortified round; in the other, the temple of Zeus Belos with bronze gates, and this exists still up to my time, and measures two furlongs each way, being of a square shape. In the midst of the temple is built a solid tower, measuring a furlong both in length and breadth; and on this tower another tower has been erected, and another again upon this, and so on up to the number of eight towers. An ascent to these has been built running outside round about all the towers; and when one reaches about the middle of the ascent, one finds a stopping-place and seats to rest upon, on which those who ascend sit down and rest. On the top of the last tower there is a large cell, and in the cell a large couch is laid, well covered, and beside it a golden table is placed; and there is no image there set up, nor does any human being spend the night there, except only one woman of the natives of the place, whomsoever the god shall choose from all the women, as the Chaldeans — who are the priests of this god — say.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 181
paragraphs: These same priests say that the god himself comes to the temple and rests on the couch. I do not believe them. The same claim is made about the temple of Theban Zeus in Egypt, where a woman also sleeps in the temple (and both women are said to abstain from relations with men). A similar practice occurs with the prophetess of Apollo at Patara in Lycia, whenever an oracle is active there. When a prophetess is appointed, she is locked in the temple overnight.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 182
paragraphs: There is moreover in the temple at Babylon another cell below, in which is a great image of Zeus sitting, made of gold, and beside it is placed a large table of gold, and his footstool and seat are of gold also; and, as the Chaldeans reported, the weight of the gold of which these things are made is eight hundred talents. Outside this cell is an altar of gold, and there is also another altar of great size, where full-grown animals are sacrificed, whereas on the golden altar it is not lawful to sacrifice any but young sucklings. On the larger altar the Chaldeans offer one thousand talents of frankincense every year at the time when they celebrate the feast in honor of this god. There was moreover in these precincts, still remaining at the time of Cyrus, a statue twelve cubits high, of solid gold. This I did not myself see, but what is related by the Chaldeans, I relate. Against this statue Dareios the son of Hystaspes formed a design, but he did not venture to take it; it was taken, however, by Xerxes the son of Dareios, who also killed the priest when he forbade him to meddle with the statue. This temple, then, is thus adorned with magnificence, and there are also many private votive-offerings.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 183
paragraphs: Of this Babylon, besides many other rulers of whom I shall make mention in the Assyrian history, and who added improvements to the walls and temples, there were also two who were women. Of these, the one who ruled first, named Semiramis — who lived five generations before the other — produced banks of earth in the plain which are a sight worth seeing; before this, the river used to flood like a sea over the whole plain.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 184
paragraphs: The queen who ruled after her, named Nitocris, was far wiser. She left behind monuments I will describe. She also saw that the Median empire was growing powerful and restless, having already captured Nineveh among other cities. She took every possible precaution against them. First, she diverted the river Euphrates, which had previously run straight through the center of the city. By digging channels upstream, she made it wind so much that it passed one particular Assyrian village three times. (The village is called Ardericca, and anyone sailing down the Euphrates from the Mediterranean still passes this village three times on three separate days.) She also raised high embankments on both sides of the Euphrates. In addition, she dug a vast lake above the city, a short distance from the river, deep enough to reach water and with a perimeter of some fifty-two miles. She used the excavated earth to raise the river embankments even higher. As the lake was dug, she had enormous stones brought to the edge. When all this was finished—the lake dug and the embankments built—she diverted the river into the new lake, filling it. While the old riverbed was empty, she accomplished two things: she lined both banks of the river through the city with baked brick, matching the riverside walls, and she built a bridge over the Euphrates from stones she had quarried for the lake, binding them together with iron and lead. During the day, square wooden platforms were laid across the stones for people to walk on. At night, the platforms were removed to prevent the inhabitants of the two halves of the city from crossing over and robbing each other. When the lake was full and the bridge finished, she turned the river back into its original course from the lake. The lake, now a marsh, served its purpose, and the citizens had a bridge.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 185
paragraphs: These defenses, then, she cast round her city from the depth; and she made the following addition which depended upon them. The city was in two divisions, and the river occupied the space between; and in the time of the former rulers, when anyone wished to pass over from the one division to the other, he had to pass over in a boat, and that, as I imagine, was troublesome. She, however, made provision also for this: when she was digging the basin for the lake, she left this other monument of herself derived from the same work, that is, she caused stones to be cut of very great length. When the stones were prepared for her and the place had been dug out, she turned aside the whole stream of the river into the place she had been digging; and while this was being filled with water, the ancient bed of the river being dried up in the meantime, she both built up with baked bricks — in the same fashion as the wall — the edges of the river where it flows through the city, and the places of descent leading from the small gateways to the river; and also about the middle of the city, as I judge, with the stones she had caused to be dug out she proceeded to build a bridge, binding together the stones with iron and lead. On the top she laid squared timbers across, to remain there while it was daytime, over which the people of Babylon made the passage across. But at night they used to take away these timbers, for this reason: that they might not go back and forth by night and steal from one another. When the place dug out had been filled into a lake by the river, and at the same time the bridge had been completed, then she conducted the Euphrates back into its ancient channel from the lake; and so the excavation, being made into a swamp, was thought to have served a good purpose, and a bridge had been set up for the men of the city.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 186
paragraphs: This same queen also contrived a trick of the following kind. Over that gate of the city through which the greatest number of people passed, she set up for herself a tomb above the very gate itself. On the tomb she engraved writing which said this: “If any of the kings of Babylon who come after me shall be in want of wealth, let him open my tomb and take as much as he desires; but let him not open it for any other cause, if he is not in want; for that will not be well.” This tomb was undisturbed until the kingdom came to Dareios. But to Dareios it seemed a monstrous thing not to make any use of this gate, and also, when there was money lying there, not to take it, considering that the money itself invited him to do so. Now the reason he would not make any use of this gate was because the corpse would have been above his head as he drove through. He then, I say, opened the tomb and found not indeed money, but the corpse, with writing which said this: “If you had not been insatiable of wealth and basely covetous, you would not have opened the resting-places of the dead.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 187
paragraphs: On his march toward Babylon, Cyrus reached the river Gyndes. This river rises in the mountains of the Matienians, flows through Dardanian territory, and empties into the Tigris, which passes the city of Opis and flows into the Red Sea. As Cyrus attempted to cross the Gyndes, which was deep enough to be navigable, one of his sacred white horses charged into the river and tried to swim across. The current swept the horse under and carried it away. Cyrus was furious at the river for this outrage. He swore he would make it so weak that women could cross it without getting their knees wet. He suspended his march on Babylon, divided his army in two, and had them dig one hundred and eighty channels on each side of the river—three hundred and sixty in all—fanning out in every direction. This vast project took the entire summer.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 188
paragraphs: Now when Cyrus on his way toward Babylon arrived at the river Gyndes — whose springs are in the mountains of the Matienians, and which flows through the Dardanians and runs into another river, the Tigris, which, flowing by the city of Opis, runs out into the Erythraian Sea — when Cyrus, I say, was attempting to cross this river Gyndes, which is a navigable stream, then one of his sacred white horses, in high spirit and wantonness, went into the river and tried to cross, but the stream swept it under water and carried it off at once. Cyrus was greatly moved with anger against the river for having acted so insolently, and he threatened to make it so feeble that for the future even women could cross it easily without wetting the knee. So after this threat he ceased from his march against Babylon and divided his army into two parts; and having divided it, he stretched lines and marked out straight channels, one hundred and eighty on each bank of the Gyndes, directed every way, and having disposed his army along them he commanded them to dig. So, as a great multitude was working, the work was indeed completed, but they spent the whole summer season at this spot working.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 189
paragraphs: When Cyrus had taken vengeance on the river Gyndes by dividing it into three hundred and sixty channels, and when the next spring was just beginning, then at length he continued his advance upon Babylon. The men of Babylon had marched forth out of their city and were awaiting him. So when in his advance he came near the city, the Babylonians joined battle with him, and having been worsted in the fight, they were shut up close within their city. But knowing well even before this that Cyrus was not apt to remain still, and seeing him lay hands on every nation equally, they had brought in provisions beforehand for very many years. So while these made no account of the siege, Cyrus was at a loss what to do, for much time went by and his affairs made no progress onward.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 190
paragraphs: Therefore, whether it was some other man who suggested it to him when he was in a strait what to do, or whether he of himself perceived what he ought to do, he did as follows. The main body of his army he posted at the place where the river runs into the city, and then again behind the city he set others, where the river issues forth from the city; and he proclaimed to his army that as soon as they should see that the stream had become passable, they should enter the city by that way. Having thus set them in their places and exhorted them in this manner, he marched away himself with that part of his army which was not fit for fighting. When he came to the lake, Cyrus also did the same things that the queen of the Babylonians had done regarding the river and the lake; that is to say, he conducted the river by a channel into the lake, which was at that time a swamp, and so made the former course of the river passable by the sinking of the stream. When this had been done in such a manner, the Persians who had been posted for this very purpose entered by the bed of the river Euphrates into Babylon, the stream having sunk so far that it reached about to the middle of a man's thigh. Now if the Babylonians had had knowledge of it beforehand, or had perceived what Cyrus was doing, they would have allowed the Persians to enter the city and then destroyed them miserably; for if they had closed all the gates that led to the river, and mounted themselves upon the ramparts that ran along the banks of the stream, they would have caught them as in a fish-trap. But as it was, the Persians came upon them unexpectedly; and owing to the size of the city (so it is said by those who dwell there) after those about the extremities of the city had suffered capture, those Babylonians who dwelt in the middle did not know that they had been captured. As they happened to be holding a festival, they went on dancing and rejoicing during this time until they learned the truth only too well.
Babylon then had thus been taken for the first time.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 191
paragraphs: As to the resources of the Babylonians — how great they are — I shall show by many other proofs, and among them by this: For the support of the great king and his army, apart from the regular tribute, the whole land of which he is ruler has been distributed into portions. Now whereas twelve months make up the year, for four of these he has his support from the territory of Babylon, and for the remaining eight months from the whole of the rest of Asia. Thus the Assyrian land is, in regard to resources, the third part of all Asia; and the government, or satrapy (as it is called by the Persians), of this territory is by far the best of all the governments. Indeed, when Tritantaichmes son of Artabazos had this province from the king, there came in to him every day an artab full of silver coin (now the artab is a Persian measure and holds more than the medimnos of Attica by three Attic choinikes). And of horses he had in this province as his private property, apart from the horses for use in war, eight hundred stallions and sixteen thousand mares, for each of these stallions served twenty mares. Of Indian hounds, moreover, such a vast number were kept that four large villages in the plain, being free from other contributions, had been appointed to provide food for the hounds.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 192
paragraphs: Such was the wealth which belonged to the ruler of Babylon. Now the land of the Assyrians has but little rain; and this little gives nourishment to the root of the grain, but the crop is ripened and the ear comes on by the help of watering from the river — not as in Egypt, by the coming up of the river itself over the fields, but by hand or with swing-buckets. For the whole Babylonian territory, like the Egyptian, is cut up into channels, and the largest of the channels is navigable for ships and runs in the direction of the sunrising in winter from the Euphrates to another river, namely the Tigris, along the bank of which lay the city of Nineveh. This territory is of all lands we know by far the best for producing grain; as to trees, it does not even attempt to bear them, either fig or vine or olive, but for producing grain it is so good that it yields as much as two-hundred-fold on average, and when it bears at its best it produces three-hundred-fold. The leaves of the wheat and barley there grow to be fully four fingers broad; and from millet and sesame seed how large a tree grows, I know myself but shall not record, being well aware that even what has already been said about the crops produced has been enough to cause disbelief in those who have not visited the Babylonian land. They use no olive oil, but only that which they make of sesame seed; and they have date-palms growing over the whole plain, most of them fruit-bearing, from which they make both solid food, wine, and honey; and they tend these in the same manner as fig-trees, and in particular they take the fruit of those palms which the Hellenes call male-palms, and tie them to the date-bearing palms, so that their gall-fly may enter the date and ripen it and that the fruit of the palm may not fall off — for the male-palm produces gall-flies in its fruit just as the wild-fig does.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 193
paragraphs: But the greatest marvel of all things in the land, after the city itself, to my mind is this which I am about to describe. Their boats — those I mean which go down the river to Babylon — are round and all of leather. For they make ribs for them of willow which they cut in the land of the Armenians, who dwell above the Assyrians, and round these they stretch hides that serve as a covering outside by way of a hull, not making broad the stern nor gathering in the prow to a point, but making the boats round like a shield. After that they stow the whole boat with straw and allow it to be carried down the stream full of cargo; and for the most part these boats bring down casks of palm-wood filled with wine. The boat is kept straight by two steering-oars and two men standing upright, one inside pulling his oar and the other outside pushing. These vessels are made both of very large size and also smaller, the largest of them having a burden of as much as five thousand talents' weight. In each one there is a live ass, and in those of larger size several. So when they have arrived at Babylon in their voyage and have disposed of their cargo, they sell by auction the ribs of the boat and all the straw, but they pack the hides upon their asses and drive them off to Armenia — for up the stream of the river it is not possible by any means to sail, owing to the swiftness of the current; and for this reason they make their boats not of timber but of hides. Then when they have come back to the land of the Armenians, driving their asses with them, they make other boats in the same manner.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 194
paragraphs: Such are their boats; and the following is the manner of dress they use: a linen tunic reaching to the feet, and over this they put on another of wool, and then a white mantle thrown round, while they wear shoes of a native fashion rather like the Boeotian slippers. They wear their hair long and bind their heads round with fillets, and they are anointed over the whole of their body with perfumes. Each man has a seal and a staff carved by hand, and on each staff is carved either an apple, a rose, a lily, an eagle, or some other device — for it is not their custom to have a staff without a device upon it.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 195
paragraphs: Such is the equipment of their bodies. And the customs established among them are as follows, the wisest in our opinion being this, which I am informed the Enetoi in Illyria also have. In every village, once a year, it was done as follows: When the maidens grew to the age for marriage, they gathered all these together and brought them in a body to one place, and round them stood a company of men. The crier made each one stand up separately and proceeded to sell them, first the most comely of all; and afterwards, when she had been sold and had fetched a large sum of money, he would put up another who was the most comely after her — and they were sold for marriage. Now all the wealthy men of the Babylonians who were ready to marry vied with one another in bidding for the most beautiful maidens; those, however, of the common sort who were ready to marry did not require a fine form, but would accept money together with less comely maidens. For when the crier had finished selling the most comely of the maidens, he would make the least shapely stand up, or any one of them who might be crippled in any way, and he would proclaim her, asking who was willing to have her in marriage for the least gold, until she was assigned to him who was willing to accept the least. The gold would come from the sale of the comely maidens, and so those of beautiful form provided dowries for those who were unshapely or crippled. But to give one's own daughter in marriage to whomsoever each man would was not allowed, nor to carry off the maiden after buying her without a surety; for it was necessary for the man to provide sureties that he would marry her before he took her away; and if they did not agree well together, the law was laid down that he should pay back the money. It was also allowed for anyone who wished to come from another village and buy. This, then, was their most honorable custom; it does not, however, still exist at the present time, but they have recently found out another way, in order that the men may not ill-treat them or take them to another city: for since the time when, being conquered, they were oppressed and ruined, each one of the common people, when he is in want of livelihood, prostitutes his female children.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 196
paragraphs: Next in wisdom to that is this other custom established among them: they bear out the sick into the marketplace, for they make no use of physicians. So people come up to the sick man and give advice about his disease, if anyone himself has ever suffered something like what the sick man has, or has seen any other who had suffered it; and coming near they advise and recommend those means by which they themselves got rid of a like disease, or saw some other get rid of it. And to pass by the sick man in silence is not permitted to them, nor until one has asked what disease he has.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 197
paragraphs: They bury their dead in honey, and their funeral laments are similar to those of Egypt. Whenever a Babylonian man has been intimate with his wife, he sits beside burning incense. His wife does the same on the other side. At dawn, they both bathe. They will not touch any vessel until they have washed. The Arabians observe the same custom.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 198
paragraphs: Now the most shameful of the customs of the Babylonians is as follows: every woman of the country must sit down in the precincts of Aphrodite once in her life and have commerce with a man who is a stranger. Many women who do not deign to mingle with the rest, because they are made arrogant by wealth, drive to the temple with pairs of horses in covered carriages, and so take their place, and a large number of attendants follow after them. But the greater number do thus: in the sacred enclosure of Aphrodite sit great numbers of women with a wreath of cord about their heads; some come and others go, and there are passages in straight lines going between the women in every direction, through which the strangers pass by and make their choice. Here, when a woman takes her seat, she does not depart again to her house until one of the strangers has thrown a silver coin into her lap and has had commerce with her outside the temple; and after throwing it he must say only these words: “I demand you in the name of the goddess Mylitta” — now Mylitta is the name given by the Assyrians to Aphrodite. The silver coin may be of any value; whatever it is, she will not refuse it, for that is not lawful for her, seeing that this coin is made sacred by the act. And she follows the man who has first thrown, and does not reject any; and after that she departs to her house, having acquitted herself of her duty to the goddess, nor will you be able thereafter to give any gift so great as to win her. So then as many as have attained to beauty and stature are speedily released, but those of them who are unshapely remain there much time, not being able to fulfill the law; for some of them remain even as much as three or four years. And in some parts of Cyprus too there is a custom similar to this.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 199
paragraphs: Those are the established customs of the Babylonians. Among them there are also three tribes that eat nothing but fish. When they catch and dry their fish in the sun, they do this: they throw them into brine, then pound them with a pestle in a mortar, and strain the result through a linen cloth. Some eat this as a paste, others bake it into a kind of bread.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 200
paragraphs: When this nation also had been subdued by Cyrus, he had a desire to bring the Massagetai into subjection to himself. This nation is reputed to be both great and warlike, and to dwell toward the East and the sunrising, beyond the river Araxes and over against the Issedonians; and some also say that this nation is of Scythian race.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 201
paragraphs: Now the Araxes is said by some to be larger and by others to be smaller than the Ister; and they say that there are many islands in it about equal in size to Lesbos, and in them people dwelling who feed in summer upon roots of all kinds which they dig up, and certain fruits from trees which have been discovered by them for food, these they store up, it is said, in the season when they are ripe, and feed upon them in winter. Moreover, it is said that other trees have been discovered by them which yield fruit of such a kind that, when they have assembled together in companies in the same place and lighted a fire, they sit round in a circle and throw some of it into the fire; and they smell the fruit which is thrown on, as it burns, and are intoxicated by the scent as the Hellenes are by wine, and when more of the fruit is thrown on they become more intoxicated, until at last they rise up to dance and begin to sing. This is said to be their manner of living. As to the river Araxes, it flows from the land of the Matienians, whence flows the Gyndes which Cyrus divided into the three hundred and sixty channels, and it discharges itself by forty branches, of which all except one end in swamps and shallow pools; and among these they say that men dwell who feed on fish eaten raw, and who are wont to use as clothing the skins of seals. But the one remaining branch of the Araxes flows with unimpeded course into the Caspian Sea.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 202
paragraphs: The Caspian Sea is a body of water by itself, connected to no other sea. The entire sea navigated by the Greeks—and the ocean beyond the Pillars of Heracles, called the Atlantic—and the Red Sea are in fact all one body of water. But the Caspian is separate. It is as long as a fifteen-day voyage under oars and as wide as an eight-day voyage at its broadest point. On its western shore rises the Caucasus, the largest and tallest of all mountain ranges, home to many diverse peoples, most of whom live entirely off wild plants. They say the trees there produce leaves that, when crushed and mixed with water, are used by the natives to paint figures on their clothing. The figures do not wash out but last as long as the wool, as if woven into the fabric from the start. These people are said to have intercourse openly, like cattle.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 203
paragraphs: On the West, then, of this Sea which is called Caspian, the Caucasus is the boundary; while toward the East and the rising sun a plain succeeds, which is of limitless extent to the view. Of this great plain, then, the Massagetai occupy a large part, against whom Cyrus had become eager to march. For there were many strong reasons which incited him to it and urged him on: first, the manner of his birth — that is, the opinion held of him that he was more than a mere mortal man — and next, the success which he had met with in his wars; for wherever Cyrus directed his march, it was impossible for that nation to escape.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 204
paragraphs: Now the ruler of the Massagetai was a woman, who was queen after the death of her husband, and her name was Tomyris. To her Cyrus sent and wooed her, pretending that he desired to have her for his wife. But Tomyris, understanding that he was wooing not herself but rather the kingdom of the Massagetai, rejected his approaches. Cyrus after this, as he made no progress by craft, marched to the Araxes, and proceeded to make an expedition openly against the Massagetai, forming bridges of boats over the river for his army to cross, and building towers upon the vessels which gave them passage across the river.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 205
paragraphs: While he was busy at this labor, Tomyris sent a herald and said thus: “O king of the Medes, cease to press forward the work which you are now pressing forward; for you cannot tell whether these things will be in the end for your advantage or not. Cease, I say, and be king over your own people, and endure to see us ruling those whom we rule. However, since I know you will not be willing to receive this counsel, but choose anything rather than to be at rest, therefore if you are greatly anxious to make trial of the Massagetai in fight, come now, leave that labor of yoking together the banks of the river, and cross over into our land, when we have first withdrawn three days' journey from the river; or, if you desire rather to receive us into your land, do this same thing yourself.” Having heard this, Cyrus called together the first men among the Persians, and having gathered these together, he laid the matter before them for discussion, asking their advice as to which of the two things he should do. Their opinions all agreed in one, bidding him receive Tomyris and her army into his country.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 206
paragraphs: But Croesus the Lydian, being present and finding fault with this opinion, declared an opinion opposite to that which had been set forth, saying as follows: “O king, I told you before also that since Zeus had given me over to you, I would avert according to my power whatever occasion of falling I might see coming near your house; and now my sufferings, which have been bitter, have proved to be lessons of wisdom to me. If you suppose that you are immortal and that you command an army which is also immortal, it will be of no use for me to declare to you my judgment. But if you have perceived that you are a mortal man yourself and command others who are so likewise, then learn this first: that for the affairs of men there is a revolving wheel, and that this in its revolution does not suffer the same persons always to have good fortune. I therefore now have an opinion about the matter laid before us which is opposite to that of these men. For if we shall consent to receive the enemy into our land, there is for you this danger in so doing: if you are worsted, you will lose in addition all your realm, for it is evident that if the Massagetai are victors, they will not turn back and flee, but will march upon the provinces of your realm. On the other hand, if you are the victor, you will not be victor so fully as if you should overcome the Massagetai after crossing over into their land and should pursue them when they fled. For against what I said before, I will set the same here again, and say that you, when you have conquered, will march straight against the realm of Tomyris. Moreover, besides what has been said, it is a disgrace and not to be endured that Cyrus the son of Cambyses should yield to a woman and so withdraw from her land. Now therefore it seems good to me that we should cross over and go forward from the crossing as far as they go in their retreat, and endeavor to get the better of them by doing as follows. The Massagetai, as I am informed, are without experience of Persian good things, and have never enjoyed any great luxuries. Cut up therefore cattle without stint, dress the meat, and set out for these men a banquet in our camp; moreover, provide without stint bowls of unmixed wine and provisions of every kind. Having done this, leave behind the most worthless part of your army, and let the rest begin to retreat from the camp toward the river. For if I am not mistaken in my judgment, when they see a quantity of good things, they will fall to the feast, and after that it remains for us to display great deeds.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 207
paragraphs: These were the conflicting opinions; and Cyrus, letting go the former opinion and choosing that of Croesus, gave notice to Tomyris to retire, as he was intending to cross over to her. She then proceeded to retire, as she had at first engaged to do; but Cyrus delivered Croesus into the hands of his son Cambyses, to whom he meant to give the kingdom, and gave him charge earnestly to honor him and to treat him well, if the crossing over to go against the Massagetai should not be prosperous. Having thus charged him and sent these away to the land of the Persians, he crossed over the river, both himself and his army.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 208
paragraphs: When he had passed over the Araxes, night having come on, he saw a vision in his sleep in the land of the Massagetai, as follows. In his sleep it seemed to Cyrus that he saw the eldest of the sons of Hystaspes having wings upon his shoulders, and that with the one of these he overshadowed Asia and with the other Europe. Now of Hystaspes the son of Arsames, who was a man of the Achaimenid clan, the eldest son was Dareios, who was then, I suppose, a youth of about twenty years of age, and he had been left behind in the land of the Persians, for he was not yet of full age to go out to the wars. So when Cyrus awoke, he considered with himself concerning the vision; and as the vision seemed to him to be of great import, he called Hystaspes, and having taken him apart by himself he said: “Hystaspes, your son has been found plotting against me and against my throne; and how I know this for certain, I will declare to you. The gods have a care for me and show me beforehand all the evils that threaten me. So in the night that is past, while sleeping, I saw the eldest of your sons having wings upon his shoulders, and with the one he overshadowed Asia and with the other Europe. To judge by this vision, it cannot be but that he is plotting against me. Therefore, go by the quickest way back to Persia and take care that, when I arrive there after subduing these regions, you set your son before me to be examined.”

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 209
paragraphs: Cyrus said this because he believed Darius was plotting against him. But in truth, the gods were showing him that he would die there and his kingdom would pass to Darius. Hystaspes replied: "O king, may no Persian ever be born who plots against you! But if one exists, may he perish swiftly. You took the Persians from slaves and made them free, from subjects and made them rulers of all. If a dream has shown you that my son is plotting, I hand him over to you to do with as you wish." With this answer, Hystaspes crossed back over the Araxes and returned to Persia to keep watch over his son Darius for Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 210
paragraphs: Hystaspes, then, having made answer with these words and having crossed over the Araxes, was going his way to the Persian land to keep watch over his son Dareios for Cyrus; and Cyrus meanwhile went forward and made a march of one day from the Araxes according to the suggestion of Croesus. After this, when Cyrus and the best part of the army of the Persians had marched back to the Araxes, and those who were unfit for fighting had been left behind, then a third part of the army of the Massagetai came to the attack and proceeded to slay — not without resistance — those who had been left behind of the army of Cyrus. Seeing the feast that was set forth, when they had overcome their enemies, they lay down and feasted; and being satiated with food and wine, they went to sleep. Then the Persians came upon them and slew many of them, and took alive many more even than they slew, and among these was the son of the queen Tomyris, who was leading the army of the Massagetai; and his name was Spargapises.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 211
paragraphs: When Tomyris learned what had happened to her army and her son, she sent a herald to Cyrus with this message: "Cyrus, insatiable for blood, do not be puffed up by what has happened. You conquered my son not in fair battle but by the fruit of the vine—the substance that fills you Persians until you lose your minds and say shameful things as it settles in your bellies. That is the weapon you used to overpower my son, not strength in combat. Now hear my good advice. Give me back my son and leave this land unpunished, even though you savaged a third of my army. If you refuse, I swear by the sun, the lord of the Massagetae, that for all your insatiable thirst, I will give you your fill of blood."

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 212
paragraphs: When these words were reported to him, Cyrus made no account of them; and the son of the queen Tomyris, Spargapises, when the wine left him and he learned in what evil case he was, entreated Cyrus that he might be loosed from his chains and gained his request; and then, as soon as he was loosed and had got power over his hands, he put himself to death.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 213
paragraphs: He ended his life in this manner. But Tomyris, as Cyrus did not listen to her, gathered together all her power and joined battle with Cyrus. This battle of all the battles fought by barbarians I judge to have been the fiercest, and I am informed it happened thus: first, it is said, they stood apart and shot at one another; and afterwards, when their arrows were all shot away, they fell upon one another and engaged in close combat with their spears and daggers. And so they continued in conflict with one another for a long time, and neither side would flee; but at last the Massagetai got the better in the fight. The greater part of the Persian army was destroyed there on the spot, and Cyrus himself brought his life to an end there, after he had reigned in all thirty years wanting one. Then Tomyris filled a skin with human blood and had search made among the Persian dead for the corpse of Cyrus; and when she found it, she let his head down into the skin, and doing outrage to the corpse she said at the same time this: “Though I yet live and have overcome you in fight, nevertheless you have undone me by taking my son with craft; but I, according to my threat, will give you your fill of blood.” Now as regards the end of the life of Cyrus there are many tales told, but this which I have related is to my mind the most worthy of belief.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 214
paragraphs: As to the Massagetai, they wear a dress which is similar to that of the Scythians, and they have a manner of life which is also like theirs. Among them there are horsemen and also men who do not ride on horses (for they have both fashions), and moreover there are both archers and spearmen, and their custom is to carry battle-axes. For everything they use either gold or bronze: in all that has to do with spear-points or arrow-heads or battle-axes, they use bronze; but for head-dresses, girdles, and belts round the arm-pits, they employ gold as ornament. In like manner with their horses: they put breast-plates of bronze about their chests, but on their bridles, bits, and cheek-pieces they employ gold. Iron, however, and silver they do not use at all, for they have none in their land, but gold and bronze in abundance.

chapters.title: Book I — Clio, Chapter 215
paragraphs: These are their customs. Each man marries one wife, but they share their wives in common. The Greeks attribute this practice to the Scythians, but in fact it belongs to the Massagetae. Whenever a man desires a woman, he hangs his quiver on the front of her wagon and lies with her without shame. They set no fixed limit on life span, but when a man grows very old, his relatives gather and sacrifice him along with some cattle. They boil the flesh together and feast on it. This they consider the most blessed death. A man who dies of disease is not eaten but buried, and it is counted as a misfortune that he did not live long enough to be sacrificed. They do not grow crops but live on livestock and fish, which the Araxes supplies in abundance. They drink milk. The only god they worship is the sun. They sacrifice horses to it, reasoning that the swiftest of mortal creatures deserves to be offered to the swiftest of the gods.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 216
paragraphs: When Cyrus had brought his life to an end, Cambyses received the royal power in succession, being the son of Cyrus and of Cassandane, daughter of Pharnaspes, for whose death, which came about before his own, Cyrus had made great mourning himself and had also proclaimed to all those over whom he bore rule that they should make mourning for her. Cambyses, I say, being the son of this woman and of Cyrus, regarded the Ionians and Aiolians as slaves inherited from his father; and he proceeded to march an army against Egypt, taking with him as helpers not only the other nations of which he was the ruler, but also those of the Hellenes over whom he had power besides.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 217
paragraphs: Now the Egyptians, before the time when Psammetichos became king over them, were wont to suppose that they had come into being first of all men. But since the time when Psammetichos, having become king, desired to know what men had come into being first, they suppose that the Phrygians came into being before themselves, but that they themselves came before all other men. Now Psammetichos, when he was not able by inquiry to find out any means of knowing who had come into being first of all men, contrived a device of the following kind.
