Taking two newborn children belonging to persons of the common sort, he gave them to a shepherd to bring up at the place where his flocks were, with a manner of bringing up such as I shall describe: charging him namely that no man should utter any word in their presence, that they should be placed by themselves in a room where none might come, and that at the proper time he should bring to them she-goats, and when he had satisfied them with milk, should do for them whatever else was needed. These things Psammetichos did and gave him this charge, wishing to hear what word the children would first let break forth, after they had ceased from wailings without sense. And accordingly so it came to pass: for after a space of two years had gone by, during which the shepherd went on acting so, at length, when he opened the door and entered, both the children fell before him in entreaty and uttered the word “bekos,” stretching forth their hands. At first, when he heard this, the shepherd kept silence; but since this word was often repeated, as he visited them constantly and attended to them, at last he declared the matter to his master, and at his command he brought the children before his face. Then Psammetichos, having himself also heard it, began to inquire what nation of men named anything “bekos,” and inquiring he found that the Phrygians had this name for bread. In this manner, guided by an indication such as this, the Egyptians were brought to allow that the Phrygians were a more ancient people than themselves.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 218
paragraphs: That it came to pass in this way, I heard from the priests of that Hephaistos who dwells at Memphis; but the Hellenes relate, besides many other idle tales, that Psammetichos cut out the tongues of certain women and then caused the children to live with these women.

With regard then to the rearing of the children, they related as much as I have said. I heard also other things at Memphis when I had speech with the priests of Hephaistos. Moreover, I visited both Thebes and Heliopolis for this very cause, namely because I wished to know whether the priests at these places would agree in their accounts with those at Memphis; for the men of Heliopolis are said to be the most learned in records of the Egyptians. Those of their narrations which I heard with regard to the gods I am not eager to relate in full, but I shall name them only, because I consider that all men are equally ignorant of these matters; and whatever things of them I may record, I shall record only because I am compelled by the course of the story.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 219
paragraphs: But as to those matters which concern men, the priests agreed with one another in saying that the Egyptians were the first of all men on earth to find out the course of the year, having divided the seasons into twelve parts to make up the whole; and this, they said, they found out from the stars. They reckon to this extent more wisely, it seems to me, than the Hellenes, inasmuch as the Hellenes throw in an intercalated month every other year, to make the seasons right, whereas the Egyptians, reckoning the twelve months at thirty days each, bring in also every year five days beyond the number; and thus the circle of their seasons is completed and comes round to the same point whence it set out. They said moreover that the Egyptians were the first who brought into use appellations for the twelve gods, and the Hellenes took up the use from them; and that they were the first who assigned altars, images, and temples to the gods, and who engraved figures on stones. With regard to most of these things, they showed me by actual facts that they had happened so. They said also that the first man who became king of Egypt was Min; and that in his time all Egypt except the district of Thebes was a swamp, and none of the regions were then above water which now lie below the lake of Moiris, to which lake it is a voyage of seven days up the river from the sea.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 220
paragraphs: And I thought they said well about the land; for it is plain in truth even to a person who has not heard of it beforehand but has only seen it, at least if he has understanding, that the Egypt to which the Hellenes come in ships is a land which has been won by the Egyptians as an addition, and that it is a gift of the river. Moreover the regions which lie above this lake, also for a distance of three days' sail — about which they did not go on to say anything of this kind — are nevertheless another instance of the same thing. For the nature of the land of Egypt is as follows: First, when you are still approaching it in a ship and are distant a day's run from the land, if you let down a sounding-line you will bring up mud, and will find yourself in eleven fathoms. This, then, so far shows that there is a silting forward of the land.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 221
paragraphs: As further evidence about this land, the priests told me that in the reign of King Moeris, whenever the river rose at least eight cubits, it flooded all of Egypt below Memphis. At the time they told me this, fewer than nine hundred years had passed since Moeris' death. Yet now, unless the river rises at least fifteen or sixteen cubits, it does not overflow. If this land continues to grow in height at the same rate, and to increase in extent in the same proportion, it seems to me that the Egyptians who live below Lake Moeris—especially those in the Delta—will eventually suffer permanent drought as the Nile can no longer reach their fields.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 222
paragraphs: From thence and as far as Heliopolis inland, Egypt is broad, and the land is all flat and without springs of water and formed of mud. The road as one goes inland from the sea to Heliopolis is about the same in length as that which leads from the altar of the twelve gods at Athens to Pisa and the temple of Olympian Zeus. Reckoning up, you would find the difference very small by which these roads fail of being equal in length — not more, indeed, than fifteen furlongs; for the road from Athens to Pisa is fifteen furlongs short of being fifteen hundred, while the road to Heliopolis from the sea reaches that number completely.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 223
paragraphs: From Heliopolis, however, as you go up, Egypt is narrow; for on the one side a mountain-range belonging to Arabia stretches along by the side of it, going in a direction from North toward the midday and the South Wind, tending upwards without a break to that which is called the Erythraian Sea; and in this range are the stone-quarries which were used in cutting stone for the pyramids at Memphis. On this side, then, the mountain ends where I have said, and then takes a turn back; and where it is widest, as I was informed, it is a journey of two months across from East to West, and the borders of it which turn toward the East are said to produce frankincense. Such, then, is the nature of this mountain-range. On the side of Egypt toward Libya another range extends, rocky and enveloped in sand: in this are the pyramids, and it runs in the same direction as those parts of the Arabian mountains which go toward the midday. So then, I say, from Heliopolis the land has no longer a great extent so far as it belongs to Egypt, and for about four days' sail up the river Egypt properly so-called is narrow; and the space between the mountain-ranges which have been mentioned is plain-land, but where it is narrowest it did not seem to me to exceed two hundred furlongs from the Arabian mountains to those which are called the Libyan. After this again Egypt is broad.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 224
paragraphs: Such is the nature of this land. From Heliopolis to Thebes is a voyage up the river of nine days, and the distance of the journey in furlongs is four thousand eight hundred and sixty, the number of the schoines being eighty-one. If these measures of Egypt in furlongs be put together, the result is as follows: I have already before this shown that the distance along the sea amounts to three thousand six hundred furlongs, and I will now declare what the distance is inland from the sea to Thebes, namely six thousand one hundred and twenty furlongs. And again, the distance from Thebes to the city called Elephantine is one thousand eight hundred furlongs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 225
paragraphs: Of this land, then, concerning which I have spoken, it seemed to myself also, according as the priests said, that the greater part had been won as an addition by the Egyptians. For it was evident to me that the space between the aforesaid mountain-ranges, which lie above the city of Memphis, once was a gulf of the sea, like the regions about Ilion, Teuthrania, Ephesos, and the plain of the Maiander — if it is permitted to compare small things with great. And small these are in comparison; for of the rivers which heaped up the soil in those regions none is worthy to be compared in volume with a single one of the mouths of the Nile, which has five mouths. Moreover, there are other rivers also, not in size at all equal to the Nile, which have performed great feats; of which I can mention the names of several, and especially the Acheloös, which, flowing through Acarnania and so issuing out into the sea, has already made half of the Echinades from islands into mainland.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 226
paragraphs: In the land of Arabia, not far from Egypt, there is a gulf of the sea running in from what is called the Erythraean Sea — very long and narrow, as I am about to describe. As to the length of the voyage along it, a man setting out from the innermost point to sail through it into the open sea would spend forty days on the journey under oars; and as to its breadth, at its widest the gulf is half a day's sail across. It has an ebb and flow of tide every day. My view is that Egypt was once just such another gulf: the one running in towards Ethiopia from the Northern Sea, and the other, the Arabian gulf I am about to describe, running from the south towards Syria, the two gulfs boring in so as almost to meet at their far points, and passing one another with only a small space left between. Now if the stream of the Nile were to turn aside into this Arabian gulf, what would prevent that gulf from being filled up with silt as the river continued to flow — certainly within twenty thousand years? For my part I am of the opinion it would be filled up even within ten thousand. How then, in all the time that has elapsed before my birth, should not a gulf even much greater than this have been filled up by a river so great and so active?

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 227
paragraphs: As for Egypt, I both believe those who say these things are so, and I am strongly of that opinion myself. I have observed that Egypt projects into the sea further than the adjoining land; that shells are found on its mountains; that an efflorescence of salt forms upon the surface, so that even the pyramids are being eaten away by it; and that of all the mountains of Egypt, only the range above Memphis has sand. Besides which, I notice that Egypt resembles neither Arabia which borders upon it, nor Libya, nor yet Syria (for Syrians are the ones who dwell along the Arabian seacoast), but has a black and easily crumbling soil — which is in truth mud and silt brought down from Ethiopia by the river. The soil of Libya, as we know, is reddish in colour and rather sandy, while that of Arabia and Syria is clayey and rocky.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 228
paragraphs: The priests also gave me a strong proof concerning this land as follows. In the reign of King Moeris, whenever the river reached a height of at least eight cubits it watered Egypt below Memphis; and not yet nine hundred years had passed since the death of Moeris when I heard these things from the priests. Yet now, unless the river rises to sixteen cubits — or fifteen at the least — it does not go over the land. I think too that those Egyptians who live below the lake of Moeris, and especially in the region called the Delta, if that land continues to grow in height according to this proportion and to expand similarly in extent, will suffer for all time to come, from the Nile failing to flood their land, the very thing they themselves said the Hellenes would one day suffer. For hearing that all the land of the Hellenes is watered by rain and not by rivers as theirs is, they said the Hellenes would one day be disappointed of a great hope and suffer the evils of famine. This saying means that if the god shall not send them rain but allow drought to prevail for a long time, the Hellenes will be destroyed by hunger; for they have in fact no other supply of water to save them except from Zeus alone.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 229
paragraphs: This has been rightly said by the Egyptians with reference to the Hellenes; but now let me tell how matters stand with the Egyptians themselves. If, as I said before, their land below Memphis (for this is the part that is increasing) continues to rise in height at the same rate as in the past, then assuredly those Egyptians who dwell here will suffer famine, if their land shall not have rain nor the river be able to flood their fields. It is certain, however, that at present they gather their crops from the earth with less labour than any other men, including other Egyptians. They have no labour in breaking up furrows with the plough, nor in hoeing, nor in any of those other tasks that other men undertake for a crop; instead, when the river has come up of its own accord and watered their fields, and after watering has withdrawn again, then each man sows his own field and turns swine into it. When he has trodden the seed into the ground with the swine, he then waits for the harvest; and when he has threshed the corn with the swine, then he gathers it in.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 230
paragraphs: If we were to follow the view of the Ionians concerning Egypt — who say that the Delta alone is Egypt, reckoning its seacoast to run from the watchtower called Perseus's to the fish-curing houses of Pelusium, a distance of forty schoeni, and extending inland as far as the city of Cercasorus, where the Nile divides and runs to Pelusium and Canobus, while as for the rest of what we call Egypt, they assign it partly to Libya and partly to Arabia — if, I say, we were to follow this account, we should thereby declare that in former times the Egyptians had no land to live in. For, as we have seen, their Delta at any rate is alluvial, and has only lately come into being (so to speak), as the Egyptians themselves say and as I believe. If then at first there was no land for them to live in, why did they waste their labour trying to prove that they had come into being before all other men? They need not have experimented with children to see what language they would first utter. I am not of the opinion that the Egyptians came into being at the same time as that land the Ionians call the Delta, but rather that they have existed always, ever since the human race came into being, and that as their land advanced forwards, many of them were left in their first dwellings while many came down gradually to the lower parts. At any rate it is certain that in old times Thebes bore the name of Egypt, and the circumference of this region measures six thousand one hundred and twenty furlongs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 231
paragraphs: If then we judge these matters rightly, the opinion of the Ionians about Egypt is not sound. But if the judgment of the Ionians is right, then I declare that neither the Hellenes nor the Ionians themselves know how to reckon, since they say the whole earth is made up of three divisions — Europe, Asia, and Libya: for they ought to add to these the Delta of Egypt, since it belongs neither to Asia nor to Libya. For according to their reckoning it cannot be the river Nile that divides Asia from Libya, since the Nile is cleft at the point of this Delta so as to flow round it, with the result that this land would come between Asia and Libya.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 232
paragraphs: We dismiss, then, the opinion of the Ionians, and offer a judgment of our own on this matter: that Egypt is all that land inhabited by Egyptians, just as Cilicia is the land inhabited by Cilicians and Assyria the land inhabited by Assyrians, and we know of no boundary properly speaking between Asia and Libya except the borders of Egypt. If, however, we adopt the view commonly held by the Hellenes, we shall suppose that the whole of Egypt, beginning from the Cataract and the city of Elephantine, is divided into two parts and thus partakes of both names, one side belonging to Libya and the other to Asia. For the Nile from the Cataract onwards flows to the sea, cutting Egypt through the middle; and as far as the city of Cercasorus the Nile flows in one single stream, but from this city onwards it divides into three channels. One, which is called the Pelusian mouth, turns towards the east; the second goes towards the west, and this is called the Canobic mouth; while the channel that runs straight on comes, as the river descends, to the point of the Delta, then cuts the Delta through its middle and so issues into the sea. In this channel we have a portion of the river's water that is neither the smallest nor the least famous — it is called the Sebennytic mouth. There are also two other mouths which branch off from the Sebennytic and go to the sea, called the Saïtic and the Mendesian mouth. The Bolbitinic and Bucolic mouths, on the other hand, are not natural but made by digging.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 233
paragraphs: Moreover, the answer given by the Oracle of Ammon also bears witness in support of my opinion that Egypt is of the extent I declare it to be in my account; and I heard of this answer after I had already formed my own opinion about Egypt. The people of the cities of Marea and Apis, dwelling in those parts of Egypt that border on Libya, held themselves to be Libyans and not Egyptians, and also being burdened by the rules of religious service — because they wished not to be debarred from the use of cows' flesh — sent to Ammon saying they had nothing in common with the Egyptians, for they dwelt outside the Delta and agreed with them in nothing; and they said they desired that it might be lawful for them to eat everything without distinction. The god, however, did not permit them to do so, but answered that Egypt was that land which the Nile comes over and waters, and that those were Egyptians who, dwelling below the city of Elephantine, drank of that river. Thus it was answered to them by the Oracle about this:

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 234
paragraphs: and the Nile, when it is in flood, goes over not only the Delta but also over the land called Libyan and over the land called Arabian, sometimes as much as two days' journey on each side, at times even more than this, at times less.

As regards the nature of the river, neither from the priests nor from any other man was I able to obtain any knowledge, though I was especially desirous to learn from them about these matters — namely why the Nile comes down increasing in volume from the summer solstice onwards for a hundred days, and then, when it has reached the number of these days, turns and ebbs, failing in its stream, so that through the whole winter season it continues to be low, and remains so until the summer solstice returns. None of these things was I able to learn from the Egyptians when I inquired of them what peculiar property the Nile has, whereby its nature is the opposite of other rivers'. And I made these inquiries desiring to know both this which I say and also why, unlike all other rivers, it does not give rise to any breezes blowing from it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 235
paragraphs: However, some of the Hellenes who wished to gain distinction for cleverness have given an account of this water in three different ways. Two of these I do not think it worth even speaking of, except just to indicate their nature. The first says that the Etesian Winds are the cause that makes the river rise, by preventing the Nile from flowing out into the sea. But the Etesian Winds often fail, and yet the Nile still does the same work it is accustomed to do; and moreover, if these winds were the cause, all the other rivers that flow in a direction opposed to the Etesian Winds ought to have been affected in the same way as the Nile, and even more so, since they are smaller and present a feebler flow of stream. Yet there are many such rivers in Syria and many in Libya, and they are affected in no such manner as the Nile.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 236
paragraphs: The second explanation shows more ignorance even than that which has been mentioned, and it is more marvellous to tell; for it says that the river produces these effects because it flows from the Ocean, and that the Ocean flows around the whole earth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 237
paragraphs: The third of the explanations is much the most plausible, but nevertheless the most mistaken of all; for this one has no more truth in it than the others, alleging as it does that the Nile flows from melting snow — whereas in fact it flows out of Libya through the midst of the Ethiopians, and so comes out into Egypt. How then should it flow from snow, when it flows from the hottest parts to those which are cooler? Indeed most of the facts are such as to convince any reasoning man that it is not at all likely it flows from snow. The first and greatest evidence is the winds, which blow hot from these regions; the second is that the land there is always rainless and without frost, whereas after snow has fallen rain must necessarily come within five days, so that if it snowed in those parts rain would fall there; the third evidence is the people dwelling there, who are black in colour because of the burning heat. Moreover, kites and swallows remain there throughout the year and do not leave the land; and cranes, fleeing the cold that sets in over Scythia, come regularly to these parts to winter. If then it snowed ever so little in the land through which the Nile flows and in which it has its rise, none of these things could take place, as necessity compels us to admit.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 238
paragraphs: As for the man who talked about the Ocean, he carried his tale into the region of the unknown, and so he need not be refuted; for I for my part know of no river Ocean existing, but I think that Homer or one of the poets before him invented the name and introduced it into his verse.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 239
paragraphs: If, however, having found fault with the opinions proposed by others, I am bound to declare an opinion of my own on these matters in doubt, I will tell what to my mind is the reason why the Nile increases in summer. In the winter season the Sun, being driven away from his former path through the heavens by the stormy winds, comes to the upper parts of Libya. If one would set forth the matter in the shortest way, all has now been said; for whatever region this god approaches most closely and stands directly above, that region may reasonably be supposed to be most in want of water, and its native streams of rivers are most dried up.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 240
paragraphs: To set the matter forth at greater length, it is thus: the Sun, passing in his course by the upper parts of Libya, acts in the following way. Since at all times the air in those parts is clear and the country is warm, because there are no cold winds, the Sun in passing through it does just what he was accustomed to do in summer when going through the midst of the heavens — that is, he draws the water to himself, and having drawn it he drives it away to the upper parts of the country, and the winds take it up and, scattering it abroad, melt it into rain; so it is natural that the winds which blow from this region, namely the South and Southwest Winds, should be much the rainiest of all winds. I think, however, that the Sun does not send away from himself all the water of the Nile each year, but that he also lets some remain with him. Then when winter becomes milder, the Sun returns again to the middle of the heavens, and from that time onwards he draws equally from all rivers; but in the meanwhile they flow in large volume, since rainwater mingles with them in great quantity, because their country receives rain then and is filled with torrent streams. In summer, however, they grow weak, since not only do the rainfalls fail, but they are also drawn upon by the Sun. The Nile, however, alone of all rivers, not having rain and being drawn by the Sun, naturally flows during winter in much less than its proper volume — that is, much less than in summer; for then it is drawn equally with all the other waters, but in winter it bears the burden alone. Thus I suppose the Sun to be the cause of these things.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 241
paragraphs: In my opinion he is also the cause that the air in these parts is dry, since he makes it so by scorching his path through the heavens; thus summer prevails always in the upper parts of Libya. If, however, the stations of the seasons had been changed, and where now in the heavens are placed the North Wind and winter were placed instead the South Wind and the midday, and where now is placed the South Wind there was the North — if this had been so, the Sun being driven from the middle of the heavens by winter and the North Wind would go to the upper parts of Europe, just as now he comes to the upper parts of Libya, and passing in his course throughout the whole of Europe I suppose he would do to the Ister what he now does to the Nile.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 242
paragraphs: As to the breeze — why none blows from the river — my opinion is that from very hot places it is not natural that anything should blow, and that a breeze is accustomed to blow from something cold.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 243
paragraphs: Let these matters then be as they are and as they were from the first. But as to the sources of the Nile, not one either of the Egyptians or of the Libyans or of the Hellenes who came into conversation with me professed to know anything, except the scribe of the sacred treasury of Athene at the city of Saïs in Egypt. To me, however, this man seemed not to be speaking seriously when he said he had certain knowledge of it; and he said the following: that there were two mountains whose tops ran up to a sharp point, situated between the city of Syene, which is in the district of Thebes, and Elephantine, and the names of the mountains were — of the one Crophi, of the other Mophi. From between these two mountains, he said, flowed the sources of the Nile, which were fathomless in depth; and half of the water flowed to Egypt and towards the North Wind, the other half to Ethiopia and the South Wind. As for the fathomless depth of the source, he said that Psammetichus king of Egypt made trial of this matter; for he had a rope twisted of many thousands of fathoms and let it down in this place, and it found no bottom. By this the scribe (if indeed what he told me was really so) gave me to understand that there were certain strong eddies and a backward flow, and that since the water dashed against the mountains, therefore the sounding-line could find no bottom when it was let down.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 244
paragraphs: From no other person was I able to learn anything about this matter; but for the rest I learned as follows by the most diligent inquiry, for I went myself as an eyewitness as far as the city of Elephantine, and from that point onwards I gathered knowledge by report. From Elephantine, as one goes up the river, there is country that slopes steeply; so that here one must attach ropes to the vessel on both sides, as one fastens an ox, and so make one's way onward; and if the rope should break, the vessel is gone at once, swept away by the violence of the stream. Through this country it is a voyage of about four days' length, and in this part the Nile is winding like the river Maeander, and the distance amounts to twelve schoeni, which one must traverse in this manner. Then you come to a level plain, in which the Nile flows around an island named Tachompso. (In the regions above Elephantine, Ethiopians dwell at once successively, who also occupy half of this island, and Egyptians the other half.) Adjoining this island there is a great lake, round which dwell Ethiopian nomad tribes; and when you have sailed through this, you come again to the stream of the Nile, which flows into this lake. After this you disembark and make a journey by land of forty days; for in the Nile sharp rocks stand up out of the water, and there are many reefs, by which it is not possible for a vessel to pass. Then, after you have passed through this country in the forty days I have mentioned, you embark again in another vessel and sail for twelve days; and after this you will come to a great city called Meroë. This city is said to be the mother-city of all the other Ethiopians, and those who dwell in it reverence among the gods Zeus and Dionysus alone, and these they greatly honour; and they have an Oracle of Zeus established, and make warlike marches whenever this god commands them by prophecies, and to whatever place he commands.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 245
paragraphs: Sailing from this city, you will come to the “Deserters” in another period of time equal to that in which you came from Elephantine to the mother-city of the Ethiopians. The name of these “Deserters” is Asmach, and this word, when translated into the tongue of the Hellenes, means “those who stand on the left hand of the king.” These were two hundred and forty thousand Egyptians of the warrior class, who revolted and went over to the Ethiopians for the following cause. In the reign of Psammetichus garrisons were stationed — one towards the Ethiopians at the city of Elephantine, another towards the Arabians and Assyrians at Daphnae of Pelusium, and another towards Libya at Marea. Even in my own day the garrisons of the Persians are ordered in the same way as these were under Psammetichus, for both at Elephantine and at Daphnae the Persians have outposts. The Egyptians of whom I speak had served as outposts for three years and no one relieved them from their guard; accordingly they took counsel together, and adopting a common plan they all in a body revolted from Psammetichus and set out for Ethiopia. Hearing this, Psammetichus set out in pursuit, and when he overtook them he entreated them much and tried to persuade them not to desert the gods of their country, their children, and their wives. At this, it is said, one of them pointed to his genitals and said that wherever this was, there they would have both children and wives. When they came to Ethiopia they gave themselves over to the king of the Ethiopians; and he rewarded them thus: there were certain of the Ethiopians who had come to be at odds with him, and he bade these men drive them out and dwell in their land. So when these men settled in the land of the Ethiopians, the Ethiopians have come to be of milder manners, having learnt the customs of the Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 246
paragraphs: The Nile, then, besides that part of its course within Egypt, is known for as far as a four months' journey by river and land: that is the number of months found by reckoning to be spent travelling from Elephantine to these “Deserters”; and the river runs from the west and the setting sun. But what lies beyond that no one can clearly say, for this land is desert by reason of the burning heat.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 247
paragraphs: This much, however, I heard from men of Cyrene, who told me they had gone to the Oracle of Ammon and had come into conversation with Etearchus king of the Ammonians; and it happened that after speaking of other matters they fell to discussing the Nile and how no one knew its sources. Etearchus said that once there had come to him men of the Nasamonians (this is a Libyan people who dwell in the Syrtis, and also in the land east of the Syrtis for no great distance), and when these Nasamonians came, and were asked by him whether they could tell him anything more than he knew about the desert parts of Libya, they said there had been among them certain sons of chief men, who were of unruly disposition; and these, when they grew up to be men, had devised various extravagant undertakings, and among them they drew lots for five of themselves to go and see the desert parts of Libya and try whether they could discover more than those who had previously explored furthest. For in the parts of Libya along the Northern Sea, beginning from Egypt and going as far as the headland of Soloeis (which is the extreme point of Libya), Libyans — and many races of them — extend along the whole coast, except such portions as the Hellenes and Phoenicians hold. But in the upper parts, which lie above the seacoast and above the peoples whose land comes down to the sea, Libya is full of wild beasts; and in the parts beyond the land of wild beasts it is full of sand, terribly waterless, and utterly desert. These young men then (they said), being sent out by their companions well supplied with water and provisions, went first through the inhabited country; after they had passed through this, they came to the country of wild beasts; and after this they passed through the desert, making their way towards the West Wind. Having crossed a great tract of sand in many days, they saw at last trees growing on a level place; and when they came up to them, they began to pluck the fruit that was on the trees. But as they began to pluck it, small men came upon them — of less stature than men of the common size — and these seized them and carried them off. Neither could the Nasamonians understand anything of their speech nor could those who were carrying them off understand the speech of the Nasamonians; and they led them (so it is said) through very great swamps, and after passing through these they came to a city in which all the men were of the same short stature as those who had carried them off, and black of skin. By the city ran a great river, which flowed from the west toward the sunrise, and in it were seen crocodiles.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 248
paragraphs: Of the account given by Etearchus the Ammonian let this much suffice, except that, as the men of Cyrene told me, he claimed the Nasamonians returned safely home, and that the people to whom they had come were all wizards. Now Etearchus conjectured this river running past the city to be the Nile; and reason compels us to think so. For the Nile flows from Libya and cuts Libya through the middle; and as I conjecture, judging of what is not known by what is evident to the view, it sets out at a distance from its mouth equal to that of the Ister. For the river Ister begins from the country of the Celts and the city of Pyrene, and so runs that it divides Europe through the middle (the Celts are outside the Pillars of Heracles and border upon the Cynesians, who dwell furthest towards the sunset of all peoples in Europe); and the Ister ends, after running through the whole of Europe, by flowing into the Euxine Sea at the place where the Milesians have their settlement of Istria.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 249
paragraphs: Now the Ister, since it flows through inhabited land, is known by the reports of many. But of the sources of the Nile no one can give an account, for the part of Libya through which it flows is uninhabited and desert. About its course, however, as much as it was possible to learn by the most diligent inquiry has been told; and it flows out into Egypt. Now Egypt lies nearly opposite to the mountain districts of Cilicia; and from there to Sinope, which lies on the Euxine Sea, is a journey in the same straight line of five days for a man travelling without baggage; and Sinope lies opposite to the place where the Ister runs out into the sea. Thus I think the Nile passes through the whole of Libya and is of equal length with the Ister.
Of the Nile, then, let this much suffice.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 250
paragraphs: Of Egypt, however, I shall give a full report, because it has more wonders than any other land, and its works too are as great beyond expression as any land has to show. For this reason, then, more shall be said about it.

The Egyptians, in keeping with their climate which is unlike any other, and with their river which shows a nature different from all other rivers, have established for themselves manners and customs that are, in almost all matters, opposite to those of other men. Among them the women go to market and carry on trade, while the men remain at home and weave; and whereas others weave by pushing the woof upwards, the Egyptians push it downwards. The men carry burdens on their heads, the women on their shoulders. The women urinate standing up, the men crouching down. They relieve themselves in their houses and eat outside in the streets, giving as their reason that one should do in secret what is unseemly though necessary, and in public what is not unseemly. No woman is priestess of any divinity, male or female; men serve as priests of all, both male and female. The sons are in no way compelled to support their parents if they do not desire to do so, but the daughters are forced to, however unwilling they may be.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 251
paragraphs: The priests of the gods in other lands wear long hair, but in Egypt they shave their heads. Among other men the custom is that in mourning those whom the matter concerns most closely have their hair cut short, but the Egyptians, when deaths occur, let their hair grow long — both that on the head and that on the chin — having before been close shaven. Other men have their daily living separate from beasts, but the Egyptians have theirs together with their beasts. Other men live on wheat and barley, but to any Egyptian who makes his living from these it is a great reproach; they make their bread of emmer wheat, which some call spelt. They knead dough with their feet and clay with their hands, with which they also gather up dung. Whereas other men, except those who have learned otherwise from the Egyptians, leave their private parts as nature made them, the Egyptians practise circumcision. As for garments, the men wear two each and the women only one. Whereas others fasten the rings and ropes of the sails on the outside of the ship, the Egyptians do this on the inside. Finally, in the writing of characters and in reckoning with pebbles, while the Hellenes carry the hand from left to right, the Egyptians do so from right to left; and doing so they say they do it in the right-handed manner and the Hellenes in the left-handed. They use two kinds of characters in writing, one called sacred and the other common.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 252
paragraphs: They are religious excessively, beyond all other men, and with regard to this they have the following customs. They drink from cups of bronze and rinse them out every day — not some only do this, but all. They wear garments of linen always newly washed, and of this they make a special point. They circumcise themselves for the sake of cleanliness, preferring to be clean rather than comely. The priests shave themselves all over the body every other day, so that no lice or any other foul thing may come upon them when they minister to the gods. The priests wear garments of linen only and sandals of papyrus, and no other garment may they take, nor other sandals. They wash themselves in cold water twice by day and twice again by night; and they perform other religious services of almost infinite number. They enjoy no few good things also, for they do not consume or spend anything of their own substance; there is sacred bread baked for them, and each of them has a great quantity of beef and goose-flesh coming in to him every day, and wine of grapes is given to them too — but it is not permitted them to taste of fish. The Egyptians do not sow beans at all in their land, and what grow of themselves they neither eat raw nor boil for food; indeed the priests cannot bear even to look upon them, thinking them an unclean kind of pulse. There is not one priest only for each of the gods but many, and of these one is chief priest; and whenever a priest dies his son is appointed to his place.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 253
paragraphs: The male oxen they consider to belong to Epaphus, and on his account they test them in the following manner. If the priest sees a single black hair on the beast, he considers it unclean for sacrifice; and one of the priests appointed for the purpose investigates these matters, both when the beast is standing upright and when it is lying on its back, drawing out its tongue moreover, to see if it is clean with respect to the appointed signs, which I shall describe in another part of this history. He also looks at the hairs of the tail to see if they are growing in the natural manner. If the beast is clean in respect of all these things, he marks it by rolling a piece of papyrus around the horns, and then when he has plastered sealing-earth over it he impresses upon it the seal of his signet-ring, and after that they take the animal away. For anyone who sacrifices a beast that is not sealed, the appointed penalty is death.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 254
paragraphs: In this way, then, the beast is tested; and their appointed manner of sacrifice is as follows. They lead the sealed beast to the altar where they are performing the sacrifice, and then kindle a fire. After that, having poured libations of wine over the altar so that it runs down upon the victim, and having called upon the god, they cut its throat; and having cut its throat they sever the head from the body. The body of the beast they flay, but upon the head they first utter many imprecations; and then those who have a market and Hellenes sojourning among them for trade carry it to the market-place and sell it, while those who have no Hellenes among them cast it into the river. This is the form of imprecation they utter over the heads, praying that if any evil is about to fall either upon those sacrificing or upon the land of Egypt in general, it may come rather upon this head. Now as regards the heads of sacrificed beasts and the pouring of wine over them, all the Egyptians have the same customs equally for all their sacrifices; and for this reason no Egyptian will eat of the head either of this or of any other kind of animal.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 255
paragraphs: But the manner of disembowelling the victims and of burning them is appointed differently for different sacrifices. I shall speak, however, of the sacrifices to that goddess whom they regard as the greatest of all, and to whom they celebrate the greatest festival. When they have flayed the bullock and uttered the imprecation, they remove the whole of its lower entrails but leave in the body the upper entrails and the fat; then they sever from it the legs and the end of the loin and the shoulders and the neck. This done, they fill the rest of the body of the animal with consecrated loaves, honey, raisins, figs, frankincense, myrrh, and every other kind of spices; and having filled it with these they offer it up, pouring over it great abundance of oil. They make their sacrifice after fasting, and while the offerings are being burned, they all beat themselves in mourning; and when they have finished beating themselves, they set forth as a feast whatever they left unburned of the sacrifice.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 256
paragraphs: The clean males of the ox kind, then, both full-grown animals and calves, are sacrificed by all the Egyptians; but the females they may not sacrifice, for these are sacred to Isis. The figure of Isis is in the form of a woman with cow's horns, just as the Hellenes represent Io in pictures, and all the Egyptians without exception revere cows far more than any other kind of cattle. For this reason no Egyptian man or woman would kiss a Hellene on the mouth, nor will they use a knife, roasting-spits, or cauldron belonging to a Hellene, nor taste of the flesh even of a clean animal if it has been cut with a Hellene's knife. They bury the cattle of this kind that die in the following manner. The females they throw into the river, but the males they bury, each people in the outskirts of their town, with one of the horns (or sometimes both) protruding to mark the place. When the bodies have rotted away and the appointed time comes, then to each city comes a boat from what is called the island of Prosopitis (this is in the Delta, and the circuit of it measures nine schoeni). On this island of Prosopitis, besides many other cities, stands the one from which the boats come to collect the bones of the oxen; the city's name is Atarbechis, and in it there is a holy temple of Aphrodite. From this city many go out in various directions, some to one city and some to another, and when they have dug up the bones of the oxen they carry them off, and all together they bury them in a single place. In the same way they bury their other cattle when these die, for the same law is laid down concerning them, and these too they abstain from killing.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 257
paragraphs: Now all who have a temple set up to the Theban Zeus, or who belong to the district of Thebes, sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep — for not all Egyptians equally reverence the same gods, except only Isis and Osiris (whom they say is Dionysus); these they all reverence alike. But those who have a temple of Mendes or belong to the Mendesian district abstain from goats and sacrifice sheep. The men of Thebes, and those who after their example abstain from sheep, say this custom was established among them for the following reason. Heracles (they say) had an earnest desire to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen by him; at last, when Heracles was insistent in entreaty, Zeus devised this trick — he flayed a ram and held in front of him the head of the ram that he had cut off, and he put on over himself the fleece, and then showed himself to Heracles. Hence the Egyptians make the image of Zeus with the face of a ram; and the Ammonians do so also after their example, being settlers from both the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, and using a language that is a mixture of both tongues. And in my opinion it is from this god that the Ammonians took the name they bear, for the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. The Thebans, then, do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred for this reason. Yet on one day of the year, at the feast of Zeus, they cut up and flay a single ram in the same manner, and cover the image of Zeus with its skin, and then they bring up to it another image of Heracles. When this is done, all who are in the temple beat themselves in lamentation for the ram, and then they bury it in a sacred tomb.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 258
paragraphs: About Heracles I heard the account that he was one of the twelve gods; but of the other Heracles whom the Hellenes know I was not able to hear anything in any part of Egypt. Moreover, to prove that the Egyptians did not take the name of Heracles from the Hellenes, but rather the Hellenes from the Egyptians — I mean those of the Hellenes who gave the name Heracles to the son of Amphitryon — of this, besides many other proofs, there is chiefly this: that the parents of this Heracles, Amphitryon and Alcmene, were both of Egyptian descent; and also that the Egyptians say they know neither the name of Poseidon nor of the Dioscuri, nor have these been accepted by them as gods among their other gods. Yet if they had received the name of any divinity from the Hellenes, they would naturally have preserved the memory of these most of all — assuming, as I suppose and as my judgment compels me to think, that in those times, as now, some of the Hellenes made voyages and were seafaring folk; so that the Egyptians would have learnt the names of these gods even more than that of Heracles. In fact, however, Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god; and (as the Egyptians themselves say) it is seventeen thousand years to the beginning of the reign of Amasis from the time when the twelve gods — of whom they count Heracles one — were begotten of the eight gods.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 259
paragraphs: I, moreover, wishing to know something certain of these matters as far as possible, made a voyage also to Tyre of Phoenicia, hearing that in that place there was a holy temple of Heracles; and I saw that it was richly furnished with many votive offerings, and especially there were in it two pillars, one of pure gold and the other of an emerald stone of such size that it shone at night. Having come into conversation with the priests of the god, I asked them how long it was since their temple had been set up; and these also I found at variance with the Hellenes, for they said that at the same time as Tyre was founded the temple of the god had been set up, and that it was a period of two thousand three hundred years since their people had begun to dwell at Tyre. I saw also at Tyre another temple of Heracles with the surname Thasian; and I came to Thasos too, and there I found a temple of Heracles set up by the Phoenicians, who had sailed out to seek for Europa and had colonised Thasos; and these things happened full five generations of men before Heracles the son of Amphitryon was born in Hellas. So then my inquiries show clearly that Heracles is an ancient god; and those of the Hellenes seem to me to act most rightly who have two temples of Heracles set up, and who sacrifice to the one as an immortal god with the title of Olympian, and make offerings of the dead to the other as a hero.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 260
paragraphs: Moreover, besides many other stories which the Hellenes tell without due consideration, this tale is especially foolish which they tell about Heracles — namely, that when he came to Egypt, the Egyptians put wreaths on him and led him in procession to sacrifice him to Zeus; and he for some time kept quiet, but when they were beginning the sacrifice of him at the altar, he roused his prowess and slew them all. I for my part am of the opinion that the Hellenes, when they tell this tale, are altogether without knowledge of the nature and customs of the Egyptians. For how should they, for whom it is not lawful to sacrifice even beasts — except swine, and the males of oxen and calves (such of them as are clean), and geese — how should these men sacrifice human beings? Besides this, how is it possible in nature that Heracles, being one person only and moreover a man (as they assert), should slay many myriads? Having said so much about these matters, we pray we may have grace from both the gods and the heroes for our speech.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 261
paragraphs: The reason why those Egyptians I have mentioned do not sacrifice goats, female or male, is this. The Mendesians count Pan among the eight gods (and these eight gods, they say, came into being before the twelve gods), and the painters and image-makers represent the figure of Pan in painting and sculpture just as the Hellenes do — with goat's face and legs, not supposing him really to be like this, but making him resemble the other gods. The reason why they represent him in this form I prefer not to say. The Mendesians, then, reverence all goats, and the males more than the females (and goatherds too have greater honour than other herdsmen); but one of the goats in particular is reverenced, and when he dies there is great mourning in all the Mendesian district. Both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes. Moreover, in my own lifetime there occurred in that district this marvel: that is to say, a he-goat had intercourse with a woman publicly, and this was done so that all men might have evidence of it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 262
paragraphs: The pig is accounted an abominable animal by the Egyptians; first, if any of them in passing touches a pig, he goes into the river and dips himself immediately in the water along with his garments. Second, swineherds, though they be native Egyptians, unlike all others do not enter any of the temples in Egypt, nor is anyone willing to give his daughter in marriage to one of them or to take a wife from among them; the swineherds marry their own daughters to each other and take wives from among one another. Now the Egyptians do not think it right to sacrifice swine to the other gods; but to the Moon and to Dionysus alone — at the same time and on the same full moon — they sacrifice swine and then eat their flesh. As to why, when they abominate swine at all their other festivals, they sacrifice them at this one, there is a story told by the Egyptians; and though I know this story, it is not a seemly one for me to tell. The sacrifice of the swine to the Moon is performed as follows: when the priest has slain the victim, he puts together the end of the tail, the spleen, and the caul, and covers them with the whole of the fat around the paunch, and then he offers them with fire; and the rest of the flesh they eat on that day of full moon on which they held the sacrifice, but on any day after this they will not taste of it. The poor among them, by reason of their scanty means, shape pigs out of dough, bake them, and offer these as sacrifices.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 263
paragraphs: Then for Dionysus, on the eve of the festival, each one kills a pig by cutting its throat before his own doors, and after that he gives the pig to the swineherd who sold it to him, to carry it away again. The rest of the feast of Dionysus is celebrated by the Egyptians in almost all respects just as it is by the Hellenes, except for choral dances; but instead of the phallos they have invented another contrivance, namely figures about a cubit high worked by strings, which women carry about the villages, with the private member made to move and not much less in size than the rest of the body; and a flute goes before, and they follow singing the praises of Dionysus. As to why the figure has this member larger than is natural, and moves it although it moves no other part of the body — about this there is a sacred story told.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 264
paragraphs: Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them. For Melampus is the one who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysus and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking, when he made it known he did not take in the whole of it; but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. Melampus, then, is the one who taught about the phallos that is carried in procession for Dionysus; and from him the Hellenes learnt to do what they do. I say, then, that Melampus, being a man of ability, devised for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysus, making changes in some few points of them. For I shall not say that what is done in the worship of the god in Egypt came accidentally to be the same as what is done among the Hellenes, for then these rites would have been in character with the Hellenic worship and not lately brought in; nor indeed shall I say that the Egyptians took either this or any other customary observance from the Hellenes. But I think it most probable that Melampus learnt the matters concerning Dionysus from Cadmus the Tyrian and from those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land we now call Boeotia.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 265
paragraphs: Moreover, the naming of almost all the gods has come to Hellas from Egypt: that it has come from the Barbarians I find by inquiry to be true, and I am of the opinion that most probably it has come from Egypt. For, except in the case of Poseidon and the Dioscuri (in accordance with what I have said before), and also of Hera, Hestia, Themis, the Charites, and the Nereïds, the Egyptians have had the names of all the other gods in their country from time immemorial. What I say here is what the Egyptians themselves think. But as for the gods whose names they profess not to know, these I think received their names from the Pelasgians — except Poseidon; about this god the Hellenes learnt from the Libyans, for no people except the Libyans have had the name of Poseidon from the first and have paid honour to this god always. Nor, it may be added, have the Egyptians any custom of worshipping heroes.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 266
paragraphs: These observances, then, and others besides which I shall mention, the Hellenes have adopted from the Egyptians; but in making the images of Hermes with the phallos, as they do, they have learnt not from the Egyptians but from the Pelasgians. The custom was received first by the Athenians of all the Hellenes, and from them by the rest. For just at the time when the Athenians were beginning to be counted among the Hellenes, the Pelasgians became dwellers with them in their land, and from this very circumstance they began to be counted as Hellenes. Whoever has been initiated in the mysteries of the Cabeiri, which the Samothracians perform (having received them from the Pelasgians), that man knows the meaning of my speech. For those very Pelasgians who became dwellers with the Athenians used to dwell before that time in Samothrace, and from them the Samothracians received their mysteries. So then the Athenians were the first of the Hellenes to make the images of Hermes with the phallos, having learnt the practice from the Pelasgians; and the Pelasgians told a sacred story about it, which is set forth in the mysteries in Samothrace.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 267
paragraphs: Now the Pelasgians formerly used to make all their sacrifices calling upon the gods in prayer, as I know from what I heard at Dodona; but they gave no title or name to any of them, for they had not yet heard any, and they called them gods (theoi) from such a notion as this, that they had set (thentes) all things in order and so had the distribution of everything. Afterwards, when much time had passed, they learnt from Egypt the names of the gods — all except Dionysus, for his name they learnt long afterwards. After a time the Pelasgians consulted the Oracle at Dodona about the names — for this prophetic seat is accounted to be the most ancient of the Oracles among the Hellenes, and at that time it was the only one. So when the Pelasgians asked the Oracle at Dodona whether they should adopt the names that had come from the Barbarians, the Oracle in reply bade them make use of the names. From that time they sacrificed using the names of the gods, and from the Pelasgians the Hellenes afterwards received them.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 268
paragraphs: But whence each of the gods had his birth, or whether they all existed from the beginning, and what forms they have — these things they did not learn until yesterday, so to speak, or the day before. For Hesiod and Homer were, I suppose, four hundred years before my time, and no more; and it is these two who made a theogony for the Hellenes, gave the titles to the gods, assigned them their honours and their arts, and set forth their forms. The poets who are said to have lived before these men were, in my opinion, really after them. Of these things the first are said by the priestesses of Dodona, and the latter — those concerning Hesiod and Homer — by myself.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 269
paragraphs: As regards the Oracles — both that among the Hellenes and that in Libya — the Egyptians tell the following tale. The priests of the Theban Zeus told me that two women in the service of the temple had been carried off from Thebes by Phoenicians, and that they had heard one of them had been sold into Libya and the other into Hellas; and these women, they said, were the ones who first founded the prophetic seats among the peoples I have named. When I asked how they knew so precisely of this tale they told, they replied that a great search had been made by the priests for these women, and they had not been able to find them, but they had afterwards heard this tale about them, which they were telling me.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 270
paragraphs: This I heard from the priests at Thebes, and what follows is said by the prophetesses of Dodona. They say that two black doves flew from Thebes in Egypt, one coming to Libya and the other to their land. The latter settled upon an oak-tree and spoke with human voice, saying that it was necessary a prophetic seat of Zeus should be established in that place; and they supposed that what was announced to them was of the gods, and accordingly made one. The dove that went away to the Libyans, they say, bade the Libyans make an Oracle of Ammon; and this also is of Zeus. The priestesses of Dodona told me these things — the eldest being named Promeneia, the next Timarete, and the youngest Nicandra; and the other people of Dodona who were engaged about the temple gave accounts agreeing with theirs.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 271
paragraphs: I, however, have an opinion about the matter as follows. If the Phoenicians did in truth carry away the consecrated women and sold one of them into Libya and the other into Hellas, I suppose that in the country now called Hellas (which was formerly called Pelasgia), this woman was sold into the land of the Thesprotians; and then being a slave there she set up a sanctuary of Zeus under a real oak-tree; for it was natural that, as an attendant of the sanctuary of Zeus at Thebes, she should in the place to which she had come keep his memory. After this, when she got a grasp of the Hellenic tongue, she established an Oracle; and she reported, I suppose, that her sister had been sold in Libya by the same Phoenicians who had sold her.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 272
paragraphs: Moreover, I think that the women were called doves by the people of Dodona because they were Barbarians, and to the hearers it seemed that they uttered their voices like birds; but after a time (they say) the dove spoke with human voice — that is, when the woman began to speak so that they could understand her. As long as she spoke a Barbarian tongue she seemed to them to be uttering her voice like a bird — for had it really been a dove, how could it have spoken with a human voice? And in saying that the dove was black, they indicate that the woman was Egyptian. The ways of delivering oracles at Thebes in Egypt and at Dodona closely resemble one another, as it happens, and the method of divination by victims has also come from Egypt.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 273
paragraphs: Moreover, it is true also that the Egyptians were the first of men to hold solemn assemblies and processions and approaches to the temples, and from them the Hellenes have learnt them; and my evidence for this is that the Egyptian celebrations of these have been held from a very ancient time, whereas the Hellenic ones were introduced only recently.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 274
paragraphs: The Egyptians hold their solemn assemblies not once in the year but often, especially and with the greatest zeal and devotion at the city of Bubastis for Artemis, and next at Busiris for Isis; for in this city is a very great temple of Isis, and this city stands in the middle of the Delta of Egypt (now Isis is, in the tongue of the Hellenes, Demeter). Thirdly, they hold a solemn assembly at the city of Saïs for Athene; fourthly, at Heliopolis for the Sun (Helios); fifthly, at the city of Buto in honour of Leto; and sixthly, at the city of Papremis for Ares.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 275
paragraphs: Now when they come to the city of Bubastis they do as follows. They sail in boats, men and women together — a great crowd of each sex in every boat; and some of the women have rattles and rattle with them, while some of the men play the flute during the whole of the voyage, and the rest, both women and men, sing and clap their hands. And when, as they sail, they come opposite to any city on the way, they bring the boat to land, and some of the women continue to do as I have said, others cry out and jeer at the women in that city, some dance, and some stand up and pull up their garments. This they do at every city along the river-bank. When they come to Bubastis they hold festival, celebrating great sacrifices, and more wine of grapes is consumed at that festival than during the whole of the rest of the year. To this place (so the natives say) they come together year by year, to the number of seventy myriads of men and women, besides children.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 276
paragraphs: Thus it is done here; and how they celebrate the festival in honour of Isis at the city of Busiris I have told before. For, as I said, they beat themselves in mourning after the sacrifice — all of them, both men and women, very many myriads of people; but for whom they beat themselves it is not permitted me by religion to say. The Carians who dwell in Egypt do this even more than the Egyptians themselves, in that they also cut their foreheads with knives; and by this it is clear that they are foreigners and not Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 277
paragraphs: At the times when they gather at the city of Saïs for their sacrifices, on a certain night they all kindle lamps in great numbers in the open air around their houses. The lamps are saucers full of salt and oil mixed, with the wick floating by itself on the surface, and this burns throughout the whole night; and to the festival is given the name Lychnocaia (the Lighting of the Lamps). Moreover, those Egyptians who have not come to this solemn assembly observe the night of the festival and themselves also light lamps — all of them — so that lamps are lit not in Saïs alone but over all Egypt. As to why light and honour are allotted to this night, a sacred story is told about it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 278
paragraphs: To Heliopolis and Buto they go year by year and do sacrifice only; but at Papremis they do sacrifice and worship as elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun begins to go down, while a few of the priests are busy with the image of the god, the greater number of them stand at the entrance of the temple with wooden clubs; and other men, more than a thousand in number who have a vow to perform, stand in a body opposite, these too all with staves of wood. The image, which is in a small wooden shrine covered with gold, they take out on the day before to another sacred building. The few, then, who have been left about the image draw a wagon with four wheels that bears the shrine and the image within it, and the other priests standing in the gateway try to prevent it from entering, and the men under a vow come to the aid of the god and strike them, while the others defend themselves. Then there comes a hard fight with staves, and they break one another's heads; and I am of opinion that many even die of the wounds they receive — though the Egyptians told me that no one died. The people of the place say they established this solemn assembly for the following reason. The mother of Ares, they say, used to dwell in this temple; and Ares, having been brought up away from her, when he grew up came there desiring to visit his mother; but the attendants of his mother's temple, not having seen him before, did not permit him to pass in, and kept him away. He then brought men to help him from another city and handled the attendants of the temple roughly, and entered to visit his mother. Hence, they say, this exchange of blows has become the custom in honour of Ares at his festival.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 279
paragraphs: The Egyptians were the first to make it a point of religion not to lie with women in temples, and not to enter a temple after going in to a woman without first bathing. For almost all other men, except the Egyptians and the Hellenes, lie with women in temples and enter a temple after going in to a woman without bathing, since they hold that there is in this respect no difference between men and beasts: they point out that they see beasts and the various kinds of birds coupling both in the temples and in the sacred enclosures of the gods; and if this were not pleasing to the god, the beasts would not do so.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 280
paragraphs: Thus these men defend what they do — which by me is disallowed. But the Egyptians are excessively careful in their observances, both in other matters concerning the sacred rites and also in the following. Egypt, though it borders upon Libya, does not abound greatly in wild animals; but such as they have are all without exception accounted sacred by them, some living with men and others not. If I were to say for what reasons the sacred animals have been thus dedicated, I should fall into discourse about matters pertaining to the gods, of which I most desire not to speak; and what I have actually said, touching lightly upon them, I said only because I was constrained by necessity. About these animals there is a custom of this kind: certain persons have been appointed from among the Egyptians, both men and women, to provide food for each kind of beast separately, and the office descends from father to son. Those who dwell in the various cities perform vows to them thus: when they make a vow to the god to whom the animal belongs, they shave the head of their children — either the whole, or the half, or the third part of it — and then weigh the hair in the balance against silver, and whatever it weighs the man gives to the person in charge of the animals, and she cuts up fish of equal value and gives it as food to the animals. Thus food for their keep has been provided. If anyone kills any of these animals, the penalty, if he did it wilfully, is death; and if without intent, such penalty as the priests may appoint. But whoever kills an ibis or a hawk, whether wilfully or not, must die.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 281
paragraphs: Of the animals that live with men there are great numbers, and would be many more but for the accidents that befall the cats. When the females have produced young they no longer resort to the males, and the males, seeking to be united with them, cannot. To this end, then, they contrive as follows: they either take away by force or remove secretly the young from the females and kill them (but after killing they do not eat them); and the females, deprived of their young and still desiring more, come therefore to the males, for the cat is a creature fond of its young. Moreover, when a fire occurs, the cats seem to be divinely possessed; for while the Egyptians stand at intervals and look after the cats, taking no care to extinguish the fire, the cats slip between the men or leap over them and jump into the fire; and when this happens, great mourning comes upon the Egyptians. In whatever houses a cat has died by a natural death, all who live in that house shave only their eyebrows; but in whatever houses a dog has died, they shave their whole body and head.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 282
paragraphs: The cats, when they are dead, are carried away to sacred buildings in the city of Bubastis, where after being embalmed they are buried; but the dogs are buried by each people in their own city in sacred tombs; and the ichneumons are buried just the same way as the dogs. The shrew-mice and the hawks they carry away to the city of Buto, and the ibises to Hermopolis. The bears (which are not commonly seen) and the wolves — not much larger in size than foxes — they bury on the spot where they are found lying.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 283
paragraphs: The nature of the crocodile is as follows. During the four most wintry months this creature eats nothing. It has four feet and is an animal belonging both to land and water; for it produces and hatches its eggs on land, and the greater part of the day it remains upon dry land, but the whole of the night in the river — for the water in truth is warmer than the unclouded open air and the dew. Of all the mortal creatures we know, this one grows to the greatest bulk from the smallest beginning; for the eggs it produces are not much larger than those of geese, and the newly hatched young is in proportion to the egg, but as he grows he becomes as much as seventeen cubits long, and sometimes even larger. He has eyes like those of a pig and large tusky teeth in proportion to the size of his body; but unlike all other beasts he grows no tongue, nor does he move his lower jaw — he brings the upper jaw down towards the lower, being in this too unlike all other beasts. He has strong claws and a scaly hide upon his back which cannot be pierced. He is blind in the water, but in the air he is of very keen sight. Since he lives in the water, he keeps his mouth full of leeches; and whereas all other birds and beasts flee from him, the trochilus is a creature that is at peace with him, since from her he receives benefit. For the crocodile, having come out of the water onto the land and then having opened his mouth (which he is accustomed to do generally towards the West Wind), the trochilus then enters his mouth and swallows down the leeches; and the crocodile, being benefited, is pleased and does no harm to the trochilus.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 284
paragraphs: For some of the Egyptians the crocodiles are sacred animals, for others they are not, but are treated on the contrary as enemies. Those who dwell around Thebes and around the lake of Moeris hold them to be most sacred, and each of these two peoples keeps one crocodile selected from the whole number, which has been trained to tameness. They put hanging ornaments of molten stone and of gold into its ears, and anklets round its front feet, and give it appointed food and sacrificial victims, and treat it as well as possible while it lives; and after it is dead they bury it in sacred tombs, embalming it. But those who dwell around the city of Elephantine even eat them, not holding them to be sacred. They are not called crocodiles but champsai; and the Ionians gave them the name of crocodile, comparing their form to that of the crocodiles (the lizards) that appear in their country in the stone walls.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 285
paragraphs: There are many ways in use of catching them, of various kinds; I shall describe the one that to me seems the most worthy of being told. A man puts the back of a pig upon a hook as bait, and lets it go into the middle of the river, while he himself on the bank has a young live pig, which he beats; and the crocodile, hearing its cries, makes for the direction of the sound, and when he finds the pig's back he swallows it down. Then they pull; and when he is drawn out to land, the hunter at once plasters up his eyes with mud, and having done so he very easily gets the mastery of him — but if he does not do so, he has much trouble.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 286
paragraphs: The river-horse is sacred in the district of Papremis, but for the other Egyptians he is not sacred. This is the appearance he presents: he is four-footed, cloven-hoofed like an ox, flat-nosed, with a mane like a horse and tusks like teeth, with a tail and voice like a horse, and in size as large as the largest ox; and his hide is so exceedingly thick that when it has been dried, shafts of javelins are made of it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 287
paragraphs: There are moreover otters in the river, which they consider sacred; and of fish also they esteem as sacred that which is called the lepidotus, and the eel; and these, they say, are sacred to the Nile. Among birds, the fox-goose.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 288
paragraphs: There is also another sacred bird called the phoenix, which I did not myself see except in painting, for in truth he comes to them very rarely — at intervals, as the people of Heliopolis say, of five hundred years. They say he comes regularly when his father dies; and if he be like the painting, he is of this size and nature — that is, some of his feathers are of gold colour and others red, and in outline and size he is as nearly as possible like an eagle. This bird, they say (but I cannot believe the story), contrives as follows. Setting out from Arabia he conveys his father, they say, to the temple of the Sun (Helios), plastered up in myrrh, and buries him in the temple of the Sun. He conveys him thus: he first forms an egg of myrrh as large as he is able to carry, and then makes trial of carrying it; and when he has made trial sufficiently, he hollows out the egg and places his father within it, and plasters over with other myrrh that part of the egg where he hollowed it out to put his father in; and when his father is laid inside, the egg (they say) proves to be of the same weight as it was before. After he has plastered it up, he conveys the whole to Egypt, to the temple of the Sun. Thus, they say, this bird does.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 289
paragraphs: There are also around Thebes sacred serpents, not at all harmful to men, which are small in size and have two horns growing from the top of the head; these they bury when they die in the temple of Zeus, for they say they are sacred to this god.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 290
paragraphs: There is, moreover, a region in Arabia situated nearly opposite the city of Buto, to which place I came to inquire about the winged serpents. When I arrived I saw bones of serpents and spines in such great quantity that it is impossible to report the number; there were heaps of spines, some large, others less large, others smaller still, and these heaps were many. This region, where the spines are scattered upon the ground, is of the nature of an entrance from a narrow mountain pass into a great plain, which plain adjoins the plain of Egypt. The story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents fly from Arabia towards Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not suffer the serpents to pass by, but kill them. On account of this deed, the Arabians say, the ibis has come to be greatly honoured by the Egyptians; and the Egyptians also agree that it is for this reason that they honour these birds.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 291
