paragraphs: The outward form of the ibis is this: it is a deep black all over, and has legs like those of a crane, a very curved beak, and in size it is about equal to a rail. This is the appearance of the black kind that fight with the serpents; but of those that most crowd round men's feet (for there are two distinct kinds of ibises), the head is bare, and also the whole of the throat, and the bird is white in feathering except for the head and neck and the extremities of the wings and the rump — in all these parts of which I have spoken it is deep black — while in the legs and the form of the head it resembles the other. As for the serpent, its form is like that of the water-snake; and it has wings not feathered but most nearly resembling the wings of a bat. Let what has now been said suffice concerning sacred animals.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 292
paragraphs: Of the Egyptians themselves, those who dwell in the part of Egypt which is sown for crops practise memory more than any other men, and are by far the most learned in history of all those of whom I have had experience. Their manner of life is as follows. For three successive days in each month they purge, hunting after health with emetics and clysters, and they think that all the diseases that exist are produced in men by the food on which they live. For the Egyptians are from other causes also the most healthy of all men, next after the Libyans — in my opinion because of their seasons, for the seasons do not change; since diseases are most apt to be produced in men by the changes of things generally, and especially by the changes of the seasons. As for their diet: they eat bread, making loaves of emmer, which they call kyllestis; and they habitually use a wine made out of barley, for they have no vines in their land. Some of their fish they dry in the sun and then eat without cooking; others they eat cured in brine. Of birds, they eat quails, ducks, and small birds without cooking, after first curing them; and everything else of the class of birds or fishes that they have, except such as have been set apart as sacred, they eat roasted or boiled.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 293
paragraphs: At the banquets of the rich among them, when they have finished eating, a man bears round a wooden figure of a dead body in a coffin, made as like the reality as possible both by painting and by carving, and measuring about a cubit or two cubits each way. This he shows to each of those drinking together, saying: “When you look upon this, drink and be merry, for you shall be such as this when you are dead.” Thus they do at their carousals.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 294
paragraphs: The customs they practise are inherited from their fathers, and they do not acquire others in addition; but besides other customs of theirs worthy of mention, they have one song, that of Linus — the same one who is sung of in Phoenicia, in Cyprus, and elsewhere, having however a name that differs according to the various nations. This song agrees exactly with what the Hellenes sing calling on the name of Linus; so that besides the many other things about which I wonder in matters concerning Egypt, I wonder especially about this — namely, where they got the song of Linus. It is clear, however, that they have sung this song from time immemorial; and in the Egyptian tongue Linus is called Maneros. The Egyptians told me that he was the only son of the man who first became king of Egypt, and that he died before his time and was honoured with these lamentations by the Egyptians; and that this was their first and only song.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 295
paragraphs: In one respect the Egyptians agree with some of the Hellenes — namely, with the Lacedaemonians, but not with the rest: that is, their younger men, when they meet their elders, give way and move out of the path; and when their elders approach, they rise from their seats. In the following, however, they do not agree with any of the Hellenes: instead of addressing one another on the roads, they do reverence, lowering the hand down to the knee.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 296
paragraphs: They wear tunics of linen about their legs with fringes, which they call calasiris; above these they throw over garments of white wool. Woollen garments, however, are not taken into the temples, nor are they buried with them, for this is not permitted by religion. In these points they are in agreement with the observances called Orphic and Bacchic (which are really Egyptian), and also with those of the Pythagoreans; for one who takes part in these mysteries is also forbidden by religious rule to be buried in woollen garments, and about this there is a sacred story told.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 297
paragraphs: Besides these things, the Egyptians have found out also to what god each month and each day belongs, and what fortunes a man will meet with who is born on any particular day, and how he will die, and what kind of man he will be; and these inventions were taken up by those of the Hellenes who occupied themselves with poetry. Portents too have been found out by them more than by all other men besides; for when a portent has occurred, they observe and write down the event that comes of it, and if ever afterwards something resembling this happens, they believe the event that follows will be similar.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 298
paragraphs: Their divination is ordered thus: the art is assigned not to any man, but to certain of the gods; for there are in their land Oracles of Heracles, of Apollo, of Athene, of Artemis, of Ares, and of Zeus, and moreover that which they hold in highest honour of all — namely the Oracle of Leto which is in the city of Buto. The manner of divination, however, is not everywhere established in the same fashion, but differs in different places.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 299
paragraphs: The art of medicine among them is distributed thus: each physician is a physician of one disease and of no more; and the whole country is full of physicians. Some profess themselves physicians of the eyes, others of the head, others of the teeth, others of the disorders of the stomach, and others of the more obscure ailments.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 300
paragraphs: Their fashions of mourning and of burial are these. Whenever any household has lost a man who is of any regard among them, the whole number of women of that house immediately plaster over their heads — or even their faces — with mud. Then, leaving the corpse within the house, they go themselves to and fro about the city and beat themselves, with their garments bound up by a girdle and their breasts exposed; and all the women related to the dead man go with them. On the other side the men beat themselves, they too having their garments bound up by a girdle. When they have done this, they then convey the body for embalming.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 301
paragraphs: In this occupation certain persons employ themselves regularly, and inherit this as a craft. Whenever a corpse is conveyed to them, they show those who have brought it wooden models of corpses made lifelike by painting, and the best of the ways of embalming they say is that of him whose name I think it impiety to mention when speaking of such a matter. The second that they show is less good than this, and also less expensive; and the third is the cheapest of all. Having told them this, they ask in which way they wish the corpse of their friend to be prepared. Then, after they have agreed for a certain price, the relatives depart, and the others, left behind in the buildings, embalm according to the best of these ways as follows. First, with a crooked iron tool they draw out the brain through the nostrils, extracting it partly thus and partly by pouring in drugs; after this with a sharp Ethiopian stone they make a cut along the side and take out the whole contents of the belly, and when they have cleaned out the cavity and rinsed it with palm-wine, they cleanse it again with pounded spices. Then they fill the belly with pure myrrh pounded up, cassia, and other spices (except frankincense), and sew it together again. Having so done, they keep it for embalming covered up in natron for seventy days, but for a longer time than this it is not permitted to embalm. When the seventy days are past, they wash the corpse and wrap the whole body in fine linen cut into bands, smearing these beneath with gum, which the Egyptians use generally in place of glue. Then the kinsfolk receive the corpse from them and have a wooden figure made in the shape of a man; and when they have had this made, they enclose the corpse within it, and having shut it up, they then store it in a sepulchral chamber, setting it to stand upright against the wall.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 302
paragraphs: Thus they deal with the corpses that are prepared in the most costly way. But for those who desire the middle way and wish to avoid great cost, they prepare the corpse as follows. Having filled their syringes with the oil that is obtained from cedar-wood, with this they immediately fill the belly of the corpse — and they do this without having cut it open or taken out the bowels, injecting the oil by the anus, and having stopped the drench from running back they keep the corpse the appointed number of days for embalming. On the last of the days they let the cedar oil come out from the belly, which they before put in; and it has such power that it brings out with it the bowels and the interior organs of the body all dissolved; and the natron dissolves the flesh, so that there is left of the corpse only the skin and the bones. When they have done this they give back the corpse at once in that condition, without working upon it any more.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 303
paragraphs: The third kind of embalming, by which are prepared the bodies of those who have less means, is as follows. They cleanse out the belly with a purge, and then keep the body for embalming during the seventy days, and immediately after that they give it back to those who brought it, to carry away.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 304
paragraphs: The wives of men of rank, when they die, are not given at once to be embalmed; nor are such women as are very beautiful, or of greater regard than others. Rather, on the third or fourth day after their death — and not before — they are delivered to the embalmers. They do so in this matter so that the embalmers may not abuse their women; for they say that one of them was once caught doing so to the corpse of a woman recently dead, and his fellow-craftsman gave information.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 305
paragraphs: Whenever anyone, either of the Egyptians themselves or of foreigners, is found to have been carried off by a crocodile or brought to his death by the river itself, the people of any city by which he may have been cast up on land must embalm him and lay him out in the fairest way they can, and bury him in a sacred burial-place; nor may any of his relations or friends touch him, but the priests of the Nile themselves handle the corpse and bury it as that of one who was something more than man.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 306
paragraphs: Hellenic customs they will by no means follow, and generally speaking they follow those of no other men whatever. This rule is observed by most of the Egyptians; but there is a large city named Chemmis in the Theban district near Neapolis, and in this city there is a temple of Perseus son of Danae, which is square-shaped, and around it grow date-palms. The gateway of the temple is built of stone and of very great size, and at the entrance two great stone statues stand. Within this enclosure is a temple-house, and in it stands an image of Perseus. These people of Chemmis say that Perseus often appears in their land and often within the temple, and that a sandal worn by him is sometimes found, measuring two cubits in length; and whenever this appears, all Egypt prospers. So they say, and they honour Perseus in Hellenic fashion thus: they hold an athletic contest, which includes the whole list of games, and they offer as prizes cattle, cloaks, and skins. When I asked why Perseus appeared to them alone, and why they were separated from all the other Egyptians in holding an athletic contest, they said that Perseus had been born of their city; for Danaus and Lynceus, they said, were men of Chemmis and had sailed to Hellas, and from them they traced a descent down to Perseus. They told me he had come to Egypt for the reason the Hellenes also give — namely to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya — and had then visited them too and recognised all his kinsfolk; and they said he had thoroughly learnt the name of Chemmis before coming to Egypt, since he had heard it from his mother, and that they celebrated an athletic contest for him by his own command.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 307
paragraphs: All these are customs practised by the Egyptians who dwell above the fens; and those settled in the fen-land have the same customs as the other Egyptians for the most part, both in other matters and in that each man lives with a single wife, as the Hellenes do. But for economy in food they have invented the following. When the river has become full and the plains have been flooded, there grow in the water great numbers of lilies, which the Egyptians call lotus. These they cut with a sickle and dry in the sun, and then they pound that which grows in the middle of the lotus, which is like the head of a poppy, and they make of it loaves baked with fire. The root of this lotus is also edible and has a rather sweet taste; it is round in shape and about the size of an apple. There are other lilies too, resembling roses in flower, which also grow in the river, and from them the fruit is produced in a separate vessel springing from the root beside the plant itself, and it very nearly resembles a wasp's comb. In this there grow edible seeds in great numbers, the size of an olive-stone, and they are eaten either fresh or dried. Besides this, they pull up from the fens the papyrus which grows every year, and the upper parts they cut off and put to other uses; but what is left below, for about a cubit in length, they eat or sell. Those who desire to have the papyrus at its very best bake it in an oven heated red-hot, and then eat it. Some of these people live on fish alone, drying them in the sun after having caught them and taken out the entrails, and when they are dry they use them for food.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 308
paragraphs: Fish that swim in shoals are not much produced in the rivers, but are bred in the lakes, and they do as follows. When the desire to breed comes upon them, they swim out in shoals towards the sea; the males lead the way, shedding forth their milt as they go, while the females, coming after and swallowing it up, become from it impregnated. When they have become full of young out in the sea, they swim back up, each shoal to its own haunts. The same males, however, no longer lead the way as before; now the lead falls to the females, and they leading the way in shoals do just as the males did — that is, they shed forth their eggs a few grains at a time, and the males coming after swallow them up. These grains are fish, and from the grains that survive and are not swallowed, the fish grow which are afterwards bred up. Now those of the fish that are caught as they swim out to sea are found to be rubbed on the left side of the head; but those caught as they swim up again are rubbed on the right side. This happens to them because as they swim down to the sea they keep close to the land on the left side of the river, and again as they swim up they keep to the same side, approaching and touching the bank as much as they can, for fear doubtless of straying from their course by reason of the stream. When the Nile begins to swell, the hollow places of the land and the depressions beside the river first begin to fill, as the water soaks through from the river; and as soon as they are full of water, at once they are filled with little fishes — and whence these are in all likelihood produced, I think I perceive. In the preceding year, when the Nile goes down, the fish first lay eggs in the mud, and then retire with the last of the retreating waters; and when the time comes round again, and the water once more comes over the land, from these eggs at once are produced the fishes of which I speak.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 309
paragraphs: Thus it is as regards the fish. For anointing, those of the Egyptians who dwell in the fens use oil from the castor-berry, which oil the Egyptians call kiki, and they do this as follows. They sow along the banks of the rivers and pools these plants, which grow of themselves in wild form in the land of the Hellenes; sown in Egypt, they produce berries in great quantity but of an evil smell. When they have gathered these, some cut them up and press the oil from them; others again roast them first and then boil them down, collecting the oil that runs out. The oil is fat and no less suitable for burning than olive oil, but it gives off a disagreeable smell.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 310
paragraphs: Against the gnats, which are very abundant, they have contrived as follows. Those who dwell above the fen-land are helped by the towers, to which they ascend when they go to rest, for by reason of the winds the gnats cannot fly up high. But those who dwell in the fen-land have contrived another way instead of the towers, and this is it. Every man of them has got a casting net, with which by day he catches fish, but in the night he puts it to the following use. He places the casting-net around the bed in which he sleeps, and then creeps in under it and goes to sleep; and the gnats, if he sleeps wrapped up in a garment or linen sheet, bite through these, but through the net they do not even attempt to bite.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 311
paragraphs: Their boats, with which they carry cargoes, are made of the thorny acacia, whose form is very like that of the Cyrenian lotus, and what exudes from it is gum. From this tree they cut pieces of wood about two cubits in length and arrange them like bricks, fastening the boat together by running a great number of long bolts through the two-cubit pieces; and when they have thus fastened the boat together, they lay cross-pieces over the top, using no ribs for the sides; and within they caulk the seams with papyrus. They make one steering-oar for it, which is passed through the bottom of the boat; and they have a mast of acacia and sails of papyrus. These boats cannot sail up the river unless there be a very fresh wind blowing, but are towed from the shore. Downstream, however, they travel as follows. They have a door-shaped crate made of tamarisk wood and reed mats sewn together, and also a stone of about two talents' weight bored with a hole. The boatman lets the crate float on in front of the boat, fastened with a rope, and lets the stone drag behind at another rope. The crate then, as the force of the stream presses upon it, goes on swiftly and draws on the baris (for so these boats are called), while the stone dragging behind and sunk deep in the water keeps its course straight. These boats they have in great numbers, and some of them carry many thousands of talents' burden.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 312
paragraphs: When the Nile comes over the land, the cities alone are seen rising above the water, resembling more nearly than anything else the islands in the Aegean Sea; for the rest of Egypt becomes a sea, and only the cities rise above the water. Accordingly, whenever this happens, they travel by water — not now by the channels of the river, but over the middle of the plain. For example, as one sails up from Naucratis to Memphis the passage is then close by the pyramids, whereas the usual passage is not the same even here, but goes by the point of the Delta and the city of Cercasorus; while if you sail over the plain to Naucratis from the sea and from Canobus, you will go by Anthylla and the city called after Archander.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 313
paragraphs: Of these, Anthylla is a city of note, and is specifically assigned to the wife of the ruler of Egypt to supply her with sandals (this has been the case since the time Egypt came under the Persians); the other city seems to me to take its name from Archander, the son-in-law of Danaus, who was son of Phthios, son of Achaeus; for it is called the City of Archander. There might indeed be another Archander, but in any case the name is not Egyptian.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 314
paragraphs: Up to this point my own observation, judgment, and inquiry are the vouchers for what I have said; but from this point onwards I am about to tell the history of Egypt according to what I heard, to which will be added something of what I have myself seen.

Of Min, who first became king of Egypt, the priests said that he banked off the site of Memphis from the river; for the whole stream of the river used to flow along the sandy mountain-range on the side of Libya, but Min formed, by embankments, that bend of the river which lies to the south about a hundred furlongs above Memphis, and thus he dried up the old stream and led the river so that it flowed in the middle between the mountains. Even now this bend of the Nile is kept by the Persians under very careful watch, that it may flow in the channel to which it is confined, and the bank is repaired every year; for if the river should break through and overflow in this direction, Memphis would be in danger of being overwhelmed by flood. When this Min, who first became king, had turned into dry land the part that was dammed off, he founded in it that city which is now called Memphis (for Memphis too is in the narrow part of Egypt); and outside the city he dug round it to the north and west a lake communicating with the river, since the east side is barred by the Nile itself. Secondly, he established in the city the temple of Hephaestus, a great work and most worthy of mention.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 315
paragraphs: After this man, the priests listed to me from a papyrus roll the names of three hundred and thirty other kings; and in all these generations of men, eighteen were Ethiopians, one was a woman — a native Egyptian — and the rest were men and of Egyptian race. The name of the woman who reigned was the same as that of the Babylonian queen, namely Nitocris. Of her they said that, desiring to take vengeance for her brother — whom the Egyptians had killed when he was their king and, after killing him, had given his kingdom to her — desiring, I say, to take vengeance for him, she destroyed many of the Egyptians by craft. She had built a very large chamber underground, and making as though she would inaugurate it, but in her mind devising other things, she invited those of the Egyptians whom she knew to have had most part in the murder, and gave a great banquet. Then, while they were feasting, she let the river in upon them by a secret conduit of large size. Of her they told me no more than this, except that when she had accomplished this, she threw herself into a room full of embers in order that she might escape vengeance.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 316
paragraphs: As for the other kings, they could tell me of no great works produced by them, and they said these kings had no renown — except only the last of them, Moeris. He (they said) produced as a memorial of himself the gateway of the temple of Hephaestus which faces the North Wind, and dug a lake, about which I shall set forth afterwards how many furlongs it measures in circuit; and in it he built pyramids of the size which I shall mention at the same time when I speak of the lake itself. He, they said, produced these works, but of the rest none produced any.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 317
paragraphs: Therefore, passing these by, I shall make mention of the king who came after these, whose name was Sesostris. He (the priests said) first of all set out with ships of war from the Arabian gulf and subdued those who dwelt along the shores of the Erythraean Sea, until as he sailed he came to a sea that could no longer be navigated by reason of shoals. Then, after he had returned to Egypt, according to the priests' report, he took a great army and marched over the continent, subduing every nation that stood in his way. Those whom he found valiant and fighting desperately for their freedom — in their lands he set up pillars that told by inscriptions his own name and the name of his country, and how he had subdued them by his power. But as to those whose cities he obtained possession of without fighting or with ease, on their pillars he inscribed words of the same tenor as those for the nations that had shown themselves courageous, and in addition he carved on them the hidden parts of a woman, wishing to signify by this that the people were cowards and effeminate.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 318
paragraphs: Thus doing he traversed the continent, until at last he passed over from Asia into Europe and subdued the Scythians and also the Thracians. These, I am of opinion, were the furthest people to which the Egyptian army came, for in their country the pillars are found to have been set up, but in the land beyond this they are no longer found. From this point he turned and began to go back; and when he came to the river Phasis, what happened then I cannot say for certain — whether the king Sesostris himself divided off a certain portion of his army and left the men there as settlers in the land, or whether some of his soldiers, weary of his distant marches, remained by the river Phasis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 319
paragraphs: For the people of Colchis are evidently Egyptian, and this I perceived for myself before I heard it from others. So when I had come to consider the matter, I asked both sides; and the Colchians had remembrance of the Egyptians more than the Egyptians of the Colchians; but the Egyptians said they believed that the Colchians were a portion of the army of Sesostris. That this was so I conjectured myself not only because they are dark-skinned and have curly hair (this of itself amounts to nothing, since there are other races that are so), but still more because the Colchians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians alone of all the races of men have practised circumcision from the first. The Phoenicians and the Syrians who dwell in Palestine confess themselves that they have learnt it from the Egyptians, and the Syrians about the rivers Thermodon and Parthenius, and the Macronians, their neighbours, say that they have learnt it recently from the Colchians. These are the only races of men who practise circumcision, and they evidently practise it in the same manner as the Egyptians. Of the Egyptians themselves and the Ethiopians I am not able to say which learnt it from the other, for undoubtedly it is a most ancient custom. But that the other nations learnt it by intercourse with the Egyptians is proved, among other things, by this strong evidence: those Phoenicians who have intercourse with Hellas cease to follow the Egyptian example in this matter, and do not circumcise their children.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 320
paragraphs: Now let me tell another thing about the Colchians to show how they resemble the Egyptians. They alone work flax in the same fashion as the Egyptians, and the two nations are like one another in their whole manner of living and in their language. The linen of Colchis is called by the Hellenes Sardonic, whereas that from Egypt is called Egyptian.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 321
paragraphs: The pillars which Sesostris of Egypt set up in the various countries are for the most part no longer to be seen extant; but in Syrian Palestine I myself saw them existing, with the inscription I have mentioned and the emblem carved upon them. Moreover, in Ionia there are two figures of this man carved upon rocks — one on the road by which one goes from the land of Ephesus to Phocaea, and the other on the road from Sardis to Smyrna. In each place there is a figure of a man cut in the rock, of four cubits and a span in height, holding in his right hand a spear and in his left a bow and arrows, with similar equipment elsewhere, being both Egyptian and Ethiopian in character; and from the one shoulder to the other across the breast runs an inscription carved in sacred Egyptian characters, saying thus: “This land with my own shoulders I won for myself.” But who he is and from where, he does not declare in these places, though in other places he has declared this. Some of those who have seen these carvings conjecture that the figure is that of Memnon; but in this they are very far from the truth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 322
paragraphs: As this Egyptian Sesostris was returning and bringing back with him many men of the nations whose lands he had subdued, when he came (said the priests) to Daphnae in the district of Pelusium on his journey home, his brother — to whom Sesostris had entrusted the charge of Egypt — invited him, and with him his sons, to a feast; and then he piled up brushwood round the house and set it on fire. Sesostris, when he discovered this, immediately took counsel with his wife (for he was bringing his wife also with him, they said), and she counselled him to lay out upon the pyre two of his sons (of whom he had six), and so make a bridge over the burning mass, that they passing over their bodies should thus escape. This, they said, Sesostris did, and two of his sons were burnt to death in this way, but the rest got away safely with their father.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 323
paragraphs: Then Sesostris, having returned to Egypt and having taken vengeance on his brother, employed the multitude that he had brought in from the peoples whose lands he had subdued as follows. These were the men who drew the stones — of very great size — that in the reign of this king were brought to the temple of Hephaestus; and these were also compelled to dig all the channels that now exist in Egypt. Thus, with no such purpose in mind, they caused Egypt, which before was all fit for riding and driving, to be no longer so from that time onwards; for from then on Egypt, though it is plain country, has become entirely unfit for riding and driving, and the cause has been these channels, which are many and run in every direction. The reason the king cut up the land thus was this: those of the Egyptians whose cities were not on the river but in the middle of the country, being in want of water when the river had gone down from them, found their drink brackish because they had it from wells.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 324
paragraphs: For this reason Egypt was cut up; and they said that this king distributed the land to all the Egyptians, giving an equal square portion to each man, and from this he made his revenue, having appointed them to pay a certain rent every year. If the river should take away anything from any man's portion, he would come to the king and declare what had happened; and the king used to send men to examine and find out by measurement how much less the piece of land had become, in order that for the future the man might pay less in proportion to the rent appointed. In this way, I think, the art of geometry was found out and afterwards came into Hellas also; for as to the sundial and the gnomon and the twelve divisions of the day, these were learnt by the Hellenes from the Babylonians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 325
paragraphs: He alone of all the Egyptian kings had rule over Ethiopia; and he left as memorials of himself, in front of the temple of Hephaestus, two stone statues of thirty cubits each, representing himself and his wife, and others of twenty cubits each representing his four sons. Long afterwards, the priest of Hephaestus refused to allow Darius the Persian to set up a statue of himself in front of them, saying that Darius had not done deeds equal to those of Sesostris the Egyptian. For Sesostris had subdued other nations, not fewer than Darius, and also the Scythians; whereas Darius had not been able to conquer the Scythians. Therefore, the priest said, it was not just that he should set up a statue in front of those which Sesostris had dedicated, if he did not surpass him in his deeds. This speech, they say, Darius took in good part.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 326
paragraphs: Now after Sesostris had ended his life, his son Pheros, they told me, received the kingdom in succession; and he made no warlike expedition, but it chanced to him to become blind by reason of the following accident. When the river had come down in flood, rising to a height of eighteen cubits (higher than ever before), and had gone over the fields, a wind fell upon it and the river became agitated by waves; and this king (they say), moved by presumptuous folly, took a spear and cast it into the midst of the eddies of the stream; and immediately upon this he had a disease of the eyes and was by it made blind. For ten years, then, he was blind, and in the eleventh year there came to him an oracle from the city of Buto, saying that the time of his punishment had expired, and that he should see again if he washed his eyes with the water of a woman who had lain only with her own husband and had not known other men. First he made trial of his own wife, and then, as he continued blind, he went on to try all the women in turn; and when he had at last regained his sight, he gathered together all the women with whom he had made the trial (except her by whose means he had regained his sight) into one city, which is now named Erythrabolus, and having gathered them there he consumed them all by fire, as well as the city itself. As for her by whose means he had regained his sight, he had her himself to wife. Then, after he had escaped the malady of his eyes, he dedicated offerings at each of the temples of renown, and especially (to mention only the most worthy of mention) he dedicated at the temple of the Sun works that are worth seeing — namely two obelisks of stone, each of a single block, measuring a hundred cubits each in length and eight cubits in breadth.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 327
paragraphs: After him, they said, there succeeded to the throne a man of Memphis, whose name in the tongue of the Hellenes was Proteus; for whom there is now a sacred enclosure at Memphis, very fair and well ordered, lying on that side of the temple of Hephaestus which faces the North Wind. Round about this enclosure dwell Phoenicians of Tyre, and this whole region is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Within the enclosure of Proteus there is a temple called the temple of the “foreign Aphrodite,” which I conjecture to be one of Helen the daughter of Tyndareus — not only because I have heard the tale how Helen dwelt with Proteus, but also especially because it is called by the name of the “foreign Aphrodite,” for no other temples of Aphrodite elsewhere have the addition of the word “foreign” to the name.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 328
paragraphs: And the priests told me, when I inquired, that the events concerning Helen happened thus. Alexander, having carried off Helen, was sailing away from Sparta to his own land, and when he had come to the Aegean Sea contrary winds drove him from his course into the Sea of Egypt; and after that, since the blasts did not cease to blow, he came to Egypt itself — and in Egypt to what is now named the Canobic mouth of the Nile and to Taricheiai. Now there was upon the shore, as still there is now, a temple of Heracles, in which if any man's slave takes refuge and has the sacred marks set upon him, giving himself over to the god, it is not lawful to lay hands upon him; and this custom has continued unchanged from the beginning down to my own time. Accordingly, the attendants of Alexander, having heard of the custom that existed about the temple, ran away from him, and sitting down as suppliants of the god, accused Alexander — because they wished to do him harm — telling the whole tale of how things were about Helen and about the wrong done to Menelaus; and they made this accusation not only to the priests but also to the warden of this river-mouth, whose name was Thonis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 329
paragraphs: Thonis, having heard their tale, immediately sent a message to Proteus at Memphis, which said as follows: “There has come a stranger, a Teucrian by race, who has done in Hellas an unholy deed; for he has deceived the wife of his own host, and is come hither bringing with him this woman herself and very much wealth, having been carried out of his way by winds to your land. Shall we then allow him to sail out unharmed, or shall we first take away from him that which he brought with him?” In reply Proteus sent back a messenger who said: “Seize this man, whoever he may be, who has done impiety to his own host, and bring him to my presence, that I may know what he will find to say.”

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 330
paragraphs: Hearing this, Thonis seized Alexander and detained his ships, and after that he brought the man himself up to Memphis, together with Helen and his wealth, and also the suppliants. When all had been brought there, Proteus began to ask Alexander who he was and from where he was sailing; and he both recounted to him his descent and told him the name of his native land, and moreover related his voyage, from where he was sailing. After this Proteus asked him whence he had taken Helen; and when Alexander went astray in his account and did not speak the truth, those who had become suppliants convicted him of falsehood, relating in full the whole tale of the wrong done. At length Proteus declared to them this sentence, saying: “Were it not that I count it a matter of great moment not to slay any of those strangers who, being driven from their course by winds, have come to my land hitherto, I should have taken vengeance on you on behalf of the man of Hellas — seeing that you, most base of men, having received from him hospitality, worked against him a most impious deed. For you went in to the wife of your own host; and even this was not enough for you, but you stirred her up with desire and have gone away with her like a thief. Moreover, even this was not enough for you, but you have come hither with plunder taken from the house of your host. Now therefore depart, since I have counted it of great moment not to be a slayer of strangers. This woman and the wealth you have, I will not permit you to carry away, but I shall keep them safe for the Hellene who was your host, until he himself comes and desires to carry them back to his home. To you and your fellow-voyagers I proclaim that you depart from your anchorage within three days and go from my land to some other; and if not, you will be dealt with as enemies.”

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 331
paragraphs: This, the priests said, was the manner of Helen's coming to Proteus; and I suppose that Homer also had heard this story, but since it was not so suitable to the composition of his poem as the other which he followed, he dismissed it — yet made it clear at the same time that he was acquainted with this story too. In his description of the wanderings of Alexander in the Iliad (nor did he elsewhere retract what he had said), it is clear that when Alexander brought Helen he was carried out of his course, wandering to various lands, and that he came, among other places, to Sidon in Phoenicia. Of this the poet has made mention in the “prowess of Diomede,” and the verses run thus:

“There she had robes many-coloured, the works of women of Sidon,/ Those whom her son himself the god-like of form Alexander/ Carried from Sidon, what time the broad sea-path he sailed over/ Bringing back Helen home, of a noble father begotten.”
And in the Odyssey also he has mentioned it in these verses:

“Such had the daughter of Zeus, such drugs of exquisite cunning,/ Good, which to her the wife of Thon, Polydamna, had given,/ Dwelling in Egypt, the land where the bountiful meadow produces/ Drugs more than all lands else, many good being mixed, many evil.”
And thus too Menelaus says to Telemachus:
“Still the gods stayed me in Egypt, to come back hither desiring,/ Stayed me from voyaging home, since sacrifice was due I performed not.”
In these lines he makes it clear that he knew of the wandering of Alexander to Egypt, for Syria borders upon Egypt, and the Phoenicians, to whom Sidon belongs, dwell in Syria.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 332
paragraphs: By these lines, and by this passage, it is also most clearly shown that the “Cyprian Epic” was not written by Homer but by some other man: for in this it is said that on the third day after leaving Sparta Alexander came to Ilion bringing Helen with him, having had a “gently-blowing wind and a smooth sea,” whereas in the Iliad it says that he wandered from his course when he brought her.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 333
paragraphs: Let us now leave Homer and the “Cyprian” Epic; but this I will say, that I asked the priests whether the tale the Hellenes tell of the events at Ilion is only an idle story, and they answered me thus: they had their knowledge by inquiry from Menelaus himself. After the rape of Helen, they said, a large army of Hellenes came to the Teucrian land to help Menelaus. When the army had come out of the ships to land and had pitched its camp there, they sent messengers to Ilion, and with these went Menelaus himself. When they entered within the wall, they demanded back Helen and the wealth that Alexander had stolen from Menelaus and carried off; and moreover they demanded satisfaction for the wrongs done. The Teucrians told the same tale then and afterwards, both with oath and without oath: namely that in deed and in truth they had neither Helen nor the wealth demanded, but that both were in Egypt; and that they could not justly be compelled to give satisfaction for what Proteus king of Egypt had. The Hellenes, however, thought that they were being mocked, and besieged the city, until at last they took it. When they had taken the wall and did not find Helen, but heard the same tale as before, then they believed the former account, and sent Menelaus himself to Proteus.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 334
paragraphs: And Menelaus, having come to Egypt and sailed up to Memphis, told the truth of these matters, and not only met with great entertainment but also received Helen unharmed, and all his own wealth besides. After he had been thus treated, however, Menelaus showed himself ungrateful to the Egyptians; for when he set out to sail away, contrary winds detained him, and since this condition lasted long, he devised an impious deed — he took two children of native Egyptians and made sacrifice of them. After this, when it became known that he had done so, he became abhorred, and being pursued he escaped and got away in his ships to Libya. But where he went after this the Egyptians were unable to tell. They said they had found out part of these things by inquiries, but the rest — namely what had happened in their own land — they told from sure and certain knowledge.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 335
paragraphs: Thus the priests of the Egyptians told me; and I myself agree with the story told about Helen, adding this consideration: if Helen had been in Ilion, she would have been given up to the Hellenes, whether Alexander consented or no. For assuredly Priam was not so mad, nor the others of his house, as to be willing to run the risk of ruin for themselves, their children, and their city, in order that Alexander might have Helen as his wife. And even supposing that for the first part of the time they had been so inclined, yet when many other Trojans besides were losing their lives as often as they fought with the Hellenes, and when of Priam's own sons two or three or even more were slain in every battle (if one may trust at all the Epic poets) — when, I say, things were coming to such a pass, I believe that even if Priam himself had had Helen as wife, he would have given her back to the Achaeans, if by so doing he might be freed from the evils that oppressed him. Nor was the kingdom coming to Alexander next, so that with Priam old the government was in his hands; but Hector, who was both older and more of a man than he, would have received it after Priam's death, and it would not have befitted Hector to allow his brother to continue his wrongdoing, seeing that great evils were coming to pass on his account both to himself privately and in general to the other Trojans. In truth, however, they lacked the power to give Helen back; and the Hellenes did not believe them, though they spoke the truth — because, as I declare my opinion, the divine power was purposing to cause them utterly to perish, and so make it evident to men that for great wrongs great also are the chastisements that come from the gods. And thus have I delivered my opinion concerning these matters.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 336
paragraphs: After Proteus, they told me, Rhampsinitos succeeded to the kingdom, and he left as his memorial the gateway to the temple of Hephaistos that faces westward. In front of the gateway he set up two statues, each twenty-five cubits tall. The Egyptians call the one on the north side Summer, and the one on the south side Winter; to Summer they pay reverence and make offerings, while to Winter they do the opposite. (a) This king, they said, gained great wealth in silver, more than any king born after him could match or even approach. Wishing to keep his treasure safe, he had a stone chamber built, with one of its walls forming part of the outside of his palace. The builder, however, had a design upon it, and he contrived as follows: he set one of the stones in such a way that it could easily be removed from the wall by two men, or even by a single man. So when the chamber was finished and the king stored his money inside it, the builder, after some time, drawing near the end of his life, called his two sons to him. He told them how he had arranged the matter when building the king's treasury, all in forethought for them, so that they might have ample means of living. He gave them the precise measurements for removing the stone, telling them that if they paid heed to this, they would be the stewards of the king's treasury. Then he died, and his sons made no long delay in setting to work. They went to the palace by night, found the stone in the wall of the chamber, dealt with it easily, and carried away a great quantity of the wealth within. (b) When the king happened to open the chamber, he was astonished to see the vessels falling short of their full amount, and he did not know whom to blame, since the seals were unbroken and the chamber had been shut close. But when, on opening the chamber a second time and a third, the money was each time seen to be diminished — for the thieves did not slacken in their assaults — he did as follows. He had traps made and set them around the vessels in which the money was kept; and when the thieves came as before and one of them entered, as soon as he came near a vessel he was caught fast in the trap. Realizing how desperate his case was, he immediately called his brother, showed him what had happened, and bade him climb in as quickly as possible and cut off his head, lest he be seen and recognized, bringing destruction upon his brother as well. To the other this seemed sound advice, and he was persuaded; he did so, and fitting the stone back into its place, he departed home carrying his brother's head with him. (c) When day came, the king entered the chamber and was utterly amazed to see the body of the thief held in the trap without its head, the chamber unbroken, and no way to come in or go out. Being at a loss, he hung the dead body up on the wall and set guards there, with orders to seize anyone seen weeping or lamenting and bring him before the king. When the body had been hung up, the mother was deeply grieved. Speaking with her surviving son, she ordered him to contrive, by whatever means he could, to take down and bring home the body of his dead brother; and if he failed to do this, she earnestly threatened that she would go and inform the king that he had the money. (d) Since the mother dealt harshly with the surviving son, and he could not persuade her with his many arguments, he contrived a device for his purpose. He provided himself with asses, filled some skins with wine, loaded them upon the asses, and drove them along. When he came opposite to those guarding the corpse, he pulled out two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied. As the wine ran out, he began to beat his head and cry out loudly, as if he did not know which of the asses to turn to first. When the guards saw the wine flowing out in streams, they ran together onto the road with drinking vessels in their hands and collected the wine that was spilling, counting it pure gain. He railed at them all violently, pretending to be angry, and when the guards tried to appease him, after a while he feigned to be pacified and to abate his anger. At last he drove his asses out of the road and began to set their loads right. Then more talk arose among them, one or two of them made jokes at him and brought him to laugh with them, and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins as well. At that they lay down then and there without further ado, intending to drink, and they took him into their company and invited him to stay with them and join them in their drinking. So he, as one might expect, was persuaded and stayed. As they welcomed him in friendly fashion as they drank, he made them a present of another skin. So at length, having drunk liberally, the guards became completely drunk, and being overcome by sleep they went to bed on the very spot where they had been drinking. He then, since it was now far on in the night, first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards. After that he placed the dead body upon the asses and drove them home, having accomplished what his mother had enjoined upon him. (e) When it was reported to the king that the dead body of the thief had been stolen away, he displayed great anger; and desiring above all to find out who it could be that devised these things, he did this — so at least they said, though I do not believe the account. He caused his own daughter to sit in a brothel and ordered her to receive all comers equally, and before lying with any of them she was to compel each one to tell her what was the most cunning and the most unholy deed he had done in all his life; and whoever should relate what had happened concerning the thief, she must seize him and not let him go. So she did as her father had enjoined. The thief, hearing the purpose for which this was done and wishing to outdo the king in cleverness, did this. From the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his cloak. Having gone in to the king's daughter and being asked the same question as the others, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother caught in a trap in the king's treasure-chamber, and the most cunning deed when he made the guards drunk and took down the dead body of his brother that had been hung up. When she heard this and tried to lay hold of him, the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse, which she grasped and held, thinking she was holding the man's own arm. But the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. (f) When this also was reported to the king, he was at first amazed at the ready invention and daring of the fellow. Then afterwards he sent round to all the cities and made proclamation, granting a free pardon to the thief and promising a great reward as well if he would come into his presence. The thief, trusting to the proclamation, came to the king, and Rhampsinitos marvelled greatly at him and gave him this daughter of his to wife, considering him to be the most knowing of all men. For just as the Egyptians were distinguished from all other men, so was he distinguished from the other Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 337
paragraphs: After this, they said, this same king descended alive into the place the Greeks call Hades, and there played at dice with Demeter. In some throws he beat her, and in others she beat him; and he came back again bringing as a gift from her a handkerchief of gold. Because of Rhampsinitos's descent, they told me, the Egyptians after his return held a festival, which I know from my own observation they still keep even in my own time; but whether they hold the feast for this reason or for some other, I cannot say. In any case, on the very day of the festival the priests weave a complete robe, and then they bind up the eyes of one of them with a headband, and leading him in the robe to the path that goes to the temple of Demeter, they depart, going back by themselves. This priest, they say, with his eyes bound, is led by two wolves to the temple of Demeter, which lies twenty furlongs from the city, and then the wolves lead him back again from the temple to the same spot.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 338
paragraphs: As for the stories told by the Egyptians, anyone to whom such things seem credible may accept them. For my part, it should be understood throughout the whole of this history that I write by hearsay what each people report in their own place. The Egyptians say that Demeter and Dionysos are rulers of the world below. The Egyptians are also the first to have reported the doctrine that the human soul is immortal, and that when the body dies, the soul enters another creature that happens at that moment to be coming to birth; and when it has gone round all the creatures of land and sea and air, it enters again into a human body as that body comes to birth, and it completes this round in a period of three thousand years. This doctrine certain Greeks adopted, some earlier and some later, as if it were their own invention, and I know the names of these men but refrain from recording them.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 339
paragraphs: Down to the time when Rhampsinitos was king, they told me, there was nothing in Egypt but orderly rule, and Egypt prospered greatly. But after him Cheops became king and brought them to every kind of misery. He shut up all the temples, and having first stopped them from sacrificing there, he then ordered all the Egyptians to work for him. Some were assigned to drag stones from the quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile; others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been ferried across the river in boats, and to haul them to the so-called Libyan mountains. They worked in shifts of a hundred thousand men at a time, for three months straight. Ten years of this oppression passed while the causeway was built along which they hauled the stones — a causeway that is, in my view, a work not much less than the pyramid itself. Its length is five furlongs, its breadth ten fathoms, and its height, where it is highest, eight fathoms, and it is made of smoothed stone with figures carved upon it. For this, they said, the ten years were spent, as well as for the underground chambers on the hill on which the pyramids stand, which he had made as burial chambers for himself on an island, having led a channel from the Nile to the place. For the construction of the pyramid itself a period of twenty years passed. The pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and its height is the same. It is built of smoothed stones fitted together in the most perfect manner, not one of the stones being less than thirty feet in length.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 340
paragraphs: This pyramid was built in the form of steps — what some call “rows” and others “bases.” After they had first made it this way, they raised the remaining stones using machines made of short pieces of timber. They lifted the stones first from the ground up to the first stage of the steps, and when a stone reached that stage, it was placed on another machine standing on the first step, and from there it was drawn up to the second stage by yet another machine. For there were as many machines as there were courses of steps — or perhaps they used one and the same machine, built to be easily carried, shifting it to each stage in turn so they could lift the stones up. Let it be told both ways, according to how it is reported. In any case, the highest parts of the pyramid were finished first, and afterwards they worked their way down, finishing the parts next to those, and last of all they finished the parts near the ground and the lowest courses. On the pyramid it is recorded in Egyptian writing how much was spent on radishes, onions, and leeks for the workmen; and if I correctly remember what the interpreter told me in reading this inscription, the sum came to one thousand six hundred talents of silver. If that is so, how much more must have been spent besides on the iron tools with which they worked, and on the bread and clothing for the workmen, considering that they were building these works for the length of time already mentioned, and were also occupied for no short period — I suppose — in cutting and transporting the stones and in excavating the underground chambers?

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 341
paragraphs: Cheops reached such a depth of wickedness, they said, that when he ran short of money he made his own daughter sit in a brothel and ordered her to charge a certain sum (they did not tell me the exact amount). She collected what her father demanded, but she also decided to leave a monument of her own. She asked each visitor for the gift of one stone. From these stones, they say, the middle pyramid of the three was built—the one that stands in front of the Great Pyramid. Each side is one hundred and fifty feet long.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 342
paragraphs: This Cheops, the Egyptians said, reigned for fifty years; and after he died, his brother Chephren succeeded to the kingdom. This king followed the same pattern as the other in every respect, including the fact that he built a pyramid. His pyramid did not reach the dimensions of the one built by his predecessor — I know this, having measured it myself — and moreover it has no underground chambers beneath it, nor does a channel from the Nile flow to it as to the other, where the water coming through a built conduit flows around an island within, and where they say Cheops himself is buried. But for a foundation he laid the first course in Ethiopian stone of varied colors. He built this pyramid forty feet lower than the other in size, placing it next to the great pyramid. The two stand on the same hill, which is about a hundred feet high. And Chephren, they said, reigned fifty-six years.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 343
paragraphs: Together, these two reigns count as one hundred and six years. During this time, the Egyptians suffered every kind of misery, and the temples stayed closed the entire time. The Egyptians hate these two kings so much that they are reluctant to even say their names. Instead, they call the pyramids after Philitis, a shepherd who grazed his flocks in the area at that time.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 344
paragraphs: After him, they said, Mykerinos became king over Egypt — the son of Cheops. His father's deeds displeased him, and he both opened the temples and gave the people, who had been ground down to the last extremity of misery, their liberty to return to their own affairs and to their sacrifices. He also handed down judgments in their lawsuits that were more just than those of all the other kings. For this reason the Egyptians praise this king above all the kings who had arisen in Egypt before him; for he not only gave good decisions, but also, when a man complained of a decision, he paid him compensation out of his own property and so satisfied his desire. But while Mykerinos was acting mercifully to his subjects and conducting himself in the way I have described, calamities befell him. The first was this: his daughter died, the only child he had in his house. Grieved beyond measure by what had happened, and wishing to bury his daughter in a more remarkable manner than others, he made a cow of wood, covered it over with gold, and then buried within it this daughter who, as I said, had died.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 345
paragraphs: This cow was not buried in the ground. It was still visible in my time, in the city of Sais, placed in a richly decorated chamber within the royal palace. Incense of every kind is burned before it daily. Each night, a lamp burns beside it all night long. In an adjacent room, there are statues that the priests at Sais told me represent the concubines of Mykerinos. Colossal wooden figures of women, about twenty in number, stand there naked. But who they really are, I can only say what I was told.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 346
paragraphs: Some, however, tell the following tale about this cow and the colossal statues — that Mykerinos fell in love with his own daughter and afterwards raped her; whereupon, they say, the girl strangled herself in grief, and he buried her in this cow; and her mother cut off the hands of the maids who had betrayed the daughter to her father — which is why the images of them have suffered the very thing the maids suffered in their lifetime. In saying this they speak foolishly, as it seems to me, especially with regard to the hands of the statues. For we ourselves saw that their hands had dropped off through the lapse of time, and they were still to be seen lying at their feet even down to my own day.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 347
paragraphs: The cow is covered with a crimson robe, except for the head and neck, which are visible, overlaid very thickly with gold; and between the horns there is the disc of the sun rendered in gold. The cow is not standing but kneeling, and in size it equals a large living cow. Every year it is carried out of its chamber — at those times, I mean, when the Egyptians beat themselves in mourning for the god whom I will not name in connection with such a matter. At those times, I say, they also carry the cow out into the light of day, for they say that she asked her father Mykerinos, when she was dying, that she might look upon the sun once each year.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 348
paragraphs: After the misfortune of his daughter, they said, a second calamity befell this king as follows. An oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that he was destined to live only six years more, and in the seventh he would end his life. Indignant at this, he sent a reproach to the oracle against the god, complaining in reply that whereas his father and uncle — who had shut up the temples, not only failed to remember the gods, but also destroyed men — had lived for a long time, he himself, who practiced piety, was destined to end his life so soon. And from the oracle a second message came, which said that it was for this very reason he was bringing his life to a swift close: he had not done what it was appointed for him to do, since it was destined that Egypt should suffer evils for a hundred and fifty years. The two kings before him had perceived this, but he had not. Hearing this and considering that the sentence had been passed beyond recall, Mykerinos procured a great many lamps, and whenever night came on, he lit them and began to drink and enjoy himself, stopping neither by day nor by night. He went about to the marshlands and to the woods and wherever he heard there were the most suitable places for enjoyment. He devised this — wanting to prove that the oracle spoke falsely — so that he might have twelve years of life instead of six, with the nights turned into days.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 349
paragraphs: This king also left behind him a pyramid, much smaller than his father's, square in shape and measuring three hundred feet lacking twenty on each side, built moreover of Ethiopian stone up to half its height. This pyramid some of the Greeks claim was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, but in saying this they are not speaking correctly. Besides, it is obvious to me that those who say this do not even know who Rhodopis was — otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which, so to speak, countless thousands of talents were spent. Moreover, they do not know that Rhodopis flourished in the reign of Amasis, not in this king's reign, for Rhodopis lived many years later than the kings who left behind the pyramids. By descent she was Thracian, and she was a slave of Iadmon son of Hephaistopolis, a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker — for he too was once the slave of Iadmon, as was proved especially by this fact: when the people of Delphi repeatedly proclaimed, in accordance with an oracle, that someone should claim the blood-money for Aesop's death, no one else came forward, but at length the grandson of Iadmon, also called Iadmon, claimed it; and so it is shown that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 350
paragraphs: As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having arrived there to practice her trade, she was ransomed from slavery for a large sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos, the brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus Rhodopis was set free, and she remained in Egypt, and by her beauty she won so much favor that she made a great deal of money — great for someone like Rhodopis — though not enough to cover the cost of such a pyramid as this. In fact, there is no need to credit her with very great wealth, since the tithe of her wealth can still be seen even now by anyone who wants to look. For Rhodopis wished to leave behind in Hellas a memorial of herself — something that no one else had thought of or dedicated in a temple — and to offer it at Delphi as her memorial. Accordingly, with the tithe of her wealth she had iron spits made, large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far as her tithe allowed. She sent them to Delphi, and they are still lying there today, heaped together behind the altar the Chians dedicated, directly opposite the inner sanctum of the temple. As it happens, the courtesans at Naucratis tend to win renown, for this woman first, about whom this story is told, became so famous that every Greek without exception came to know the name of Rhodopis; and after her, one named Archidiche was sung about throughout Hellas, though she was less talked about than the former. As for Charaxos, after ransoming Rhodopis and returning to Mytilene, he was savagely abused by Sappho in an ode. About Rhodopis, then, I will say no more.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 351
paragraphs: After Mykerinos, the priests said, Asychis became king of Egypt, and he built for Hephaistos the temple gateway that faces the sunrise — by far the most beautiful and largest of the gateways. While all of them have figures carved upon them and countless other architectural ornaments, this one has them far more than the rest. In this king's reign, they told me, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was passed for the Egyptians allowing a man to borrow the money he needed by offering as security the dead body of his father. An additional clause was added: the lender was to have a claim on the whole burial chamber belonging to the borrower, and the borrower who offered this security, if he refused to repay the debt, would be subject to this penalty — that neither he himself would be allowed burial when he died, either in the family tomb or any other, nor would he be allowed to bury any kinsman who died. Wishing to surpass the kings of Egypt before him, this king left as his memorial a pyramid that he made of bricks, on which there is an inscription carved in stone that says: “Do not despise me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, for I surpass them as much as Zeus surpasses the other gods. For with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever mud stuck to the pole, they gathered up and made into bricks, and in this way they finished me.”
Such were the deeds this king performed;

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 352
paragraphs: and after him reigned a blind man from the city of Anysis, whose name was Anysis. In his reign the Ethiopians, led by their king Sabacos, marched against Egypt with a great host. So this blind man fled and took refuge in the marshlands, and the Ethiopian ruled over Egypt for fifty years, during which he did the following: whenever an Egyptian committed a transgression, he would never put him to death, but he sentenced each man according to the gravity of the offense, ordering them to throw up an embankment before the city each offender came from. In this way the cities were raised still higher than before; for they had first been embanked by those who dug the channels in the reign of Sesostris, and then again in the reign of the Ethiopian, and so they were raised very high. While other cities in Egypt also stood high, I think it was at Bubastis in particular that the earth was piled up most. In this city there is a temple very much worth mentioning, for though there are other larger and more costly temples, none is more pleasing to the eye than this one. Now Bubastis in the Greek tongue is Artemis,

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 353
paragraphs: and her temple is laid out thus: except for the entrance, it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile — not joining one another, but each extending as far as the entrance of the temple, one flowing around on one side and the other on the other. Each is a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees. The gateway rises to a height of ten fathoms and is adorned with figures six cubits high, very striking. This temple stands in the middle of the city, and can be looked down upon from all sides as one walks around; for since the city has been banked up to a height, while the temple has not been moved from where it was originally built, one can look down into it. Around it runs a stone wall with figures carved upon it, and within is a grove of very large trees planted around a great temple-house, inside which stands the image of the goddess. The breadth and length of the temple is a furlong in every direction. Opposite the entrance there is a road paved with stone for about three furlongs, leading through the marketplace toward the east, with a breadth of about four hundred feet. On either side grow trees reaching to the sky, and the road leads to the temple of Hermes. This, then, is how the temple is arranged.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 354
paragraphs: The final deliverance from the Ethiopian came about, they said, as follows. He fled away because he had seen a vision in his sleep, in which it seemed to him that a man came and stood beside him and advised him to gather together all the priests of Egypt and cut them in half through the middle. Having seen this dream, he said it seemed to him that the gods were showing this to him in order to give him a pretext — so that he might commit an impious act against religion and thus receive some punishment either from the gods or from men. He would not, however, do so. In truth, he said, the time had expired during which it had been prophesied that he would rule Egypt before departing from it. For while he was still in Ethiopia, the oracles the Ethiopians consult had told him it was fated that he should rule Egypt for fifty years. Since this time was now running out, and the vision of the dream also disturbed him, Sabacos departed from Egypt of his own accord.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 355
paragraphs: Then when the Ethiopian had gone away out of Egypt, the blind man returned from the marshland and began to rule again, having lived for those fifty years on an island he had made by piling up ashes and earth. Whenever any Egyptian visited him bringing food — as each had been appointed to do without the Ethiopian's knowledge — he also bade them bring some ashes as their gift. No one was able to find this island before Amyrtaios; that is, for more than seven hundred years the kings who rose before Amyrtaios were not able to find it. The name of this island is Elbo, and its size is ten furlongs on each side.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 356
paragraphs: After him the priest of Hephaistos, whose name was Sethos, came to the throne. This man, they said, neglected and held in no regard the warrior class of the Egyptians, thinking he would have no need of them. Besides other slights he put upon them, he also took from them the plots of grain-land which had been granted to them as a special gift in the reigns of previous kings — twelve plots to each man. After this, Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians, marched a great army against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a tight corner, entered the sanctuary of the temple and lamented before the image of the god the danger hanging over him. As he was lamenting, sleep came over him, and in his vision it seemed that the god came and stood beside him and encouraged him, saying he would suffer no harm if he went out to meet the army of the Arabians, for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in what he had seen in his sleep, he took with him, they said, those Egyptians who were willing to follow, and encamped at Pelusion, for that was the route of the invasion. Not one of the warrior class followed him, but shopkeepers, artisans, and men of the marketplace. Then, after they arrived, field mice swarmed by night upon their enemies and ate through their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handgrips of their shields, so that the next day they fled, and being without weapons to defend themselves, great numbers of them fell. To this day this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding a mouse on his hand, and by letters inscribed he says these words: “Let whoever looks upon me learn to fear the gods.”

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 357
paragraphs: Up to this point in the story, it was the Egyptians and their priests who gave the account, declaring that from the first king down to this priest of Hephaistos who reigned last, there had been three hundred and forty-one generations of men, and in that span there had been the same number of chief priests and kings. Now three hundred generations of men equal ten thousand years, since a hundred years is three generations; and in the forty-one generations that remain — those I mean which were added to the three hundred — there are one thousand three hundred and forty years. So in the period of eleven thousand three hundred and forty years, they said, no god had arisen in human form, nor even before or after that time, among the remaining kings who arose in Egypt, did they report that anything of the kind had happened. During this time they said the sun had moved four times from his accustomed place of rising — where he now sets he had twice risen, and where he now rises he had twice set; and in the meantime nothing in Egypt had changed from its usual state, neither in the produce of the earth, nor in what comes to them from the river, nor in matters of disease or death.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 358
paragraphs: When the historian Hecataeus visited Thebes and traced his ancestry back to a god in the sixteenth generation, the priests of Zeus did much the same for him as they did for me (though I did not trace my own genealogy). They led him into the great inner hall of the temple and showed him wooden statues—as many as I described. Each chief priest sets up a statue of himself during his lifetime. The priests counted and showed the statues, demonstrating that each was the son of the one before, going through all the statues from the most recent all the way back to the earliest. When Hecataeus traced his descent and connected himself to a god in the sixteenth generation, they challenged him with their own genealogy, refusing to accept that any man was descended from a god. They traced their counter-genealogy like this: each statue, they said, was a piromis born of a piromis (meaning a good and noble man). They showed three hundred and forty-five statues, each piromis descended from piromis, without ever connecting the line to either a god or a hero.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 359
paragraphs: From their declaration it followed that the beings represented by the statues were human in form and far from being gods. But they said that before these men, gods were the rulers of Egypt. They did not mingle with humans. One of them always held supreme power. The last god to rule Egypt was Horus, the son of Osiris—the god the Greeks call Apollo. He deposed Typhon and became the last divine king of Egypt. Osiris in Greek is Dionysus.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 360
paragraphs: Among the Greeks, Heracles, Dionysos, and Pan are reckoned the latest-born of the gods; but for the Egyptians, Pan is a very ancient god and is one of those known as the eight gods, while Heracles belongs to the second rank, called the twelve gods, and Dionysos is of the third rank, those born from the twelve gods. Now as to Heracles I have already shown how many years old he is according to the Egyptians themselves, reckoning down to the reign of Amasis; Pan is said to have existed even longer than these, while Dionysos is given the fewest years in comparison to the others, and even for him they count fifteen thousand years down to the reign of Amasis. The Egyptians say they know this for certain, since they have always kept records and written down the years as they passed. Now the Dionysos said to have been born of Semele daughter of Cadmos was born about sixteen hundred years before my time; Heracles, son of Alcmene, about nine hundred years; and the Pan born of Penelope — for the Greeks say Pan was born of her and Hermes — came into being after the Trojan Wars, about eight hundred years before my time.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 361
paragraphs: Of these two accounts, every man may adopt the one he finds more credible when he hears it. I, for my part, have already stated my own opinion about them.
