For if these too, like Heracles son of Amphitryon, had appeared before all men's eyes and lived their lives into old age in Hellas — I mean Dionysos son of Semele and Pan son of Penelope — then one might have said that these also had been born as mere men, bearing the names of gods who had come into being long before. But as it is, with regard to Dionysos the Greeks say that as soon as he was born, Zeus sewed him up in his thigh and carried him to Nysa, which is above Egypt in the land of Ethiopia; and as for Pan, they cannot say where he went after he was born. From this it has become clear to me that the Greeks learned the names of these gods later than those of the other gods, and they trace their lineage as though their birth occurred at the time they first learned their names.
So far, then, the history is told by the Egyptians themselves;

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 362
paragraphs: but I will now recount what other nations also tell, and what the Egyptians report in agreement with the others, about what happened in this land; and I will also add something of what I have seen myself.

Being set free after the reign of the priest of Hephaistos, the Egyptians, since they could not live any length of time without a king, set twelve kings over themselves, dividing all of Egypt into twelve parts. These kings intermarried with one another and reigned together, making agreements that they would not try to overthrow one another by force, nor seek any advantage over one another, but would live in perfect friendship. The reason they made these agreements and guarded them so strictly from being broken was this: an oracle had been given to them at the outset, when they first began to exercise their rule, that whichever of them poured a libation with a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos would become king over all Egypt — for they used to assemble together in all the temples.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 363
paragraphs: Moreover, they resolved to join together and leave a common memorial of themselves. Having decided this, they had a labyrinth built, situated a little above the Lake of Moiris and almost opposite the so-called City of Crocodiles. I saw this myself, and I found it greater than words can describe. For if one should put together and reckon up all the buildings and great works produced by the Greeks, they would prove inferior in labor and expense to this labyrinth — though it is true that both the temple at Ephesos and the one at Samos are works worth noting. The pyramids too were greater than words can say, and each one of them is equal to many Greek works, great as those may be; but the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids. It has twelve roofed courts, with gates facing each other, six on the north side and six on the south, adjoining one another, and the same wall surrounds them all on the outside. It contains two kinds of chambers, one kind below ground and the other above them — three thousand in number, fifteen hundred of each kind. The upper chambers we saw ourselves, going through them, and we speak of them having looked with our own eyes. But the underground chambers we only heard about, for the Egyptians in charge of them refused to show them on any account, saying that there lay the tombs of the kings who had first built this labyrinth and of the sacred crocodiles. So we speak of the chambers below from what we received by hearsay, while the chambers above we saw ourselves and found to be works of more than human greatness. The passages through the chambers and the windings through the courts, which were beautifully adorned, offered endless matter for wonder, as we went from a court into the chambers beyond, from the chambers into colonnades, from the colonnades into other rooms, and then from the chambers again into other courts. Over all of these is a roof made of stone like the walls, and the walls are covered with carved figures; each court is surrounded by pillars of white stone fitted together most perfectly. At the end of the labyrinth, at one corner, there is a pyramid forty fathoms high, on which large figures are carved, and an underground passage leads to it.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 364
paragraphs: Such is this labyrinth; but an even greater wonder is offered by the lake called the Lake of Moiris, along whose side this labyrinth was built. The measure of its circumference is three thousand six hundred furlongs (sixty schoines), which is the same number of furlongs as the extent of Egypt itself along the sea. The lake lies stretched lengthwise from north to south, and at its deepest it is fifty fathoms deep. That this lake is artificial and dug by hand is obvious, for in about the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising fifty fathoms above the water, with the same height built below the water as well; and upon each is set a colossal stone statue seated on a throne. So the pyramids are a hundred fathoms in total height, and these hundred fathoms are equal to a furlong of six hundred feet — the fathom being six feet or four cubits, the feet being four palms each, and the cubits six palms. The water in the lake does not come from the land nearby, for that country is very short of water, but has been brought there from the Nile by a canal: for six months the water flows into the lake, and for six months out again into the Nile. Whenever the water flows out, it brings into the royal treasury a talent of silver a day from the fish caught, and twenty pounds a day when the water is flowing in.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 365
paragraphs: The inhabitants of the region also told me that this lake had an underground outlet to the Syrtis in Libya, turning toward the interior of the continent on the western side and running along the mountain above Memphis. Since I did not see anywhere the earth dug out from this excavation — a matter that caught my attention — I asked those living nearest the lake where the excavated earth had been taken. They told me where it had been carried off, and I readily believed them, for I knew by report that a similar thing had been done at Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians. There, certain thieves had once devised a plan to carry off the wealth of Sardanapallos son of Ninos, the king — wealth that was very great and kept in underground treasure-houses. They began from their own dwelling, and estimating their direction they dug underground toward the king's palace; and the earth brought out from the excavation they used to carry away, when night came on, to the river Tigris which flows past the city of Nineveh, until at last they accomplished what they desired. In the same way, as I heard, the digging of the lake in Egypt was carried out — except that it was done not by night but by day; for as they dug, the Egyptians carried to the Nile the earth they excavated, and the river, receiving it, naturally bore it away and dispersed it. This is how the lake is said to have been dug.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 366
paragraphs: The twelve kings continued to rule justly, but in the course of time the following happened. After sacrificing in the temple of Hephaistos, they were about to make a libation on the last day of the festival, and the chief priest, bringing out for them the golden cups they customarily used to pour libations, miscounted and brought out only eleven for the twelve kings. Then the one standing last in order, Psammetichos, since he had no cup, took off his bronze helmet, and holding it out to receive the wine, he proceeded to make his libation. Likewise all the other kings were accustomed to wear helmets, and they happened to have them on at that moment. Now Psammetichos held out his helmet with no treacherous intent; but they, noting what Psammetichos had done and recalling the oracle — how it had been declared to them that whichever of them should pour a libation with a bronze cup would be sole king of Egypt — remembering, I say, the saying of the oracle, did not indeed think it right to kill Psammetichos, since they found on inquiry that he had not done it with any premeditation. But they decided to strip him of almost all his power and to drive him away into the marshland, and that from the marshland he should have no dealings with the rest of Egypt.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 367
paragraphs: This Psammetichos had previously been a fugitive from the Ethiopian Sabacos, who had killed his father Necos; from him, I say, he had been a fugitive in Syria. When the Ethiopian departed as a result of the vision in the dream, the Egyptians of the district of Saïs brought him back to his own country. Afterwards, when he was king, it was his fate to be a fugitive a second time on account of the helmet, being driven by the eleven kings into the marshland. Holding that he had been gravely wronged by them, he considered how he might take vengeance on those who had driven him out. When he sent to the oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, where the Egyptians have their most truthful oracle, he was given the reply that vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. He was strongly inclined not to believe that bronze men would come to help him; but not long afterwards, certain Ionians and Carians who had sailed out for plunder were forced to come ashore in Egypt, and having landed and being clad in bronze armor, one of the Egyptians, never having seen men in bronze armor before, came to the marshland and brought word to Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. He, perceiving that the saying of the oracle was coming to pass, dealt in a friendly manner with the Ionians and Carians, and with large promises persuaded them to take his side. Then, having persuaded them, with the help of the Egyptians who favored his cause and of these foreign mercenaries, he overthrew the kings.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 368
paragraphs: Having gained power over all Egypt, Psammetichos built the southern gateway of the temple of Hephaistos at Memphis. He also built a court for Apis, where the sacred bull is kept when it appears—a court opposite the gateway, surrounded by a colonnade and covered with carved figures. Instead of pillars, the colonnade is supported by colossal statues twelve cubits tall. Apis is Epaphos in Greek.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 369
paragraphs: To the Ionians and Carians who had helped him, Psammetichos granted portions of land to settle in, opposite one another with the river Nile between them; these were called the “Encampments.” These portions of land he gave them, and besides he paid them all he had promised. Moreover, he placed with them Egyptian boys to be taught the Greek language, and from these — who learned the language thoroughly — are descended the present class of interpreters in Egypt. The Ionians and Carians occupied these portions of land for a long time; they lay toward the sea, a little below the city of Bubastis, on what is called the Pelusian mouth of the Nile. King Amasis later removed these men from there and settled them at Memphis, making them into a bodyguard for himself against the Egyptians. And since they settled in Egypt, we who are Greeks know with certainty, through our dealings with them, everything that happened in Egypt from the reign of king Psammetichos onward; for these were the first men of foreign speech to settle in Egypt. In the land from which they were removed, there still remained down to my own time the sheds where their ships had been drawn up and the ruins of their houses.
Thus, then, Psammetichos obtained Egypt:

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 370
paragraphs: and I have made mention of the oracle in Egypt often before this, and I will now give an account of it, since it is worth describing. This oracle in Egypt is sacred to Leto and is established in a great city near the mouth of the Nile called the Sebennytic, as one sails up the river from the sea; and the name of this city where the oracle is found is Buto, as I have said before. In this Buto there is a temple of Apollo and Artemis; and the temple-house of Leto, in which the oracle is, is both great in itself and has a gateway ten fathoms in height. But what most astonished me of the things to be seen there, I will now describe. Within this sacred enclosure stands a shrine of Leto made of a single stone, both in height and in length, of which all the walls in these two directions are equal, each being forty cubits; and for the covering of the roof another stone lies on top, with a cornice measuring four cubits.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 371
paragraphs: This shrine, then, of all the things I saw in that temple, is the most marvelous, and next to it comes the island called Chemmis. It lies in a deep, broad lake beside the temple at Buto, and the Egyptians say that this island is a floating island. I myself did not see it either floating about or moved from its place, and I am astonished to hear of it, wondering whether it really is a floating island. On this island of which I speak there is a great temple-house of Apollo, and three separate altars are set up within, and many palm trees and other trees are planted there, some fruit-bearing and some not. The Egyptians, when they say that it floats, add this story: on this island, which formerly was not floating, Leto, being one of the eight gods who came into existence first, and dwelling in the city of Buto where she has her oracle, received Apollo from Isis as a charge and preserved him, concealing him on the island now said to be floating, at the time when Typhon came in pursuit, searching everywhere, desiring to find the son of Osiris. They say that Apollo and Artemis are the children of Dionysos and Isis, and that Leto became their nurse and protector; and in the Egyptian tongue Apollo is Oros, Demeter is Isis, and Artemis is Bubastis. From this story and from no other Aeschylus son of Euphorion took what I am about to say, in which he differs from all earlier poets: he represented Artemis as the daughter of Demeter. For this reason, they say, the island became a floating one.
Such is the story they tell;

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 372
paragraphs: but as for Psammetichos, he was king over Egypt for fifty-four years, of which for twenty-nine years he was encamped before Azotos, a great city of Syria, besieging it until at last he took it; and this Azotos, of all the cities we know, held out longest under a siege.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 373
paragraphs: Psammetichos' son was Necos, and he became king of Egypt. He was the first to attempt the canal connecting the Nile to the Red Sea, which Darius the Persian later completed. The canal is a four-day voyage in length and wide enough for two triremes to be rowed side by side. The water comes from the Nile. The canal runs from a point slightly above the city of Bubastis, past the Arabian city of Patumos, and into the Red Sea. The first part runs along the Arabian side of the Egyptian plain, past the ridge that extends south of Memphis, where the stone quarries are. The canal follows the base of this ridge from west to east, then turns south through a gap in the hills toward the Arabian Gulf. The shortest and most direct route from the northern sea to the southern (or Red) Sea is across the strip from Mount Casion on the border of Egypt and Syria—a distance of exactly a thousand furlongs. That is the most direct route. The canal is much longer because it winds. A hundred and twenty thousand Egyptians died during the digging under Necos. He eventually stopped because an oracle warned him he was working for the benefit of a barbarian. (The Egyptians call anyone who does not speak their language a barbarian.)

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 374
paragraphs: After abandoning the canal, Necos turned to warfare. He had triremes built, some for the Mediterranean and some for the Arabian Gulf on the Red Sea. Their ship sheds can still be seen. He used these ships when he needed them. On land, Necos fought and defeated the Syrians at Magdolos. After the battle, he captured the great Syrian city of Cadytis. He dedicated the clothes he wore during these victories to Apollo, sending them to the temple of the Branchidai near Miletos. After a total reign of sixteen years, Necos died and passed the throne to his son Psammis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 375
paragraphs: While this Psammis was king of Egypt, envoys came to him from the Eleians, who boasted that they arranged the Olympic contest in the most just and honorable manner possible, and thought that not even the Egyptians, the wisest of men, could devise anything else to be added to their rules. When the Eleians came to Egypt and stated what they had come for, the king called together those of the Egyptians reputed to be the wisest, and when the Egyptians had gathered, they heard the Eleians describe everything it was their duty to do concerning the contest. After they had explained everything, they said they had come to learn what else the Egyptians might find to suggest, anything juster than this. The Egyptians, after consulting together, asked the Eleians whether their own citizens took part in the contest, and they answered that it was permitted to anyone who wished, both of their own people and of the other Greeks equally, to compete. Upon this the Egyptians said that in arranging the games this way they had utterly missed the mark of justice; for it could not be otherwise than that they would side with the man of their own state if he were competing, and thus act unfairly to the stranger. If they really wished, as they claimed, to arrange the games justly, and if this was the reason they had come to Egypt, they advised them to arrange the contest so that only foreigners might compete in it, and no Eleian would be allowed to compete. Such was the suggestion made by the Egyptians to the Eleians.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 376
paragraphs: When Psammis had been king of Egypt for only six years and had made an expedition to Ethiopia, and immediately afterwards ended his life, Apries son of Psammis inherited the kingdom in succession. This man came to be the most prosperous of all the kings up to that time, except only his forefather Psammetichos, and he reigned twenty-five years, during which he led an army against Sidon and fought a sea-battle with the king of Tyre. Since, however, it was fated that evil should come upon him, it came through a matter which I shall relate at greater length in the Libyan history, and only briefly here. Apries sent a great expedition against the Kyrenians and met with a correspondingly great disaster; and the Egyptians, considering him to blame for this, revolted against him, supposing that Apries had deliberately sent them out to obvious ruin so that — as they said — there might be a slaughter of them and he might the more securely rule over the rest of the Egyptians. Indignant at this, both the men who had returned from the expedition and the friends of those who had perished openly revolted.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 377
paragraphs: Hearing of this, Apries sent Amasis to them to put a stop to it by persuasion; and when he had come and was trying to restrain the Egyptians, as he was speaking and telling them not to revolt, one of the Egyptians stood up behind him and placed a helmet on his head, saying as he did so that he was putting it on to crown him king. To Amasis what was done was not entirely unwelcome, as he showed by his behavior; for as soon as the rebellious Egyptians had set him up as king, he prepared to march against Apries. Apries, hearing this, sent one of his own attendants to Amasis, a man of reputation whose name was Patarbemis, ordering him to bring Amasis alive into his presence. When Patarbemis came and summoned Amasis, the latter, who happened to be sitting on horseback, lifted up his leg and behaved in an unseemly manner, telling him to take that back to Apries. Nevertheless, they say, Patarbemis pressed him to go to the king, since the king had sent to summon him, and he replied that for some time past he had been preparing to do so, and that Apries would have no cause to fault him. Then Patarbemis, perceiving his intent both from what he said and from seeing his preparations, departed in haste, wishing to inform the king as quickly as possible of what was going on. When he returned to Apries without bringing Amasis, the king, paying no attention to what he said, but moved by violent anger, ordered his ears and nose to be cut off. And the rest of the Egyptians who still remained on his side, when they saw the man of greatest reputation among them suffering such shameful outrage, waited no longer but joined the others in revolt and delivered themselves over to Amasis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 378
paragraphs: Apries, learning of this second defection, armed his foreign mercenaries and marched against the Egyptians. He had around thirty thousand Carian and Ionian mercenaries. His royal palace was in the city of Sais—a large and impressive building. Apries and his mercenaries marched to attack the Egyptians, and Amasis and his forces marched to resist them. Both armies came to the city of Momemphis and prepared for battle.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 379
paragraphs: There are seven classes of Egyptians: one is called that of the priests, another that of the warriors, and the rest are cowherds, swineherds, shopkeepers, interpreters, and boatmen. This is the number of the classes of the Egyptians, and their names are given them from the occupations they follow. Of these, the warriors are called Calasirians and Hermotybians, and they come from the following districts — for all Egypt is divided into districts.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 380
paragraphs: The Hermotybians come from the districts of Busiris, Sais, Chemmis, Papremis, the island called Prosopitis, and half of the district of Natho. At their peak, they numbered one hundred and sixty thousand. None of them practices any trade. They devote themselves entirely to warfare.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 381
paragraphs: The districts of the Calasirians are those of Thebes, Bubastis, Aphthis, Tanis, Mendes, Sebennytos, Athribis, Pharbaithos, Thmuïs, Onuphis, Anytis, and Myecphoris — this last being on an island opposite the city of Bubastis. These are the districts of the Calasirians; at their greatest strength they numbered two hundred and fifty thousand men. Nor is it lawful for them, any more than for the others, to practice any trade; rather they practice only the profession of war, handing down the tradition from father to son.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 382
paragraphs: Whether the Greeks have learned this also from the Egyptians, I cannot say for certain, since I see that the Thracians too, and the Scythians, Persians, Lydians, and almost all the barbarians regard those of their citizens who learn the crafts, and their descendants, as less honorable than the rest; while those who keep themselves free from all practice of manual arts are reckoned noble, and especially those devoted to war. However that may be, the Greeks have all learned this, and especially the Lacedemonians; but the Corinthians least of all look down on those who practice handicrafts.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 383
paragraphs: The following privilege was specially granted to this class, and to no others of the Egyptians except the priests: each man had twelve yokes of land specially granted to him, free of taxes. A yoke of land measures a hundred Egyptian cubits every way, and the Egyptian cubit happens to be equal to that of Samos. This was a privilege granted to all of them, and they also had certain additional benefits taken in turn, and not by the same men twice. A thousand of the Calasirians and a thousand of the Hermotybians served as bodyguard to the king each year, and besides their yokes of land they received a daily allowance of five pounds of bread per man, two pounds of beef, and four half-pints of wine. This was the allowance given to those serving as the king's bodyguard for the time being.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 384
paragraphs: So when Apries, leading his foreign mercenaries, and Amasis, at the head of the whole body of the Egyptians, approached one another and came to the city of Momemphis, they joined battle. Although the foreign troops fought well, they were far outnumbered and were defeated because of this. Apries is said to have supposed that not even a god could cause him to cease from his rule, so firmly did he think it was established. In that battle, then, he was defeated, and being taken alive he was brought away to the city of Saïs, to what had formerly been his own dwelling but was henceforth the palace of Amasis. There he was kept in the palace for some time, and Amasis treated him well. But at last, since the Egyptians blamed Amasis, saying that he was not acting rightly in keeping alive a man who was the greatest enemy of both themselves and him, he handed Apries over to the Egyptians, and they strangled him; afterwards they buried him in the burial place of his fathers, which is in the temple of Athene, close to the sanctuary, on the left as you enter. The men of Saïs buried all those of this district who had been kings within the temple; for the tomb of Amasis too, though farther from the sanctuary than that of Apries and his forefathers, is also within the temple court. It consists of a colonnade of stone of great size, with pillars carved to resemble date palms and otherwise sumptuously adorned; and within the colonnade are double doors, and inside the doors a burial chamber.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 385
paragraphs: Inside this colonnade are double doors. Behind the doors is the burial chamber. Also in Sais is the burial place of a god whose name I consider it impious to mention in this context. It is in the temple of Athena, behind and extending along the entire wall of the goddess' house. In the sacred enclosure stand tall stone obelisks. Beside them is a lake, decorated with a stone rim—beautifully finished—and about the same size, I thought, as the lake called the Round Pool on Delos.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 386
paragraphs: On this lake they perform by night the drama of the god's sufferings. The Egyptians call these performances Mysteries. I know the full details of how they are conducted, but I will say no more. Similarly, about the rites of Demeter, which the Greeks call the Thesmophoria, I will keep silent—except for what may be spoken without impiety. The daughters of Danaos brought this ceremony from Egypt and taught it to the Pelasgian women. Afterward, when the Dorians drove out the entire population of the Peloponnese, the rite was lost, except among the Arcadians, who were not driven out and remained.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 387
paragraphs: Apries having thus been overthrown, Amasis became king. He was from the district of Saïs, and the name of the city he came from is Siuph. At first the Egyptians despised Amasis and held him in little regard, because he had been a commoner of no distinguished family; but afterwards Amasis won them over by cleverness rather than obstinacy. Among countless other valuable possessions of his, there was a golden foot-basin in which both Amasis himself and all his guests always used to wash their feet. He broke this up, and from the metal he had an image of a god made, and set it up in the city, where it was most prominent. The Egyptians continually visited the image and paid it great reverence. Then Amasis, hearing what the townspeople were doing, called the Egyptians together and explained the matter to them, saying that the image had been made from the foot-basin into which the Egyptians had formerly vomited, urinated, and washed their feet, whereas now they were showing it great reverence. “And just so,” he continued, “I myself have now fared like the foot-basin; for though formerly I was a commoner, I am now your king,” and he bade them accordingly honor him and hold him in regard.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 388
paragraphs: In this way he won the Egyptians to himself, so that they consented to be his subjects. His ordering of affairs was as follows. In the early morning and until the time when the marketplace filled, he willingly conducted whatever business was brought before him, but after that he spent his time drinking and jesting with his boon-companions, behaving frivolously and playfully. His friends, troubled by this, admonished him in words such as these: “O king, you are not governing yourself rightly by descending to such trifling behavior. You ought rather to be sitting the whole day in dignity on a dignified throne and conducting your business; and so the Egyptians would know for certain that they were ruled by a great man, and you would have a better reputation. As it is, you are behaving in no way like a king.” And he answered them thus: “Those who have bows string them when they wish to use them, and when they have finished using them they unstring them again; for if they were always kept strung, they would break, so that the men could not use them when they had need. So too is the state of a man: if he were always in earnest and did not relax himself for sport at the proper time, he would either go mad or become struck with stupor before he was aware of it; and knowing this well, I give a portion of my time to each of the two ways of living.” Such was his answer to his friends.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 389
paragraphs: It is said, however, that even when he was a commoner, Amasis was a lover of drinking and jesting, and not at all seriously disposed. Whenever his means of livelihood failed him through his drinking and luxurious living, he would go about and steal; and those he stole from would accuse him of having their property, and when he denied it, they would bring him before the judgment of an oracle whenever there was one in the place. Many times he was convicted by the oracles, and many times he was acquitted. When he finally became king, he did as follows: as for all those gods who had acquitted him and pronounced him not to be a thief, he paid no regard to their temples, gave nothing for their further adornment, and did not even visit them to offer sacrifice, considering them worthless and their oracles lying; but as for those who had convicted him of being a thief, to these he paid the very greatest regard, considering them to be true gods and to give oracles that did not lie.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 390
paragraphs: First, at Saïs, he built and completed for Athene a temple gateway which is a great marvel, and in this he far surpassed all who had done the like before him, both in height and size — so large are the stones and of such quality. Secondly, he dedicated great colossal statues and very large man-headed sphinxes, and for restoration he brought in other stones of monstrous size. Some of these he had brought from the quarries opposite Memphis, others of very great size from the city of Elephantine, a voyage of not less than twenty days from Saïs. Of all these things, what I wonder at most is this: a monolithic shrine which he brought from the city of Elephantine. They spent three years bringing it, and two thousand men were assigned to convey it, all of them of the class of boatmen. The length of this shrine outside is twenty-one cubits, the breadth fourteen cubits, and the height eight. These are the outside measurements of the monolith shrine; inside, the length is eighteen cubits and five-sixths of a cubit, the breadth twelve cubits, and the height five cubits. It lies by the entrance of the temple; for they did not draw it inside the temple because, as is said, while the shrine was being drawn along, the master craftsman groaned aloud, seeing that much time had been spent and he was worn out by the labor, and Amasis took this to heart as an omen and did not allow them to haul it any further. Others on the other hand say that a man was killed by it, one of those heaving it with levers, and that it was not drawn in for that reason.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 391
paragraphs: Amasis also dedicated in all the other important temples works worth seeing for their size, including at Memphis the colossal statue that lies on its back in front of the temple of Hephaistos, whose length is seventy-five feet. On the same base, made of the same stone, stand two colossal statues each twenty feet in length, one on each side of the large statue. There is also another stone statue of the same size at Saïs, lying in the same manner as the one at Memphis. Moreover, Amasis was the one who built and completed for Isis her temple at Memphis, which is of great size and very much worth seeing.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 392
paragraphs: In the reign of Amasis, Egypt is said to have been more prosperous than at any previous time, both from what the river gave to the land and from what the land gave to its people. The country at that time contained twenty thousand inhabited cities. It was Amasis who established the law that every Egyptian must appear once a year before the governor of his district and declare his means of livelihood. Anyone who failed to do so, or could not prove he lived by honest means, was punished by death. The Athenian Solon brought this law from Egypt and established it at Athens. It is an excellent law, and I hope it stays in force forever.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 393
paragraphs: Amasis became a friend of the Greeks. Among other tokens of friendship, he granted the city of Naucratis to Greeks who came to Egypt, giving them a place to live. For those who did not wish to settle but came on trading voyages, he set aside areas where they could erect altars and sacred precincts to their gods. The largest, most famous, and most used of these is called the Hellenion. It was founded jointly by the following cities: of the Ionians, Chios, Teos, Phocaea, and Clazomenae; of the Dorians, Rhodes, Cnidos, Halicarnassos, and Phaselis; of the Aeolians, Mytilene alone. The Hellenion belongs to these cities, and they are the ones who appoint the market supervisors. Other cities that claim a share have no right to one. Separately, the Aeginetans established a precinct of Zeus, the Samians one of Hera, and the Milesians one of Apollo.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 394
paragraphs: In ancient times, Naucratis was the only port of entry in Egypt. Anyone who arrived at any other mouth of the Nile was required to swear he had not come there intentionally. Having sworn his innocence, he had to sail his ship to the Canobic mouth. If contrary winds made this impossible, he had to transport his cargo by barge around the Delta to Naucratis. Such was the privileged status of Naucratis.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 395
paragraphs: Moreover, when the Amphictyons had let out the contract for building the temple which now stands at Delphi, agreeing to pay a sum of three hundred talents — for the temple that formerly stood there had burned down of itself — the people of Delphi had to provide a quarter of the payment. Accordingly the Delphians went round to various cities collecting contributions, and in doing so they got as much from Egypt as from anywhere, for Amasis gave them a thousand talents’ weight of alum, while the Greeks who lived in Egypt gave them twenty pounds of silver.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 396
paragraphs: Amasis also made a pact of friendship and alliance with the people of Cyrene. He decided to take a wife from there—either because he wanted a Greek wife, or simply out of friendship for Cyrene. He married a woman named Ladice, said by some to be the daughter of Battus, by others of Arcesilaus, and by still others of Critobulos, a prominent citizen. When Amasis lay with her, he found himself unable to consummate the marriage, though he had no trouble with his other wives. After this continued for some time, Amasis told Ladice he believed she had used witchcraft on him, and that nothing could save her from the worst death of any woman. Ladice denied everything, but Amasis was unmoved. So she silently vowed to Aphrodite that if Amasis lay with her successfully that night, she would send a statue to the goddess at Cyrene. Immediately after the vow, Amasis was able to perform. From then on, every time he came to her, he succeeded. He loved her very much after that. Ladice fulfilled her vow and sent the statue, which was still in good condition in my time, set up facing outward from the city of Cyrene. When Cambyses conquered Egypt and learned who Ladice was, he sent her home to Cyrene unharmed.

chapters.title: Book II — Euterpe, Chapter 397
paragraphs: Amasis also dedicated offerings in Greece. At Cyrene, he gave a gold-plated image of Athena and a painted portrait of himself. At the temple of Athena at Lindos, he gave two stone statues and a remarkable corselet of linen. At the temple of Hera on Samos, he gave two wooden portraits of himself, which were still standing in my time in the great temple, behind the doors. He made these gifts to Samos because of the friendship between himself and Polycrates, son of Aeaces. His gifts to Lindos were not because of any friendship but because the temple of Athena at Lindos was said to have been founded by the daughters of Danaos, who landed there while fleeing the sons of Aegyptus. Those were the offerings of Amasis. He was the first man to conquer Cyprus and compel it to pay tribute.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 398
paragraphs: It was against this Amasis that Cambyses son of Cyrus was making his expedition, taking with him not only the other peoples over whom he ruled but also Greeks, both Ionians and Aiolians; and the cause of the expedition was as follows. Cambyses sent an envoy to Egypt and asked Amasis to give him his daughter, making the request on the advice of an Egyptian who urged it on Amasis out of a grudge, for the following reason: at the time when Cyrus had sent to Amasis asking for a physician of the eyes, the best in Egypt, Amasis had picked him out of all the physicians in Egypt and torn him away from his wife and children, and handed him over to Persia. Having this grievance, the Egyptian urged Cambyses on by advising him to ask Amasis for his daughter, so that Amasis would either be grieved if he gave her, or if he refused to give her, would offend Cambyses. Amasis, vexed and afraid of the power of the Persians, knew neither how to give nor how to refuse, for he was well aware that Cambyses meant to keep her not as a wife but as a concubine. Reckoning it this way, he did the following: there was a daughter of the former king Apries, very tall and of comely form, the only surviving member of his house, and her name was Nitetis. This girl Amasis adorned with fine clothing and gold, and sent off to Persia as his own daughter. But after a time, when Cambyses greeted her, calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: “O king, you do not realize how you have been deceived by Amasis; for he dressed me up in finery and sent me off, giving me to you as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries, against whom Amasis rose up along with the Egyptians and murdered him, though he was his lord and master.” These words, and the occasion that produced them, led Cambyses son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 399
paragraphs: Such is the account given by the Persians; but as for the Egyptians, they claim Cambyses as one of their own, saying that he was born of this very daughter of Apries, for they say it was Cyrus who sent to Amasis for his daughter, not Cambyses. In saying this, however, they are not speaking correctly; nor can they have failed to notice — for the Egyptians are as well acquainted as any other people with the laws and customs of the Persians — first, that it is not their custom for a bastard to become king when there is a son born of a true marriage; and secondly, that Cambyses was the son of Cassandane, daughter of Pharnaspes, a man of the Achaimenid family, and not the son of the Egyptian woman. But they distort the truth of history, claiming kinship with the house of Cyrus. So much, then, for these matters.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 400
paragraphs: The following story is also told, which for my part I do not believe — that one of the Persian women came in to visit the wives of Cyrus, and when she saw children of comely form and tall standing by Cassandane's side, she loudly praised them and expressed great admiration; and Cassandane, who was the wife of Cyrus, said: “Nevertheless, though I am the mother of such children as these, Cyrus treats me with dishonor and holds in honor the woman he has brought in from Egypt.” Thus she spoke, they say, being vexed by Nitetis, and upon that Cambyses, the elder of her sons, said: “For this reason, mother, when I am grown to be a man, I will turn what is above in Egypt to below and what is below to above.” He is reported to have said this when he was perhaps about ten years old, and the women were astonished at it. He, they say, always kept it in mind, and so at last, when he had become a man and had obtained royal power, he made the expedition against Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 401
paragraphs: Another thing also contributed to this expedition, which was as follows. There was among the foreign mercenaries of Amasis a man who was by race from Halicarnassos, named Phanes, who was both capable in judgment and valiant in matters of war. This Phanes, having (as one may suppose) some quarrel with Amasis, fled away from Egypt in a ship, desiring to come to speech with Cambyses. Since he was of no small repute among the mercenaries and was very closely acquainted with all the affairs of Egypt, Amasis pursued him and considered it a matter of some importance to capture him. He pursued him by sending after him the most trusted of his eunuchs with a trireme, who captured him in Lykia; but having captured him, he did not bring him back to Egypt, since Phanes got the better of him by a trick — he made his guards drunk and escaped to Persia. So when Cambyses had resolved to march against Egypt and was in difficulty about the march — how he should get safely through the waterless region — this man came to him and, besides informing him about the other affairs of Amasis, also advised him concerning the march, telling him to send to the king of the Arabians and ask him for safe passage through this region.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 402
paragraphs: By this way alone is there a known entrance into Egypt. From Phoenicia to the borders of the city of Cadytis belongs to the Syrians known as Palestinians; and from Cadytis — which is a city I suppose not much smaller than Sardis — from this city, the coastal trading stations as far as the city of Ienysos belong to the king of Arabia, and then from Ienysos onward the country belongs to the Syrians again, as far as the Serbonian lake, along which Mount Casion stretches toward the sea. After the Serbonian lake, in which the story is that Typhon is hidden, from this point onward the land is Egypt. The region lying between the city of Ienysos on the one hand and Mount Casion and the Serbonian lake on the other — which is of no small extent, as much as a three days' journey — is grievously lacking in water.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 403
paragraphs: I will now mention something that few travelers to Egypt have noticed. Twice a year, earthenware jars full of wine are imported to Egypt from all parts of Greece and from Phoenicia. Yet you almost never see an empty wine jar anywhere in Egypt. What happens to them all?

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 404
paragraphs: In what way, then, one will ask, are they used up? This also I will explain. The head-man of each place must collect all the earthenware jars from his own town and convey them to Memphis, and those at Memphis must fill them with water and carry them to these same waterless regions of Syria. So the jars, which come regularly to Egypt and are emptied there, are carried off to Syria to be added to those that have come before. It was the Persians who thus prepared this approach to Egypt, supplying it with water in the manner described, from the time when they first took possession of Egypt. But at the time I speak of, since water was not yet provided, Cambyses, acting on the advice of his Halicarnassian guest, sent envoys to the Arabian king and asked from him — and obtained — safe passage, having given him pledges of friendship and received them from him in return.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 405
paragraphs: The Persians provided this water supply route through the desert after they conquered Egypt. But at the time of Cambyses' invasion, when the route had no water stations, Cambyses took Phanes' advice and sent a messenger to the Arabian king to request safe passage, giving and receiving pledges of friendship. No people revere the oath of friendship more than the Arabs. When two men wish to make a pledge, a third man stands between them. Using a sharp stone, he makes a cut on the inside of each man's palm near the base of the middle fingers. He takes a thread from each man's cloak, dips it in blood, and smears seven stones placed between them, invoking Dionysus and Ourania. When this ceremony is complete, the man who made the pledge introduces the foreigner (or fellow citizen, if the pledge is between citizens) to his friends, and they too consider themselves bound by the oath. The Arabs recognize only two gods: Dionysus and Ourania. They say they cut their hair in the same style as Dionysus, shaving it in a circle around the head and cutting the temples short. They call Dionysus Orotalt and Ourania Alilat.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 406
paragraphs: So when the Arabian king had given his pledge of friendship to the men who had come to him from Cambyses, he arranged matters as follows: he took camel skins, filled them with water, and loaded them onto the backs of all the living camels he had, and driving them to the waterless region, there he awaited the army of Cambyses. This is the more credible of the accounts given, but the less credible must also be told, since it is a current story. There is a great river in Arabia called Corys, which runs out into the sea called Erythraian. From this river, it is said, the king of the Arabians, having had a conduit pipe made by stitching together raw ox-hides and other skins long enough to reach the waterless region, conveyed water through these, if you please, and had great cisterns dug in the waterless region to receive the water and preserve it. Now it is a journey of twelve days from the river to that waterless region, and the story adds that he conveyed the water by three conduit pipes to three different parts of it.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 407
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Psammenitos the son of Amasis was camped at the Pelusian mouth of the Nile, waiting for Cambyses. Cambyses did not find Amasis alive when he invaded Egypt. Amasis had died after a forty-four-year reign, during which he had suffered no great misfortune. When he died, he was embalmed and placed in the tomb he had built for himself in the temple. During the reign of his son Psammenitos, the Egyptians witnessed the greatest portent ever seen: it rained in Egyptian Thebes. Rain had never fallen there before that time, and has not fallen since, according to the Thebans themselves. In upper Egypt, rain simply does not fall. Yet on this occasion, it rained in Thebes—a drizzle.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 408
paragraphs: When the Persians had marched all the way through the waterless region and were encamped near the Egyptians intending to join battle, the foreign mercenaries of the Egyptian king, who were Greeks and Carians, holding a grudge against Phanes because he had brought a foreign-speaking army against Egypt, contrived against him as follows: Phanes had children whom he had left behind in Egypt. These they brought to their camp into the sight of their father, and they set up a mixing-bowl between the two camps. Then they brought up the children one by one and cut their throats so that the blood ran into the bowl. When they had gone through every one of the children, they brought wine and water and poured them into the bowl, and only after all the mercenaries had drunk of the blood did they join battle. Then, after a battle fought with great stubbornness in which very many fell on both sides, the Egyptians at length turned and fled.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 409
paragraphs: I was witness, moreover, to a great marvel, which the local inhabitants pointed out to me. Of the bones scattered about of those who fell in this fight — each side lying separately, since the bones of the Persians were heaped on one side, where they had been laid apart at the start, and those of the Egyptians on the other — the skulls of the Persians are so weak that if you hit them with just a pebble you will make a hole in them, while those of the Egyptians are so exceedingly strong that you would hardly break them by striking them with a large stone. The cause of this, they said — and I for my part readily believe them — is that the Egyptians from early childhood shave their heads, and the bone is thickened by exposure to the sun. This is also the reason why they do not become bald: for among the Egyptians you see fewer bald-headed men than among any other race. This, then, is why they have strong skulls. The reason the Persians have weak ones is that from infancy they keep their heads delicately in the shade by wearing tiaras, that is, felt caps. So much for that. I saw a similar thing at Papremis in the case of those who were slain along with Achaimenes son of Dareios, by Inaros the Libyan.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 410
paragraphs: When the Egyptians turned and fled from the battle, they fled in disorder; and as they were shut up in Memphis, Cambyses sent a ship from Mytilene up the river carrying a Persian herald to summon the Egyptians to terms of surrender. But when they saw the ship entering Memphis, they poured forth from the fortress in a body, destroyed the ship, and tore the men in it limb from limb, and carried their remains into the fortress. After this, the Egyptians, being besieged, surrendered in due course. The Libyans who dwell on the borders of Egypt, struck with terror by what had happened to Egypt, surrendered themselves without resistance, both imposing a tribute on themselves and sending presents. Likewise the people of Kyrene and Barca, equally terrified with the Libyans, acted in a similar way. Cambyses accepted the gifts from the Libyans graciously, but as for the gifts from the Kyrenians, finding fault with them — I suppose because they were too small in amount (for the Kyrenians in fact sent five hundred pounds of silver) — he took the silver by handfuls and scattered it with his own hand among his soldiers.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 411
paragraphs: On the tenth day after he received the surrender of the fortress of Memphis, Cambyses set the king of the Egyptians Psammenitos, who had been king for six months, to sit in the suburb of the city, in order to humiliate him. Him, along with other Egyptians, he placed there, and proceeded to test his spirit as follows. Having dressed his daughter in the clothing of a slave, he sent her out with a pitcher to fetch water, and with her he sent other maidens also, chosen from the daughters of the leading men, dressed just as the king's daughter was. As the maidens passed by their fathers with cries and lamentation, the rest of the men began to cry out and lament aloud, seeing their children being ill-used. But Psammenitos, when he saw it before his eyes and perceived what was happening, bent himself down to the earth. Then, after the water-bearers had passed by, Cambyses next sent his son together with two thousand other Egyptians of the same age, with ropes around their necks and bits placed in their mouths; and these were being led away to execution to avenge the death of the Mytilenians who had been destroyed at Memphis with their ship — for the Royal Judges had decided that for each man, ten of the noblest Egyptians should lose their lives in retaliation. When Psammenitos saw them passing by him and perceived that his son was leading the way to death, he did the same as he had done for his daughter, while the other Egyptians sitting around him lamented and showed signs of grief. When these too had passed by, it happened that a man of his table companions, advanced in years, who had been stripped of all his possessions and had nothing beyond what a beggar owns, and was asking alms from the soldiers, passed by Psammenitos son of Amasis and the Egyptians sitting in the suburb of the city. When Psammenitos saw him, he uttered a great cry of lamentation, called his companion by name, and beat himself on the head. Now there were, it seems, men set to watch him, who reported to Cambyses everything he did on each occasion as they passed. Cambyses marveled at what he had done and sent a messenger to ask him: “Psammenitos, your master Cambyses asks you why, when you saw your daughter mistreated and your son going to his death, you did not cry out or lament for them, whereas you honored with these signs of grief the beggar who, as he hears from others, is in no way related to you?” Thus he asked, and the other answered: “O son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great to lament aloud, but my companion's trouble called for tears, seeing that he has been stripped of great wealth and has come to beggary on the threshold of old age.” When this saying was reported by the messenger, it seemed to them well spoken. And, as the Egyptians report, Croesus shed tears — for he too, as fortune would have it, had accompanied Cambyses to Egypt — and the Persians present shed tears also, and some pity entered into Cambyses himself. He ordered that the life of Psammenitos's son be spared from among those being put to death, and he also ordered that Psammenitos himself be raised from his place in the suburb of the city and brought into his presence.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 412
paragraphs: As for the son, those who went for him found that he was no longer alive but had been cut down first of all; Psammenitos himself, however, they raised from his place and brought into the presence of Cambyses, with whom he continued to live for the rest of his time without suffering any violence. And if he had known how to keep himself from meddling with mischief, he would have received Egypt to rule over, since the Persians are accustomed to honor the sons of kings, and even when kings have revolted from them, they give back the power into the hands of their sons. That this is their established rule, one may judge by many instances besides, and especially by the case of Thannyras son of Inaros, who received back the power his father had held, and by that of Pausiris son of Amyrtaios, who also received back his father's power — though it is certain that no men ever to this time did more harm to the Persians than Inaros and Amyrtaios. As it was, however, Psammenitos devised evil and received the reward that was due: he was found to be inciting the Egyptians to revolt; and when this became known to Cambyses, Psammenitos drank bull's blood and died at once. So he came to his end.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 413
paragraphs: From Memphis Cambyses came to the city of Saïs with the purpose of doing what he in fact did. For when he had entered the palace of Amasis, he immediately ordered that the corpse of Amasis be brought out of its burial place. When this had been done, he commanded them to scourge it, pluck out its hair, and stab it, and to dishonor it in every other possible way. When they had done this until they were worn out — for the corpse, being embalmed, withstood the violence and did not fall apart in any place — Cambyses ordered it consumed with fire, thereby enjoining a thing not permitted by religion; for the Persians hold fire to be a god. To consume corpses with fire is by no means according to the custom of either people: of the Persians for the reason mentioned, since they say it is not right to give the dead body of a man to a god; while the Egyptians have the established belief that fire is a living wild beast that devours everything it catches, and when sated with the food it dies itself together with what it devours. It is by no means their custom to give the corpse of a man to wild beasts, which is why they embalm it, so that it may not be eaten by worms as it lies in the tomb. Thus Cambyses was ordering them to do what was not permitted by the customs of either people. However, the Egyptians say that it was not Amasis who suffered this outrage, but another Egyptian who was of the same bodily stature as Amasis; the Persians did this outrage to him, thinking they were doing it to Amasis. For they say that Amasis had learned from an oracle what was about to happen concerning himself after his death, and accordingly, to avert the evil threatening to come upon him, he buried the body of this man who was scourged within his own burial chamber near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body as far as possible in the innermost recess of the chamber. These instructions said to have been given by Amasis regarding his burial and the other man are not, in my opinion, ones that were really given at all; I think rather that the Egyptians make this pretense out of pride, with no good ground.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 414
paragraphs: After this Cambyses planned three separate expeditions: one against the Carthaginians, another against the Ammonians, and a third against the “Long-lived” Ethiopians, who dwell in that part of Libya bordering the Southern Sea. In forming these plans, he resolved to send his naval force against the Carthaginians, a body chosen from his land army against the Ammonians, and as for the Ethiopians, to send spies first, both to see whether the so-called Table of the Sun truly existed among these Ethiopians, and in addition to this to spy out everything else as well — pretending, however, to be bearers of gifts for their king.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 415
paragraphs: The Table of the Sun is said to be this: a meadow outside the city, filled with the boiled meat of every kind of four-footed animal. The city's officials place the meat there at night. During the day, anyone who wishes may come and eat. The locals say the earth itself produces the food each night. That is the account of the so-called Table of the Sun.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 416
paragraphs: Such is the nature of the so-called Table of the Sun as described. So when Cambyses had resolved to send the spies, he at once sent for those of the Ichthyophagoi who understood the Ethiopian tongue to come from the city of Elephantine. While they were going to fetch these men, he gave the order for the fleet to sail against Carthage. But the Phoenicians said they would not do so, for they were bound not to by solemn vows, and they would not be acting piously by making an expedition against their own sons. Since the Phoenicians were unwilling, the rest were rendered unequal to the attempt. Thus the Carthaginians escaped being enslaved by the Persians; for Cambyses did not think it right to use force to compel the Phoenicians, both because they had delivered themselves over to the Persians of their own accord and because the entire naval force depended on the Phoenicians. The men of Cyprus too had delivered themselves over to the Persians and were joining in the expedition against Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 417
paragraphs: As soon as the Ichthyophagoi arrived at Cambyses from Elephantine, he sent them to the Ethiopians, instructing them what they should say and giving them gifts to carry: a purple garment, a collar of twisted gold with bracelets, an alabaster box of perfumed ointment, and a jar of palm wine. Now these Ethiopians to whom Cambyses was sending them are said to be the tallest and most handsome of all men; and besides other customs they are reported to differ from other men in, there is this particular one regarding their royal power — whichever of their nation they judge to be the tallest and to have strength in proportion to his stature, that man they appoint to reign over them.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 418
paragraphs: So when the Ichthyophagoi had come to this people, they presented their gifts to the king who ruled over them and said: “The king of the Persians Cambyses, wishing to become your friend and guest-friend, sent us with orders to come and speak with you, and he gives you these gifts, which are the things he himself most delights to use.” The Ethiopian, however, perceiving that they had come as spies, spoke to them as follows: “Neither did the king of the Persians send you bearing gifts because he thought it a matter of great importance to become my guest-friend, nor do you speak the truth — for you have come as spies of my kingdom — nor again is he a righteous man; for if he were righteous, he would not have coveted a land other than his own, nor would he be leading men into slavery at whose hands he has suffered no wrong. Now then, give him this bow and say these words: The king of the Ethiopians gives this advice to the king of the Persians, that when the Persians can draw bows of this size as easily as I draw this one, then he may march against the Long-lived Ethiopians, provided he be superior in numbers; but until then, let him feel gratitude to the gods that they do not put it into the minds of the sons of the Ethiopians to acquire another land in addition to their own.”

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 419
paragraphs: Having said this and having unbent the bow, he delivered it to those who had come. Then he took the purple garment and asked what it was and how it had been made. When the Ichthyophagoi told him the truth about the purple-fish and the dyeing of the fabric, he said that the men were deceitful and so were their garments. Next he asked about the twisted gold of the collar and the bracelets, and when the Ichthyophagoi explained how they were fashioned, the king burst into laughter and said, supposing them to be fetters, that in his country they had stronger fetters than these. Thirdly he asked about the perfumed ointment, and when they told him how it was made and how it was used for anointing, he said the same as he had said about the garment. Then when he came to the wine, and learned how it was made, he was exceedingly delighted with the taste of the drink, and asked besides what food the king ate and what was the longest time a Persian man lived. They told him he ate bread, explaining to him first how wheat was grown, and they said that eighty years was the longest term of life appointed for a Persian. In reply the Ethiopian said he did not wonder that they lived but a few years, when they fed on dung; for indeed they would not be able to live even as many years as this, if they did not renew their vigor with the drink — pointing to the wine — for in this respect, he said, his people were far behind the Persians.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 420
paragraphs: Then when the Ichthyophagoi asked the king in return about the length of days and the manner of life of his people, he answered that the majority of them reached the age of a hundred and twenty years, and some went beyond even this; their food was boiled flesh and their drink was milk. When the spies marveled at the number of years, he led them to a certain spring, in the water of which they washed and came out with their skin more sleek, as if it were a spring of oil; and from it came a scent as of violets. The water of this spring, the spies said, was so extraordinarily weak that nothing could float upon it, not wood nor anything lighter than wood — everything sank to the bottom. If this water they have is really such as it is said to be, it would no doubt be the cause why the people are so long-lived, since they use it for every purpose of life. Then when they left this spring, he led them to a prison for men, where all were bound in fetters of gold. Among these Ethiopians bronze is the rarest and most precious of all things. When they had seen the prison, they also saw the so-called Table of the Sun:

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 421
paragraphs: and after this they saw last of all their receptacles for dead bodies, which are said to be made of crystal in the following way. When they have dried the corpse, whether by the Egyptian method or by some other, they cover it entirely with plaster and then adorn it with painting, making the figure resemble the living man as closely as possible. After this they place around it a block of crystal hollowed out, for they dig this up in great quantities, and it is very easy to work. The dead body, being in the middle of the block, is visible through it, but produces no unpleasant smell nor any other unseemly effect, and all its parts are visible, just like the dead body itself. For a year the nearest relatives keep the block in their house, giving the dead man the first share of everything and offering him sacrifices; and after this period they carry it out and set it up around the city.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 422
paragraphs: After they had seen everything, the spies departed to go back; and when they reported these things, Cambyses was enraged at once and proceeded to march his army against the Ethiopians, not having ordered any provision of food nor even considered that he was proposing to march an army to the furthest ends of the earth. But, like one who is mad and not in his right senses, when he heard the report of the Ichthyophagoi he began the march, ordering those of the Greeks present to remain behind in Egypt, and taking with him the whole of his land force. When in the course of his march he had reached Thebes, he detached about fifty thousand of his army and ordered them to enslave the Ammonians and set fire to the seat of the oracle of Zeus, while he himself with the rest of his army went on against the Ethiopians. But before the army had covered a fifth of the way, all the provisions they had completely ran out; and then, after the provisions, the beasts of burden too were eaten up and were gone. Now if Cambyses, perceiving this, had changed his plan and led his army back, he would have been a wise man despite his first mistake; as it was, however, he paid no regard but went forward without stopping. The soldiers, therefore, as long as they could get anything from the ground, prolonged their lives by eating grass. But when they came to the sand, some did a fearful deed — out of each company of ten they selected one by lot and devoured him. When Cambyses heard this and was alarmed at their eating of one another, he gave up the expedition against the Ethiopians and set out to go back again, and arrived at Thebes having lost a great number of his army. Then from Thebes he came down to Memphis and allowed the Greeks to sail home.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 423
paragraphs: So fared the expedition against the Ethiopians. As for those of the Persians sent to march against the Ammonians, they set out from Thebes and went on their way with guides; and it is known that they reached the city of Oasis, inhabited by Samians said to be of the Aischrionian tribe, seven days' journey from Thebes over sandy desert — a place called in the Greek language the “Isle of the Blessed.” The army is said to have reached this point, but from there onward, except for the Ammonians themselves and those who have heard the story from them, no one can say anything about them; for they neither reached the Ammonians nor returned back. This is what the Ammonians themselves add to the story: they say that as the army was going from this Oasis through the sandy desert to attack them, and had reached a point about midway between them and the Oasis, while they were taking their morning meal a violent south wind blew upon them, and carrying with it heaps of desert sand, buried them under it, and so they disappeared and were seen no more. That, the Ammonians say, is what became of this army.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 424
paragraphs: When Cambyses arrived at Memphis, the sacred bull Apis appeared to the Egyptians. (The Greeks call him Epaphos.) As soon as Apis appeared, the Egyptians put on their finest clothes and began celebrating. Cambyses saw the Egyptians feasting and assumed they were celebrating his military disasters. He summoned the officials of Memphis and demanded to know why the Egyptians had held no festivities when he was in Memphis before but were doing so now, when he had returned with a diminished army. They told him that their god had appeared—something that happened only after long intervals—and that it was customary for all Egypt to celebrate when he came. Cambyses said they were liars and sentenced them to death for lying.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 425
paragraphs: Having put these men to death, he next summoned the priests into his presence; and when the priests answered him in the same manner, he said that if a tame god had come to the Egyptians, it would not escape his knowledge. Saying this, he ordered the priests to bring Apis into his presence, and they went to bring him. Now this Apis, or Epaphos, is a calf born of a cow that is not permitted afterwards to conceive any other offspring; and the Egyptians say that a flash of light comes down from heaven upon this cow, and from it she produces Apis. This calf that is called Apis is black and has the following signs: a white square upon the forehead, on the back the likeness of an eagle, double hairs in the tail, and on the tongue a mark like a beetle.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 426
paragraphs: This Apis (or Epaphos) is a calf born of a cow that can never conceive again. The Egyptians say a bolt of light strikes the cow from heaven and she conceives Apis. The calf they call Apis has these marks: it is black, with a white square on its forehead, the image of an eagle on its back, double hairs in its tail, and a scarab mark under its tongue. When the priests brought Apis, Cambyses—half mad as he was—drew his dagger and aimed for the bull's belly but struck its thigh. He laughed and said to the priests: "Wretched people, are these your gods—creatures of flesh and blood that feel the blade? This is a god worthy of the Egyptians. But you will not laugh at me and get away with it." He ordered the priests to be whipped and any Egyptian caught celebrating to be killed. So the festival was broken off. The priests were punished. Apis, wounded in the thigh, lay in the temple, weakening.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 427
paragraphs: When Apis had ended his life from the wound, the priests buried him without Cambyses's knowledge. But Cambyses, as the Egyptians say, immediately after this evil deed became completely mad — not having been really in his right senses even before that time. The first of his evil deeds was to put to death his brother Smerdis, who was his brother by the same father and same mother. This brother he had sent away from Egypt to Persia out of envy, because Smerdis alone of all the Persians had been able to draw the bow which the Ichthyophagoi brought from the Ethiopian king, to the extent of about two finger-breadths, while none of the other Persians had proved able to do so. Then when Smerdis had gone off to Persia, Cambyses saw a vision in his sleep of this kind: it seemed to him that a messenger came from Persia and reported that Smerdis, sitting upon the royal throne, had touched the heavens with his head. Fearing therefore lest his brother should kill him and reign in his place, he sent Prexaspes to Persia — the man he trusted most of all the Persians — with orders to kill him. Prexaspes accordingly went up to Susa and killed Smerdis; some say he took him out on a hunt and killed him there, others that he brought him to the Erythraian Sea and drowned him.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 428
paragraphs: This, they say, was the first beginning of Cambyses's evil deeds; and next, after this, he put to death his sister, who had accompanied him to Egypt and to whom he was also married, she being his sister by both parents. He had taken her in marriage in the following manner (for before this the Persians had not been accustomed at all to marry their sisters). Cambyses fell in love with one of his sisters and wished to take her to wife; so, since he had it in mind to do what was not customary, he called the Royal Judges and asked them whether there was any law permitting one who desired to marry his sister. Now the Royal Judges are men chosen from among the Persians, and they hold office until they die or until some injustice is found in them — that long, and no longer. They pronounce decisions for the Persians and are the expounders of the ancestral ordinances, and all matters are referred to them. When Cambyses asked them, they gave him an answer that was both upright and safe, saying that they had found no law permitting a brother to marry his sister, but apart from that they had found a law to the effect that the king of the Persians might do whatever he wished. Thus on one hand they did not tamper with the law out of fear of Cambyses, while at the same time, to avoid perishing themselves by upholding the law, they found another law alongside the one asked about, in favor of the man who wanted to marry his sisters. So Cambyses at that time took as his wife the one he was in love with, but not long afterwards he took another sister as well. Of these, it was the younger whom he put to death, she having accompanied him to Egypt.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 429
paragraphs: About her death, as about the death of Smerdis, two different stories are told. The Greeks say that Cambyses had pitted a lion cub against a puppy, and this wife of his was also watching. When the puppy was being overpowered, another whelp, its brother, broke its chain and came to its aid; and having become two instead of one, the whelps then got the better of the cub. Cambyses was pleased at the sight, but she, sitting beside him, began to weep. Cambyses noticed and asked her why she wept, and she said she had wept when she saw that the whelp had come to help its brother, because she remembered Smerdis and perceived that no one would come to his aid. The Greeks say it was for this saying that she was killed by Cambyses. The Egyptians, however, say that as they were sitting at table, the wife took a lettuce and pulled off the leaves all round, then asked her husband whether the lettuce was more beautiful stripped like this or with leaves on, and he said “with leaves on.” She then spoke thus: “Yet you once produced the likeness of this lettuce, when you stripped bare the house of Cyrus.” Moved to anger, he leapt upon her, and she, being pregnant, miscarried and died.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 430
paragraphs: These were the acts of madness done by Cambyses toward those of his own family, whether his madness was produced really on account of Apis or from some other cause, as many ills are wont to seize upon men; for it is said, moreover, that Cambyses had from birth a certain grievous malady — the one called by some the “sacred” disease. And it was certainly nothing strange that, when the body was suffering from a grievous malady, the mind should not be sound either.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 431
paragraphs: The following are also acts of madness he did to the other Persians. To Prexaspes, the man he honored most and who used to carry his messages — whose son, moreover, was cupbearer to Cambyses, no small honor itself — it is said that he spoke as follows: “Prexaspes, what kind of a man do the Persians consider me to be, and what do they say concerning me?” He answered: “Master, in all other respects you are greatly praised, but they say you are overly given to the love of wine.” So he spoke concerning the Persians; and upon that Cambyses was roused to anger and answered thus: “It appears, then, that the Persians say I am given to wine, and that therefore I am beside myself and not in my right mind; and their earlier praise was not sincere.” For before this, it seems, when the Persians and Croesus were sitting with him in council, Cambyses had asked them what kind of a man they thought he was compared with his father Cyrus; and they had answered that he was better than his father, for he not only possessed everything his father had possessed but had also added Egypt and the Sea. So said the Persians; but Croesus, who was present and was not satisfied with their judgment, spoke thus to Cambyses: “To me, O son of Cyrus, you do not seem to be equal to your father, for you do not yet have such a son as he left behind him in you.” Hearing this, Cambyses was pleased and commended the judgment of Croesus.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 432
paragraphs: So recalling this, he said in anger to Prexaspes: “Learn then for yourself now whether the Persians speak the truth, or whether, when they say this, it is they themselves who are out of their senses. For if I, shooting at your son there standing before the entrance of the chamber, hit him in the very middle of the heart, the Persians will be shown to be speaking falsely; but if I miss, then you may say the Persians are speaking truly and that I am not in my right mind.” Having said this, he drew his bow and hit the boy; and when the boy had fallen down, it is said that he ordered them to cut open his body and examine the place where he was hit, and as the arrow was found to be stuck in the heart, he laughed and was delighted, and said to the boy's father: “Prexaspes, it has now been made clear, as you see, that I am not mad, but that it is the Persians who are out of their senses; and now tell me: whom of all men did you ever see before this time hit the mark so well in shooting?” Then Prexaspes, seeing that the man was not in his right senses and fearing for himself, said: “Master, I think that not even God himself could have hit the mark so fairly.” Thus he acted at that time. On another occasion he condemned twelve Persians, men equal to the best, on a trivial charge, and buried them alive head downward.

chapters.title: Book III — Thalia, Chapter 433
paragraphs: When he was doing these things, Croesus the Lydian thought it right to admonish him with the following words: “O king, do not indulge your youthful heat and passion in everything, but restrain and hold yourself back. It is a good thing to be prudent, and forethought is wise.
