Now the revenues came to them from the mainland and from the mines: from the gold mines in Scapte Hyle there came in usually eighty talents a year, and from those on Thasos itself a smaller amount than this—but so much that, in general, the Thasians, without any tax on the produce of their soil, had a revenue from the mainland and from the mines amounting yearly to two hundred talents, and when the amount was at its highest, to three hundred.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 47
paragraphs: I myself saw these mines, and by far the most marvelous of them were those the Phoenicians discovered, who made the first settlement on this island with Thasus; and the island took the name it now has from this Thasus the Phoenician. These Phoenician mines are in the part of Thasos between the places called Aenyra and Coenyra, and opposite Samothrace, where there is a great mountain that has been entirely turned up in the search for metal. So much for that matter; and the Thasians, at the king's command, both razed their walls and brought all their ships to Abdera.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 48
paragraphs: After this, Darius began to test the Hellenes—what they intended, whether to go to war with him or surrender. He sent out heralds, therefore, and appointed them to go, some to one place and some to another, throughout Hellas, ordering them to demand earth and water for the king. These, I say, he sent to Hellas; and meanwhile he was sending other heralds to his own tributary cities along the seacoast, and bidding them have warships built, and vessels to transport horses as well.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 49
paragraphs: These cities, then, were preparing these things; and meanwhile, when the heralds had come to Hellas, many of those who lived on the mainland gave what the Persian demanded, and all those who lived on the islands did so, whomever the heralds came to with their demand. The islanders, I say, gave earth and water to Darius, and among them also those of Aegina. When these had done so, the Athenians at once went urgently against them, supposing that the Aeginetans had given in with hostile intent against themselves, so as to make an expedition against them together with the Persians; and they were also glad to get hold of a pretext against them. So they went back and forth to Sparta and accused the Aeginetans of what they had done, as having proved themselves traitors to Hellas.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 50
paragraphs: In consequence of this accusation, Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, king of the Spartans, crossed over to Aegina intending to seize the Aeginetans most guilty in the matter. But as he was trying to seize them, certain of the Aeginetans opposed him, and among them especially Crius son of Polycritus, who said that Cleomenes should not carry off a single Aeginetan with impunity, for he was doing this (he said) without the authority of the Spartan state, having been persuaded to it by the Athenians with money; otherwise he would have come and seized them in company with the other king. He said this because of a message received from Demaratus. Then Cleomenes, as he was leaving Aegina, asked Crius what his name was, and he told him the truth; and Cleomenes said to him: “Now then, Ram, bind your horns with bronze, for you will have a great trouble to contend with shortly.” (The Greek word krios also means “ram.”)

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 51
paragraphs: Meanwhile Demaratus son of Ariston had stayed behind in Sparta and was bringing charges against Cleomenes. He too was king of the Spartans, but of the inferior house—which, however, is inferior in no other way, since it is descended from the same ancestor; the house of Eurysthenes has always been honored more, apparently because he was the elder brother.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 52
paragraphs: For the Lacedaemonians, who on this matter agree with none of the poets, say that Aristodemus son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, being their king, himself led them (and not the sons of Aristodemus) to this land which they now possess. Then, not long afterward, the wife of Aristodemus, whose name was Argeia—she was the daughter, they say, of Autesion son of Tisamenus son of Thersander son of Polyneices—is said to have borne twins; and Aristodemus lived only long enough to see his children, and then ended his life by sickness. The Lacedaemonians of that time resolved, according to established custom, to make the elder of the children their king; but they did not know which of them they should take, because they were alike and of equal size. When they were unable to find out, or even before this, they inquired of their mother; but she said that even she herself did not know one from the other. This she said, although she actually knew quite well, because she desired that somehow both might be made kings. The Lacedaemonians were therefore in a difficulty; and being in a difficulty, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do in the matter. The Pythian priestess bade them regard both children as their kings, but honor most the first in age. So, they say, did the priestess give them her answer; and when the Lacedaemonians were no less at a loss how to find out the elder of them, a Messenian named Panites made a suggestion to them. This Panites, I say, suggested to the Lacedaemonians that they watch the mother and see which of the children she washed and fed first of the two; and if she was seen to do this always in the same order, they would have all they were seeking and wished to discover; but if she too was uncertain and did it in a different order at different times, it would be plain to them that she had no more knowledge than anyone else, and they must turn to some other way. The Spartans, following the Messenian's suggestion, watched the mother of the sons of Aristodemus and found that she gave preference thus to the firstborn, both in feeding and in washing, not knowing she was being watched. They therefore took the child honored by its mother and brought it up in the public hall as the firstborn, and named it Eurysthenes; and the other was called Procles. When they had grown up, both of them, they say, were at variance with one another throughout their whole lives, although they were brothers, and their descendants continued in the same way.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 53
paragraphs: This is the account given by the Lacedaemonians alone of all the Hellenes; but what follows I write in accordance with the general report of the Hellenes: namely, that the names of these kings of the Dorians are correctly enumerated by the Hellenes back to Perseus son of Danaë (leaving out the god), and are shown to be of Hellenic stock—for from that point they were already reckoned as Hellenes. I said “up to Perseus,” and did not trace the descent from a yet higher point, because no name of a mortal father is given for Perseus, as Amphitryon is for Heracles. With good reason, then, I have said “rightly up to Perseus”; but if one enumerates their ancestors in succession going back from Danaë daughter of Acrisius, the rulers of the Dorians will prove to be Egyptians by direct descent.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 54
paragraphs: Thus I have traced the descent according to the account given by the Hellenes; but according to the story as told by the Persians, Perseus himself was an Assyrian and became a Hellene, whereas the ancestors of Perseus were not Hellenes. As for the ancestors of Acrisius—who according to this account were not related to Perseus at all—they say that these were, as the Hellenes also report, Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 55
paragraphs: Let it suffice to have said so much about these matters; and as to the question how and by what exploits they, being Egyptians, received the sceptres of royalty over the Dorians, we shall omit these things, since others have told them. But the matters with which other narrators have not dealt—of these I will make mention.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 56
paragraphs: These are the royal rights that the Spartans have given their kings: two priesthoods, of Zeus Lacedaemon and Zeus Uranios; the right to make war against whatever land they choose, and that no Spartan shall hinder this right—or, if he does, he shall be subject to the curse; that on campaigns the kings shall go out first and return last; that a hundred picked men shall be their guard on expeditions; and that they shall use in their marches to war as many cattle as they wish, and take both the hides and the chine-portions of all that are sacrificed.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 57
paragraphs: These are their privileges in war; and in peacetime things have been assigned to them as follows. If any sacrifice is performed at public expense, it is the kings' privilege to sit down to the feast before all others, and for the attendants to begin with them first, and to serve each of them a portion double that given to the other guests; they shall have the first pouring of libations and the hides of the animals slain in sacrifice. On every new moon and seventh day of the month, each of them shall be delivered at public expense a full-grown victim at the temple of Apollo, a measure of barley-groats, and a Laconian quarter of wine; at all the games they shall have seats of honor specially set aside for them. Moreover, it is their privilege to appoint as protectors of strangers (proxenoi) whomever they wish of the citizens, and each to choose two “Pythians” (now the Pythians are men sent to consult the god at Delphi, and they eat with the kings at public expense). If the kings do not come to the public dinner, the rule is that there shall be sent out to their houses two quarts of barley-groats for each and half a pint of wine; but if they are present, they shall be given double shares of everything. They shall be honored in the same way when they have been invited to dinner by private persons. The kings, it is ordained, shall also have charge of the oracles given, but the Pythians too shall have knowledge of them. The rule is moreover that the kings alone give decision on the following cases only: about the maiden who inherits her father's property, namely who ought to have her if her father has not betrothed her to anyone, and about public ways; and if any man wishes to adopt a son, it must be done in the presence of the kings. It is ordained that they shall sit in council with the Senators, who are twenty-eight in number; and if they do not come, those of the Senators most closely related to them shall have the kings' privileges, and give two votes besides their own, making three in all.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 58
paragraphs: These rights have been assigned by the Spartan state to the kings during their lifetime; and after they are dead, these which follow. Horsemen ride around and announce what has happened throughout the whole of the Laconian land, and in the city women go about and strike on a copper kettle. Whenever this happens, two free persons from each household must go into mourning, a man and a woman, and heavy penalties are appointed for those who fail to do this. Now the custom of the Lacedaemonians concerning the deaths of their kings is the same as that of the barbarians who dwell in Asia, for most of the barbarians practice the same customs regarding the death of their kings. Whenever a king of the Lacedaemonians dies, from the whole territory of Lacedaemon, not counting the Spartans, a certain fixed number of the “dwellers round” (the perioeci) are compelled to go to the funeral ceremony.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 59
paragraphs: When many thousands of these and of the Helots and of the Spartans themselves have been gathered together in the same place, with their women intermingled, they beat their foreheads with a will and make lamentation without stint, saying that the one who has died last of their kings was the best of all. Whenever any of their kings has been killed in war, they prepare an image to represent him, laid on a couch with fine coverings, and carry it out to be buried. After the burial, no assembly is held among them for ten days, nor any meeting for the choice of magistrates; but they keep mourning during these days. In another respect too they resemble the Persians: when the king is dead and another is appointed king, this newly incoming king releases any Spartan who was a debtor to the king or to the state—just as among the Persians the new king who comes to the throne remits to all the cities the arrears of tribute due.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 60
paragraphs: In the following respect too the Lacedaemonians resemble the Egyptians: their heralds, flute-players, and cooks inherit the crafts of their fathers, and a flute-player is the son of a flute-player, a cook of a cook, and a herald of a herald. Other men do not lay hands on the office because they have loud and clear voices and so shut them out of it; they practice their craft by inheritance from their fathers.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Thus are these things done; and at the time of which we speak, while Cleomenes was in Aegina doing deeds which were for the common service of Hellas, Demaratus was bringing charges against him—not so much because he cared about the Aeginetans as because he felt envy and jealousy of him. So Cleomenes, after he returned from Aegina, planned to depose Demaratus from the kingship, making an attempt upon him on the following grounds. Ariston, being king in Sparta and having married two wives, yet had no children born to him; and since he did not acknowledge that he himself was the cause of this, he married a third wife, and married her in this way. He had a friend, a man of the Spartans, to whom of all the citizens Ariston was most attached; and this man happened to have a wife who was by far the fairest of all the women in Sparta, one who had become the fairest after having been the foulest. For since she was ugly in appearance, her nurse, considering that she was the daughter of wealthy parents and was ill-favored in looks, and seeing moreover that her parents were distressed by it, devised the following plan. Every day she would carry her to the temple of Helen, which is at the place called Therapne, lying above the temple of Phoebus; and whenever the nurse carried her there, she would place her before the image and pray to the goddess to deliver the child from her ugliness. Once, as the nurse was leaving the temple, it is said that a woman appeared to her, and having appeared, asked what she was carrying in her arms; and she told her she was carrying a child. At this the other bade her show the child to her, but she refused, for she had been forbidden by the parents to show it to anyone; but the woman kept pressing her to show it. So, perceiving that the woman really wanted to see it, the nurse showed her the child. Then the woman stroked the child's head and said that she would be the fairest of all the women in Sparta; and from that day her appearance was changed. Afterwards, when she came of age, she was married to Agetus son of Alcides, this friend of Ariston of whom we spoke.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 62
paragraphs: Now Ariston, it seems, was continually stung by desire for this woman, and so contrived as follows. He made an agreement with his comrade, whose wife this woman was, that he would give him as a gift any one thing he chose from his own possessions; and he asked his comrade to make him a like return. The comrade, fearing nothing for his wife, since he saw that Ariston too had a wife, agreed; and on these terms they imposed oaths on one another. After this, Ariston on his side gave that which Agetus had chosen from Ariston's treasures, whatever the thing was; then he himself, seeking to obtain the like return, tried to take away his comrade's wife. The comrade said that he consented to give anything else except this one thing only; but at last, compelled by the oath and by the treacherous deception, he allowed her to be taken from him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 63
paragraphs: Thus Ariston had brought into his house the third wife, having dismissed the second; and this wife, not having fulfilled the ten months but in a shorter period of time, bore him the Demaratus of whom we were speaking. One of his servants reported to him, as he was sitting in council with the Ephors, that a son had been born to him. He then, knowing the time when he had taken the wife, and reckoning the months on his fingers, said, denying with an oath: “The child would not be mine.” The Ephors heard this but thought it a matter of no importance at the time; and the child grew up, and Ariston repented of what he had said, for he thought Demaratus was certainly his own son. He gave him the name “Demaratus” for this reason: because before these events the Spartan people as a whole had made a vow, praying that a son might be born to Ariston as one who was preeminent in renown above all the kings who had ever arisen in Sparta.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 64
paragraphs: For this reason the name Demaratus (“prayer of the people”) was given to him. As time went on, Ariston died, and Demaratus obtained the kingdom; but it was fated, apparently, that these things should become known and cause Demaratus to be deposed from his kingdom. That is why Demaratus came to be greatly at variance with Cleomenes, both on that earlier occasion when he withdrew the army from Eleusis, and especially now, when Cleomenes had crossed over to seize those Aeginetans who had gone over to the Medes.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Cleomenes, eager to take revenge on Demaratus, arranged matters with Leotychides, son of Menares, son of Agis — a man of the same royal house as Demaratus. The condition was this: if Leotychides were installed as king in Demaratus's place, he would join Cleomenes on the campaign against the Aeginetans. Leotychides already had reason enough to hate Demaratus, and the cause was as follows. Leotychides had been betrothed to Percalos, the daughter of Chilon son of Demarmenos. But Demaratus plotted against him and deprived him of the marriage, seizing Percalos himself beforehand and taking her for his own wife. This was the origin of the feud between Leotychides and Demaratus. And now, at Cleomenes's prompting, Leotychides stood up and swore an accusation against Demaratus, claiming that he had no right to the throne of Sparta because he was not truly the son of Ariston. After this formal charge he pressed his suit, recalling the old remark that Ariston had made when his servant came to announce that a son had been born to him: Ariston, counting up the months, had denied with an oath that the child was his. Leotychides seized on this utterance and argued that Demaratus was not Ariston's son and therefore had no right to rule Sparta. As witnesses he produced those Ephors who happened to have been sitting in council with Ariston at the time and had heard him say it.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 66
paragraphs: At last, since the dispute went on without resolution, the Spartans decided to send to Delphi and ask the oracle whether Demaratus was indeed the son of Ariston. The question was referred to the Pythian prophetess through Cleomenes's arrangement, and Cleomenes won over to his side Cobon son of Aristophantus, the most powerful man in Delphi. Cobon then persuaded Perialla, the prophetess of the oracle, to give the answer that Cleomenes wanted. So when the envoys arrived and put their question to the god, the Pythia declared that Demaratus was not the son of Ariston. Later, however, the whole business came to light: Cobon was driven into exile from Delphi, and Perialla was removed from her office as prophetess.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 67
paragraphs: That is how the deposing of Demaratus from the kingship came about. As for his flight as an exile from Sparta to the Medes, it happened on account of an insult, as I shall now relate. After he had been stripped of the crown, Demaratus was serving in a public office to which he had been elected. It was the time of the festival of the Gymnopaediae, and Demaratus was among the spectators. Leotychides, who had now become king in his place, sent his servant to ask Demaratus mockingly and insultingly what sort of thing it was to hold a magistracy after having been king. Stung by the question, Demaratus replied that he himself had now had experience of both, whereas Leotychides had not — and that this question would prove the beginning of either endless misfortune or endless good fortune for the Lacedaemonians. With these words he veiled his head, left the theater, and went home. There he at once made ready and sacrificed an ox to Zeus, and after the sacrifice he summoned his mother.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 68
paragraphs: When his mother came, he placed some of the inner parts of the sacrificed animal in her hands and entreated her, saying: “Mother, I beg you, in the name of the other gods and above all of this Zeus, guardian of our household, to tell me the truth — who is really and truly my father? For Leotychides, in his quarrel with me, claimed that you came to Ariston already pregnant by your former husband. Others, repeating what is surely an empty tale, say that you went in to one of the servants, the keeper of the asses, and that I am his son. I therefore beseech you by the gods to tell me the truth. For if you did any of the things that are said of you, you did not do them alone — many other women have done the same. And the common report in Sparta is that there was no seed in Ariston capable of begetting children; for if there had been, his earlier wives would also have borne him children.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 69
paragraphs: Thus he spoke, and she answered him as follows: “My son, since you entreat me so earnestly to tell you the truth, the whole truth shall be told. When Ariston had brought me into his house, on the third night an apparition came to me in the likeness of Ariston; and after lying with me it placed upon me the garlands it was wearing and then went away. Soon afterward Ariston himself came. When he saw me wearing the garlands, he asked who had given them to me, and I said that he had. He denied it, but I began to swear to it, saying that he did wrong to deny it, for he had come only a short while before, lain with me, and given me the garlands. Then Ariston, seeing that I was taking an oath, realized that the matter was of the gods. And so indeed it was: the garlands were found to come from the hero-shrine that stands beside the outer door of our house — the shrine they call the temple of Astrabacus — and the diviners likewise answered that it was this very hero. So, my son, you now have the whole truth, as much as you wished to learn. You are begotten either of this hero — and Astrabacus is your father — or else of Ariston himself, for it was on that night that I conceived you. As for the point on which your enemies most eagerly seize — that Ariston, when your birth was announced, declared in the hearing of many that you were not his son, because the ten months had not yet been completed — he spoke that word out of ignorance of such matters. Women bring forth children at the ninth month as well, and even at the seventh, and not all after the full ten. I bore you, my son, at the seventh month; and Ariston himself before long recognized that he had uttered that saying in folly. Accept then no other reports about your birth; you have heard the entire truth. And as for Leotychides and all who spread such tales — may their own wives bear them children by keepers of asses!”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Having heard what he wished to learn, Demaratus took provisions for the road and set out, pretending that he was going to Delphi to consult the oracle — but his destination was Elis. The Lacedaemonians, suspecting he was trying to escape, set off in pursuit; but before they caught him Demaratus had already crossed from Elis to Zacynthus. The Spartans crossed after him and seized his attendants, though the Zacynthians refused to give up the man himself. From there Demaratus crossed over into Asia, to the court of King Darius, who received him with great honor as a guest and granted him land and cities. That is how Demaratus came to Asia — a man who had distinguished himself among the Lacedaemonians in many ways, by both deeds and counsels, and who, above all, had won them an Olympic victory in the four-horse chariot race, the only king of Sparta ever to do so.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 71
paragraphs: With Demaratus deposed, Leotychides son of Menares succeeded to the kingship. A son was born to him named Zeuxidemus, whom some of the Spartans called Cyniscus. Zeuxidemus, however, never became king of Sparta, for he died before Leotychides, leaving behind a son, Archidamus. After losing Zeuxidemus, Leotychides took a second wife, Eurydame, the sister of Menios and daughter of Diactorides. By her he had no male issue but a daughter, Lampito, whom Archidamus son of Zeuxidemus married, Leotychides himself giving her in marriage.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Leotychides, however, did not himself live out his old age in Sparta; he paid a penalty for what had been done to Demaratus, and this is how. He went as commander of the Lacedaemonians on a campaign into Thessaly, and although he could have reduced the whole country to subjection, he accepted a large bribe instead. He was caught in the act right there in camp, sitting on a glove stuffed full of money. Brought to trial, he was exiled from Sparta and his house was razed to the ground. He went into exile at Tegea and ended his life there.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 73
paragraphs: All of that happened later. At the time of which I am speaking, Cleomenes — having brought the affair of Demaratus to a successful end — at once took Leotychides with him and marched against the Aeginetans, furious at the insults they had offered him. The Aeginetans, now that both kings had come against them, decided that further resistance was pointless. The Spartans picked out ten of the most prominent men of Aegina, ranked by wealth and by birth, and took them off as prisoners — among them Crios son of Polycritus and Casambus son of Aristocrates, who held the greatest power on the island. Having carried them to Attica, they handed them over for safekeeping to the Athenians, who were Aegina's bitterest enemies.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 74
paragraphs: After this, when it came to light that he had engineered the plot against Demaratus, Cleomenes grew frightened of the Spartans and withdrew to Thessaly. From there he went to Arcadia and began to stir up trouble, binding the Arcadians together against Sparta. Among other oaths by which he made them swear that they would follow him wherever he led, he was especially eager to bring the Arcadian leaders to the city of Nonacris and have them swear by the water of the Styx. For near this city, according to the Arcadians, is the water of the Styx, and there is in fact something of the kind: a thin trickle of water drips from a rock into a hollow gully, and a wall of rough stones runs around the gully. Nonacris, where this spring is located, is an Arcadian town near Pheneos.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 75
paragraphs: When the Lacedaemonians learned what Cleomenes was up to, they grew afraid and proceeded to bring him back to Sparta to rule on the same terms as before. But no sooner had he returned than a madness seized him — he had never been entirely of sound mind — and whenever he met one of the Spartans on the street he would strike him in the face with his staff. As he kept doing this and had plainly lost his reason, his kinsmen bound him in stocks. While he was so bound, he noticed that his guard had been left alone by the others, and he asked him for a knife. At first the guard, a Helot, would not give it, but Cleomenes threatened him with what he would do afterwards if he refused, and at last the man was intimidated into handing it over. Then Cleomenes, once he had the blade, began to mutilate himself from the legs upward, slicing his flesh lengthways up from the legs to the thighs, from the thighs to the loins and flanks, until at last he reached his belly; cutting this into strips he died. Most of the Greeks say that this happened to him because he bribed the Pythian prophetess to give the answer she did about Demaratus. The Athenians alone say it was because, when he invaded Eleusis, he laid waste the sacred precinct of the Two Goddesses. The Argives say it was because he dragged out from their sanctuary of Argos those of their people who had fled there for refuge after the battle, slew them, and even set fire to the grove itself, thinking it of no account.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 76
paragraphs: For when Cleomenes was consulting the oracle at Delphi, he was told that he would conquer Argos. So he led the Spartans out and came to the river Erasinos, which is said to flow from the Stymphalian lake — that lake, they say, empties into an unseen chasm, then reappears above ground in the territory of Argos, and from that point onward the Argives call the water Erasinos. When he reached the river, Cleomenes offered sacrifice to it. The omens were entirely unfavorable for crossing, so he declared that he admired the Erasinos for not betraying the men of its own country — but that the Argives would not escape him even so. After this he withdrew and marched his army down to Thyrea. There, sacrificing a bull to the Sea, he shipped them across to the territory of Tiryns and Nauplia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 77
paragraphs: Learning of this, the Argives hurried to the coast to meet them. Near Tiryns, at the place called Hesipeia, they camped opposite the Lacedaemonians, leaving only a narrow strip of ground between the two armies. The Argives were not afraid of a straight fight, but only of being undone by some trick — for it was to this, they thought, that the oracle given by the Pythia jointly to them and to the Milesians applied. It ran as follows:

“But when the female at length shall conquer the male in the battle, — conquer and drive him forth, and glory shall gain among Argives — then many wives of the Argives shall tear both cheeks in their mourning; so that a man shall say some time, of the men that came after, ‘Quelled by the spear it perished, the three-coiled terrible serpent.’”

All of this together frightened the Argives, and with this in mind they decided to make use of the enemy's herald. Having decided, they acted on it: whenever the Spartan herald announced some order to the Lacedaemonians, the Argives did the same thing.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 78
paragraphs: When Cleomenes realized that the Argives were doing whatever the Lacedaemonian herald announced, he passed the word among his men that when the herald proclaimed breakfast they should instead take up their arms and attack the Argives. This was done: while the Argives, acting on the herald's call, were eating their morning meal, the Lacedaemonians fell upon them. Many were killed, and many more took refuge in the sacred grove of Argos. The Lacedaemonians set up a watch and sat around the grove. Then Cleomenes did the following.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 79
paragraphs: He had some deserters with him, and by questioning them he got the names he needed. He then sent a herald to summon out the Argives shut up in the sanctuary, calling each one by name and saying that their ransom had already been paid. (Among the Peloponnesians the standard ransom is fixed at two minae of silver per prisoner.) One by one Cleomenes called about fifty Argives out and put them to death. For some time those still inside the enclosure did not notice what was happening — the grove was dense, and those inside could not see what was going on outside — until one of them climbed a tree and saw from above what was being done. After that, they would not come out when they were called.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 80
paragraphs: Cleomenes then ordered all the Helots to pile up brushwood around the sacred grove, and when they had done so, he set it on fire. As it was burning, he asked one of the deserters to which god the grove was sacred, and the man answered that it was sacred to Argos. When he heard this, Cleomenes groaned aloud and said, “Apollo, god of oracles, you have surely deceived me badly, saying that I should conquer Argos. I now suspect that the oracle has already been fulfilled for me.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 81
paragraphs: After this Cleomenes sent the greater part of his army back to Sparta, but he himself took a thousand of the best men and went to the temple of Hera to sacrifice. When he wanted to offer the sacrifice upon the altar, the priest forbade him, saying that it was not lawful by sacred custom for a foreigner to sacrifice there. Cleomenes, however, ordered the Helots to drag the priest away from the altar and scourge him, and he himself performed the sacrifice. After that he returned to Sparta.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 82
paragraphs: After his return, his political enemies brought him up before the Ephors, alleging that he had accepted bribes and so had failed to take Argos when he could easily have done so. He answered them — whether lying or telling the truth I cannot say for certain — that once he had captured the sanctuary of Argos, it seemed to him that the god's oracle had been fulfilled, and therefore he did not think it right to attempt the city itself until he had consulted the omens and learned whether the goddess would allow him or stand against him. As he was taking the auspices in the temple of Hera, a flame of fire blazed out from the breasts of the cult statue, and by this he knew the truth of the matter: that he would not take Argos. Had the flame blazed from the head of the image, he would have conquered the city entire from top to bottom; but since it came from the breasts, everything the god had wanted him to accomplish had already been done. So he spoke, and the Spartans found his account credible and reasonable, and he easily escaped his accusers.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 83
paragraphs: Argos, however, was so stripped of men that its slaves seized control of the whole state, running and managing it until the sons of the slain grew to manhood. These, trying to recover Argos for themselves, drove the slaves out; and the slaves, expelled, fought their way into possession of Tiryns. For a time the two parties kept friendly relations with each other, but eventually there came to the slaves a prophet named Cleander, a Phigalian from Arcadia by birth. This man persuaded the slaves to attack their old masters, and as a result there was a long war between them, until at last the Argives, with difficulty, prevailed.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 84
paragraphs: The Argives, then, say that this is why Cleomenes went mad and came to a bad end. The Spartans themselves, however, say that Cleomenes was not driven mad by any divine power. He had taken, they say, to drinking wine unmixed with water, a habit he picked up from keeping company with Scythians, and that is what made him mad. The nomadic Scythians, after Darius had invaded their country, were eager to take revenge on him, and sent to Sparta proposing an alliance: the Scythians were to invade Media by way of the river Phasis, while the Spartans were to march up inland from Ephesus, and the two forces would meet at an appointed place. The Spartans say that when the Scythians arrived on this business, Cleomenes spent a great deal of time with them — too much, in fact — and that by this association he learned to drink wine unmixed; and this, as the Spartans believe, is what drove him mad. Ever since then, when they want to drink stronger wine, they say “Fill it up, Scythian style.” That is what the Spartans say about Cleomenes. To me, though, it seems that his fate was the retribution he paid for Demaratus.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 85
paragraphs: When the Aeginetans heard that Cleomenes was dead, they sent envoys to Sparta to denounce Leotychides for the business of the hostages being kept at Athens. The Lacedaemonians convened a court and judged that Leotychides had outrageously wronged the Aeginetans; they sentenced him to be handed over, taken to Aegina, and surrendered in place of the men still held at Athens. But just as the Aeginetans were about to take Leotychides away, Theasides son of Leoprepes, a man of standing in Sparta, spoke to them. “What are you planning to do, men of Aegina? To carry off the king of the Spartans, handed over to you by his own fellow citizens? The Spartans may have voted this in anger now, but be careful lest at some later date — if you do it — they bring down ruin on your country. ” Hearing this, the Aeginetans held back from taking him. Instead they came to an agreement: Leotychides would accompany them to Athens and have the men returned to Aegina.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 86
paragraphs: When Leotychides arrived in Athens and asked for the hostages to be given back, the Athenians — unwilling to hand them over — produced excuses for refusing, claiming that since two kings had deposited them, it was not right to return them to one without the other. When it became clear that the Athenians would not give them up, Leotychides said to them:

“Athenians, do whichever of the two you prefer. You know as well as I do that if you give them up, you do what religion commands; if you refuse, you do the opposite. But I want to tell you what once happened at Sparta in a matter of a deposit. We Spartans tell how there lived in Lacedaemon, about two generations before my time, a man named Glaucus, son of Epicydes. He was said to have attained the highest merit in every respect, and especially was well spoken of for his honesty by all who then dwelt in Lacedaemon; and the story we tell of him is this. A man from Miletus once came to Sparta wishing to speak with him, with the following reasons: ‘I am a Milesian,’ he said, ‘and I have come here hoping to benefit from your honesty, Glaucus. There was much report of your uprightness throughout Greece, and especially in Ionia, and I reflected that Ionia is perpetually in danger, whereas the Peloponnese is secure, and that wealth rarely stays long with the same men. So, turning these things over in my mind, I decided to convert half of my property into silver and lodge it with you, well assured that if placed with you it would be safe. I beg you, therefore, take the money, and take these tokens and keep them; whoever asks for it back producing the matching tokens, to him return it.’ So spoke the stranger from Miletus, and Glaucus accepted the deposit on those terms. A long time passed, and the sons of the man who had made the deposit came to Sparta, spoke with Glaucus, and, producing the tokens, asked for the money to be returned. Glaucus turned them away, saying, ‘I do not remember the matter, nor can I recall anything of what you mention; but I want to think it over and do what is just. If I received it, I want to give it back honestly; if I did not, I will treat you according to the customs of the Greeks. I therefore defer settling the matter with you for three months from today.’ The Milesians went away in grief, thinking themselves cheated of the money. But Glaucus set out for Delphi to consult the oracle. When he asked the oracle whether he might seize the money by a false oath, the Pythia rebuked him in these lines:

“‘Glaucus, son of Epicydes, yes — for the moment, this, to defeat their word by an oath and take the money, is more profitable. Swear, then, since death awaits even the man who swears truly. But know that Oath has a son — nameless, handless, footless — yet without feet he pursues, without hands he seizes, and utterly destroys the house and race of the man who offends. The line of the man who swears truly fares better hereafter.’

When he heard this, Glaucus begged the god to pardon him for what he had said, but the prophetess answered that to tempt the god and to do the deed were equivalent. So Glaucus sent for the Milesians and gave them back their money. Now, Athenians, the reason I set out to tell you this story is this: at the present time there is not a single descendant of Glaucus living, nor any hearth reckoned as his; he has been utterly destroyed, torn up by the roots out of Sparta. So it is best not even to entertain the thought of doing anything with a deposit except to return it, when those who made it ask for it back.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 87
paragraphs: When Leotychides had finished speaking and the Athenians still would not listen to him, he went back home. The Aeginetans, before paying the penalty for their earlier wrongs — when to please the Thebans they had offered insult to the Athenians — now acted as follows. Resentful of the Athenians' behavior and believing themselves wronged, they made preparations to avenge themselves. While the Athenians were celebrating their four-yearly festival at Sunion, the Aeginetans lay in wait for the sacred ship that was being sent to the festival, seized it — it was full of the leading men of Athens — and, having captured it, threw the men in chains.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 88
paragraphs: Having suffered this outrage from the Aeginetans, the Athenians no longer held back from contriving every possible injury against them. There was in Aegina a man of note named Nicodromus son of Cnoethus. He had a grievance against the Aeginetans, who had previously driven him out of the island, and when he heard that the Athenians were now resolved to do harm to Aegina, he came to an agreement with them to hand the island over to them, telling them on what day he would make his attempt and by what day they must be ready to come to his support.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 89
paragraphs: After this, Nicodromus, acting on his agreement with the Athenians, seized what is called the Old City. The Athenians, however, did not come to his support at the proper moment, for they did not happen to have enough ships to engage the Aeginetans. While they were busy asking the Corinthians to lend them ships, their whole plan fell to pieces. The Corinthians, who were then on very friendly terms with them, gave the Athenians twenty ships at their request, selling them for five drachmas apiece — since by their law they were not allowed to give them away for nothing. With these ships and their own, the Athenians sailed for Aegina with a total of seventy manned vessels, arriving one day later than the day agreed upon.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Meanwhile Nicodromus, since the Athenians had not come to help at the proper time, boarded a ship and escaped from Aegina, and some other Aeginetans went with him. The Athenians gave them Sunion to settle in, and from that base these men continued to plunder the Aeginetans still on the island.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 91
paragraphs: That is what happened afterwards. At the time we are speaking of, the well-to-do on Aegina overcame the common people, who had risen against them along with Nicodromus. Once they had the rebels in their power, they led them out to execution. From this came a curse which they could not expiate by any sacrifice, despite everything they tried; instead, they were driven off their island before the goddess relented. They had taken about seven hundred of the commoners prisoner, and were leading them out to die, when one of them broke free of his bonds and fled for refuge to the entrance of the temple of Demeter the Lawgiver. He seized the ring of the door and clung to it; and when they found that they could not pry him loose no matter how hard they pulled, they cut off his hands and carried him off, while his hands remained clinging to the door-handle.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 92
paragraphs: So the Aeginetans treated one another. When the Athenians arrived, they fought against them with seventy ships, were beaten at sea, and called on the same allies as before — the Argives — for help. The Argives, however, would no longer come, having a grievance because ships from Aegina, pressed into service by Cleomenes, had put in to the Argolid and the crews had landed alongside the Lacedaemonians; men from Sicyonian ships had landed with them too in that same invasion. As punishment, the Argives had fined both states, a thousand talents in all: five hundred each. The Sicyonians acknowledged that they had done wrong and agreed to pay a hundred talents to settle their debt. The Aeginetans, however, refused to admit any wrongdoing and dug in their heels. For this reason, when Aegina now asked for help, no Argive came at the state's expense; but volunteers came, about a thousand of them, led by a commander named Eurybates, who had trained as a pentathlete. Most of these men never returned home — they were killed by the Athenians on Aegina. Eurybates himself, fighting in single combat, killed three opponents in succession and was himself killed by the fourth, Sophanes of Deceleia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Aeginetans, however, engaged the Athenians at sea while the Athenian ships were in disarray, defeated them, and captured four of their vessels together with their crews.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 94
paragraphs: So the Athenians were at war with the Aeginetans. Meanwhile the Persian was pressing forward with his own design: his servant kept reminding him constantly about the Athenians, and the sons of Pisistratus were near at hand bringing charges against the city without stop, while Darius himself was looking for this very pretext to subdue those parts of Greece that had not given him earth and water. He dismissed Mardonius from command, since his expedition had ended miserably, and appointed other generals to lead the attack against Eretria and Athens: Datis, a Mede by birth, and Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, the king's nephew. He sent them out with orders to reduce Athens and Eretria to slavery and bring the captives before him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 95
paragraphs: When these newly appointed commanders, marching from the king, reached the Aleïan plain in Cilicia at the head of a large and well-equipped land army, the whole naval armament also arrived, drawn from the several nations that had been assigned to provide it. There too came the horse-transports that Darius the year before had ordered his tributaries to have ready. Into these they embarked their cavalry, and having loaded the land-army on the ships, they set sail for Ionia with six hundred triremes. Instead of keeping their course along the mainland towards the Hellespont and Thrace, they set out from Samos and made their voyage through the Icarian Sea, between the islands — because, I think, they feared above all the coastline around Mount Athos, since the previous year, going that way, they had suffered a terrible disaster. Besides, Naxos was forcing their hand, since it had not been subdued the first time.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 96
paragraphs: When they reached Naxos, coming at it across the Icarian Sea — for it was against Naxos that the Persians intended to strike first, remembering their earlier failure — the Naxians fled at once into the mountains and did not wait to resist. The Persians enslaved those they caught and set fire to the sanctuaries and to the town. That done, they put to sea to attack the other islands.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 97
paragraphs: While they were doing this, the Delians too abandoned Delos and fled for refuge to Tenos. When the armament was sailing in, Datis went on ahead and did not let the ships anchor off the island of Delos itself, but had them moor at Rheneia across the strait. Then, having found out by inquiry where the Delians had gone, he sent a herald to address them with this message: “Holy men, why have you fled, thinking of me what is not fitting? I myself have at least this much sense, and beyond that I have been commanded by the king to do no harm to the land in which the two deities were born — neither to the land nor to its inhabitants. Return, therefore, to your own homes and dwell once more on your island.” Thus he proclaimed to the Delians by herald, and he then piled up on the altar three hundred talents' weight of frankincense and burned it.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 98
paragraphs: After this Datis sailed off with his army to make war first on Eretria, taking Ionians and Aeolians with him. After he had put to sea from Delos, the island trembled — for the first and last time, as the Delians told me, from before that day down to my own time. Surely the god had intended this as a portent to mankind of the evils that were to come. For in the time of Darius son of Hystaspes, of Xerxes son of Darius, and of Artaxerxes son of Xerxes — three generations in succession — more evils befell Greece than in the twenty generations before Darius, some inflicted on her by the Persians, others by her own leaders warring against one another for supremacy. It was thus no unreasonable thing that Delos, previously unshaken, should be shaken. And an oracle had been given about it that ran:
“Delos, too, will I move, unmoved though it has been before.”

In the Greek tongue these names have the following meanings: Darius means “Compeller,” Xerxes “Warrior,” Artaxerxes “Great Warrior.” So indeed the Greeks might rightly call these kings in their own language.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Having left Delos, the barbarians put in at the islands along the way, gathering additional forces and taking the islanders' sons as hostages. Sailing round them in turn, they also came to Carystos. The Carystians, however, would neither give them hostages nor agree to join an expedition against their neighbors — meaning Eretria and Athens — so the Persians began to besiege the town and ravage its territory, until in the end the Carystians too gave way and came over to the king's side.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 100
paragraphs: The Eretrians, meanwhile, on being told that the Persian armament was sailing against them, asked the Athenians for help. The Athenians did not refuse — they sent as their supporters the four thousand who had been settled on the land of the wealthy Chalcidians. The Eretrians, however, had no solid plan of action. Though they had called for the Athenians, they were in fact divided between two minds: some proposed abandoning the city and fleeing to the heights of Euboea, while others, expecting to gain personally from the Persians, were preparing to hand the place over. Aeschines son of Nothon, one of the leading Eretrians, having learned how matters stood on both sides, told the Athenians who had come the whole state of affairs and begged them to depart for their own land so that they would not be destroyed as well. The Athenians took his advice and did just that.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 101
paragraphs: While they crossed over to Oropos and saved themselves, the Persians sailed on and put in along the coast of Eretrian territory at Temenos, Choereae, and Aegilia. Having seized these places, they at once began to disembark their cavalry and made ready to advance on the enemy. The Eretrians, however, did not intend to march out and meet them in the field; their aim, since the party in favor of staying had prevailed, was to hold out as long as they could by defending the walls. A fierce assault was made on the wall, and for six days there were heavy losses on both sides; on the seventh, Euphorbus son of Alcimachus and Philagrus son of Cyneas, men of note among the citizens, handed the city over to the Persians. Once inside, the Persians plundered and set fire to the temples, in retribution for the temples burned at Sardis, and according to the orders of Darius reduced the inhabitants to slavery.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 102
paragraphs: Having taken Eretria, the Persians stayed a few days and then sailed for Attica, pressing on hard in the belief that the Athenians would behave just as the Eretrians had. And since Marathon was the place in Attica most suitable for cavalry and also closest to Eretria, it was there that Hippias son of Pisistratus was guiding them.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 103
paragraphs: When the Athenians learned of this, they too marched out to Marathon to defend their territory, led by ten generals. The tenth of these was Miltiades, whose father Cimon son of Stesagoras had been forced to go into exile from Athens on account of Pisistratus son of Hippocrates. While in exile, Cimon happened to win a victory at the Olympic games with the four-horse chariot, matching in this achievement his half-brother Miltiades, who had the same mother. Then at the next Olympics he won again with the same mares but allowed Pisistratus to be proclaimed the victor; by handing over the victory he was permitted to return home under an agreement for peace. After he had won yet again at a later Olympic festival with the same mares, it was his fate to be killed by the sons of Pisistratus — Pisistratus himself being no longer alive. They sent men to ambush him by night near the City Hall and had him killed there. Cimon's grave is in the outer part of the city, across the road called the Hollow Way, and directly opposite him are buried those mares that had won him three Olympic victories. The mares of Euagoras the Laconian achieved the same feat, but no others did. Now at that time the elder of Cimon's sons, Stesagoras, was being raised in the house of his uncle Miltiades in the Chersonese, while the younger was being brought up at Athens with Cimon himself, bearing the name Miltiades after Miltiades the founder of the colony in the Chersonese.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 104
paragraphs: This Miltiades, then, at the time of which I speak, had come from the Chersonese and was now a general of the Athenians, having escaped death in two different forms. The Phoenicians, pursuing him as far as Imbros, had done everything they could to capture him and bring him before the king. After he escaped them and returned to his own country, and seemed at last to be safe, his enemies, who had been lying in wait for him at home, prosecuted him in court for his tyranny in the Chersonese. Having escaped their efforts too, he was elected by the people and appointed a general of the Athenians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 105
paragraphs: First of all, while they were still in the city, the generals dispatched a herald to Sparta — Pheidippides, an Athenian who was by profession a long-distance runner. As Pheidippides himself told the Athenians on his return, Pan met him on Mount Parthenion above Tegea; calling out his name, Pan told him to ask the Athenians why they gave him no attention, when he was well disposed toward them and had often been useful to them before, and would be useful again. The Athenians, when their fortunes had been set right, believed the tale to be true and established a temple to Pan below the Acropolis; and from that message on, they propitiate him with yearly sacrifices and a torch-race.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 106
paragraphs: On this occasion, however — the time when he said Pan had appeared to him — Pheidippides, having been sent by the generals, was in Sparta the day after he left Athens. When he came before the magistrates he said: “Men of Lacedaemon, the Athenians beg you to come to their aid and not to allow a city most anciently established among the Greeks to fall into slavery at the hands of barbarians. Eretria has already been enslaved, and Greece has been made the weaker by the loss of a famous city.” He delivered the message with which he had been charged, and they were willing enough to help the Athenians, but it was not possible for them to move at once, since they did not wish to break their law. It was the ninth day of the month, and on the ninth day, they said, they would not march out, nor before the moon was full.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 107
paragraphs: So the Spartans waited for the full moon. Meanwhile Hippias son of Pisistratus was guiding the barbarians in to Marathon, having had the previous night a dream in which it seemed to him that he lay with his own mother. From this he concluded that he would return to Athens, recover his rule, and die an old man in his own land. That was how he interpreted the dream. Now, as he was leading the troops in, he first set ashore the slaves from Eretria on the island of Aegleia, belonging to Styra. When the ships came to land at Marathon, he had them moored there, and as the barbarians came ashore he was busy positioning them in their places. While he was doing this, he was seized by a violent fit of sneezing and coughing; and since he was an old man, most of his teeth were loosened by it, and with one great cough he dislodged a tooth. The tooth dropped onto the sand, and he searched eagerly for it; when it could not be found, he groaned and said to those near him: “This land is not ours, nor shall we be able to make it subject. Whatever share of it belonged to me, the tooth has now claimed.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 108
paragraphs: So Hippias concluded that his dream had been thus fulfilled. Meanwhile the Athenians, drawn up in the sacred precinct of Heracles, were joined by the Plataeans, who came to their aid in full force. For the Plataeans had given themselves to the Athenians, and the Athenians had undertaken many labors on their behalf. The surrender had come about like this. Being oppressed by the Thebans, the Plataeans had first tried to give themselves to Cleomenes son of Anaxandridas and to the Lacedaemonians, who happened to be in the area. But the Lacedaemonians would not accept them and said: “We live too far off, and our help to you would be cold comfort. You might be enslaved many times over before any of us heard of it. We advise you instead to give yourselves to the Athenians — they are your neighbors, and they are no bad allies.” The Lacedaemonians gave this advice not so much out of goodwill for the Plataeans as out of a wish that the Athenians should be caught up in trouble and conflict with the Boeotians. The Plataeans did not fail to follow the counsel. While the Athenians were offering sacrifice to the twelve gods, the Plataeans seated themselves as suppliants at the altar and so handed themselves over. When the Thebans learned of this, they marched against the Plataeans, and the Athenians came to their defense. Just as the two sides were about to join battle, the Corinthians, who happened to be there, would not allow them to fight but reconciled the quarrel. Both parties put the matter in their hands, and the Corinthians fixed the boundaries of the land on the condition that the Thebans should leave alone any Boeotians who did not wish to be counted among them. After this decision the Corinthians departed. But as the Athenians were withdrawing, the Boeotians attacked them, and in the resulting battle were defeated. The Athenians then advanced beyond the boundaries the Corinthians had set for the Plataeans and made the river Asopus itself the border between Thebes and the territory of Plataea and Hysiae. That is how the Plataeans had given themselves to the Athenians, and now they had come to Marathon to bring them support.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 109
paragraphs: The opinions of the Athenian generals were divided. One side argued that they should not fight a battle, since they were too few to engage the Median army; the other side, among them Miltiades, argued that they should. The worse opinion was on the point of prevailing. But since the man chosen by lot as polemarch of Athens had a vote in addition to the ten generals (for in those days the Athenians gave the polemarch an equal vote with the generals), and the polemarch at that time was Callimachus of the deme of Aphidnae, Miltiades came to him and said: “Callimachus, it rests with you now either to bring Athens into slavery, or to leave her free and so bequeath to all future generations a memorial even greater than Harmodius and Aristogiton left. For at this moment the Athenians face a greater danger than any they have faced since they became a people. If they submit to the Medes, it is already decided what they shall suffer, being handed over to Hippias; but if this city prevails, she may become the foremost of all the cities of Greece. How that may happen, and why the decision has fallen to you of all men, I shall now explain. Of us ten generals, the opinions are divided, some urging battle, some opposing it. If we do not fight, I expect some great spirit of discord will fall upon the Athenians and so shake them that they will go over to the Medes. But if we fight a battle before any rot can set in among the people, then — if the gods grant us a fair field — we can win. All of this now lies with you and depends on you. If you join my side, your country is free and your native city will be the first among the cities of Greece. If you choose the side of those who oppose battle, you will have the opposite of all the goods I have described.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 110
paragraphs: With these words Miltiades won Callimachus over, and with the polemarch's vote added, the decision was taken to fight. After this, the generals who had voted for battle, as each one's day of command came round, handed over their command to Miltiades; and he accepted it, but would not yet bring on a battle — not until his own day of command arrived.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 111
paragraphs: When his turn at last came round, the Athenians were drawn up for battle in the following order. On the right wing was the polemarch Callimachus (the Athenian custom then being that the polemarch commanded the right wing); next after him, in order, came the tribes arranged by their numbers, one after the other; and last, drawn up on the left wing, were the Plataeans. Ever since this battle, when the Athenians offer sacrifices at the solemn assemblies of the four-yearly festivals, the Athenian herald prays “that blessings may come to the Athenians and to the Plataeans alike.” On this occasion, as the Athenians were forming up at Marathon, something like this was done: their line, made equal in length to the Median line, came to be of only a few ranks' depth in the middle — the weakest point — while each wing was given greater numbers and so reinforced.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 112
paragraphs: Once they were in place and the sacrifices proved favorable, the Athenians were released and set off at a run to attack the barbarians. The space between the armies was no less than eight stades. The Persians, seeing them coming at a run, prepared to receive them, convinced in their own minds that the Athenians were suicidally insane, given how few they were and that they were pressing forward on the run without any cavalry or archers. So the barbarians thought. But the Athenians, when in full body they crashed into the enemy, fought in a memorable fashion. They were the first of all the Greeks I know of to charge the enemy at a run, and the first to endure the sight of Median clothing and the men who wore it — for up to that time even the very name of the Medes had been a terror to Greek ears.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 113
paragraphs: The fighting at Marathon went on for a long time. In the center of the line, where the Persians themselves and the Sacae were drawn up, the barbarians were winning — here they had broken the Greek ranks and were pursuing them inland. But on both wings, the Athenians and the Plataeans each had the advantage; and being victorious there, they let the routed part of the barbarians flee unmolested, drew the two wings together, and fought the troops who had broken their center. In that fight the Athenians prevailed. They followed the fleeing Persians, cutting them down as they went, until they came to the sea; then they called for fire and began to lay hold of the ships.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 114
paragraphs: In this part of the battle the polemarch Callimachus was killed, having shown himself a brave man, and one of the generals, Stesilaus son of Thrasylaus, was killed too. Cynegirus son of Euphorion, as he was grasping the ornament at the stern of a ship, had his hand cut off with an axe and fell. Many other Athenians of distinction were also killed.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 115
paragraphs: In this way the Athenians took seven of the ships, but with the rest the barbarians pushed off from land. Picking up the Eretrian captives from the island where they had left them, they sailed around Sunion with the intention of reaching the city before the Athenians could. A charge went around Athens that they had conceived this plan through a scheme of the Alcmaeonids: these men, it was said, had made an arrangement with the Persians and signaled to them with a shield once the Persians were back aboard their ships.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 116
paragraphs: While the Persians were sailing around Sunion, the Athenians hurried back to the city at top speed to defend it, and they arrived before the barbarians got there. Having come from the shrine of Heracles at Marathon, they encamped at another shrine of Heracles — the one at Cynosarges. The barbarians, for their part, came and lay with their ships at anchor in the sea off Phalerum (which was then the port of Athens), and after riding there for some time, they sailed back to Asia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 117
paragraphs: In this battle at Marathon about six thousand four hundred of the barbarians were killed, and one hundred and ninety-two of the Athenians. Such was the tally of the dead on both sides. And there happened there a marvel of this kind: an Athenian named Epizelos son of Couphagoras, fighting in the close combat and acquitting himself bravely, was deprived of the sight of his eyes, though he had received no blow on any part of his body and had not been hit by any missile; from that moment to the end of his life he remained blind. I was told that the story he used to tell about what had befallen him was this: that it seemed to him a tall man in full armor stood against him, whose beard cast a shadow across his whole shield; that this apparition passed him by, but killed the man standing next to him. This is the tale Epizelos used to tell, as I was informed.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 118
paragraphs: Datis, meanwhile, as he was making his way to Asia with his army, saw a dream when he was at Myconos. The nature of the vision is not recorded, but as soon as day dawned he had the ships searched. In a Phoenician vessel he found an image of Apollo plated with gold, and he asked where it had been carried off from. When he was told the name of the temple, he sailed in his own ship to Delos, and finding the Delians now returned to the island, he deposited the statue in the temple and charged the Delians to convey it back to Delion in Theban territory, which lies on the seacoast just opposite Chalcis. Having given that order, Datis sailed away. The Delians, however, never returned the statue; it was the Thebans themselves who, twenty years later, brought it back to Delion, prompted by an oracle.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 119
paragraphs: As for the Eretrians who had been reduced to slavery, when Datis and Artaphernes reached Asia they brought them up to Susa. King Darius, though he had raged against the Eretrians before their capture because they had wronged him without provocation, treated them no more harshly once he saw them in his power as prisoners. He settled them as colonists in the Cissian country on one of his own estates, a place called Ardericca, two hundred and ten stades from Susa and forty stades from the well that yields three kinds of substance: asphalt, salt, and oil, drawn up in the following manner. The liquid is brought up by a sweep, to which half a skin has been fastened in place of a bucket; a man plunges this into the well, draws it up, and pours it into a cistern, from which it runs off in three separate channels. The asphalt and salt solidify at once; the oil — which the Persians call rhadinace — is black and gives off a disagreeable smell. Here King Darius settled the Eretrians, and down to my own day they still occupy this land and keep their original language. So much, then, for what happened to the Eretrians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 120
paragraphs: Two thousand of the Lacedaemonians came to Athens after the full moon, hurrying so hard to arrive in time that they reached Attica on the third day out of Sparta. Although they were too late for the battle, they still wanted to see the Medes, so they went out to Marathon and looked at the bodies of the slain. Then they went home, praising the Athenians and the work they had done.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 121
paragraphs: It is a matter of wonder to me, and I do not accept the report, that the Alcmaeonidae could ever have flashed a shield to the Persians by pre-arrangement, with the wish that the Athenians should fall under the barbarians and under Hippias. They are plainly shown to have been haters of tyrants as much as, or more than, Callias son of Phaenippus, the father of Hipponicus — Callias, who was the only Athenian who dared, when Pisistratus was driven out of Athens, to buy up the goods that were being auctioned off by the state, and who in other ways also devised every kind of hostility against him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 122
paragraphs: This Callias deserves to be remembered by everyone for a number of reasons: first, as already said, because he was an excellent man in the cause of his country's freedom; then for what he did at the Olympic games, where he won the horse race and came in second in the chariot race, having already before won at the Pythian games, so that he was distinguished in the eyes of all Greece by the sums he spent; and finally because he showed himself so generous with his three daughters, for when they came of age for marriage he gave each of them a most splendid dowry and also indulged their wishes — whichever man in Athens each one chose as her husband, to that man he gave her.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 123
paragraphs: Similarly, the Alcmaeonidae were haters of tyrants to the same degree as he, or more. So it is a matter of wonder to me, and I do not accept the charge that they were the ones who displayed the shield — seeing that throughout the entire time of the tyranny they were in exile, and that it was by their contrivance that the sons of Pisistratus were made to give up their rule. They, to my judgment, did far more to set Athens free than Harmodius and Aristogiton. For those two, by killing Hipparchus, only enraged the rest of the house of Pisistratus and did not cause the others to stop their tyranny; whereas the Alcmaeonidae manifestly freed Athens — at least if it is true, as I have set forth before, that they were the ones who persuaded the Pythian prophetess to instruct the Lacedaemonians to set Athens free.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 124
paragraphs: It might perhaps be suggested that they had some grievance against the Athenian people and that for this reason they tried to betray their own city. But on the contrary, there were no men in higher repute among the Athenians than they, and none who had been more greatly honored. It is therefore not reasonable to suppose that they would have displayed a shield for any such purpose. That a shield was displayed cannot be denied — it was done. But as to who displayed it, I cannot say more than that.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 125
paragraphs: Now the family of the Alcmaeonidae had already been prominent at Athens from the earliest times, and they became very greatly distinguished from the time of Alcmaeon and of Megacles after him. For Alcmaeon son of Megacles made himself of use to the Lydians sent from Croesus at Sardis to the oracle at Delphi, and assisted them energetically. When Croesus heard from the Lydians who had gone to the oracle that this man had served him well, he summoned him to Sardis, and when he arrived Croesus offered him as a gift as much gold as he could carry away on his own person at one time. With such a gift in view, Alcmaeon made preparations and resorted to these devices. He put on a large tunic, letting a deep fold of it hang open at the front, and he pulled on the widest boots he could find. So equipped he went into the treasury to which they led him. There he threw himself onto a heap of gold dust, and first he packed along the sides of his legs as much gold as his boots would hold; then he filled the whole fold of his tunic with gold and sprinkled some of the gold dust on his hair and took some into his mouth. Having done this, he came out of the treasury, dragging his boots with difficulty and looking like anything on earth except a man — for his mouth was stuffed full and every part of him was bulging. Croesus burst out laughing when he saw him, and not only gave him everything he was carrying but presented him with even more besides, of no less value. So this family became enormously wealthy, and this same Alcmaeon of whom I speak became a breeder of chariot horses and won a victory at Olympia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 126
paragraphs: Then in the next generation after this, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon raised the family still higher, so that it became much more famous among the Greeks than before. Cleisthenes son of Aristonymus, son of Myron, son of Andreas, had a daughter named Agariste, and he made it his purpose to find the best man in Greece and marry her to him. So when the Olympic games were being held and Cleisthenes won them with a four-horse chariot, he had it proclaimed that any Greek who considered himself worthy to be Cleisthenes's son-in-law should come to Sicyon by the sixtieth day, or sooner if he wished, for Cleisthenes meant to conclude the marriage within a year, counting from that sixtieth day. All those Greeks who took pride either in themselves or in their high birth came as suitors, and for them Cleisthenes had built a running-track and a wrestling-ground kept expressly for their use.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 127
paragraphs: From Italy came Smindyrides son of Hippocrates of Sybaris, who of all men on earth had attained the highest degree of luxury (for Sybaris was at that time at the height of its prosperity), and Damasus of Siris, son of that Amyris who was called the Wise; these came from Italy. From the Ionian gulf came Amphimnestus son of Epistrophus of Epidamnus; from Aetolia came Males, the brother of that Titormus who surpassed all Greeks in strength and who fled the company of men to the remotest part of the Aetolian land. From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon the tyrant of the Argives — the Pheidon who established the standard weights and measures still used in the Peloponnese, and who outdid all other Greeks in outrageous arrogance, for he removed the Elean presidents of the games from their posts and presided over the Olympic games himself; I say, his son, and with him Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paios, the son of that Euphorion who, according to the Arcadian story, entertained the Dioscuri in his home and from then on made a point of welcoming everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaios of Elis — these came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, son of that Alcmaeon who had gone to Croesus, and with him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who surpassed the other Athenians in both wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 128
paragraphs: Such was the number of suitors. When they had arrived by the appointed day, Cleisthenes first asked them about their native countries and the genealogy of each, and then kept them for a year, testing continually their courage, character, upbringing, and temperament, both in his conversations with each of them individually and in their company as a group. He tested them by taking the younger ones out for athletic exercises, and, above all, at their daily meals together: for during all the time he kept them there, he did everything of the kind that could be done, and entertained them magnificently. It so happened that the ones who pleased him most were those who had come from Athens, and of these he preferred Hippocleides son of Tisander, both for his personal qualities and because he was connected by descent with the Cypselid family of Corinth.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 129
paragraphs: Then, when the day appointed for the wedding feast had come, and for Cleisthenes himself to declare which of the suitors he was choosing, Cleisthenes sacrificed a hundred oxen and feasted both the suitors and all the people of Sicyon. When the meal was finished, the suitors began to compete with one another in music and in speeches for the company's entertainment; and as the drinking went on and Hippocleides was commanding great attention, he told the flute-player to strike up a dance tune. The flute-player did so, and Hippocleides danced. He pleased himself with his own dancing, but Cleisthenes was beginning to look on the whole thing with suspicion. After a while Hippocleides called for a table to be brought in, and when it came, he first danced Laconian figures on top of it, then Attic ones, and then, thirdly, he planted his head on the table and kicked his legs in the air. Cleisthenes, during the first and second performances, though he was already revolted at the thought of having Hippocleides for a son-in-law because of his dancing and shamelessness, restrained himself, not wanting to burst out at him in anger. But when he saw him waving his legs around in the air, he could hold back no longer and said: “Son of Tisander, you have danced your marriage away!” And Hippocleides answered: “Hippocleides doesn't care!”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 130
paragraphs: And from that came the proverb. Then Cleisthenes called for silence and said to the company: “Gentlemen, suitors of my daughter, I commend you all, and if it were possible I would gratify you all — choosing none of you above the rest and rejecting none. But since that cannot be, as I am deliberating about one girl only, I cannot please all of you.
