The Ethiopians wore leopard-skins and lion-skins tied upon them, and they had bows made of a strip of palm-wood, of great length, no less than four cubits, and for them small reed arrows with a sharpened stone tip instead of iron — the same stone they use for engraving seals. In addition they had spears tipped with a sharpened gazelle horn in place of a spear-head, and knob-studded clubs. Before going into battle they used to smear half their bodies with white and the other half with red. The commander of both the Arabians and of the Ethiopians who lived above Egypt was Arsames, son of Darius and of Artystone, the daughter of Cyrus whom Darius loved most of all his wives and of whom he had an image made in beaten gold.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Such, then, was the commander of the Ethiopians above Egypt and of the Arabians — namely Arsames. But the Ethiopians from the direction of the sunrise (for the Ethiopians were in two contingents) had been assigned to serve with the Indians, differing from the other Ethiopians in no way except in their language and in the nature of their hair: the eastern Ethiopians have straight hair, while those of Libya have hair more thickly curled than any other men's. These Asian Ethiopians were armed for the most part like the Indians, but on their heads they wore the skin of a horse's forehead, flayed off together with the ears and mane, the mane serving as a crest, while the ears were set up straight and stiff. In place of shields they used protections of crane-skin held in front of them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 71
paragraphs: The Libyans marched in leather gear and carried javelins hardened in fire at the point. They acknowledged as their commander Massages son of Oarizus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 72
paragraphs: The Paphlagonians served with plaited helmets on their heads, small shields, spears of no great size, and also javelins and daggers; on their feet they wore native boots reaching halfway up the shin. The Ligyes, Matieni, Mariandyni, and Syrians served with the same equipment as the Paphlagonians; these Syrians are called Cappadocians by the Persians. The commanders were Dotus son of Megasidrus over the Paphlagonians and Matieni, and Gobryas son of Darius and Artystone over the Mariandyni, Ligyes, and Syrians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 73
paragraphs: The Phrygians had equipment very much like that of the Paphlagonians, with slight differences. The Phrygians, according to the Macedonians, used to be called Briges during the time when they were natives of Europe and lived among the Macedonians; but after they had migrated to Asia, together with their country they changed their name and came to be called Phrygians. The Armenians were armed just like the Phrygians, being settlers from them. The commander of both together was Artochmes, who was married to a daughter of Darius.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 74
paragraphs: The Lydians had arms very closely resembling those of the Greeks. The Lydians were in older times called Maeonians, and they were renamed after Lydus son of Atys, exchanging their earlier name. The Mysians wore native helmets on their heads, carried small shields, and used javelins hardened at the tip by fire. They are settlers from the Lydians, and from Mount Olympus they take the name Olympieni. The commander of the Lydians and Mysians was Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, the same man who invaded Marathon together with Datis.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 75
paragraphs: The Thracians served wearing fox-skins on their heads and tunics over their bodies, with multicolored cloaks thrown loosely over them; on their feet and lower legs they wore fawn-skin boots. In addition they had javelins, small round shields, and short daggers. After they had crossed over into Asia, these men came to be called Bithynians; but formerly, as they themselves say, they were called Strymonians, since they had lived by the river Strymon; they say they were driven out of their old homes by the Teucrians and Mysians. The commander of the Thracians who lived in Asia was Bassakes son of Artabanus.

They carried small shields of raw oxhide, and each man carried two hunting-spears of Lycian make. On their heads they wore bronze helmets to which the ears and horns of an ox were attached, also in bronze, with crests on top; and their lower legs were wrapped with strips of red cloth. Among these men there is an oracle of Ares.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 77
paragraphs: The Maeonian Cabalians, who are called Lasonians, had the same equipment as the Cilicians — what that was I shall explain when in the course of my catalogue I come to the Cilician contingent. The Milyans carried short spears, and their garments were fastened with brooches; some of them had Lycian bows, and on their heads they wore leather caps. The commander of all these was Badres son of Hystanes.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 78
paragraphs: The Moschi wore wooden caps on their heads and carried shields and small spears with long points set on them. The Tibareni, Macrones, and Mossynoeci served with equipment like the Moschi's, and they were arrayed together under the following commanders: the Moschi and Tibareni under Ariomardus, son of Darius and Parmys, daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus; the Macrones and Mossynoeci under Artayctes son of Cherasmis, the governor of Sestos on the Hellespont.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 79
paragraphs: The Mares wore on their heads native plaited helmets and carried small hide shields and javelins. The Colchians wore wooden helmets, carried small shields of raw oxhide, short spears, and also knives. The commander of the Mares and Colchians was Pharandates son of Teaspis. The Alarodians and Saspires served armed like the Colchians; their commander was Masistius son of Siromitres.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 80
paragraphs: The island tribes who marched with the army from the Erythraean Sea — those who inhabited the islands where the king settles the people called the “Removed” — had clothing and arms very similar to those of the Medes. Their commander was Mardontes son of Bagaeus, who the year after these events was commander of the army at Mycale and lost his life in the battle.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 81
paragraphs: These were the nations that served in the land campaign and had been assigned to the infantry. Of this army the men mentioned above were the commanders; they were the ones who drew it up in divisions, counted it, and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of ten thousands. The commanders of hundreds and of tens were appointed by the commanders of ten thousands; and there were others who led divisions and nations.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 82
paragraphs: These, I say, who have been mentioned, were the commanders of the army. But over them, and over the whole infantry together, the commanders were Mardonius son of Gobryas, Tritantaechmes son of that Artabanus who had given the opinion that they should not make the march against Greece, Smerdomenes son of Otanes (both of them sons of Darius's brothers, and thus cousins of Xerxes), Masistes son of Darius and Atossa, Gergis son of Ariazus, and Megabyzus son of Zopyrus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 83
paragraphs: These were the generals of the whole infantry apart from the ten thousand; and of these ten thousand picked Persians the general was Hydarnes son of Hydarnes. These Persians were called the “Immortals,” because whenever any one of them made the number incomplete, whether by death or disease, another was chosen in his place, and they were never either more or fewer than ten thousand. Of all the nations, the Persians showed the greatest splendor of ornament and were themselves the best men. Their equipment was as described above, and besides this they were conspicuous among the rest for the lavish amount of gold they wore. They brought with them carriages, and in them concubines and a multitude of well-appointed attendants; and provisions for them, apart from those of the other soldiers, were carried on camels and pack animals.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 84
paragraphs: The nations that served as cavalry are the following — though not all the nations supplied cavalry, only those listed here. The Persians were equipped in the same way as their infantry, except that on their heads some of them wore beaten metalwork, whether of bronze or iron.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 85
paragraphs: There are also certain nomads called Sagartians, Persian in race and in language, whose dress is a blend of the Persian and the Pactyan. These furnished eight thousand cavalry, and they are not accustomed to carry weapons of either bronze or iron except daggers; instead they rely on ropes twisted of leather, and they trust to these when they go into war. Their way of fighting is this: when they come to grips with the enemy, they throw the ropes with nooses on the end, and whatever the man catches by the throw — horse or rider — he drags it to himself, and thus, entangled in the toils, the victims are destroyed.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 86
paragraphs: Such is the manner of fighting of these men, and they were arrayed next to the Persians. The Medes had the same equipment as their infantry, and the Cissians likewise. The Indians were armed in the same way as their foot soldiers, and they both rode horses and drove chariots drawn by horses or wild asses. The Bactrians were equipped as their infantry were, and the Caspians likewise. The Libyans too were equipped as their infantry, and all of them drove chariots. So too the Caspians and the Paricanians had equipment like their infantry, and they all rode on camels, which were no slower than horses.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 87
paragraphs: These were the only nations that served as cavalry, and their total number proved to be eighty thousand, apart from camels and chariots. The rest of the cavalry was arrayed in squadrons, but the Arabians were placed last of all, since the horses could not bear the camels, and so they were stationed last to keep the horses from being frightened.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 88
paragraphs: The cavalry commanders were Harmamithras and Tithaeus, both sons of Datis. But the third, Pharnouches, who had shared command of the cavalry with them, had been left behind at Sardis sick. For as they were setting out from Sardis, an unwelcome accident happened to him: as he was riding along, a dog darted under his horse's feet, and the horse, not having seen it beforehand, took fright, reared up, and threw Pharnouches off its back. Falling, he vomited blood, and his illness turned into consumption. As for the horse, his servants at once did as he had ordered: they led it away to the spot where it had thrown its master and cut off its legs at the knees. That is how Pharnouches was removed from his command.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 89
paragraphs: The number of the triremes proved to be twelve hundred and seven, and these were the peoples who supplied them. The Phoenicians, together with the Syrians who live in Palestine, furnished three hundred; they were equipped thus: on their heads they wore leather caps very like the Greek kind, and they wore linen corselets and carried rimless shields and javelins. The Phoenicians, according to their own account, lived in ancient times by the Erythraean Sea, and from there passed over and now inhabit the coast of Syria. This part of Syria, all the way to Egypt, is called Palestine. The Egyptians furnished two hundred ships. On their heads they wore plaited helmets; they had hollow shields with wide rims and spears for sea-fighting, and great battle-axes. Most of them wore corselets and carried large knives.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Such was the equipment of the Egyptians. The Cyprians furnished a hundred and fifty ships and were themselves equipped as follows: their kings had their heads wound with turbans, while the rest wore tunics; in other respects they were like the Greeks. Among these there are various races: some come from Salamis and Athens, others from Arcadia, others from Cythnus, others from Phoenicia, and still others from Ethiopia, as the Cyprians themselves report.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 91
paragraphs: The Cilicians furnished a hundred ships; these men too wore native helmets on their heads, and for shields they carried round targets of raw oxhide. They wore woolen tunics, and each man carried two javelins and a sword, the sword very like the Egyptian knife. These people used to be called Hypachaeans in old times, and they took their later name from Cilix son of Agenor, a Phoenician. The Pamphylians furnished thirty ships and were equipped in Greek style. These Pamphylians are descended from those who were scattered from Troy together with Amphilochus and Calchas.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 92
paragraphs: The Lycians furnished fifty ships. They wore corselets and greaves, and carried bows of cornel-wood, featherless reed arrows, javelins, and a goat-skin slung over the shoulder; on their heads they wore feather-wreathed felt caps, and they carried daggers and falchions as well. The Lycians were formerly called Termilae, being originally from Crete, and they took their later name from Lycus son of Pandion, an Athenian.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Asian Dorians furnished thirty ships; they carried Greek arms and were originally from the Peloponnese. The Carians supplied seventy ships; they were equipped mostly like Greeks but also had falchions and daggers. What their former name was has been told in the first part of the history.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 94
paragraphs: The Ionians furnished a hundred ships and were equipped like Greeks. The Ionians, during the long time they lived in the Peloponnese, in the country now called Achaea, and before Danaus and Xuthus came to the Peloponnese, were called, as the Greeks report, Pelasgians of the Coast, and then were called Ionians after Ion son of Xuthus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 95
paragraphs: The islanders furnished seventeen ships and were armed like Greeks; these too are a Pelasgian race, though they came later to be called Ionian by the same principle as the Ionians of the Twelve Cities, who came from Athens. The Aeolians supplied sixty ships; they were equipped like Greeks and used in old times to be called Pelasgians, as the Greeks report. The people of the Hellespont — except those of Abydus (for the men of Abydus had been appointed by the king to stay in place and guard the bridges) — the rest of those who served in the expedition from the Pontic region furnished a hundred ships and were equipped like Greeks. These are colonists of the Ionians and Dorians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 96
paragraphs: On all the ships there served as fighting men Persians, Medes, or Sacae. Of the ships, those that sailed best were supplied by the Phoenicians, and among the Phoenicians the best were those of Sidon. Over all these men, and over those of them who were assigned to the land army as well, there were native chieftains for each people; but since the inquiry does not oblige me, I make no mention of them in passing — first because the chieftains of each nation were not persons worthy of mention, and second because within each nation there were as many chieftains as there were cities. These men went with the expedition not as commanders but like the rest, serving as slaves; for the generals who held absolute power and commanded the various nations — that is, those who were Persians — have already been named by me.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 97
paragraphs: The commanders of the naval force were these: Ariabignes son of Darius, Prexaspes son of Aspathines, Megabazus son of Megabates, and Achaemenes son of Darius. That is, the Ionian and Carian contingent was commanded by Ariabignes, son of Darius and of the daughter of Gobryas; the Egyptians by Achaemenes, full brother of Xerxes; and the rest of the armament by the other two. In all, the thirty-oared and fifty-oared galleys, the light craft, and the long horse-transport vessels had been gathered together, as it turned out, to a total of three thousand.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Of those who sailed in the ships, the men of most note after the commanders were these: from Sidon, Tetramnestus son of Anysus; from Tyre, Matten son of Siromus; from Aradus, Merbalus son of Agbalus; from Cilicia, Syennesis son of Oromedon; from Lycia, Cyberniscus son of Sicas; from Cyprus, Gorgus son of Chersis and Timonax son of Timagoras; from Caria, Histiaeus son of Tymnes, Pigres son of Hysseldomus, and Damasithymus son of Candaules.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Of the rest of the officers I make no mention in passing (since I am not obliged to), but only of Artemisia, who astonishes me most of all that she should have joined the expedition against Greece, being a woman. After her husband died, she held the power herself; and though she had a son who was a grown young man, she went on the expedition driven by her own high spirit and manly courage, under no compulsion. Her name, as I said, was Artemisia; she was the daughter of Lygdamis, and by descent she was on her father's side of Halicarnassus and on her mother's of Crete. She ruled over the people of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyrus, and Calydna, and supplied five ships. Her ships were reputed the best in the whole fleet after those of Sidon, and of all his allies she gave the king the best counsel. The states I say she led, I declare to be all of Dorian race: the people of Halicarnassus are Troezenians, and the rest are Epidaurians. So much, then, for the naval force.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 100
paragraphs: When Xerxes had had the army numbered and arranged in its divisions, he resolved to drive through it himself and review it, and he then proceeded to do so. Driving past each nation in turn in a chariot, he inquired about them, and his scribes wrote down the names, until he had gone from end to end both of the cavalry and of the infantry. When he had done this, the ships were drawn down into the sea, and Xerxes, changing from his chariot to a Sidonian ship, sat down under a golden canopy and sailed along past the prows, questioning each contingent as he had done with the land army and having the answers written down. The captains had taken their ships out to about four plethra from the beach and were holding them there, all with the prows turned in an even line toward the shore and the fighting men fully armed for war; Xerxes inspected them sailing in the channel between the prows and the beach.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 101
paragraphs: When he had sailed through the fleet and had disembarked from his ship, he sent for Demaratus son of Ariston, who was marching with him against Greece. When Demaratus was brought, Xerxes asked him this: “Demaratus, it now pleases me to ask you something I wish to know. You are not only a Greek, but also, as I have been told both by you and by the other Greeks who speak with me, of a city that is neither the smallest nor the weakest in Greece. Tell me, therefore, whether the Greeks will bring themselves to raise a hand against me. In my own view, even if all the Greeks and the other peoples of the west were gathered together, they would not be strong enough in battle to withstand my attack, if they should be my enemies. Still, I would like to hear your own opinion, whatever you have to say about these matters.” So he asked, and the other replied: “O king, shall I speak the truth to you, or that which will please?” Xerxes bade him speak the truth, saying that he would suffer nothing unpleasant in consequence, any more than he had before.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 102
paragraphs: When Demaratus heard this, he spoke as follows: “O king, since you bid me by all means to speak the truth, and so to speak as one who shall not afterwards be convicted by you of having lied, I say this: with Greece, poverty is always a native growth, but valor is one that has been brought in, gained by intelligence and the force of law. By means of this valor Greece defends herself continually, both against poverty and against a master's rule. Now, I have words of praise for all the Greeks settled in the Dorian lands, but what I am about to say concerns not all of them, only the Lacedaemonians. Of them I say, first, that there is no possibility they will ever accept your terms, which bring slavery to Greece; and second, that they will stand against you in battle even if all the other Greeks are on your side. As for numbers, do not ask how many they must be to do this. If a thousand of them have taken the field, they will fight with you — or if it is fewer than that, or more.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Xerxes, hearing this, laughed and said: “Demaratus, what a thing is this you have said — that a thousand men will fight with so vast an army! Come, tell me: you say that you yourself were once king of these men. Will you, then, be willing right now to fight with ten men? And yet, if your state is such throughout as you describe, you, their king, ought by your own laws to stand in battle against twice as many as another man — that is, if each one of them is a match for ten of my army, I expect you to be a match for twenty. Thus the report you give of them would be borne out. But if you, who make so great a boast, are men of the same size and quality as the Greeks I commonly deal with, yourself included, then take care that what has been said does not turn out to be an empty boast. For come, let me examine the matter by every probability. How could a thousand men, or ten thousand, or even fifty thousand, all equally free and not ruled by one man, stand against so great an army? Since, as you know, there will be more than a thousand of us for each one of them, supposing them to be five thousand in number. Now if they were ruled by one man after our fashion, they might, out of fear of him, become braver than is their nature, or they might be driven by the lash to fight with greater numbers while being fewer themselves. But left to their own freedom, they would do neither. For my part I suppose that even if they were matched equally in numbers, the Greeks would hardly dare fight the Persians alone. With us, the thing you speak of is to be found in single men — not often, but rarely; for there are some Persian spearmen of mine who will consent to fight three Greeks at a time. You have had no experience of such men, and so you speak very much at random.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 104
paragraphs: To this Demaratus replied: “O king, from the first I was sure that if I told the truth, I would not be speaking anything pleasing to you. But since you compelled me to speak the very truth, I told you about the affairs of the Spartans. Yet you know better than anyone how I am at this present time affectionately disposed toward them — seeing that they first stripped me of the rank and privileges inherited from my fathers, and then made me a stateless exile. Your father took me in, gave me a livelihood and a house to live in. It is surely not reasonable to suppose that a prudent man would push aside the friendliness offered to him; rather he would accept it gratefully. I do not profess that I can fight ten men, or even two; if I had my choice, I would not even fight one. But if there were necessity, or some great cause pressing me into combat, I would most willingly fight one of those men who claim each to be a match for three Greeks. So too the Lacedaemonians, one against one, are inferior to no men, and in a body they are the best of all. For though they are free, they are not free in all things: over them is set Law as their master, whom they fear far more than your people fear you. At any rate, whatever their master commands, they do; and he commands always the same thing — he forbids them to flee out of battle before any multitude of men, but orders them to stay at their post and either win the victory or lose their life. If I seem to you to be speaking foolishly in saying these things, I prefer from now on to be silent about the rest; I spoke now only because I was forced. May it nevertheless turn out as you wish, O king.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 105
paragraphs: Such was his reply, and Xerxes turned the matter into laughter and felt no anger, but dismissed him kindly. After their conversation, having appointed Mascames son of Megadostes to be governor at Doriscus, removing the one whom Darius had appointed, Xerxes marched his army on through Thrace to invade Greece.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 106
paragraphs: Mascames, whom he left behind here, proved to be a man of such qualities that to him alone Xerxes used to send gifts, reckoning him the best of all the men whom he or Darius had appointed as governors. He used to send him gifts every year, and so did Artaxerxes son of Xerxes afterwards to Mascames's descendants. For even before this campaign, governors had been appointed throughout Thrace and everywhere around the Hellespont; but all of these — both in Thrace and on the Hellespont — were conquered by the Greeks after this expedition, except only the one at Doriscus. Many tried to take Mascames at Doriscus, but none ever succeeded. For this reason the gifts are sent continually for him from whatever Persian king reigns at the time.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 107
paragraphs: Of those who were conquered by the Greeks, Xerxes reckoned no one a man of worth except Boges, who was at Eion; him he never ceased praising, and he paid very high honor to his children who survived him in Persia. Boges indeed proved worthy of great praise. When he was being besieged by the Athenians under Cimon son of Miltiades, and could have come out under a truce and returned home to Asia, he chose not to do so, for fear the king might think he had survived through cowardice; instead, he held out to the last. When there were no longer any provisions within the wall, he heaped up a great pyre, cut the throats of his children, his wife, his concubines and his servants, and threw them into the fire; after that he scattered all the gold and silver of the city from the wall into the river Strymon, and having done so, he threw himself into the fire. For this reason he is justly praised by the Persians to this day.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 108
paragraphs: From Doriscus Xerxes was pushing on to invade Greece, and as he went he compelled those he came across to join his march. For the whole country as far as Thessaly had, as I have set out before, been reduced to subjection and was tributary to the king, having been conquered by Megabazus and afterwards by Mardonius. Marching out of Doriscus, he passed first by the Samothracian strongholds, the westernmost of which is a city called Mesambria. Next comes Stryme, a city of the Thasians; between them flows the river Lisus, which at that time did not suffice to supply water for Xerxes's army but ran dry. This country was once called Gallaice, but is now called Briantice; strictly, however, it too belongs to the Cicones.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 109
paragraphs: Having crossed the dry bed of the river Lisus, he passed the Greek cities of Maroneia, Dicaea, and Abdera. These he passed by, along with the following notable lakes lying near them: the Ismarian lake, between Maroneia and Stryme; the Bistonian lake near Dicaea, into which two rivers, the Travus and the Compsatus, pour their waters. At Abdera he passed no noteworthy lake, but did pass the river Nestus, which there flows into the sea. Then, beyond these places, he went past cities of the mainland; near one of them happens to lie a lake about thirty stades in circumference, full of fish and very brackish, which the baggage animals alone drank dry by watering there. The name of this city is Pistyros.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 110
paragraphs: These coastal Greek cities, then, he passed, leaving them on his left. The Thracian tribes whose territory he marched through were the following: the Paeti, Cicones, Bistones, Sapaeans, Dersaeans, Edonians, and Satrae. Of these, those who lived along the coast accompanied him with their ships, while those of them who lived inland — the ones I have just listed — were compelled to accompany him on land, except the Satrae.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 111
paragraphs: The Satrae, so far as we know, have never yet submitted to any man; they remain to my own day still free, alone of all the Thracians. For they live in high mountains, covered with forests of every kind and with snow, and they are also highly skilled in war. These are the people who possess the oracle of Dionysus; that oracle is in their highest mountains. Of the Satrae, those who act as the interpreters of the shrine are the Bessi; a prophetess utters the oracles, as at Delphi; and beyond this there is nothing of a notable character.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 112
paragraphs: Having passed through the country just described, Xerxes next went by the strongholds of the Pierians, one of which is called Phagres and the other Pergamos. This way he made his march, passing close under the walls of these places and keeping Mount Pangaeum on his right, which is both great and lofty and has mines of gold and silver held by the Pierians and the Odomantians, and especially by the Satrae.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Thus passing by the Paeonians, Doberes, and Paeoples, who live beyond Pangaeum toward the north, he went on westward until at last he came to the river Strymon and the city of Eion, of which Boges — the man I was speaking of a little earlier — was commander as long as he lived. The country about Mount Pangaeum is called Phyllis; it stretches westward as far as the river Angites, which flows into the Strymon, and southward as far as the Strymon itself. At this river the Magi offered sacrifices for good omens, slaughtering white horses.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 114
paragraphs: After these rites and many other charms for the river, at the Nine Ways in the land of the Edonians they crossed by the bridges, for they had found the Strymon already bridged. On being told that the place was called the Nine Ways, they buried alive there that number of boys and girls, children of the local inhabitants. Burying alive is a Persian custom: I am told that Amestris, the wife of Xerxes, when she had grown old, repaid her own life to the god who is said to dwell beneath the earth by burying twice seven children of Persian men of note.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 115
paragraphs: As the army marched on from the Strymon, it found a shore running toward the setting sun, and it passed by the Greek city of Argilus, which is situated there. This region, and the country lying above it, is called Bisaltia. Then, keeping on his left the gulf off Posideion, he went through the plain called the plain of Syleus, passing the Greek city of Stageirus, and so came to Acanthus, taking along with him as he went every one of these tribes and of those who dwell around Pangaeum, just as he had done with those I listed before — those by the coast serving in the fleet, those inland accompanying him on foot. This road along which Xerxes the king led his army, the Thracians neither disturb nor sow over, but hold it in the greatest reverence to this day.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 116
paragraphs: When he reached Acanthus, Xerxes proclaimed a formal guest-friendship with its people, presented them with Median dress, and praised them, seeing their zeal in his service and hearing of the work they had done on the digging.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 117
paragraphs: While Xerxes was at Acanthus, it happened that the man who had been in charge of the making of the channel, Artachaees by name, died of sickness. He was held in high regard by Xerxes, belonged to the Achaemenid family, was in stature the tallest of all the Persians — falling short by only four fingers of being five royal cubits in height — and he had the loudest voice of any man. Xerxes was deeply grieved at the loss of him, and carried him out and buried him with great honor, and the whole army joined in heaping up a mound for him. The people of Acanthus, on the instruction of an oracle, sacrifice to this Artachaees as a hero, invoking his name in their worship.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 118
paragraphs: Xerxes, then, was deeply grieved at the loss of Artachaees. Meanwhile the Greeks who were entertaining his army and providing Xerxes with his dinners had been brought to utter ruin, to the point that they were being driven from house and home. For instance, when the Thasians entertained Xerxes's army and provided him with dinner on behalf of their towns on the mainland, Antipater son of Orgeus, a man of standing among the citizens equal to the best and appointed to this business, reported that four hundred talents of silver had been spent on that single meal.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 119
paragraphs: In the other cities also, those placed in charge of the business reckoned roughly the same cost. For the dinner was arranged as follows, having been ordered a long time in advance and reckoned a matter of the greatest importance. In the first place, as soon as they heard of it from the heralds who carried the proclamation around, the citizens in each city distributed grain among their households, and everyone kept grinding wheat and barley meal for many months. Then they fattened cattle, finding and obtaining the finest animals at a high price, and they kept birds both of the land and of the water in cages or in pools, all for the entertainment of the army. Then again they had drinking-cups and mixing-bowls made of gold and silver, and all the other table service; these were made for the king himself and for those who dined with him, but for the rest of the army only the appointed rations were provided. When the army came to any place, a tent was already pitched ready in which Xerxes himself took his rest, while the rest of the army stayed in the open air. When dinner-time came, it was the hosts who had to toil; while the others, once they had eaten their fill and passed the night there, the next day tore down the tent, took all the movable furniture with them, and moved on, leaving nothing behind.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 120
paragraphs: It was then that a saying was well uttered by Megacreon, a man of Abdera, who advised the Abderites to go in a body, themselves and their wives, to their temples, and sit down as suppliants of the gods, begging that for the future too the gods would ward off from them the half of whatever evils threatened. He told them to feel great thankfulness to the gods for the past, since King Xerxes had not seen fit to eat twice a day. For if it had been ordered that breakfast also be provided in the same style as dinner, it would have remained for the Abderites either not to await Xerxes's coming at all, or, if they stayed, to be crushed by misfortune more than any other men on earth.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 121
paragraphs: They, then, hard pressed as they were, carried out what had been ordered of them. From Acanthus Xerxes, after ordering the generals to wait for the fleet at Therma, let the ships sail apart from himself; (Therma is the city on the Thermaic gulf, which takes its name from it). He did this because he had been told that this was the shortest route. For from Doriscus as far as Acanthus the army had been marching thus: Xerxes had divided the whole land army into three divisions. One of them he assigned to march along the sea, accompanying the fleet; its commanders were Mardonius and Masistes. Another third of the army was ordered to march by the inland route, under the command of Tritantaechmes and Gergis. Meanwhile the third subdivision, with which Xerxes himself went, marched in the middle between them, under the command of Smerdomenes and Megabyzus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 122
paragraphs: The fleet, when it had been released by Xerxes and had sailed through the channel dug across Athos (which runs across to the gulf on which the cities of Assa, Pilorus, Singus, and Sarte are situated), having taken up a contingent from these cities as well, sailed from there with a fair passage into the Thermaic gulf. Rounding Ampelos, the headland of Torone, it left on one side the following Greek cities, from which it took up contingents of ships and men: Torone, Galepsus, Sermyle, Mecyberna, and Olynthus. This region is called Sithonia.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 123
paragraphs: Xerxes's fleet, cutting across from the headland of Ampelos to that of Canastraeum — which juts farthest into the sea of all Pallene — took on contingents of ships and men from Potidaea, Aphytis, Neapolis, Aege, Therambus, Scione, Mende, and Sane, for these are the cities that occupy the region now called Pallene, once called Phlegra. Sailing along the coast of this country also, the fleet continued on its course toward the place already mentioned, taking up contingents from the cities that come next after Pallene and border the Thermaic gulf; their names are: Lipaxus, Combreia, Lisae, Gigonus, Campsa, Smila, and Aeneia. The region in which these cities stand is called Crossaea to this very day. Sailing from Aeneia, with whose name I end the list, the fleet came straight into the Thermaic gulf and into the region of Mygdonia, and so arrived at the aforesaid Therma and at the cities of Sindus and Chalestra on the river Axius. This river is the boundary between Mygdonia and Bottiaea, the narrow coastal strip of which is occupied by the cities of Ichnae and Pella.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 124
paragraphs: While his naval force was camped about the river Axius, the city of Therma, and the cities in between, waiting for the king's arrival, Xerxes and the land army were advancing from Acanthus, cutting through the middle by the shortest route to reach Therma. They passed through Paeonia and Crestonia to the river Cheidorus, which rises in the land of the Crestonians, flows through Mygdonia, and comes out alongside the marsh by the river Axius.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 125
paragraphs: As the army was proceeding along this route, lions attacked the camels that carried his provisions. The lions used to come down regularly at night, leaving their haunts, but they touched nothing else — neither baggage animal nor man — only the camels. I wonder what the cause was, what it was that made the lions leave everything else alone and attack the camels only, creatures they had never seen before and had never had any experience of.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 126
paragraphs: In these parts there are many lions and many wild oxen, the kind with the very large horns that are often brought into Greece. The range of these lions is bounded on one side by the Nestus, which flows through Abdera, and on the other by the Achelous, which flows through Acarnania: you will not see a lion in any part of Europe east of the Nestus, nor in the remaining part of the continent west of the Achelous. They are found only in the space between these rivers.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 127
paragraphs: When Xerxes reached Therma, he established the army there. The encampment occupied no less than the following stretch of coast: starting from the city of Therma and from Mygdonia, it extended as far as the rivers Lydias and Haliacmon, which form the boundary between Bottiaea and Macedonia by mingling their waters into one and the same stream. In these places the barbarians were encamped; and of the rivers listed, only the Cheidorus, flowing from Crestonian territory, proved insufficient for the drinking of the army and ran dry.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 128
paragraphs: Then Xerxes, seeing from Therma the mountains of Thessaly, Olympus and Ossa, and noting that they were very lofty, and being informed that between them lay a narrow channel through which the Peneios flows, and hearing that by this way there was a good road leading into Thessaly, conceived a desire to sail there and look at the outlet of the Peneios — for he was intending to take the inland route, through the land of the upland Macedonians, until he should reach the Perrhaebians, passing by the city of Gonnos; this way, he was told, was safest. Having conceived the wish, he acted on it: he embarked on a Sidonian ship (the one he always used when he wanted to do something of this kind), and he gave the signal for the other ships to put out to sea too, leaving the land army behind. When Xerxes had looked at the outlet of the Peneios, he was struck with great wonder, and summoning his guides he asked them whether it was possible to turn the river aside and bring it out to the sea by another route.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 129
paragraphs: Thessaly, it is said, was in old times a lake, enclosed on all sides by very lofty mountains; for the parts of it lying to the east are shut in by the ranges of Pelion and Ossa, which join each other at their lower slopes, those to the north by Olympus, those to the west by Pindus, and those to the south by Othrys. The region in the middle, between all these named mountains, is Thessaly, forming as it were a hollow. Many rivers flow into it — especially five of note: the Peneios, Apidanus, Onochonos, Enipeus, and Pamisos — which gather their waters from the mountains that ring Thessaly and run into the plain with separate names, finally flowing into the sea by one single narrow channel, after mingling all their waters together. As soon as they are mingled, the Peneios prevails over the rest with its name and obliterates the separate names. It is said that in ancient times, when this channel and outlet between the mountains did not yet exist, these rivers, together with Lake Boebeis, had no names as they do now; but by their waters they made the whole of Thessaly into a sea. The Thessalians themselves say that Poseidon made the channel through which the Peneios flows; and reasonably so, since anyone who believes that it is Poseidon who shakes the earth and that the chasms produced by earthquakes are his work would, on seeing this place, say that it was made by Poseidon — for the parting of the mountains is clearly, to my mind, the work of an earthquake.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 130
paragraphs: So when Xerxes asked whether there was any other possible outlet to the sea for the Peneios, the guides answered with exact knowledge of the truth: “O king, for this river there is no other outlet reaching the sea than this one alone; for all Thessaly is encircled by mountains like a crown.” To this Xerxes is said to have replied: “Then the Thessalians are prudent men. This, it seems, was what they wished to guard against in good time when they changed their policy — reflecting, among other things, on this in particular: that they have a country which is, as it seems, easy to conquer and can be taken quickly, for one would only need to let the river flood their land by throwing up an embankment to keep it from going through the narrow channel and diverting its course from the present one, so as to put the whole of Thessaly under water, except the mountains.” He said this with reference to the sons of Aleuas, because they, Thessalians, were the first of the Greeks to give themselves over to the king; and Xerxes believed they were offering him friendship on behalf of their whole nation. Having so spoken, and having looked at the place, he sailed back to Therma.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 131
paragraphs: He spent many days in the region of Pieria, for meanwhile a third of his army was cutting the road over the Macedonian mountains, so that the whole host could pass by this way into the land of the Perrhaebians. Now too the heralds returned who had been sent to Greece to demand earth, some empty-handed, others bearing earth and water.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 132
paragraphs: Among those who gave what was demanded were these: the Thessalians, Dolopians, Enienes, Perrhaebians, Locrians, Magnesians, Malians, Achaeans of Phthiotis, and Thebans, along with the rest of the Boeotians except the Thespians and Plataeans. Against these the Greeks who took up war against the barbarian swore an oath: that whatever Greeks had given themselves over to the Persian without being compelled, if the Greeks' own affairs came to a good end, they would dedicate a tithe of them as an offering to the god at Delphi.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 133
paragraphs: Such was the oath taken by the Greeks. But Xerxes had not sent heralds to Athens or Sparta to demand earth, for this reason: when Darius earlier had sent men for this very purpose, the Athenians threw those who made the demand into the pit and the Spartans threw them into a well, telling them to take earth and water from there and carry them to the king. For this reason Xerxes did not send envoys to make this demand. What evil came upon the Athenians in consequence of this treatment of the heralds, I cannot say — except that their land and city were laid waste; but I do not think this happened for that reason.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 134
paragraphs: On the Lacedaemonians, however, the wrath of Talthybius, Agamemnon's herald, fell. In Sparta there is a temple of Talthybius, and there are also descendants of his called Talthybiads, to whom the right of carrying out all heralds' missions from Sparta has been given. After this event, the Spartans could not, when sacrificing, obtain favorable omens. This state of things lasted a long time, and the Lacedaemonians were grieved, reckoning it a great misfortune. Assemblies were called repeatedly and a proclamation made asking whether any Lacedaemonian was willing to die for Sparta. At length Sperthias son of Aneristus and Bulis son of Nicolaus, Spartans of noble birth and of the very first rank in wealth, voluntarily offered themselves up to Xerxes to pay the penalty for Darius's heralds who had perished at Sparta. So the Spartans sent these men to the Medes to be put to death.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 135
paragraphs: Not only is the courage shown by these men worthy of admiration, but also the sayings they uttered. On their way to Susa they came to Hydarnes — a Persian by birth, commander of the peoples of the Asian seaboard — and he offered them hospitality and entertained them. While they were his guests he asked them: “Lacedaemonians, why do you refuse to become friends of the king? You can see that the king knows how to honor good men, if you look at me and my fortunes. So you too, Lacedaemonians, if you gave yourselves over to the king — since you already have the reputation with him of being good men — each of you would rule some Greek country as the king's gift.” To this they answered: “Hydarnes, your advice to us is not equally balanced, for you advise having experience of one side only and no experience of the other. You know well what slavery is, but you have never yet tasted freedom, to know whether it is sweet or not. If you had tried it, you would advise us to fight for it not with spears only, but with axes.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 136
paragraphs: That was their answer to Hydarnes. When they had gone up to Susa and come into the king's presence, the spear-bearers of the guard first ordered them, and tried to compel them by force, to do obeisance to the king by prostrating themselves. They said they would do no such thing, even if the guards pushed them down head-first, for it was not their custom to do obeisance to a man, and they had not come there for that purpose. After resisting this, they spoke words to this effect: “O king of the Medes, the Lacedaemonians have sent us in place of the heralds killed at Sparta, to pay the penalty for their lives.” At this, Xerxes, moved by a spirit of magnanimity, replied that he would not be like the Lacedaemonians, who had violated the customs accepted by all men by killing heralds; he would not do himself what he blamed them for doing, nor would he free the Lacedaemonians from their guilt by killing these men in return.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 137
paragraphs: So, for the moment, the wrath of Talthybius was laid to rest, even though the Spartans had done no more than this, and even though Sperthias and Bulis returned home to Sparta. Long afterwards, however — during the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians — it was roused again, as the Lacedaemonians say. In this I see most clearly the hand of Divinity. That the wrath of Talthybius fell upon messengers and did not cease until it had been fully paid out was only just. But that it happened to fall upon the sons of the very men who had gone up to the king because of that wrath — namely Nicolaus son of Bulis and Aneristus son of Sperthias (the same Aneristus who took the town of Halieis, a colony of Tiryns, by sailing into its harbor with a merchant ship full of fighting men) — this makes it clear to me that it came about by divine action caused by the wrath. For these men, sent by the Lacedaemonians as envoys to Asia, were betrayed by Sitalces son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and by Nymphodorus son of Pythes, a man of Abdera, and were captured at Bisanthe on the Hellespont. Brought to Attica, they were put to death by the Athenians, along with Aristeas son of Adeimantus of Corinth. These events took place many years after the king's expedition; but I now return to my earlier narrative.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 138
paragraphs: The king's expedition was called, in name, an expedition against Athens; but in fact it was aimed at all of Greece. The Greeks, long since informed of it, were not all affected in the same way. Some of them, having given earth and water to the Persian, were confident, expecting that they would suffer no injury from the barbarian; while others, who had not given, were in great fear, seeing that there were not ships enough in Greece to receive the invader in battle as far as numbers went, and that the majority of the states were unwilling to take up the war but readily embraced the side of the Medes.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 139
paragraphs: I am forced here to declare an opinion that most men will find distasteful, but I will not refrain from saying what I plainly see to be the truth. If the Athenians, seized with fear of the danger threatening them, had abandoned their country, or if, without abandoning it, they had stayed and given themselves up to Xerxes, no one would have opposed the king at sea. And if no one had opposed Xerxes at sea, on land things would have gone somewhat like this: even if the Peloponnesians had thrown many rings of walls across the Isthmus, the Lacedaemonians would have been deserted by their allies — not willingly, but of necessity, since their allies would have been subdued city by city by the barbarian's fleet, and the Spartans would have been left alone. Left alone, and showing great deeds of valor, they would have died nobly. Either that, or, seeing the rest of the Greeks going over to the Medes, they would have come to terms with Xerxes before that. Either way, Greece would have fallen under Persian rule. As for the supposed benefit of walls thrown across the Isthmus, I cannot see what good they would have been once the king commanded the sea. As it is, if anyone should say that the Athenians were the saviors of Greece, he would not miss the truth. For whichever way they turned, the balance was likely to tip. They were the ones who, preferring that Greece should continue to exist in freedom, roused up all of Greece that had not already gone over to the Medes — and, after the gods at least, they were the ones who repelled the king. Not even the dreadful oracles that came from Delphi and cast them into dread induced them to abandon Greece. They stayed and endured to receive the invader into their land.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 140
paragraphs: The Athenians had sent men to Delphi to consult the oracle. After these had performed the usual rites in the sacred precinct, when they had entered the inner sanctuary and taken their seats, the Pythian priestess — whose name was Aristonice — uttered this oracle to them:

“Why do you sit, you wretched ones? Flee to the uttermost limits, leaving your home and the heights of the wheel-round city behind you! Lo, there remains now neither head nor body in safety — neither the feet below, nor the hands, nor anything between is left to you; all are destroyed together, for fire and the passionate War-god, driving on the Syrian car at speed, shall hurl them down to ruin. Not yours alone — he shall make many other great strongholds perish, yes, he shall deliver many temples of the gods to the ravening fire: temples that even now stand with the sweat of their terror streaming down, shaking with dread; and lo! from the topmost roof to the pavement dark blood trickles, foretelling the dire, unavoidable evil. Forth from the shrine with you, and steep your soul in sorrow!”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 141
paragraphs: Hearing this, the Athenian envoys were thrown into deep distress. As they were giving themselves over to despair at the evil prophesied to them, Timon son of Androboulus, a Delphian of reputation equal to the first, advised them to take a suppliant's bough and approach the oracle a second time, consulting it as suppliants. The Athenians did as he advised and said: “Lord, we beg you, utter to us some better oracle about our native land, out of respect for these suppliant boughs we have come bearing to you. Otherwise we will certainly not depart from the sanctuary, but will stay here where we are now, even until we bring our lives to an end.” When they had spoken these words, the priestess gave them a second oracle as follows:

“Pallas cannot prevail to appease great Zeus on Olympus, though with many words and close-woven wiles she beseech him. But I will tell you this more, and clench it with adamantine steel: when all else is taken — whatever the boundary of Cecrops encloses within, and the dark ravines of divinest Cithaeron — a wall of wood at last Zeus grants to the Trito-born goddess, alone to remain unbroken, which shall profit you and your children. Stay not there for the horsemen to come, nor for the countless foot-soldiers; stay not for the host from the mainland, but turn your back to the foe and withdraw; for yet in time you shall face him again. Salamis, thou divine, thou shalt bring sons of women to perish, either when grain is sown or when it is gathered in.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 142
paragraphs: This seemed to them, as indeed it was, a milder utterance than the first. So they had it written down and departed with it to Athens. When the messengers on their return reported to the people, many differing opinions were expressed by those who tried to interpret the oracle, and among them these, standing most at odds with one another: some of the older men said that they thought the god had prophesied that the Acropolis would survive, for the Acropolis of the Athenians had in old times been fenced with a thorn hedge, and they took the phrase “wall of wood” to refer to this hedge. Others, on the contrary, said that the god meant their ships by this, and they advised leaving everything else aside and getting these ready. Those who claimed the ships were the wall of wood were, however, shaken in their interpretation by the last two verses the priestess uttered:
“Salamis, thou divine, thou shalt bring sons of women to perish, either when grain is sown or when it is gathered in.”

On these verses the opinion of those who said that the ships were the wall of wood was disturbed, for the professional interpreters of oracles took these to mean that they were fated, if they prepared for a sea-battle, to be defeated around Salamis.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 143
paragraphs: Now there was a certain Athenian who had been lately coming forward to take his place among the leading men, whose name was Themistocles, called son of Neocles. This man said that the oracle-interpreters were not making a correct guess at the whole meaning. He argued that if these words really referred to the Athenians, the oracle would not have been worded so mildly but rather thus: “Salamis, thou merciless,” instead of “Salamis, thou divine,” — at least if the inhabitants were destined to perish around it. Properly understood, the oracle had been uttered by the god not against the Athenians but against the enemy. He therefore advised them to prepare for a sea-battle, for in this lay their wall of wood. When Themistocles had thus declared his opinion, the Athenians judged it was to be preferred to the advice of the oracle-interpreters, who had bidden them not to make ready for a sea-fight and in fact not to raise their hands in opposition at all, but to abandon the land of Attica and settle elsewhere.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 144
paragraphs: Another opinion of Themistocles had already, at the right moment, proved to be the best. The Athenians had had large sums accumulating in the public treasury from the revenue of the mines at Laurium, and were planning to distribute them among themselves, ten drachmas to each man. Themistocles persuaded them to give up this plan of distribution and instead to build with this money two hundred ships for the war — meaning the war with Aegina. For that war, as it turned out, was the salvation of Greece at that time, by compelling the Athenians to become a naval power. The ships, though not used for the purpose for which they had been built, thus proved of service to Greece when Greece needed them. These ships, then, the Athenians already had, having built them beforehand; in addition it was necessary to build others. After the oracle was given, they decided in council to receive with their ships in full force the barbarian invading Greece — following the god's commands — together with those Greeks willing to join them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 145
paragraphs: These were the oracles that had been given to the Athenians. When those Greeks who had the better mind about Greece met together in one place, considered their affairs and exchanged assurances with one another, they decided that their first step of all should be to reconcile their mutual enmities and bring to an end the wars they were currently waging against one another. Other states had wars on their hands, but especially the Athenians had one with the Aeginetans. After this, having been informed that Xerxes was at Sardis with his army, they resolved to send spies to Asia to observe the king's strength, and to send envoys to Argos to make an alliance against the Persian, and others to Sicily to Gelon son of Dinomenes, and others to Corcyra, urging them to come to the help of Greece, and others again to Crete — with the aim that if possible the Greek race might unite as one and that all might act together toward the same end, since dangers threatened all Greeks equally. Gelon's power was said to be great, far greater than any other Greek state's.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 146
paragraphs: Having so resolved, they reconciled their quarrels, and then first sent three men as spies to Asia. On arriving at Sardis, these men gathered information about the king's army, but were discovered. After being examined by the generals of the land army, they were being led off to their deaths. Their death had been decreed — but Xerxes, on being informed of this, found fault with the generals' decision and sent some of his spear-bearing bodyguards, with orders to bring the spies before him if they were still alive. They found them still alive and brought them into the king's presence. Xerxes, having ascertained for what purpose they had come, commanded the spearmen to take them around and show them the whole army, both infantry and cavalry, and when they had had their fill of looking at it, to let them go unharmed to whatever country they wished.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 147
paragraphs: Such was his order, and he added this saying at the same time: if the spies had been put to death, the Greeks would not have learned beforehand how far beyond description his power was; and on the other hand, by killing three men they would not have done the enemy much damage. But when these men returned to Greece, he thought the Greeks, hearing of his might, would hand over their freedom to him of their own accord, before the expedition even took place; and in that case there would be no need for him to take the trouble of marching against them. This opinion of his is much like his way of thinking at other times. For when Xerxes was at Abydos, he saw grain ships from the Pontus sailing through the Hellespont on their way to Aegina and the Peloponnese. Those sitting beside him, on being told that the ships belonged to the enemy, were ready to capture them and looked to the king to see when he would give the word. But Xerxes asked where the men were sailing, and they replied, “Master, to your enemies, carrying grain to them.” He then said: “Are we not sailing to the same place ourselves, provided with grain as well as the other necessities? How then do these men wrong us, seeing that they are carrying provisions that will serve us?”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 148
paragraphs: The spies, having thus observed everything and afterwards been released, returned to Europe. Meanwhile those Greeks who had sworn alliance against the Persian, after sending out the spies, next sent envoys to Argos. The Argives report that their own affairs happened like this. They were informed, they say, at the very first of the enterprise being set on foot by the barbarian against Greece; and upon being informed, and perceiving that the Greeks would try to get them as allies against the Persians, they sent messengers to consult the god at Delphi, asking how they should act to obtain the best outcome for themselves — since lately six thousand of them had been slain by the Lacedaemonians under Cleomenes son of Anaxandridas, and this was in fact why they sent to inquire. On consulting the oracle, the Pythia gave them this answer:
“You who are hated by your neighbors, but loved by the immortal gods — keep your spear within bounds, and sit well guarded behind it. Guard the head well, and the head shall save the limbs and body.”

Such, they say, was the Pythia's earlier reply to them. And afterwards, when the Greek messengers came, as I said, to Argos, they entered the council chamber and said what they had been charged to say. The Council's response was this: the Argives were ready to do as requested, on condition that they made peace with the Lacedaemonians for thirty years, and that they had half the leadership of the whole confederacy; and yet by strict right (they said) the whole leadership belonged to them, but it was enough to have half.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 149
paragraphs: So the Council replied, they say, even though the oracle had forbidden them to make the alliance with the Greeks. They were eager, they say, for a thirty-year truce from hostilities, despite their fear of the oracle, so that (as they allege) their sons might grow to manhood during those years; they feared that if there was no truce and another disaster befell them fighting the Persian on top of the one they had already suffered, they might for all time to come be subject to the Lacedaemonians. To what the Council said, those of the envoys who were from Sparta replied that regarding the truce they would refer the matter to their public assembly, but regarding the leadership they were themselves empowered to answer, and they did so: they had two kings, while the Argives had one; it was not possible to remove either of the two Spartan kings from leadership, but nothing prevented the Argive king from having an equal vote with each of theirs. Then, say the Argives, they could not bear the grasping selfishness of the Spartans; they chose to be ruled by the barbarians rather than yield in any way to the Lacedaemonians, and they ordered the envoys to leave the territory of Argos before sunset, or else be treated as enemies.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 150
paragraphs: This is the Argives' own report about these matters. But another story is told in Greece, to the effect that Xerxes sent a herald to Argos before setting out to campaign against Greece. When this herald arrived, he said: “Men of Argos, King Xerxes says this to you: we hold that Perses, from whom we are descended, was the son of Perseus son of Danaë, born of Andromeda daughter of Cepheus; and by this account it would seem that we are descended from you. It is not fitting, then, that we should go on an expedition against those from whom we trace our descent, nor that you should set yourselves against us by helping others. Rather, it is fitting that you keep still and remain by yourselves; for if things turn out as I intend, I shall hold no people in higher honor than you.” On hearing this, the Argives, it is said, considered the matter a weighty one, and so at first they made no offer of help, nor did they ask for any share. But later, when the Greeks tried to bring them into the alliance, then — knowing well that the Lacedaemonians would not give them a share in the command — they asked for a share in command merely as a pretext for staying neutral.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 151
paragraphs: Some Greeks also report an event which, in agreement with this account, occurred many years after these things. It so happened that at Susa, the city of Memnon, there were Athenian envoys come about another matter — Callias son of Hipponicus and those who went up with him — and at that same time the Argives had also sent envoys to Susa, who asked Artaxerxes son of Xerxes whether the friendship they had formed with Xerxes still stood, if they themselves wished to maintain it, or whether he now considered them enemies; and King Artaxerxes answered that it most certainly still stood, and that there was no city he reckoned a greater friend than Argos.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 152
paragraphs: Now, whether Xerxes actually sent a herald to Argos saying these things, and whether the Argive envoys who went up to Susa really questioned Artaxerxes about friendship, I cannot say for certain; and I offer no opinion on the matter other than what the Argives themselves report. But I do know this: if all the nations of men were to bring together in one place the evils they have suffered, wishing to make an exchange with their neighbors, each people, once they had closely examined the evils their fellows had suffered, would gladly carry back home those they had brought. So the Argives have not acted the most shamefully of all. I, however, am bound to report what is reported, though I am not bound to believe it entirely; and let this remark be taken as holding good for every narrative in my history. For I must add that it is also reported that the Argives were actually the ones who invited the Persian to invade Greece, because their war with the Lacedaemonians had ended badly, and they were ready to suffer anything rather than the calamity that was then upon them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 153
paragraphs: So much for the Argives. Meanwhile envoys had come from the allies to Sicily to confer with Gelon, among them Syagrus from the Lacedaemonians. The ancestor of this Gelon — the man who came as a settler to Gela — was a native of the island of Telos, which lies off Triopion; and when Gela was being founded by the Lindians of Rhodes and by Antiphemus, he was not left behind. In the course of time his descendants became and continued to be priests of the mysteries of the chthonic goddesses, an office acquired by Telines, one of their ancestors, in the following way. Certain men of Gela, defeated in a factional struggle, had fled to Mactorium, the city above Gela. These men Telines brought back to Gela from exile, with no force of arms, but only with the sacred rites of these goddesses. From whom he received them, or whether he obtained them for himself, I cannot say; but trusting in these rites, he brought the exiles back on the condition that his descendants would be priests of the mysteries of the goddesses. It has made me wonder that Telines could have carried out so great a deed, given what I have been told. Such deeds, to my mind, do not come from any ordinary man, but from one of brave spirit and manly vigor; whereas Telines, according to the inhabitants of Sicily, was on the contrary effeminate in character and rather faint-hearted.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 154
paragraphs: He, then, had obtained the priesthood I speak of. When Cleander son of Pantares came to the end of his life after having been tyrant of Gela for seven years — finally killed by Sabyllus, a man of Gela — the monarchy passed to his brother Hippocrates. While Hippocrates was tyrant, Gelon, a descendant of Telines the priest of the mysteries, served as a spear-bearer of his bodyguard along with many others, including Aenesidemus son of Pataecus. Before long he was promoted for his valor to command the whole cavalry. For when Hippocrates laid siege in succession to Callipolis, Naxos, Zancle, and Leontini, and also to Syracuse and many towns of the barbarians, Gelon showed himself a most brilliant warrior in these wars; and of the cities just mentioned, not one — except Syracuse — escaped being reduced to subjection by Hippocrates. The Syracusans, however, after being defeated in battle at the river Elorus, were rescued by the Corinthians and Corcyreans, who brought the quarrel to a settlement on the condition that the Syracusans should hand Camarina over to Hippocrates. Camarina had in ancient times belonged to the Syracusans.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 155
paragraphs: When it was Hippocrates's fate, after having been tyrant for the same number of years as his brother Cleander, to be killed at the city of Hybla — where he had gone on an expedition against the Sicels — Gelon, under the pretext of helping Hippocrates's sons Euclides and Cleander, when the citizens were no longer willing to submit, in fact, after winning a battle over the men of Gela, stripped Hippocrates's sons of power and became ruler himself. After this stroke of luck, Gelon restored those Syracusans called the “landholders” who had been driven into exile by the common people and by their own slaves (called Cyllyrians). He brought them from the city of Casmene back to Syracuse, and in this way gained possession of Syracuse too — for the common people of Syracuse, when Gelon marched against them, handed over both the city and themselves to him.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 156
paragraphs: Having got Syracuse in his power, he cared less for Gela, of which he was also ruler, and handed it over to his brother Hieron, while he himself set about strengthening Syracuse. At once that city rose and shot up in prosperity. First, he brought all the people of Camarina to Syracuse and made them citizens, then razed Camarina to the ground. Next he did the same to more than half of the people of Gela as he had done to the Camarinans. As for the Megarians of Sicily, when they were besieged and surrendered by capitulation, he took the wealthy among them — who had stirred up the war against him and were expecting to be executed — and brought them to Syracuse and made them citizens; but the common people of Megara, who had no share in the guilt of that war and expected to suffer no evil, these too he brought to Syracuse and sold them as slaves for export out of Sicily. He did the same thing with the Euboeans of Sicily, making the same distinction between them. He dealt thus with both cities because he reckoned a body of common people to be a most unpleasant element in a state.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 157
paragraphs: In the manner described, then, Gelon had become a powerful tyrant. At this time, when the Greek envoys arrived at Syracuse, they came to confer with him and said: “The Lacedaemonians and their allies have sent us to get you to join them against the barbarian. We assume you know well of the man who is about to invade Greece — that a Persian is planning to bridge the Hellespont and lead an expedition against Greece, bringing with him out of Asia all the armies of the East, under the pretext of marching on Athens, but in fact intending to bring all of Greece under his power. You, seeing that you have risen to great power and have no small portion of Greece as your share, being ruler of Sicily, come to the aid of those striving to free Greece, and help to set her free. For if all Greece is gathered into one, it forms a great body, and we are a match for those coming against us. But if some of us go over to the enemy and others refuse to help, so that the sound part of Greece is only a small part, then at once there is a danger that all Greece may fall to ruin. Do not imagine that if the Persian defeats us in battle he will not also come against you — guard against this beforehand. In coming to our aid you are helping yourself. A thing planned wisely generally turns out well in the end.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 158
paragraphs: So spoke the envoys; and Gelon came down on them very sharply, saying: “Greeks, it is a selfish speech with which you have dared to come and invite me to be your ally against the barbarian. When, some time ago, I asked you to join me in fighting an army of barbarians, a quarrel having arisen between me and the Carthaginians, and when I called upon you to take vengeance on the people of Egesta for the death of Dorieus son of Anaxandridas, while at the same time I offered to help you in freeing the trading posts, from which you have reaped great advantages and profits — then neither for my sake did you come to my aid, nor did you come to exact vengeance for the death of Dorieus. And as far as you are concerned, all those places are even now under the rule of barbarians. But since things turned out well for us and took a better course, now that the war has come round and reached you, at last a memory of Gelon has arisen in your minds. Even so, though I have been slighted by you, I will not act as you did; I am prepared to come to your aid, supplying two hundred triremes, twenty thousand hoplites, two thousand cavalry, two thousand archers, two thousand slingers, and two thousand light-armed men to run alongside the cavalry; and moreover I undertake to supply grain for the whole Greek army until we have finished the war. I pledge these things on this condition: that I be commander and leader of the Greeks against the barbarian. On any other terms I will neither come myself nor send others.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 159
paragraphs: Hearing this, Syagrus could not contain himself and said: “Deeply, I believe, would Agamemnon son of Pelops groan, if he heard that the Spartans had had the leadership taken from them by Gelon and the Syracusans. No — make no further mention of the condition that we should hand the leadership over to you. If you wish to come to Greece's aid, know that you will be under the command of the Lacedaemonians; and if you insist on not being under command, do not come to our help at all.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 160
paragraphs: Seeing that Syagrus's reply was hostile, Gelon now put forward his final proposal: “Spartan stranger, reproaches that sink into a man's heart are apt to rouse his spirit in anger against them; yet although you have spoken insults against me, you will not provoke me into making an unseemly reply. But since you so firmly lay claim to the leadership, it would be more fitting for me to do so than for you, seeing that I am leader of an army many times as large and of ships many more. Since, however, this condition is so distasteful to you, we will yield somewhat on our original demand. Suppose you were to be leaders of the land army and I of the fleet; or if it pleases you to lead the sea forces, I am willing to be leader on land. Either you must be content with these terms, or you will go away without the alliance I have to give.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 161
paragraphs: Gelon made these offers, and the Athenian envoy, answering before the Lacedaemonian, replied: “O king of the Syracusans, it was not a leader Greece needed when she sent us to you, but an army. You, however, do not hold out to us any hope that you will send an army, unless you have the leadership of Greece; and you are striving to become commander of the Greek forces. So long as you demanded to be leader of the entire Greek army, it was enough for us Athenians to keep silence, knowing that the Lacedaemonian could answer for us both. But now, since, rebuffed from the demand for the whole, you are asking to command the naval force, we tell you this: not even if the Lacedaemonian allows it will we permit you to command the fleet. This at least is our own right, if the Lacedaemonians do not themselves desire it. If they wish to be leaders, we do not contest it with them; but no one else shall we permit to command the ships. For then to no purpose would we possess a naval force larger than that of any other Greek people, if, being Athenians, we should yield the leadership to Syracusans — we, who boast of a race the most ancient of all, the only Greeks never to have migrated from one land to another, and who had a man whom Homer the epic poet said was the best of all who came to Ilium in drawing up an army and arranging it in battle order. So we are not justly to be reproached if we say these things.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 162
paragraphs: To this Gelon replied: “Athenian stranger, it seems you have the commanders, but no men to be commanded. Since, then, you will not yield at all and want the whole, you had best go home as fast as you can and tell the Greeks that the spring has been taken out of their year.” The meaning of the saying is this: that the spring is plainly the noblest part of the year, and so he meant to say that his army was the noblest part of the Greek army; thus Greece, deprived of his alliance, was, he said, as if the spring had been taken out of the year.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 163
