paragraphs: The Greek envoys, having finished their conference with Gelon, sailed away. Gelon for his part, on the one hand fearing for the Greeks that they might not be able to overcome the barbarian, and on the other thinking it intolerable that he, as tyrant of Sicily, should go to the Peloponnese and be under the command of the Lacedaemonians, gave up this plan and followed another. As soon as he was informed that the Persian had crossed the Hellespont, he sent Cadmus son of Scythes, a man of Cos, with three fifty-oared galleys to Delphi, carrying large sums of money and friendly proposals, to wait there and see how the battle would turn out: if the barbarian should win, he was to give him the money and also offer him earth and water from the lands over which Gelon ruled; if the Greeks should win, he was to bring it all back.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 164
paragraphs: This Cadmus, before these events, had inherited from his father the government of Cos in a prosperous state; and, under no compulsion or threat of danger but moved simply by uprightness of character, he had voluntarily placed the government in the hands of the people of Cos and departed to Sicily, where he took the city of Zancle (which had changed its name to Messene) from the Samians and colonized it anew. This Cadmus, having come there in the manner described, Gelon was now sending, having picked him out because of the integrity he had found in him in other matters. In addition to his other honorable actions, Cadmus left this deed to be remembered — and not the least of them. Having charge of that great sum of money that Gelon had entrusted to him, though he might easily have taken it for himself, he did not choose to do so; but when the Greeks had prevailed in the sea-fight and Xerxes had withdrawn and gone home, he too returned to Sicily bringing back the entire sum with him.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 165
paragraphs: The following story is also told by those living in Sicily: that Gelon, even though he would have had to be under the Lacedaemonians' command, would have come to the aid of the Greeks — but that Terillus son of Crinippus, the tyrant of Himera, having been driven out of Himera by Theron son of Aenesidemus, the ruler of the Acragantines, was at this very time bringing in an army of Phoenicians, Libyans, Iberians, Ligurians, Elisycans, Sardinians, and Corsicans, to the number of three hundred thousand, with Hamilcar son of Hanno, king of the Carthaginians, as their commander. Terillus had persuaded Hamilcar partly by the guest-friendship between them, but especially by the zealous help of Anaxilaus son of Cretines, the tyrant of Rhegium, who to help his father-in-law tried to bring Hamilcar into Sicily and gave him his own sons as hostages. For Anaxilaus was married to Terillus's daughter, whose name was Cydippe. So, they say, it was for this reason that Gelon could not come to the aid of the Greeks, and therefore sent the money to Delphi.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 166
paragraphs: In addition, they report that it happened that Gelon and Theron won their victory over Hamilcar the Carthaginian on the very same day when the Greeks won at Salamis over the Persian. This Hamilcar, who was a Carthaginian on his father's side but Syracusan on his mother's, and who had become king of the Carthaginians on his merits, when the engagement took place and he began to be defeated in the battle, disappeared, as I am told; for neither alive nor dead did he appear again anywhere on earth, though Gelon used every effort to search for him.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 167
paragraphs: Moreover there is also this story reported by the Carthaginians themselves — and they give what is probable in itself. While the barbarians were fighting the Greeks in Sicily from early morning till late afternoon (for to such length, it is said, the combat was drawn out), Hamilcar was all this time in the camp, sacrificing to obtain good omens, burning whole victims on a great pyre. When he saw the rout of his own army — being at that moment, it happened, in the act of pouring a libation over the offerings — he threw himself into the fire, and so was burned up and disappeared. However it was that Hamilcar vanished — whether in such a way as this, as the Phoenicians report, or in some other way — the Carthaginians now offer sacrifices to him, and at that time they set up memorials to him in all the cities of their colonies, and the greatest of them in Carthage itself.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 168
paragraphs: So much for affairs in Sicily. As for the Corcyreans, they answered the envoys as follows — and then acted as I shall now relate. The same men who had gone to Sicily tried to enlist the Corcyreans' help too, using the same arguments they had used with Gelon; and the Corcyreans at the time promised to send a force and to help in the defense, declaring that they must not permit Greece to be ruined without an effort on their part, for if it suffered disaster they would themselves be reduced to subjection from the very first day, and they must give aid to the utmost of their power. Thus speciously they replied; but when the time came to send help, they manned sixty ships, having other intentions in mind, and after much delay finally put out to sea and reached the Peloponnese. Then near Pylos and Taenarum in the Lacedaemonian territory they kept their ships at anchor, waiting, like Gelon, to see how the war would turn out; for they did not expect the Greeks to prevail but thought the Persian would easily get the better of them and be ruler of all Greece. They were acting deliberately in order to be able to say to the Persian something like this: “O king, when the Greeks tried to get our help in this war, we, who possess a not inconsiderable force, and could have supplied a ship contingent second only to the Athenians, refused to oppose you or to do anything contrary to your wish.” By such a speech they hoped to gain some advantage over the others, and so, I believe, it would have turned out. Meanwhile they had an excuse ready-made for the Greeks too, which is the one they actually used: when the Greeks reproached them for not coming to help, they said they had manned sixty triremes but had been unable to get past Cape Malea because of the Etesian winds; that was why they had not come to Salamis — not from any want of courage on their part that they had missed the sea-fight.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 169
paragraphs: Thus the Corcyreans evaded the Greek request. But the Cretans, when the Greeks sent to try to obtain their help, did this: they joined together and sent men to consult the god at Delphi, asking whether it would be better for them to come to Greece's aid. The Pythia answered: “You fools, do you think those woes too few that Minos sent upon you in his wrath because of the help you gave to Menelaus? For whereas they did not join with you in avenging Minos's death at Camicus, you nevertheless joined with them in avenging the woman who was carried off from Sparta by a barbarian.” When the Cretans heard this answer reported, they refrained from giving aid.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 170
paragraphs: The story goes that Minos, having come to Sicania (which is now called Sicily) in search of Daedalus, died there a violent death; and after a time the Cretans, prompted by a god — all of them except the men of Polichne and Praesus — came with a great force to Sicania and for seven years besieged the city of Camicus, which in my time was occupied by the Acragantines. At last, unable either to take the city or to remain before it, since they were hard pressed by famine, they broke off the siege and departed. On their way back, when they were off the coast of Iapygia, a great storm caught them and cast them onto the coast; their ships were shattered, and since they no longer saw any means of returning to Crete, they founded there the city of Hyria. There they stayed and were transformed, becoming, instead of Cretans, Messapians of Iapygia, and, instead of islanders, mainlanders. Then from the city of Hyria they founded those other settlements which the Tarentines, long afterwards, tried to destroy and suffered great disaster in the attempt — so great that this proved to be the greatest slaughter of Greeks known to us, not only of the Tarentines themselves but of those citizens of Rhegium whom Micythus son of Choerus compelled to come to the Tarentines' aid: three thousand of them were slain there. Of the Tarentines themselves who fell, there was no counting. This Micythus was a servant of Anaxilaus, left by him in charge of Rhegium; he was the one who, after being expelled from Rhegium, settled at Tegea in Arcadia and dedicated those many statues at Olympia.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 171
paragraphs: The story of the Rhegians and Tarentines has been a digression in my narrative. In Crete, however, as the men of Praesus relate, after it had been thus stripped of inhabitants, settlements were made by various peoples, but especially by Greeks; and in the second generation after the death of Minos came the Trojan war, in which the Cretans proved not the most contemptible of those who came to help Menelaus. After that, when they had returned home from Troy, famine and plague fell upon both the people and their livestock, until at last Crete was stripped of its inhabitants for the second time, and a third population of Cretans now occupies it together with the survivors of the former. This, then, the Pythia recalled to them and so stopped them from coming to the aid of the Greeks, though they wished to.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 172
paragraphs: As for the Thessalians, at first they had taken the side of the Persians unwillingly, and they gave proof that they were not pleased with what the Aleuadae were plotting. For as soon as they heard that the Persian was about to cross over into Europe, they sent envoys to the Isthmus; at the Isthmus were assembled representatives of Greece chosen by those cities that had the better mind for Greece. Coming before these men, the Thessalian envoys said: “Greeks, you must guard the pass by Olympus, so that Thessaly and all Greece may be sheltered from the war. We are prepared to join you in guarding it, but you must send a large force as well; for if you do not, know well that we shall come to terms with the Persian. It is not right that we, standing as outposts so far in advance of the rest of Greece, should perish alone in your defense. And if you are unwilling to come to our aid, you cannot apply any force against us to compel us to do the impossible; rather we shall try to devise some means of safety for ourselves.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 173
paragraphs: Thus spoke the Thessalians; and the Greeks, hearing them, resolved to send to Thessaly by sea a force of foot soldiers to guard the pass. When the army had been assembled, it sailed through the Euripus and, reaching Alus in Achaea, disembarked there and marched into Thessaly, leaving the ships behind at Alus. They arrived at Tempe, the pass leading from lower Macedonia into Thessaly along the river Peneios, between the mountains of Olympus and Ossa. There the Greeks encamped, assembled to the number of about ten thousand hoplites, and the Thessalian cavalry was added to them. The commander of the Lacedaemonians was Euaenetus son of Carenus, who had been chosen from among the polemarchs and was not of the royal house; and of the Athenians, Themistocles son of Neocles. They remained, however, only a few days there. Envoys came from Alexander son of Amyntas the Macedonian, who advised them to depart and not stay to be trampled underfoot in the pass by the invading host, indicating to them at the same time the great size of the army and the number of the ships. On receiving this counsel, they followed it, for they thought the advice was good, and the Macedonian was plainly well disposed toward them. Also, I think, fear persuaded them, when they learned that there was another pass into Thessaly besides this one — by upper Macedonia through the Perrhaebians and by the city of Gonnos — the way, in fact, by which Xerxes's army did make its entrance. So the Greeks went down to their ships again and returned to the Isthmus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 174
paragraphs: Such was the expedition to Thessaly, which took place when the king was about to cross from Asia into Europe and was already at Abydos. The Thessalians, now stripped of allies, took the side of the Medes with a good will and no longer half-heartedly, so that in the course of events they proved highly useful to the king.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 175
paragraphs: When the Greeks had returned to the Isthmus, they deliberated, in the light of what Alexander had said, where and in what places they should make their stand. The opinion that prevailed was to guard the pass at Thermopylae: it was seen to be narrower than the one leading into Thessaly, and at the same time it was a single pass and also nearer their own country. As for the path by which those of the Greeks who were taken by the enemy at Thermopylae were captured, they did not even know of its existence until they were told of it by the people of Trachis after they had arrived at Thermopylae. This pass, then, they resolved to guard, and not to allow the barbarian to pass into Greece. They also resolved that the fleet should sail to Artemisium in the territory of Histiaea, for these two positions are close to one another, so that each division could have information of what was happening to the other. The places are situated as I shall describe.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 176
paragraphs: As for Artemisium first: coming out of the Thracian Sea, the open waters contract from great width to the narrow channel that lies between the island of Sciathos and the mainland of Magnesia; and after the strait there follows immediately, on Euboea, the beach called Artemisium, on which stands a temple of Artemis. Secondly, the passage into Greece by Trachis is, where it is narrowest, about fifty feet wide; but this is not the narrowest part of the whole region. That lies in front of Thermopylae and also behind it: at Alpeni, which lies behind Thermopylae, and again at the river Phoenix near the town of Anthela, the road is only a single wheel-track wide. On the west of Thermopylae there is a mountain impassable and sheer, rising to a great height and extending toward the range of Oeta, while on the east of the road the sea with its marshy pools comes up right against it. In this pass there are hot springs, which the natives call the “Pots,” and an altar of Heracles is set up near them. A wall had once been built at this pass, and in old times there was a gate set in it; this wall was built by the Phocians out of fear, because the Thessalians had come from the land of the Thesprotians to settle in the Aeolian land that they now occupy. Since the Thessalians, as they supposed, were trying to subdue them, the Phocians guarded themselves against this in advance; and at that time they also let the water of the hot springs run over the passage, to turn the place into a ravine, and contrived every possible means that the Thessalians should not invade their land. The old wall had been built long before and was by now mostly fallen into ruin with age. The Greeks resolved to set it up again, and at this spot to repel the barbarian from Greece. Very close to the road is a village called Alpeni, from which the Greeks counted on getting their supplies.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 177
paragraphs: These places, then, the Greeks perceived to be suited to their purpose; for they considered everything carefully beforehand and calculated that the barbarians would not be able to take advantage either of their superior numbers or of their cavalry. They therefore resolved to receive the invader of Greece here. When they were informed that the Persian was in Pieria, they broke up from the Isthmus and set out on campaign, some going by land to Thermopylae, others making for Artemisium by sea.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 178
paragraphs: The Greeks, I say, were hurrying to the defense, each assigned to his own post. Meanwhile the men of Delphi, struck with dread, consulted the god's oracle on behalf of themselves and on behalf of Greece, and the answer given was that they should pray to the Winds, for these would be powerful helpers of Greece in battle. The Delphians, having accepted the oracle, first reported the answer to those of the Greeks who desired to remain free; and by reporting it at a time when they were in great dread of the barbarian, they laid up for themselves an undying store of gratitude. After this the Delphians set up an altar for the Winds at Thyia, where there is a sacred precinct of Thyia the daughter of Cephisus — from whom the place also takes its name — and they approached the Winds with sacrifices.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 179
paragraphs: Following the oracle, the Delphians still make propitiatory offerings to the Winds to this day. Meanwhile, the fleet of Xerxes set out from the city of Therma, and ten of its ships — the fastest sailors — crossed straight toward Skiathos, where three Greek ships, one from Troizen, one from Aegina, and one from Athens, were stationed as an advance watch. When their crews spotted the barbarian ships, they turned and fled:

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 180
paragraphs: The Troizenian ship, under the command of Prexinos, was pursued and captured at once by the barbarians. They then took the handsomest of her fighting men and cut his throat at the prow of the ship, treating it as a good omen that the first Greek they had captured was preeminent for beauty. The name of this sacrificed man was Leon — and perhaps his name itself played some part in what befell him.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 181
paragraphs: The Aeginetan ship, commanded by Asonides, gave them more trouble to capture, because Pytheas son of Ischenoös was serving as a fighting man on board. He proved himself an extraordinarily valiant man that day: as the ship was being taken, he held out fighting until he was hacked to pieces. When he fell and still did not die but had breath left in him, the Persians serving as marines on the ships were so impressed by his courage that they did everything they could to save his life — applying myrrh ointments to heal his wounds and wrapping him in bands of the finest linen. When they rejoined their main fleet, they displayed him to the whole army, marveling at him and treating him well. But the rest of the men they had captured from that ship they treated as slaves.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 182
paragraphs: Two of the three ships, then, were captured in this way. But the third, commanded by the Athenian Phormos, ran aground in its flight at the mouth of the river Peneios. The barbarians seized the vessel but not its crew, for as soon as the Athenians had beached the ship, they leapt out and made their way through Thessaly back to Athens.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 183
paragraphs: The Greeks stationed at Artemisium were informed of these events by fire-signals from Skiathos. Struck with fear at the news, they shifted their anchorage from Artemisium to Chalkis, intending to guard the Euripos, while leaving daylight watchers on the heights of Euboea. Meanwhile, three of the ten barbarian ships sailed up to the reef called Myrmex, which lies between Skiathos and Magnesia. The barbarians had brought a stone pillar with them for this purpose, and they set it up on the reef. Then, with the difficulties of the passage now cleared, they set out from Therma with their main fleet and sailed to this point with all their ships, eleven days having passed since the king began his march from Therma. They were informed about this reef, which lies directly in the middle of the fairway, by Pammon of Skyros. Sailing all day, the barbarians completed the voyage to Sepias in Magnesia and to the beach between the city of Casthanaia and the headland of Sepias.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 184
paragraphs: Up to this point, and as far as Thermopylae, the army had suffered no disaster; and by my reckoning its numbers were still as follows. Of the 1,207 ships that had come from Asia, the original crews supplied by the various nations amounted to 241,400 men — reckoning 200 men per ship. On each of these ships, in addition to the native fighting men, there served thirty Persian, Median, or Sacan marines, amounting to 36,210 more. To this and the previous numbers I will add the crews of the fifty-oared galleys, estimating eighty men, more or less, in each. Of these vessels, as was mentioned earlier, there were 3,000 gathered together, which would yield 240,000 men. This, then, was the naval force from Asia, totaling 517,610 in all. The infantry numbered 1,700,000, and the cavalry 80,000; and to these I will add the Arabian camel-drivers and the Libyan charioteers, reckoning them at 20,000. The result is that the combined naval and land forces amount to 2,317,610 men. This is the tally of the army brought up out of Asia itself, not counting the attendants who accompanied it or the grain-transports and the men who sailed in them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 185
paragraphs: There is still to be counted, in addition to all this, the force being led from Europe; of this I must give a probable estimate. The Greeks of Thrace and of the islands off the Thracian coast supplied 120 ships, which yields a total of 24,000 men. As for the land-force supplied by the Thracians, Paionians, Eordians, Bottiaians, the race inhabiting Chalkidike, the Brygians, Pierians, Macedonians, Perraibians, Enianians, Dolopians, Magnesians, Achaians, and all those who dwell along the Thracian coast — of these various nations I estimate there were 300,000. These added to those from Asia make a grand total of 2,640,000 fighting men, plus another 1,610.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 186
paragraphs: With the fighting force at this number, the attendants who accompanied them and the men in the small vessels that carried grain, along with those in the other vessels that sailed with the army — I suppose these were not fewer than the fighting men but more. I will assume them to be equal in number, neither more nor less; and so, being equal in number to the fighting body, they make up the same total. Thus 5,283,220 was the number of men whom Xerxes son of Darius led as far as Sepias and Thermopylae.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 187
paragraphs: That is the number of Xerxes's whole army. But of the women who baked bread for it, and of the concubines and eunuchs, no one can state an exact figure; nor, again, of the draft-animals and other beasts of burden, or of the Indian hounds that accompanied it — none of these could anyone count, because of their sheer multitude. So it does not surprise me that the streams of some rivers failed them; what astonishes me is how the provisions were enough to feed so many multitudes. For I calculate that if each man received only a quart of wheat per day and nothing more, the daily consumption would amount to 110,340 medimnoi — and I am not counting anything for the women, eunuchs, pack-animals, or dogs. Of all these men, so many myriads in number, not one was more worthy in beauty and stature than Xerxes himself to possess this power.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 188
paragraphs: The fleet, then, set forth and sailed, and when it had put in at the shore of Magnesia on the beach between the city of Casthanaia and the headland of Sepias, the first ships to arrive moored by the land while the others rode at anchor behind them. Because the beach was not large, they lay at anchor with their prows projecting seaward, in a formation eight ships deep. So they lay through the night; but at early dawn, after a clear sky and windless calm, the sea began to heave violently, and a great storm struck them with a strong east wind — the wind that the locals call Hellespontias. Those who noticed the wind rising and were so moored that they could do so drew their ships up on shore before the storm hit, and both they and their ships escaped. As for the ships caught out at sea, some were cast away at the place called Ipnoi in Pelion, others on the beach, some were wrecked on the headland of Sepias itself, others at the city of Meliboia, and others were thrown up on shore at Casthanaia. The violence of the storm was irresistible.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 189
paragraphs: There is a story that the Athenians had called upon Boreas for help, at the suggestion of an oracle — for another pronouncement of the god had come to them, bidding them call upon their brother-in-law to be their helper. According to Greek legend, Boreas has a wife from Attica, Oreithuia daughter of Erechththeus. Because of this kinship, the Athenians — so the tale goes — concluded that Boreas was their brother-in-law. When they perceived the wind rising as they lay with their ships at Chalkis in Euboea, or even before then, they offered sacrifices and called upon Boreas and Oreithuia to help them and destroy the ships of the barbarians, as he had done before around Mount Athos. Whether it was for this reason that Boreas fell upon the barbarians as they lay at anchor, I cannot say; but however that may be, the Athenians claim that Boreas had come to their aid in earlier times, and that on this occasion too he accomplished the things I have described. When they returned home, they set up a temple dedicated to Boreas beside the river Ilissos.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 190
paragraphs: In this disaster, the number of ships lost was no fewer than 400, according to the lowest estimates — along with men beyond counting and an immense quantity of valuables. Indeed, the shipwreck proved very profitable to Ameinocles son of Cretines, a Magnesian who held lands around Sepias: he picked up many golden cups that washed ashore afterwards, and many silver ones too, and discovered Persian treasure-chests, and acquired other gold objects more than can be described. Yet though this man became very rich from his finds, he was otherwise unfortunate — he too suffered calamity, being tormented by the slaying of a child.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 191
paragraphs: Of the grain-transports and other vessels that perished, no count was made; the loss was so great that the fleet's commanders, struck with fear that the Thessalians might attack them now that they had been brought into such a sorry state, threw a high palisade around their camp built from the wreckage. The storm raged for three days; but at last the Magians, offering sacrifices of victims and singing incantations to the Wind to appease it by enchantments — and, in addition, offering to Thetis and the Nereids — caused it to stop on the fourth day, or else it abated of its own accord for some other reason. They sacrificed to Thetis because the Ionians had told them the story that she was carried off from that place by Peleus, and that the whole headland of Sepias belonged to her and the other Nereids.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 192
paragraphs: The storm had ceased on the fourth day; meanwhile, the day-watchers had run down from the heights of Euboea on the day after the first storm began, and were keeping the Greeks informed of everything that had happened with the shipwreck. On learning this, the Greeks first prayed to Poseidon the Savior and poured libations, then hurried back to Artemisium, expecting that only very few enemy ships would be left to come against them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 193
paragraphs: So they came for a second time and stationed their ships around Artemisium; and from that time to this they still use the title 'Savior' for Poseidon. Meanwhile, once the wind had ceased and the swell had calmed, the barbarians dragged their ships into the sea and sailed along the mainland shore. Having rounded the tip of Magnesia, they sailed straight into the gulf leading toward Pagasai. In this gulf of Magnesia there is a place where, it is said, Heracles was left behind by Jason and his comrades, having been sent from the Argo to fetch water, when they were sailing for the fleece to Aia in Colchis — for from that spot, once they had taken on water, they planned to launch their ship into the open sea. That is why the place is called Aphetai. Here, then, the fleet of Xerxes took up its moorings.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 194
paragraphs: It happened that fifteen of these ships put out to sea considerably later than the rest, and they caught sight of the Greek ships at Artemisium. The barbarians assumed these were their own vessels and sailed toward them, only to fall among the enemy. Their commander was Sandokes son of Thamasios, governor of Kyme in Aiolia, whom King Darius had once taken and crucified (he being one of the Royal Judges) for this reason: Sandokes had delivered an unjust verdict for money. After he had been hung up, Darius reconsidered and found that his services to the royal house outweighed his offenses; realizing this, and seeing that he had acted more hastily than wisely, Darius let him go. So he escaped from King Darius and survived; but now, sailing in toward the Greeks, he was not destined to escape a second time. For when the Greeks saw them sailing up, they perceived the mistake, put out against them, and captured them without difficulty.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 195
paragraphs: Aridolis, tyrant of Alabanda in Caria, was captured in one of these ships, and in another the Paphian commander Penthylos son of Demonoös, who had brought twelve ships from Paphos but lost eleven of them in the storm off Sepias, and was now captured sailing in toward Artemisium with the one that had escaped. These men the Greeks sent in chains to the Isthmus of the Corinthians, after questioning them about what they wanted to learn concerning Xerxes's army.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 196
paragraphs: The barbarian fleet, then — except for the fifteen ships under Sandokes — had arrived at Aphetai. Meanwhile Xerxes with the land army, having marched through Thessaly and Achaia, had already entered the country of the Malians two days earlier, after holding a contest in Thessaly for his own horses and also testing the Thessalian cavalry — because he had been told it was the best among the Greeks. In this trial the Greek horses were far outmatched by the others. Of the rivers in Thessaly, only the Onochonos failed to provide enough water for the army; but of the rivers in Achaia, even the largest of them, the Epidanos, barely held out.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 197
paragraphs: When Xerxes reached Alos in Achaia, the guides who were informing him about the route, wishing to tell him everything, reported to him a local legend concerning the temple of Zeus Laphystios: how Athamas son of Aiolos plotted death for Phrixos together with Ino, and how afterwards, by command of an oracle, the Achaians lay the following requirements on his descendants. Whoever is the eldest of this race is forbidden to enter the City Hall, and they themselves keep watch (the City Hall is called by the Achaians the 'Hall of the People'). If he does enter it, he may not come out until he is about to be sacrificed. They added that many who were about to be sacrificed had fled in fear to another country, and if they later returned home and were caught, they were placed in the City Hall. They also told how the victim is sacrificed thickly wreathed in garlands, and with what form of procession he is led to the altar. This is done to the descendants of Kytissoros son of Phrixos, because, when the Achaians were making Athamas son of Aiolos a sacrificial victim to purge the sins of the land by oracular command, and were just about to sacrifice him, this Kytissoros arrived from Aia of the Colchians and rescued him — and by doing so brought the wrath of the gods down upon his own descendants. Having heard these things, Xerxes, when he reached the sacred grove, refrained from entering it himself and commanded his whole army to do the same; and he paid reverence to both the house and the sacred precinct of the descendants of Athamas.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 198
paragraphs: These, then, were the events in Thessaly and Achaia. From there Xerxes proceeded to the Malian land, along a gulf of the sea in which there is an ebb and flow of the tide every day. Around this gulf there is a level space, in parts broad but in other parts very narrow; and lofty, inaccessible mountains surrounding this region enclose the whole Malian land and are called the rocks of Trachis. The first city on this gulf as one comes from Achaia is Antikyra, past which flows the river Spercheios out of the land of the Enianians and into the sea. About twenty furlongs from this river there is another called Dyras, which is said to have sprung up in order to bring aid to Heracles when he was burning. Then again, about twenty furlongs from this, there is another river called Melas.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 199
paragraphs: From this river Melas the city of Trachis is five furlongs distant; and here, in the area where Trachis stands, is the widest part of the whole district as regards the space from the mountains to the sea, the plain measuring 22,000 plethra. In the mountain range that encloses the land of Trachis there is a cleft to the south of Trachis itself; and through this cleft the river Asopos flows, running along the foot of the mountain.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 200
paragraphs: There is also another river called Phoinix, to the south of the Asopos, not large, which flows out of these mountains into the Asopos. At the river Phoinix is the narrowest place, for here a road has been constructed wide enough for only a single wheel-track. From the river Phoinix it is fifteen furlongs to Thermopylae; and in the space between the river Phoinix and Thermopylae there is a village called Anthela, past which the Asopos flows before emptying into the sea. Around this village there is a wide space containing a temple dedicated to Demeter of the Amphictyons, seats for the Amphictyonic councillors, and a temple dedicated to Amphictyon himself.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 201
paragraphs: King Xerxes, then, was encamped within the region of Trachis in the Malian land, and the Greeks within the pass. This place is called by the Greeks in general Thermopylae, but by the local inhabitants and those who dwell around it, Pylai. Both sides were encamped in this vicinity; the one held all the country beyond Trachis toward the north, and the others the country stretching toward the south and midday on this side of the continent.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 202
paragraphs: These were the Greeks who awaited the Persian attack in this place: of the Spartans, three hundred hoplites; of the men of Tegea and Mantineia, a thousand, half from each; from Orchomenos in Arcadia, one hundred and twenty; and from the rest of Arcadia, a thousand — so many Arcadians in all. From Corinth, four hundred; from Phlius, two hundred; and from Mykene, eighty: these were the contingents from the Peloponnese. From the Boeotians came seven hundred of the Thespians and four hundred of the Thebans.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 203
paragraphs: In addition to these, the Opuntian Locrians had been summoned to come in their full force, along with a thousand of the Phokians: for the Greeks themselves had sent word to them, saying through messengers that they had come as forerunners of the others, that the rest of the allies were expected any day, that their sea was safely guarded — watched by the Athenians and the Aeginetans and those appointed to serve in the fleet — and that they had nothing to fear. For it was no god, they said, who was coming to attack Greece, but a man; and no mortal was born, nor would be, without some evil mingled into his fortunes at birth, with the greatest evils befalling the greatest men. The one marching against them, being mortal, would therefore be destined to fail in his expectations. Hearing this, they came to help the others at Trachis.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 204
paragraphs: Although each city had its own commanders, the one most held in regard and leader of the whole army was the Lacedaemonian Leonidas son of Anaxandrides, son of Leon, son of Eurycratides, son of Anaxander, son of Eurycrates, son of Polydoros, son of Alcamenes, son of Teleclos, son of Archelaos, son of Hegesilaos, son of Doryssos, son of Leobotes, son of Echestratos, son of Agis, son of Eurysthenes, son of Aristodemos, son of Aristomachos, son of Cleodaios, son of Hyllos, son of Heracles — who had obtained the kingdom of Sparta against expectation.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 205
paragraphs: Having two elder brothers, Cleomenes and Dorieos, Leonidas had been far from expecting to become king. But since Cleomenes had died without a male child, and Dorieos was by then no longer alive either — he too had ended his life in Sicily — the kingdom came to Leonidas, both because he was of greater age than Cleombrotos (who was the youngest son of Anaxandrides) and because he had married the daughter of Cleomenes. At this time he went to Thermopylae, having chosen the three hundred men appointed by law — men who happened to have sons — and he took with him as well, before arriving, those Thebans whom I mentioned when I counted the troops, whose commander was Leontiades son of Eurymachos. The reason Leonidas was eager to take these men of all the Greeks with him was that the Thebans were strongly accused of taking the side of the Medes; so he summoned them to the war to discover whether they would send troops with him or openly renounce the Greek alliance. They sent men — but with other intentions in their hearts.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 206
paragraphs: These the Spartans had sent out first with Leonidas, so that the other allies, seeing them, would join the campaign, and for fear that they too might side with the Medes if they heard that the Spartans were delaying their action. Afterwards, once they had completed their festival (the festival of the Carneia stood in their way), they intended to leave a garrison in Sparta and come to help in full force with all speed. Likewise the rest of the allies had thought to do the same, for it happened that the Olympic festival fell at the same time as these events. Since they did not suppose the fighting at Thermopylae would be decided so quickly, they sent only the forerunners of their force.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 207
paragraphs: Such were their intentions. Meanwhile the Greeks at Thermopylae, when the Persian drew near the pass, grew afraid and deliberated about retreating from their position. The rest of the Peloponnesians thought it best to fall back to the Peloponnese and hold the Isthmus as a guard; but Leonidas, when the Phokians and Locrians objected indignantly to this view, cast his vote for staying there and at the same time sending messengers to the various states, asking them to come up and help, since they were too few to repel the Median army.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 208
paragraphs: While they were deliberating, Xerxes sent a mounted scout to see how many they were and what they were doing. For he had heard while still in Thessaly that a small force had gathered at this spot, led by Lacedaemonians, with Leonidas — who was of the line of Heracles — at their head. When the horseman rode up toward their camp, he could see them, but not the whole army: those posted within the wall that they had repaired and were guarding could not be seen, but he observed those outside, whose station was in front of the wall. It happened at that moment that the Lacedaemonians were the ones posted outside. So he saw some of the men practicing athletic exercises and others combing their long hair; and as he looked upon these things he marveled, while also taking careful note of their number. When he had observed everything exactly, he rode back unmolested, for no one tried to pursue him, and he found himself treated with complete indifference. On his return, he reported to Xerxes everything he had seen.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 209
paragraphs: Hearing this, Xerxes could not guess the truth of the matter — that they were preparing to die and to deal out death to the enemy as far as they could. It seemed to him that they were simply acting ridiculously. So he sent for Demaratos son of Ariston, who was in his camp, and when he came, Xerxes questioned him about each of these things, wanting to discover what the Lacedaemonians were doing. Demaratos said: “You heard from my own mouth earlier, when we were setting out to march against Greece, what sort of men these are; and having heard it, you made me a laughingstock, because I told you what I foresaw would come to pass. For to me, O king, the greatest of all ends is to speak the truth continually before you. Hear me now too: these men have come to fight us for the passage, and this is what they are preparing to do. They have a custom that whenever they are about to risk their lives, they attend to the arrangement of their hair. Be assured, however, that if you overcome these men and the rest who remain behind in Sparta, there is no other race of men that will withstand your onset, O king, or raise hands against you; for you are now about to fight the noblest kingdom and city among the Greeks, and their best men.” To Xerxes what was said seemed utterly incredible, and he asked again how it was possible that so few would fight against his host. Demaratos said, “O king, treat me as a liar if you do not find that these things come to pass as I say.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 210
paragraphs: Even so, he did not convince Xerxes, who let four days pass, expecting that the Greeks would take flight; but on the fifth day, when they still had not departed but remained — obstinate, as he thought, in their impudence and folly — he became enraged and sent the Medes and the Kissians against them, ordering that the men be taken alive and brought into his presence. When the Medes charged forward and attacked the Greeks, many of them fell, and others kept coming up continually, and they were not driven back, though they suffered heavy losses. They made it plain to everyone, and to the king himself not least, that human beings are many but men are few. This combat went on throughout the day.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 211
paragraphs: When the Medes were being roughly handled, they withdrew from the battle, and the Persians — those whom the king called the “Immortals,” commanded by Hydarnes — took their place and came up to attack, supposing that at least they would easily overcome the enemy. But when they too engaged the Greeks, they had no more success than the Medes — exactly the same — since they were fighting in a cramped pass, using shorter spears than the Greeks and unable to take advantage of their greater numbers. The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, fought memorably. Among other feats, being perfectly skilled warriors facing unskilled foes, they would turn their backs to the enemy and feign flight; and the barbarians, seeing them apparently fleeing, would chase after them with shouts and clashing of arms. Then, just as the Lacedaemonians were about to be caught, they would wheel and face the barbarians — and in this turn they would cut down countless multitudes of Persians. A few of the Spartans themselves also fell on these occasions. Since the Persians were unable to achieve any success, whether by attacking the entrance in divisions or by any other means, they pulled back.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 212
paragraphs: During these assaults it is said that the king, looking on, leapt up from his seat three times, struck with fear for his army. So they fought that day. On the following day the barbarians fared no better: because the men opposing them were few, they engaged in the expectation that the Greeks would be found disabled and no longer capable of raising their hands in battle against them. But the Greeks were drawn up by companies as well as by nationalities, and they fought in turn, each in succession — except for the Phokians, who were posted on the mountain to guard the path. So the Persians, finding nothing different from what they had met the day before, withdrew from the fight.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 213
paragraphs: While the king was at a loss as to what to do next, Epialtes son of Eurydemos, a Malian, came to speak with him, supposing he would win a great reward. This man told him of the path leading over the mountain to Thermopylae, and so brought about the destruction of the Greeks remaining there. Afterwards, fearing the Lacedaemonians, he fled to Thessaly; and while he was in exile, the Deputies placed a price on his life when the Amphictyons met for their assembly at Pylai. Some time later, having returned to Antikyra, he was slain by Athenades, a man of Trachis. Now this Athenades killed Epialtes for another reason, which I shall describe later in this history; but for this deed he was honored by the Lacedaemonians nonetheless.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 214
paragraphs: Thus, some time after these events, Epialtes was killed. There is, however, another account that says Onetes son of Phanagoras, a man of Carystos, and Corydallos of Antikyra were the ones who showed the Persians the way around the mountain; but I cannot accept this at all. For in the first place we must judge by this fact: that the Deputies of the Greeks did not proclaim a reward for the lives of Onetes and Corydallos, but for Epialtes the Trachinian — they surely having obtained the most exact information. Secondly, we know that Epialtes went into exile from his country to escape this very charge. It is true that Onetes might have known of this path, even if he were not a Malian, had he spent much time in the country; but it was Epialtes who led them around the mountain by the path, and so I record him as the guilty man.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 215
paragraphs: Xerxes, then, pleased with what Epialtes undertook to accomplish, at once and with great joy dispatched Hydarnes and the men whom Hydarnes commanded, and they set out from the camp around the time when the lamps are lit. This path had been discovered by the Malians who dwell in that land, and having discovered it they once used it to guide the Thessalians against the Phokians, at the time when the Phokians had fortified the pass with a wall and so were sheltered from attacks. So long ago as that had the Malians shown the pass to be worthless. The path runs as follows: it begins from the river Asopos, which flows through the cleft, and both the mountain and the path share the same name — Anopaia. This Anopaia stretches over the ridge of the mountain and ends near the town of Alpenos, which is the first town of the Locrians toward Malis, and by the stone called Black Buttocks and the seats of the Kercopes, where the pass is at its very narrowest.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 217
paragraphs: By this path, so situated, the Persians — having crossed the Asopos — marched all through the night, with the mountains of the Oitaians on their right and those of the Trachinians on their left. When dawn appeared, they had reached the summit of the mountain. At this part of the mountain, as I have already said, a thousand Phokian hoplites were keeping guard, to protect their own country and to watch the path — for while the pass below was being guarded by those I have mentioned, the path over the mountain was being guarded by the Phokians, who had undertaken the task for Leonidas at their own offer.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 218
paragraphs: While the Persians were climbing, they were hidden from the Phokians because the whole mountain was covered with oak trees. The Phokians became aware of them after they had completed the ascent, in this way: the day was still, and the Persians made no small noise — as was natural when leaves lay strewn on the ground under their feet. At that, the Phokians sprang up and began to put on their armor, and by this time the barbarians were close at hand. The barbarians, when they saw men arming themselves, were astonished, for they had expected no one to appear to oppose them, and instead they had encountered an armed force. Hydarnes, seized with fear that the Phokians might be Lacedaemonians, asked Epialtes what people this force belonged to; and when he had been accurately informed, he drew up the Persians for battle. The Phokians, when the enemy's arrows came thick upon them, fled at once to the topmost peak of the mountain, convinced that it was against them that the enemy had come, and there they prepared to meet their death. So they, at least, were in this frame of mind. Meanwhile the Persians under Epialtes and Hydarnes paid no attention to the Phokians, but descended the mountain with all speed.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 219
paragraphs: To the Greeks at Thermopylae, first of all the soothsayer Megistias, looking into the sacrificed victims, announced the death that would come to them at dawn. Next, deserters brought word that the Persians had gone around. These men signaled it to them while it was still night. And thirdly came the day-watchers, who had run down from the heights when day was already breaking. Then the Greeks deliberated, and their opinions were divided: some urged that they should not abandon their post, while others opposed this advice. After this, they dispersed from the assembly: some went away, scattering each to their own cities, while others were ready to remain there together with Leonidas.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 220
paragraphs: It is also reported, however, that Leonidas himself sent them away, out of concern that they should not perish, but thinking it unseemly for himself and for the Spartans present to abandon the post they had originally come to guard. I am inclined rather to this latter opinion: that because Leonidas perceived the allies were disheartened and unwilling to face the danger with him to the end, he ordered them to leave, while he held that for himself to depart was not honorable, whereas if he remained, great glory would be left behind him, and the prosperity of Sparta would not be blotted out. For the Pythian prophetess had given the Spartans an oracle, when they consulted her about this war at its outset, to the effect that either Lacedaemon must be destroyed by the barbarians, or their king must lose his life. The prophetess gave this answer in hexameter verses, which ran as follows:

“But as for you, you men who dwell in wide-spaced Sparta — either your glorious city is sacked by the sons of Perseus, or, if not, then a king of the Heraclean line, dead, shall be mourned by all within the borders of broad Lacedaemon. Him neither the might of bulls nor the raging of lions shall stop; for he has might like Zeus's; and I say he will not be restrained until he has utterly torn apart one or the other of these.”

I am of the opinion that Leonidas, considering these things and wanting to lay up glory for himself above all other Spartans, dismissed the allies — rather than that those who departed did so in such disorderly fashion because they were divided in opinion.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 221
paragraphs: Of this, the following strikes me as proof as convincing as any: Leonidas is known to have tried to dismiss even the soothsayer who accompanied the army, Megistias the Acarnanian — said to be descended from Melampus — so that he would not perish with them, after he had declared from the victims what was about to come upon them. Megistias, however, when ordered to leave, would not himself depart; but he sent away his son, who was with him in the army, besides whom he had no other child.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 222
paragraphs: The allies who were dismissed, then, departed, obeying the word of Leonidas, and only the Thespians and the Thebans remained behind with the Lacedaemonians. Of these, the Thebans stayed against their will, not because they wished to — Leonidas kept them, counting them as hostages — but the Thespians very willingly, for they said they would not leave Leonidas and those with him, but stayed behind and died with them. Their commander was Demophilos son of Diadromes.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 223
paragraphs: Xerxes, meanwhile, having made libations at sunrise, waited for some time — until about the hour when the marketplace fills — and then advanced on them. This had been instructed by Epialtes, since the descent of the mountain is shorter, and the distance to cover much less, than the roundabout ascent. So the barbarians under Xerxes were advancing to the attack; and the Greeks under Leonidas, feeling they were going out to meet death, now pushed out much further than before into the broader part of the defile. When the wall's fence was being guarded, they had on the previous days fought retreating before the enemy into the narrow part of the pass; but now they engaged them outside the narrows, and very many of the barbarians fell. For behind them, the divisional leaders with whips in their hands struck every man, driving them ever forward. Many were forced into the sea and perished, and many more still were trodden down alive by one another; and there was no keeping count of the number who died. For, knowing the death about to come upon them because of those going around the mountain, the Greeks displayed against the barbarians the whole extent of their strength — disregarding danger and acting as though possessed by a spirit of recklessness.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 224
paragraphs: By this time, the spears of most of them were broken in the fighting, and they were killing the Persians with their swords. In this combat fell Leonidas, having proved himself a very good man, and with him other notable Spartans, whose names I was told as men who had shown themselves worthy — indeed, I was told the names of all the three hundred. On the Persian side there also fell here, besides many other notables, two sons of Darius — Abrocomes and Hyperanthes — born to Darius by Phratagune the daughter of Artanes. Artanes was the brother of King Darius and the son of Hystaspes, the son of Arsames. In giving his daughter in marriage to Darius, he also gave her his whole fortune with her, because she was his only child.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 225
paragraphs: Two brothers of Xerxes, then, fell here fighting. Meanwhile a great struggle arose between the Persians and the Lacedaemonians over the body of Leonidas, until the Greeks by sheer valor dragged it away from the enemy and put their opponents to flight four times. This fight continued until the men who had come with Epialtes arrived; and when the Greeks learned that these had come up, from that moment the character of the combat changed. They drew back to the narrow part of the road, passed beyond the wall, and took up position together on the hillock — all in one body — except for the Thebans. This hillock stands at the entrance, where the stone lion now stands as a memorial to Leonidas. Here, defending themselves with daggers (those who still had them), and with their hands, and with their teeth, they were overwhelmed by the missiles of the barbarians — some of whom had pursued them directly and had torn down the fence of the wall, while others had come around and surrounded them on every side.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 226
paragraphs: Such were the proofs of courage given by the Lacedaemonians and Thespians. Yet the Spartan Dienekes is said to have proved himself the best man of all — the same man who, they report, made this remark before engaging the Medes: when he was told by one of the men of Trachis that when the barbarians shot their arrows they darkened the sun by the sheer number of them, so vast was their host, he was not dismayed but, making light of the Median numbers, replied that their guest from Trachis had brought them very good news — for if the Medes darkened the sun, their battle against them would be fought in the shade, not in the sun.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 227
paragraphs: This and other sayings of the kind, they report, Dienekes the Lacedaemonian left behind as memorials of himself. After him, the bravest of the Lacedaemonians are said to have been two brothers, Alpheos and Maron, sons of Orsiphantos. Of the Thespians, the man who gained the most honor was Dithyrambos son of Harmatides.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 228
paragraphs: The men were buried where they fell; and for them, along with those who were killed before being dismissed by Leonidas, there is an inscription that reads:
“Here once, facing three hundred myriads of foes in battle, four thousand men from the Peloponnese made their stand.”
This is the inscription for the whole body; and for the Spartans alone there is this:
“Stranger, carry this word, we ask, to the Spartans — that lying here in this spot we remain, faithfully keeping their laws.”
This, then, for the Lacedaemonians; and for the soothsayer, as follows:

“This is the tomb of famed Megistias, whom the Median enemies slew where the Spercheios flows as they forded the stream — soothsayer who then, knowing clearly the fates that were coming, could not bring himself to abandon Sparta's good leaders in the fight.”

It was the Amphictyons who honored them with these inscriptions and memorial pillars, except in the case of the inscription to the soothsayer: that one, for the soothsayer Megistias, was composed by Simonides son of Leoprepes on account of guest-friendship.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 229
paragraphs: Two of these three hundred, it is said — Eurystos and Aristodemos — could, had they agreed together, either have both come safely home to Sparta (since they had been dismissed from the camp by Leonidas and were lying at Alpenoi with severe eye disease), or, if they did not wish to return home, they might have died along with the rest. When they could have done one of these two things, they could not agree; and being divided in opinion, Eurystos, it is said, when informed that the Persians had gone around, asked for his armor, put it on, and ordered his Helot to lead him to the fighting. Once the Helot had led him there, the man ran off and escaped, but Eurystos plunged into the thick of the fighting and so lost his life. Aristodemos, however, was left behind, fainting. Now if Aristodemos alone had been ill and had therefore returned home to Sparta, or if both men had come back together, I do not suppose the Spartans would have shown any anger toward them. But as it was — since one of them had lost his life, and the other, clinging to an excuse the first man could equally have used, had refused to die — it was inevitable that the Spartans felt great indignation against Aristodemos.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 230
paragraphs: Some say that Aristodemos came safely to Sparta in this way and on the pretext I have described; but others say he had been sent as a messenger from the camp, and that when he could have come up in time to find the battle still going on, he was not willing to do so, but lingered on the road and so saved his life, while his fellow messenger reached the battle and was killed.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 231
paragraphs: When Aristodemos, then, had returned home to Lacedaemon, he met with reproach and dishonor. The dishonor he suffered was this: no Spartan would give him fire or speak to him, and he bore the reproach of being called Aristodemos the Coward.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 232
paragraphs: He, however, made good all the guilt charged against him at the battle of Plataea. But it is reported that another man also survived of these three hundred, whose name was Pantites, having been sent as a messenger to Thessaly; and when he returned to Sparta and found himself dishonored, he is said to have hanged himself.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 233
paragraphs: The Thebans, whose commander was Leontiades, being with the Greeks, had for a time continued to fight against the king's army, compelled by necessity. But when they saw that the Persian cause was prevailing — then, and not before, while the Greeks with Leonidas were making their way in haste to the hillock — they broke off from them and, holding out their hands, approached the barbarians, saying (what was in fact quite true) that they were on the side of the Medes, that they had been among the first to give earth and water to the king, and that they had come to Thermopylae under compulsion, being blameless for the losses inflicted on the king. By saying this they preserved their lives, for they also had the Thessalians to bear witness to their words. But they did not altogether meet with good fortune: some had even been cut down as they were approaching; and when the rest came and the barbarians had them in their power, most of them were branded by order of Xerxes with the royal marks, beginning with their leader Leontiades — the same whose son Eurymachos was later killed by the Plataeans after being made commander of four hundred Thebans and seizing the city of the Plataeans.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 234
paragraphs: So the Greeks at Thermopylae fought. Xerxes then summoned Demaratos and questioned him, first saying this: “Demaratos, you are a good man — I infer it from the truth of your words, for everything you said turned out just as you said. Now, however, tell me: how many Lacedaemonians remain, and how many of them are like these in matters of war? Or are they all of them such?” Demaratos said: “O king, the total number of Lacedaemonians is great and their cities are many; but what you wish to know, you shall learn. In Lacedaemon there is the city of Sparta, with about eight thousand men; these are all equal to those who fought here. The other Lacedaemonians are not equal to these, but they are good men too.” Xerxes then said, “Demaratos, by what means can we get the better of these men with the least trouble? Come, explain this to us — you know the course of their counsels, since you were once their king.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 235
paragraphs: He answered: “O king, if you are truly taking counsel with me, it is right that I tell you the best course. What if you were to send three hundred ships of your fleet to attack the Laconian coast? There is an island lying near it called Kythera, of which Chilon, one of our wisest men, used to say that it would be of greater benefit to the Spartans if it sank beneath the sea than if it remained above — for he was always anticipating that something would happen from that quarter of the kind I am now describing to you. It was not that he knew of your expedition beforehand, but that he feared equally every armament of men. So let your forces set out from this island and keep the Lacedaemonians in fear; and while they have a war of their own close to their doors, there will be no fear for you that, when the rest of Greece is being conquered by your land army, they will come to the rescue there. Then, after the rest of Greece has been brought into subjection, the Lacedaemonian power will from that moment stand alone and therefore weak. If, however, you do not do this, here is what you must expect: there is a narrow isthmus leading to the Peloponnese, and there you must look for battles more severe than those which have already taken place, since all the Peloponnesians have sworn to a league against you. But if you follow the course I have described, this isthmus and the cities within it will come over to your side without a battle.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 236
paragraphs: After him spoke Achaimenes, Xerxes's brother and also commander of the fleet, who happened to be present at this conversation and was afraid that Xerxes might be persuaded to do this. “O king,” he said, “I see that you are listening to the words of a man who envies your good fortune — or who is even a traitor to your cause. For truly the Greeks delight in that very temper; they envy a man for his good luck, and they hate whatever is stronger than themselves. If, on top of the other misfortunes we have suffered — since four hundred of our ships have been wrecked — you now send off another three hundred from the fleet's station to sail around the Peloponnese, then your opponents become a match for you in battle; whereas while the fleet is all assembled together it is hard for them to deal with, and they will not be a match for you at all. Moreover, the whole naval force will support the land force and be supported by it, if they go forward together; but if you divide them, neither will you be of use to them nor they to you. My determination is rather to put your own affairs in good order and not to concern yourself with the affairs of the enemy — where they will mount the war, or what they will do, or how many they are. It is enough that they take thought for themselves, and we likewise for ourselves. And if the Lacedaemonians come out to fight the Persians, they will certainly not heal the wound from which they are now suffering.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 237
paragraphs: To him Xerxes replied as follows: “Achaimenes, I think you speak well, and so I will do. But Demaratos is saying what he believes to be best for me, though his opinion is overruled by yours. For I will certainly not accept what you said — namely that he is not well-disposed to my cause — judging both by what he has said before now and by this truth: that though one fellow-citizen envies another's good fortune and shows hostility by silence, nor would one citizen, when consulted by a fellow-citizen, suggest the course that seemed best to him (unless he had attained a great height of virtue — and such men are few), yet guest-friend to guest-friend in prosperity is as well-disposed as anyone on earth, and if his friend consults him, he will give him the best advice. As for slander against Demaratos — who is my guest-friend — I bid everyone refrain from it in the future.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 238
paragraphs: Having said this, Xerxes went to inspect the bodies of the dead. As for Leonidas, on hearing that he had been the king and commander of the Lacedaemonians, he ordered them to cut off his head and crucify the body. It has been made clear to me by many other proofs, but by none more strongly than by this, that King Xerxes had been more enraged with Leonidas while alive than with any other man on earth; for otherwise he would never have inflicted this outrage on his corpse, since of all the men I know, the Persians are most accustomed to honor those who are good men in war. Those to whom it was appointed to do these things, then, proceeded to do so.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 239
paragraphs: I will now return to the point in my narrative where I left off. The Lacedaemonians had been informed before all others that the king was preparing an expedition against Greece, and so they sent to the oracle at Delphi, where that reply was given them which I reported shortly before. They got this information in a strange way. Demaratos son of Ariston, after fleeing for refuge to the Medes, was not friendly to the Lacedaemonians — such is my opinion, which likelihood supports — but whether he did what follows out of goodwill or out of malicious triumph over them, it is open to anyone to conjecture. When Xerxes had decided to make a campaign against Greece, Demaratos, being in Susa and having been informed of it, wished to report it to the Lacedaemonians. He could find no other way to send the news without being discovered, but he contrived as follows: he took a folding tablet, scraped off the wax that was on it, and then wrote the king's plan on the wood of the tablet itself; after doing so, he melted the wax and poured it back over the writing, so that the tablet (being carried with apparently no writing on it) would not cause trouble with the keepers of the road. When it arrived at Lacedaemon, the Lacedaemonians could not make sense of it, until at last, as I am told, Gorgo, daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas, suggested a plan she herself had thought of, telling them to scrape the wax and they would find writing on the wood. Doing as she said, they found the writing and read it, and after that they sent word to the other Greeks. These events, it is said, came to pass in this way.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Those Greeks appointed to serve in the fleet were these: the Athenians furnished 127 ships, and the Plataeans, moved by valor and zeal for the service though having no practice in seamanship, joined the Athenians in manning their ships. The Corinthians furnished forty ships, the Megarians twenty; the Chalcidians manned twenty ships that the Athenians supplied them with; the Aeginetans furnished eighteen ships, the Sikyonians twelve, the Lacedaemonians ten, the Epidaurians eight, the Eretrians seven, the Troizenians five, the Styrians two, the Keians two ships and two fifty-oared galleys, while the Opuntian Locrians also came to help the rest with seven fifty-oared galleys.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 2
paragraphs: These were those who joined the expedition to Artemisium, and I have listed them by the number of ships they each supplied. So the number of ships assembled at Artemisium (apart from the fifty-oared galleys) was 271; and the commander holding supreme authority was provided by the Spartans — namely Eurybiades son of Eurycleides — since the allies said they would not follow Athenian leadership, and unless a Lacedaemonian were leader they would break up the expedition that was to be undertaken.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 3
paragraphs: It had originally been proposed, even before they sent to Sicily to seek allies, that the fleet should be placed in the charge of the Athenians. When the allies opposed this, the Athenians yielded, as they had it deeply at heart that Greece should be saved, and they saw that if there were disagreement among themselves over the leadership, Greece would perish. In this they judged rightly, for discord among those of the same race is worse than unified war, by as much as war is worse than peace. Being convinced of this truth, they did not contend, but gave way for as long as they urgently needed the allies — as their later conduct proved. For when, having driven the Persian away from themselves, they were now fighting for his land and no longer for their own, they used the arrogance of Pausanias as a pretext and stripped the Lacedaemonians of the leadership. But that happened later.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 4
paragraphs: At this time, however, even these Greeks who had come to Artemisium, when they saw that a great number of ships had put in at Aphetai and the whole area was filled with the enemy's armament, were struck with fear — for the barbarians' fortunes had turned out differently from what they expected — and they deliberated about retreating from Artemisium into the inner parts of Greece. When the Euboeans realized what they were considering, they asked Eurybiades to stay there with them for a short time, until they could remove their children and households from the land. When they failed to persuade him, they went elsewhere and persuaded Themistocles, the Athenian commander, by a payment of thirty talents, on condition that the fleet should stay and fight the sea-battle in front of Euboea.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Themistocles induced the Greeks to stay in this way: to Eurybiades he passed five talents of the sum, pretending that the money came from himself. When Eurybiades had been persuaded by him to change his mind, Adeimantos son of Okytos, the Corinthian commander, was the only one of all the others who still held out, saying that he would sail away from Artemisium and not stay with the rest. To him, then, Themistocles said with an oath: “You at least shall not leave us, for I will give you greater gifts than the king of the Medes would send you if you deserted your allies.” So saying, he at the same time sent three talents of silver to Adeimantos's ship. So all these had been persuaded by gifts to change their minds, the Euboeans' request had been met, and Themistocles himself made money on the side. It was not known that he had kept the rest of the money; those who received a share of it were fully convinced it had come from the Athenian state for this purpose.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 6
paragraphs: So they remained in Euboea and fought a sea-battle, which came about as follows. When the barbarians had arrived at Aphetai about the beginning of the afternoon, having been told even before arriving that a few Greek ships were stationed at Artemisium, and now seeing them for themselves, they were eager to attack, to see if they could capture them. They thought it not yet good to sail directly against them, for this reason: for fear that the Greeks, when they saw them coming, would set out in flight and darkness would catch them as they fled — in which case, they reckoned, the Greeks would likely escape; whereas, by their calculation, not even the fire-bearer should get away and save his life.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 7
paragraphs: With this in mind, they contrived as follows: they detached two hundred of their ships and sent them around to sail past Caphereus and around Geriastos to the Euripos, going outside Skiathos so as not to be sighted by the enemy as they rounded Euboea. Their intention was that, with these coming up that way and blocking the Greeks' retreat while they themselves advanced directly, they would surround them on every side. Having devised this plan, they proceeded to dispatch the ships assigned to the task, while they themselves had no intention of attacking the Greeks that day, or until the agreed signal should be displayed by those sailing around to show they had arrived. So these ships, they were sending around; meanwhile at Aphetai they were counting the rest.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 8
paragraphs: During this time, while they were counting their ships, the following happened. In that camp there was a man of Skione named Skyllias, the best diver of all men in his day, who had also saved many goods for the Persians in the shipwreck at Pelion and had acquired many for himself as well. This Skyllias, it appears, had had the intention even before this of deserting to the Greek side, but up to that point had not found it possible. In what manner he actually came over to the Greeks after this attempt, I cannot say for certain, but I am astonished if the story is true that is reported: it is said that he dove into the sea at Aphetai and did not come up until he reached Artemisium, having traversed somewhere about eighty furlongs through the sea. There are several other tales told about this man that seem likely to be false, but some also true. Regarding this matter, let it be stated as my opinion that he came to Artemisium in a boat. When he arrived, he at once informed the commanders about the shipwreck — how it had happened — and about the ships that had been sent off to sail around Euboea.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 9
paragraphs: On hearing this, the Greeks consulted with one another, and after much was said, the prevailing opinion was that they should remain there that day and camp on shore, then, after midnight was past, set out to meet the ships sailing around. But afterwards, as no one sailed out to attack them, they waited for the late afternoon and sailed out themselves to attack the barbarians, wanting to test both their manner of fighting and the maneuver of breaking through their line.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Seeing them sailing out against them with so few ships, not only the rest of Xerxes's army but also their commanders judged them to be moved by sheer madness, and they too launched their ships, supposing they would easily capture them. Their expectation was reasonable enough, since they saw that the Greeks' ships were few while theirs were many times as numerous and sailed better. With their minds set on this, they came round and enclosed them in the middle. At this, those Ionians who were kindly disposed to the Greeks and were serving in the expedition against their will, counted it a great grief when they saw the Greeks surrounded, feeling sure that not one of them would return home — so weak did they think the power of the Greeks to be. But those to whom what was happening was a source of pleasure were vying with one another, each trying to be the first to capture an Athenian ship and receive gifts from the king — for in their camps the Athenians were talked about more than anyone else.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 11
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Greeks, when the signal was given, first placed themselves with prows facing the barbarians and drew the sterns of their ships together in the middle; and when the signal was given a second time, although shut into a small space and facing prow to prow, they set to work vigorously; and they captured thirty barbarian ships, along with Philaon son of Chersis, the brother of Gorgos king of Salamis, a man of great standing in the army. The first of the Greeks to capture an enemy ship was an Athenian, Lycomedes son of Aischraios, who received the prize for valor. So these, contending in this sea-battle with uncertain result, were parted from each other by the coming on of night. The Greeks sailed back to Artemisium and the barbarians to Aphetai, the contest having turned out very different from their expectations. In this sea-fight Antidoros of Lemnos alone of the Greeks serving with the king deserted to the Greek side, and the Athenians for this deed gave him a piece of land on Salamis.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 12
paragraphs: When darkness had come on — although it was the middle of summer — very heavy rain fell, which lasted through the whole night, with crashing thunder from Mount Pelion. Dead bodies and pieces of wreckage were cast up at Aphetai, becoming entangled around the prows of the ships and striking against the oar-blades. The men of the army stationed there, hearing all this, became afraid, expecting that they would surely perish, such were the troubles they had come into.
