In this evil state, seeing that he was running for his life and was likely to suffer much torment before death, he did a deed that is scarcely credible. Being fastened on a block bound with iron, he obtained an iron tool that had somehow been brought in, and at once devised a feat as courageous as any we know: for having first calculated how the remaining part of his foot might be freed from the block, he cut off the flat of his own foot. After that, since he was still guarded by warders, he broke through the wall and ran off to Tegea, traveling during the nights and in daytime entering a wood and resting there. Although the Lacedaemonians searched for him in full force, he reached Tegea on the third night. The Lacedaemonians were struck with great wonder both at his courage (when they saw the severed piece of foot lying there) and at their inability to find him. So he escaped them then, taking refuge at Tegea, which at that time was not friendly with the Lacedaemonians. Once healed, and having procured a wooden foot for himself, he became an open enemy of the Lacedaemonians. In the end, however, the enmity he had fallen into with the Lacedaemonians was not to his advantage; for he was caught by them while practicing divination in Zakynthos and was put to death.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 38
paragraphs: The death of Hegesistratos, however, occurred later than the events at Plataea; at this time he was at the Asopos, having been hired by Mardonius for no small sum, sacrificing and showing zeal for his cause both because of his enmity toward the Lacedaemonians and because of the money he was earning. But as the sacrifices were not favorable for battle either for the Persians themselves or for those Greeks with them (they too had their own diviner, Hippomachos the Leucadian), and as the Greeks had men constantly streaming in and growing in number, Timagenides son of Herpys, a Theban, counseled Mardonius to set a guard on the pass of Kithairon, saying that the Greeks were pouring in every day and he would thus cut off large numbers.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 39
paragraphs: Eight days had now passed while they sat opposite one another, when Timagenides gave this advice to Mardonius. Mardonius, seeing that the advice was good, sent the cavalry, when night came on, to the pass of Kithairon leading toward Plataea — which the Boeotians call “Three Heads” and the Athenians “Oak Heads.” Sent in this way, the cavalry did not act in vain: they caught five hundred pack-animals coming out into the plain, carrying provisions from the Peloponnese to the army, along with the men accompanying the carts. Having taken this prize, the Persians began slaughtering them without sparing either beast or man; and when they were sated with killing, they surrounded what was left and drove them into the camp to Mardonius.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 40
paragraphs: After this deed they spent two more days, neither side willing to begin a battle; for the barbarians advanced as far as the Asopos to test the Greeks, but neither side would cross the river. However, Mardonius's cavalry made attacks continually and did damage to the Greeks; for the Thebans, strongly on the Medes' side, pressed the war with vigor, and always led the way up to the moment of fighting; and after this, the Persians and Medes took up the work and were the ones who displayed valor in their turn.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 41
paragraphs: For ten days nothing more was done than this; but when the eleventh day came, while they still sat opposite one another at Plataea, the Greeks by now having grown much more numerous and Mardonius being greatly vexed at the delay, Mardonius son of Gobryas and Artabazos son of Pharnakes — a man esteemed by Xerxes above almost all Persians — came to speak with each other. In their discussion, the opinions expressed were these. Artabazos's opinion was that they must set the whole army in motion as soon as possible and move to the walls of the Thebans, where great stores of grain had been brought in for them and fodder for their beasts; there they should settle quietly and get their business done as follows. They had, he said, great quantities of gold (both coined and uncoined) as well as silver and drinking cups, and he advised that these should be sent around without stint to the Greeks, especially to those who were leaders in their various cities; these, he said, would speedily surrender their freedom. He advised that they not risk a battle. His opinion, then, was the same as the Thebans', for he too had some true foresight. But Mardonius's opinion was more vehement and more obstinate, and he was by no means disposed to yield; for he said he thought their army far superior to that of the Greeks, and gave as his opinion that they should engage in battle as quickly as possible and not allow them to assemble in still greater numbers than were already gathered. As for the sacrifices of Hegesistratos, they should leave them alone and not try to force a favorable sign, but follow Persian custom and engage in battle.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 42
paragraphs: When he expressed this judgment, no one opposed him, and so his opinion prevailed; for it was he, and not Artabazos, who had been given command of the army by the king. He therefore summoned the commanders of the divisions and the generals of the Greeks with him, and asked whether they knew of any oracle about the Persians that said they were destined to be destroyed in Greece. Those summoned to council fell silent, some not knowing the oracles and others knowing them but thinking it unsafe to speak; then Mardonius himself said: “Since you either know nothing or do not venture to speak, I will tell you, for I know very well. There is an oracle saying that the Persians are destined, when they come to Greece, to plunder the temple at Delphi, and having plundered it to perish, every one of them. We, therefore, precisely because we know this, will not go to that temple, nor will we attempt to plunder it; and for this reason we shall not perish. So those of you who happen to wish well to the Persians, rejoice so far as this matter is concerned, and be assured that we shall overcome the Greeks.” Having spoken to them thus, he next commanded them to prepare everything and set all in order, since at dawn of the next day a battle would be fought.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Now this oracle, which Mardonius said referred to the Persians, I know for my part was composed with reference to the Illyrians and the army of the Enchelians, not to the Persians at all. However, the oracle composed by Bakis with reference to this battle —

“The gathering of Greeks together and cry of barbarian voices, where the Thermodon flows, by the banks of the grassy Asopos; here very many shall fall before destiny gave them to perish, bow-bearing Medes in fight, when the fatal day approaches them” —
these sayings, and others like them composed by Musaios, I know had reference to the Persians. Now the river Thermodon flows between Tanagra and Glisas.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 44
paragraphs: After the inquiry about the oracles and the exhortation given by Mardonius, night came on and the guards were set. When night was well advanced and it seemed that there was quiet everywhere in the camps, the men being in their deepest sleep, then Alexander son of Amyntas, commander and king of the Macedonians, rode his horse up to the Athenian guard-posts and asked to have speech with their generals. While the greater number of the guards stayed at their posts, some ran to the generals, and when they reached them they said that a man had come riding on a horse out of the Median camp who revealed nothing further, only named the generals and said he wished to have speech with them.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 45
paragraphs: On hearing this, they at once accompanied the men to the guard-posts; and when they had arrived, Alexander said to them: “Athenians, I entrust these words of mine to you as a deposit, charging you to keep them secret and tell them to no one except Pausanias, so that you may not bring me to ruin. For I would not utter them if I did not care greatly for the general safety of Greece, seeing that I am a Greek myself by original descent and would not wish to see Greece enslaved instead of free. I tell you, then, that Mardonius and his army cannot get the sacrifices to turn out as he wishes, otherwise you would long since have fought. Now, however, he has resolved to let the sacrifices alone and to bring on a battle at dawn; for, as I conjecture, he fears you may assemble in greater numbers. Therefore prepare yourselves. If Mardonius should after all put off the battle and not bring it on, stay where you are and hold out patiently, for they have provisions only for a few days remaining. And if this matter turns out according to your wish, each of you ought then to remember me too with regard to liberation, since I have done so hazardous a deed for the Greeks' sake out of zeal for you, wishing to reveal to you Mardonius's design so that the barbarians may not fall upon you unprepared. I am Alexander the Macedonian.” Having spoken, he rode back to the camp and to his own position.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 46
paragraphs: Then the Athenian generals came to the right wing and reported to Pausanias what they had heard from Alexander. At this, he, struck with fear of the Persians, spoke as follows: “Since, then, the battle comes on at dawn, it is right that you Athenians take your stand opposite the Persians, and we opposite the Boeotians and those Greeks now posted against you. The reason is that you are acquainted with the Medes and their manner of fighting, having fought them at Marathon, while we have no experience of these men and are ignorant of them; for not one Spartan has tested himself against the Medes in combat, though we have experience of the Boeotians and the Thessalians. It is right, therefore, that you take up your arms and come to this wing, and we go to the left.” To this the Athenians answered: “To us also, long ago at the very first, when we saw the Persians being drawn up opposite you, it occurred to say these very things, which you now bring forward before we have uttered them; but we feared that these words might not please you. Since, however, you yourselves have mentioned this, know that your words have given us pleasure, and that we are ready to do what you propose.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 47
paragraphs: Both sides, then, were content to do this, and as dawn appeared they began exchanging their positions with one another. But the Boeotians, perceiving what was being done, reported it to Mardonius, who on hearing it at once tried to change positions himself, bringing the Persians across so as to face the Lacedaemonians. When Pausanias learned that this was being done, he perceived that he was not unobserved, and led the Spartans back again to the right wing; and Mardonius likewise returned to his left.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 48
paragraphs: When they had been brought back to their former positions, Mardonius sent a herald to the Spartans who spoke as follows: “Lacedaemonians, you are said by those here to be very good men — they admire you because you do not flee in war nor leave your post, but stay and either destroy your enemies or perish yourselves. In this, however, as it now appears, there is no truth. For before we engaged in battle and came to hand-to-hand combat, we saw you already in flight and leaving your station, desiring to make trial first with the Athenians while you arrayed yourselves opposite our slaves. These are not at all the deeds of good men in war; we were greatly deceived in you. We expected, because of your renown, that you would send a herald to us, challenging us and desiring to fight the Persians alone; we on our part were ready to do this, but found you saying nothing of the kind — rather, you cowered in fear. Now, therefore, since you were not the first to say this, we are. Why do we not fight at once — you on behalf of the Greeks (since you have the reputation of being the best), and we on behalf of the barbarians — with equal numbers on both sides? And if we think it good that the rest should fight too, then let them fight afterward; but if we think it enough that we alone should fight, let us fight it out to the end, and whichever of us are victors, let them be counted victorious with their whole army.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 49
paragraphs: The herald, having spoken thus, waited some time; and then, as no one answered him, he departed and went back. On his return he reported to Mardonius what had happened to him. Mardonius, greatly rejoiced and elated by his empty victory, sent the cavalry to attack the Greeks. And when the horsemen rode up to attack, they damaged the whole Greek army by hurling javelins and shooting arrows, being mounted archers and therefore hard to fight against; they also disturbed and choked up the spring Gargaphia, from which the whole Greek army was drawing its water. Now the Lacedaemonians alone were posted near this spring, and it was at some distance from the rest of the Greeks (each being posted where they happened to be), while the Asopos was close at hand; but when they were kept away from the Asopos, they would go back and forth to this spring — for the horsemen and archers prevented them from fetching water from the river.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Such being the situation, the Greek generals — their army cut off from its water and being harassed by the cavalry — assembled to consult about these and other matters, coming to Pausanias on the right wing. For other things troubled them even more than these I have mentioned, since they had no provisions left, and their attendants who had been sent to the Peloponnese for the purpose of getting them had been cut off by the cavalry and could not reach the camp.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 51
paragraphs: The generals in council with one another resolved that, if the Persians put off the battle for that day, they would go to the Island. This is ten furlongs from the Asopos and the spring Gargaphia where they were then encamped, and lies in front of the Plataeans' city. And if it be asked how there can be an island on the mainland, here is how: the river parts in two upstream, flowing from Kithairon down into the plain, with about three furlongs between its streams, and then joins again into one; its name is Oëroe, said by the natives to be the daughter of Asopos. To this place, I say, they decided to move so that they might have an abundant water supply and not be damaged by the cavalry, as they now were while they stood directly opposite. They proposed to make the move when the second watch of the night had come, so that the Persians might not see them set out and harass them with the cavalry in pursuit. They also planned, after arriving at this place — around which, as I say, Oëroe the daughter of Asopos flows, parting into two streams as she runs down from Kithairon — to send half the army to Kithairon during that same night to pick up the attendants who had gone for provisions, since those were cut off from them in Kithairon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 52
paragraphs: Having so resolved, during that whole day they had unceasing trouble while the cavalry pressed them. But when the day drew to a close and the cavalry's attacks had ceased, then, as night was coming on and the hour arrived at which they had agreed to retire from their place, most of them set out and began to withdraw — but not keeping it in mind to go to the agreed place. On the contrary, once they had begun to move, they readily took the chance to flee from the cavalry toward the city of the Plataeans; and in their flight they came as far as the temple of Hera, which stands before the Plataean city, twenty furlongs from the spring Gargaphia. Having arrived there, they halted in front of the temple.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 53
paragraphs: These, then, were camping around the temple of Hera. Pausanias, seeing them retiring from the camp, gave the word to the Lacedaemonians also to take up their arms and follow after the others who had gone before, supposing these were going to the agreed place. When all the other commanders were ready to obey Pausanias, Amompharetos son of Poliades, commander of the Pitanate division, said he would not flee from the strangers, nor would he willingly disgrace Sparta; he expressed wonder at what was being done, not having been present at the earlier discussion. Pausanias and Euryanax were greatly disturbed that he did not obey them — and still more that they might be forced to leave the Pitanate division behind, since he refused. They feared that, if they left it in order to carry out what they had agreed with the other Greeks, Amompharetos himself would perish being left behind, along with the men with him. With this in mind they kept the Lacedaemonian force from moving, while they tried to persuade him that it was not right for him to do this.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 54
paragraphs: They, then, were exhorting Amompharetos, the only one of the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans left behind. Meanwhile the Athenians were keeping themselves quietly in the place where they had been posted, knowing the Spartan spirit — that they tend to say one thing and mean another. When the army began to move, the Athenians sent a horseman from their own number to see whether the Spartans were attempting to set out, or whether they really had no intention of retreating, and they told him to ask Pausanias what they ought to do.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 55
paragraphs: When the herald came to the Lacedaemonians, he saw they were still in their place and their leaders had come to strife with one another. For although Euryanax and Pausanias both urged Amompharetos not to risk remaining behind with his men, alone of all the Lacedaemonians, they did not persuade him at all, and at last they had come to outright strife. Meanwhile the Athenian herald had arrived and was standing beside them. Amompharetos, in his disputing, took up a rock in both hands and set it at Pausanias's feet, saying that with this pebble he cast his vote not to flee from the strangers — meaning the barbarians. Pausanias, calling him a madman and out of his senses, bade the Athenian herald — who was asking what he had been charged to ask — be told the state of their affairs; and at the same time he asked the Athenians to come toward the Lacedaemonians and to do the same as they did regarding the retreat.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 56
paragraphs: He, then, went back to the Athenians. As dawn still found them arguing with one another, Pausanias, who had stayed still throughout all this time, gave the signal and led all the rest away over the low hills, supposing that Amompharetos would not stay behind when the other Lacedaemonians departed — in which he was in fact right. With them went the Tegeans too. Meanwhile the Athenians, following the orders given them, were going in the direction opposite to the Lacedaemonians; for these clung to the hills and the lower slope of Kithairon out of fear of the cavalry, while the Athenians marched below in the direction of the plain.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 57
paragraphs: As for Amompharetos, at first he did not believe Pausanias would ever dare to leave him and his men behind, and he insisted they stay there and not abandon their post; but when Pausanias and his troops were well away in front, then he perceived that they had actually left him behind. He made his division take up their arms and led them slowly toward the main body. This main body, having gone about ten furlongs, waited for Amompharetos's division, halting at the river Moloeis and the place called Argiopion, where also stands a temple of Eleusinian Demeter. It stopped there for this reason: so that, if Amompharetos and his division should not leave the place where they had been posted but should remain there, it might be able to come back to their aid. So Amompharetos and his men were coming up to join them, and the barbarians' cavalry was at the same time beginning to attack them in full force. For the horsemen acted on this day as they had been in the habit of doing every day: seeing the place empty where the Greeks had been posted in the previous days, they rode their horses further and further forward, and as soon as they came up with them began to attack.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Then Mardonius, when he learned that the Greeks had departed during the night and saw their place deserted, called Thorax of Larissa and his brothers Eurypylos and Thrasydeios and said: “Sons of Aleuas, will you still say anything now, seeing these places deserted? You who dwell near them used to say that the Lacedaemonians did not flee from battle but were men unsurpassed in war. These men you saw before this changing their post, and now we all see that they have run away during the past night. By this they made plain, when the time came for them to contend in battle with those who were truly the best of all men, that after all they were men of no worth, who had been making a display of valor among the Greeks — a worthless race. As for you, since you had no experience of the Persians, I was very willing to excuse you for praising these men, of whom you did know something good; but much more did I marvel that Artabazos should have been afraid of the Lacedaemonians, and that in his fear he uttered that most cowardly opinion — namely, that we should move our army away and go to the city of the Thebans to be besieged there — an opinion about which the king shall yet be informed by me. But we will speak of these things elsewhere. For now, we must not allow them to act thus, but must pursue them until they are caught and pay the penalty to us for all they did to the Persians in time past.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Having said this, he led the Persians on at a run, after they had crossed the Asopos, on the track of the Greeks, supposing they were running away from him; and he directed his attack against the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans only, not seeing the Athenians, whose march was toward the plain, because of the hills. The rest of the barbarian division commanders, seeing that the Persians had set off in pursuit of the Greeks, all at once raised the signals for battle and began to pursue, each as fast as they could, with no order or sequence of posts.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 60
paragraphs: These, then, came on shouting and in confused numbers, thinking to make short work of the Greeks. Pausanias, when the cavalry began to attack, sent a horseman to the Athenians and said: “Athenians, now that the greatest contest is set before us — one whose outcome is the freedom or slavery of Greece — we, the Lacedaemonians, and you, the Athenians, have been deserted by our allies, who have run away during the past night. Now, therefore, it is determined what we must do about this: we must defend ourselves and protect one another as best we may. If the cavalry had set out to attack you first, we and the Tegeans (who with us refuse to betray the cause of Greece) would have been bound to go to your aid; but as it is, since the whole body has come against us, it is right that you should come to that portion of the army which is hardest pressed, to give aid. However, if something has befallen you that makes it impossible to come help, do us a kindness by sending the archers to us. We know that you have been by far the most zealous in this present war, so we trust you will listen to this request too.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 61
paragraphs: When the Athenians heard this they were eager to come to their help and assist them as much as possible; but as they were already on their way, they were attacked by those Greeks on the king's side who had been ranged opposite them, so that they were no longer able to come to the Lacedaemonians' aid — the force attacking them gave them much trouble. Thus the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans were left alone, numbering together with light-armed men fifty thousand of the former and three thousand Tegeans (the Tegeans were not separated at all from the Lacedaemonians). They began to offer sacrifice, meaning to engage in battle with Mardonius and the force that had come against them. Then, since their offerings did not prove favorable and many of them were being killed in the meantime and many more wounded — for the Persians had made a palisade of their wicker shields and were discharging their arrows in vast numbers and without sparing — Pausanias, seeing the Spartans hard pressed and the offerings not favorable, fixed his gaze on the temple of Plataean Hera and called on the goddess to help, praying that they might by no means be cheated of their hope.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 62
paragraphs: While he was still calling on her, the Tegeans sprang forward before the rest and advanced against the barbarians; and immediately after Pausanias's prayer the sacrifices proved favorable for the Lacedaemonians as they offered them. So when at last this came to pass, they too advanced against the Persians; and the Persians put aside their bows and came against them. Then first there was fighting over the wicker shields, and when these had been overturned, the fighting by the temple of Demeter was fierce and went on for a long time, until at last they came to grappling; for the barbarians would seize hold of the spears and break them off. In courage and strength the Persians were not inferior to the others, but they had no defensive armor, and moreover they were unversed in war and unequal to their opponents in skill; they would dart out one at a time or in groups of about ten, some more, some fewer, and fall upon the Spartans and perish.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 63
paragraphs: In the place where Mardonius himself was — riding on a white horse and having around him the thousand best Persians picked from the rest — there they pressed upon their opponents most of all. As long as Mardonius was alive, they held out and in defending themselves cut down many of the Lacedaemonians; but when Mardonius was killed and the men ranged around his person (the strongest portion of the whole army) had fallen, then the others also turned and gave way before the Lacedaemonians. Their manner of dress, without defensive armor, was a very great cause of destruction to them, since in truth they were fighting light-armed against hoplites.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 64
paragraphs: So satisfaction for the murder of Leonidas was paid by Mardonius, according to the oracle given to the Spartans; and the most famous victory known to us was won by Pausanias son of Cleombrotos, son of Anaxandrides, whose earlier ancestors have been named in connection with Leonidas, since as it happens they are the same for both. Now Mardonius was killed by Arimnestos, a man of standing in Sparta, who afterwards, when the Median wars were over, with three hundred men fought a battle against the entire Messenian army then at war with the Lacedaemonians, at Stenycleros; and both he was killed and the three hundred along with him.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 65
paragraphs: When the Persians were put to flight at Plataea by the Lacedaemonians, they fled in disorder to their own camp and to the palisade they had built in Theban territory. It is a marvel to me that, though they fought beside the sacred grove of Demeter, not one of the Persians was found to have entered the enclosure or to have been killed within it — but around the temple, on unconsecrated ground, the greater part of the slain fell. I suppose (if one ought to suppose anything about divine matters) that the goddess herself refused to receive them, because they had set fire to the temple — the so-called “palace” at Eleusis.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Thus far, then, had this battle gone. Artabazos son of Pharnakes, however, had been displeased from the very first that Mardonius remained behind after the king had gone, and afterwards had continually raised objections and done nothing, always urging them not to fight a battle. Since he was not pleased with what Mardonius was doing, for himself he acted as follows. The men under his command — and he had with him no small force, as much as forty thousand — when the fighting began, knowing well what the outcome of the battle would be, he led them carefully, having first given orders that all should go by the way he led them and at the same pace he went. Having given these orders, he led his troops on the pretense of taking them into battle; and when he was well on his way, he saw the Persians already in flight. Then he no longer led his men in the same order as before, but set off at a run, fleeing by the quickest route — not to the palisade or to the wall of the Thebans, but toward Phokis, eager to reach the Hellespont as quickly as possible.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 67
paragraphs: These, I say, were thus directing their march. Meanwhile, while the other Greeks on the king's side were deliberately slack in the fight, the Boeotians fought with the Athenians for a long time. The Thebans who took the Median side had no small zeal for the cause, and they fought and were not slack — so that three hundred of them, the first and best of all, fell there by the hands of the Athenians. When these too turned to flight, they fled to Thebes, not to the same place as the Persians; and the main body of the other allies fled without having fought steadily with anyone or shown any deeds of valor.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 68
paragraphs: This too is additional proof to me that all the fortunes of the barbarians depended on the Persians — namely that at that time these men fled before they had even engaged the enemy, because they saw the Persians doing so. Thus all were in flight except only the cavalry, including that of the Boeotians; and this rendered a service to the fugitives by constantly staying close to the enemy and keeping their own side's fugitives separated from the Greeks.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 69
paragraphs: The victors, then, were pressing after Xerxes's troops, pursuing and slaughtering them. During this panic, news was brought to the other Greeks — those who had taken position around the temple of Hera and had been absent from the battle — that a battle had taken place and Pausanias's troops were winning. On hearing this, without forming any order, the Corinthians and those near them turned to go along the skirts of the mountain and the low hills on the way leading straight up to the temple of Demeter, while the Megarians, Phliasians, and those near them went by the plain along the smoothest route. But when the Megarians and Phliasians drew near the enemy, the Theban cavalry caught sight of them from a distance hurrying along in no order, and rode up to attack — their cavalry commander being Asopodoros son of Timander. Falling upon them, they killed six hundred, and pursued and drove the rest to Kithairon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 70
paragraphs: These, then, perished thus ingloriously. Meanwhile the Persians and the rest of the throng, having fled for refuge to the palisade, succeeded in getting up onto the towers before the Lacedaemonians came up; and once up, they reinforced the defensive wall as best they could. When the Lacedaemonians came up to attack it, a vigorous fight for the wall began between them. As long as the Athenians were away, they defended themselves and had much the advantage over the Lacedaemonians, who did not understand the art of fighting against walls; but when the Athenians came up to help, then there was a fierce fight for the wall lasting a long time, and at last, by valor and endurance, the Athenians mounted the wall and made a breach, through which the Greeks poured in. The Tegeans were the first to enter the wall, and they plundered Mardonius's tent, taking, besides the other things in it, the manger of his horse, which was all of bronze and a sight worth seeing. This manger of Mardonius was dedicated by the Tegeans as an offering in the temple of Athena Alea; but everything else they took, they brought to the common stock of the Greeks. The barbarians, once the wall was captured, no longer formed themselves into any close body, nor did any of them think of making a stand, but they were utterly at a loss, as you would expect from men in a panic with many tens of thousands shut up in a small space; and the Greeks were able to slaughter them, so that out of an army of three hundred thousand — subtracting the forty thousand Artabazos took with him in his flight — of the remainder not three thousand men survived. Of the Lacedaemonians from Sparta, ninety-one were killed in battle; of the Tegeans, sixteen; and of the Athenians, fifty-two.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 71
paragraphs: Among the barbarians, those who proved themselves the best men were, of the foot, the Persians, and of the cavalry, the Sacans; and for a single man, Mardonius, it is said, was the best. Of the Greeks, though both Tegeans and Athenians proved themselves good men, the Lacedaemonians surpassed them in valor. Of this I have no other proof (for all these were victorious over their opposite numbers), except this: that they fought the strongest part of the enemy's force and overcame it. The man who, in my opinion, by far proved himself the best was that Aristodemos who, having come back alone of the three hundred safely from Thermopylae, had reproach and dishonor attached to him. After him the best were Poseidonios, Philokyon, and Amompharetos the Spartan. However, when there was discussion of which of them had shown himself the best, the Spartans present gave it as their opinion that Aristodemos had evidently wished to be killed, because of the charge against him, and so, as if in a frenzy and leaving his place in ranks, had performed great deeds, whereas Poseidonios had proved himself a good man although he had not wanted to be killed — and to that extent he was the better of the two. This, however, they perhaps said out of ill will. All those I named of the men killed in this battle were especially honored, except Aristodemos; but Aristodemos, because he had wanted to be killed on account of the aforementioned charge, was not honored.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 72
paragraphs: These gained the greatest renown of those who fought at Plataea. As for Callicrates — the handsomest man to come to the camp, not only of the Lacedaemonians but of all the Greeks of his time — he was not killed in the battle itself; but while Pausanias was offering sacrifice, he was struck by an arrow in the side as he was sitting in his place in the ranks. While the rest were fighting, he, having been carried out of the ranks, was dying a lingering death. He said to Arimnestos, a Plataean, that it did not grieve him to die for Greece, but only that he had not proved his strength of hand, and that no deed of valor had been performed by him worthy of the spirit he had in him to perform great deeds.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 73
paragraphs: Of the Athenians, the man who gained most glory is said to have been Sophanes son of Eutychides of the deme of Dekeleia — a deme whose inhabitants long ago performed a deed that has been of service to them ever since, as the Athenians themselves report. For when, in olden times, the sons of Tyndareus invaded Attica with a great army to bring back Helen, and were laying waste the demes — not knowing to what hiding place Helen had been taken — then they say that the men of Dekeleia (or, as some say, Dekelos himself), aggrieved by the insolence of Theseus and fearing for the whole land of the Athenians, told them the whole matter and led them to Aphidnai, which Titakos, a man sprung from the soil, delivered up by treachery to the sons of Tyndareus. As a result of this deed, the Dekeleians have continued to enjoy freedom from dues at Sparta and front seats at the games — privileges still in effect to this day. Indeed, in the war which arose many years after these events between the Athenians and Peloponnesians, when the Lacedaemonians laid waste all the rest of Attica, they spared Dekeleia from harm.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 74
paragraphs: To this deme belonged Sophanes, who showed himself the best of all the Athenians in this battle. Of him there are two different stories told. One says he carried an iron anchor bound by bronze chains to the belt of his corslet, which he would throw down whenever he came up with the enemy, so (they say) that when the enemy came out of their ranks, they could not move him from his place; and when a flight of his opponents took place, his plan was to take up the anchor first and then pursue them. So this story goes. But the other story, disputing the truth of the one above, reports as follows: on his shield, which was always moving about and never remaining still, he bore an anchor as a device — and not an iron one bound to his corslet.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 75
paragraphs: There was another distinguished deed done by Sophanes: when the Athenians were besieging Aegina, he challenged to a fight and killed Eurybates the Argive, who had been victor in the pentathlon at the games. To Sophanes himself it happened, after these events, that while he was general of the Athenians together with Leagros son of Glaucon, he was killed — after proving himself a good man — by the Edonians at Daton, fighting for the gold mines.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 76
paragraphs: When the barbarians had been laid low by the Greeks at Plataea, a woman approached — the concubine of Pharandates son of Teaspis, a Persian — coming over of her own free will from the enemy. When she perceived that the Persians had been destroyed and that the Greeks were victorious, she descended from her carriage and came up to the Lacedaemonians while they were still engaged in the slaughter. She had adorned herself with many gold ornaments, and her attendants likewise, and she had put on the finest of her robes. Seeing that Pausanias was directing everything there — being already familiar with his name and lineage, which she had heard often — she recognized Pausanias, took hold of his knees, and said: “O king of Sparta, deliver your suppliant from the slavery of the captive. For you have already done me a service by destroying these men, who have respect for neither demigods nor gods. I am by race of Cos, the daughter of Hegetorides son of Antagoras; and the Persian took me by force in Cos and kept me a prisoner.” He answered: “Woman, be of good courage — both because you are a suppliant, and also, if in addition it chances that you are speaking the truth and are the daughter of Hegetorides of Cos, who is bound to me as guest-friend more than any other man dwelling in those parts.” Having said this, he for the time put her in charge of the Ephors present; and afterwards he sent her to Aegina, where she herself wished to go.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 77
paragraphs: After the woman's arrival, the Mantineians arrived, when all was over. Learning they had come too late for the battle, they were greatly grieved and said they deserved to be punished. Being informed that the Medes with Artabazos were in flight, they pursued them as far as Thessaly, though the Lacedaemonians tried to prevent them from pursuing fugitives. On their return home, they sent the leaders of their army into exile. After the Mantineians came the Eleians; they too, like the Mantineians, were greatly grieved and departed home; and these also, on their return, sent their leaders into exile. So much for the Mantineians and Eleians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 78
paragraphs: At Plataea, among the Aeginetans' troops, was Lampon son of Pytheas, one of the leading men of Aegina, who was moved to go to Pausanias with a most impious proposal; having come in haste, he said: “Son of Cleombrotos, a deed has been done by you that is of marvellous greatness and glory, and God has permitted you, by rescuing Greece, to lay up for yourself the greatest renown of all the Greeks we know of. Now do also what remains to be done after this, so that yet greater reputation may attach to you, and that in future every barbarian may beware of being the first to commit outrageous deeds against Greeks. For when Leonidas was killed at Thermopylae, Mardonius and Xerxes cut off his head and crucified him. Repay him like with like, and you will have praise first from all the Spartans, and then secondly from the other Greeks also; for if you impale the body of Mardonius, you will have taken vengeance for Leonidas, your father's brother.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 79
paragraphs: He said this thinking to give pleasure; but Pausanias answered him: “Stranger of Aegina, I admire your friendly spirit and your forethought for me, but you have missed a good opinion nevertheless; for after exalting me and my family and my deed, you then cast me down to nothing by advising me to commit an outrage on a dead body, and by saying that if I do this I will be better reported of. Such things are more fitting for barbarians than for Greeks — and even in barbarians we find fault with such deeds. However that may be, I do not wish to please, in any such way as this, either Aeginetans or others who delight in such things. It is enough for me that I keep free of unholy deeds — yes, and of unholy speech too — and so please the Spartans. As for Leonidas, whom you bid me avenge, I declare that he has been greatly avenged already, and honored by the countless lives taken of these men — and not only he, but also the rest who ended their lives at Thermopylae. As for you, do not come to me again with such a proposal, nor give me such advice; and be thankful, moreover, that you go unpunished for it now.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 80
paragraphs: Having heard this, he went his way. Pausanias then issued a proclamation that no one should lay hands on the spoils, and he ordered the Helots to gather the things together. They accordingly dispersed about the camp and found tents furnished with gold and silver, beds overlaid with gold and silver, mixing bowls of gold, and cups and other drinking vessels. They also found sacks laid on wagons, in which there turned out to be cauldrons of gold and silver; and from the dead bodies lying there they stripped bracelets, collars, and also their swords if they were of gold — for embroidered clothing was of no account. The Helots stole many of the things and sold them to the Aeginetans, but many also they delivered up — as many as they could not conceal. So the great wealth of the Aeginetans first came from this: they bought the gold from the Helots, pretending that it was bronze.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 81
paragraphs: Then having gathered the things together, and set apart a tithe for the god at Delphi (with which was dedicated the golden tripod that rests upon the three-headed bronze serpent and stands close by the altar), and also for the god at Olympia (with which they dedicated a bronze statue of Zeus ten cubits high), and finally for the god at the Isthmus (with which was made a bronze statue of Poseidon seven cubits high) — having set apart these things, they divided the rest, and each took what they were due, including the concubines of the Persians and the gold, silver, and other things, and also the beasts of burden. How much was set apart and given to those who had proved the best men at Plataea is not reported by anyone, though for my part I suppose gifts were made to them too. To Pausanias, however, ten of each thing were set apart and given — women, horses, talents, camels, and so on for the other things.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 82
paragraphs: It is also said that what follows was done. Xerxes in his flight from Greece had left to Mardonius the furnishings of his own tent. Pausanias, accordingly, seeing Mardonius's furnishings adorned with gold and silver and with hangings of different colors, ordered the bakers and cooks to prepare a meal as they were accustomed to do for Mardonius. When they did as commanded, it is said that Pausanias, seeing couches of gold and silver with luxurious coverings, tables of gold and silver, and the magnificent apparatus of the feast, was astonished at the good things set before him; and for sport he ordered his own servants to prepare a Laconian meal. When the banquet was served and the difference between the two was great, Pausanias laughed and sent for the Greek commanders; and when they had come together, Pausanias said, pointing to the preparation of the two meals: “Greeks, I assembled you for this reason — because I wished to show you the senselessness of this leader of the Medes, who, having such fare as this, came to us, who have such sorry fare as you see here, to take it away from us.” Thus Pausanias is said to have spoken to the Greek commanders.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 83
paragraphs: In later time, after these events, many of the Plataeans also found chests of gold, silver, and other treasures. Moreover, afterwards the following was seen concerning the bodies here, after the flesh had been stripped from the bones: the Plataeans had gathered the bones all into one place, and there was found a skull with no suture but all of one bone, and also a jawbone (the upper part of the jaw) which had teeth joined together and all of one bone — both the cutting teeth and the grinding teeth; and there were also seen the bones of a man five cubits tall.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 84
paragraphs: The body of Mardonius, however, had disappeared on the day after the battle, taken by whom I cannot say for certain; but I have heard the names of many men from various cities who are said to have buried Mardonius, and I know that many received gifts from Artontes son of Mardonius for having done this. Who it was, though, who took up and buried the body of Mardonius, I cannot discover for certain; but Dionysophanes, an Ephesian, is reported with some plausibility to have been the one who buried Mardonius.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 85
paragraphs: He was buried, then, in some such manner. The Greeks, having divided the spoils at Plataea, proceeded to bury their dead, each nation apart. The Spartans made themselves three separate burial-places: in one they buried the younger Spartans, among whom were Poseidonios, Amompharetos, Philokyon, and Callicrates; in the second, the rest of the Spartans; in the third, the Helots. They then buried their dead thus. The Tegeans buried theirs together in a place apart from these; the Athenians, theirs together; the Megarians and Phliasians, those who had been killed by the cavalry. The burial-places of all these contained bodies; but as for the burial-places of other cities to be seen at Plataea, these, as I am told, are all merely mounds of earth without bodies in them, raised by the various peoples on account of posterity, because they were ashamed of their absence from the fight. Among others there is one called the burial-place of the Aeginetans, which I hear was raised at the request of the Aeginetans by Cleades son of Autodicos, a Plataean who was their public guest-friend, no less than ten years after these events.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 86
paragraphs: When the Greeks had buried their dead at Plataea, they at once resolved in common council to march on Thebes and demand that the Thebans surrender those who had taken the side of the Medes — chief among them Timagenides and Attaginos, who were leaders equal to the first; and if the Thebans did not give them up, they resolved not to retire from the city until they had taken it. Having so resolved, they came accordingly on the eleventh day after the battle and began to besiege the Thebans, demanding that the men be handed over. When the Thebans refused, they began to lay waste their land and attack their wall.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 87
paragraphs: So, as the ravages did not cease, on the twentieth day Timagenides spoke as follows to the Thebans: “Thebans, since the Greeks have resolved not to abandon the siege until either they have taken Thebes or you have delivered us up to them, let the land of Boeotia no longer suffer on our account. If they desire money and are demanding our surrender as a pretext for this, let us give them money taken out of the state's treasury — for we took the Medes' side together with the state, not by ourselves alone; but if they are truly conducting the siege to get us into their hands, then we will give ourselves up for trial.” It was thought that he spoke well and at the right time, and the Thebans at once sent a herald to Pausanias offering to hand over the men.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 88
paragraphs: After they had come to agreement on these terms, Attaginos escaped out of the city; and when his sons were delivered up to Pausanias, he released them from the charge, saying that the sons had no share in the guilt of taking the Medes' side. As for the other men the Thebans handed over, they supposed they would get a trial and relied on being able to ward off the danger by payment of money; but Pausanias, when he had received them, suspecting this very thing, first dismissed the whole army of allies, then took the men to Corinth and put them to death there. These were the things that happened at Plataea and at Thebes.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 89
paragraphs: Artabazos son of Pharnakes, meanwhile, in his flight from Plataea was by now getting well on his way. When he came to the Thessalians, they offered him hospitality and asked about the rest of the army, knowing nothing of what had happened at Plataea. Artabazos, knowing that if he told them the whole truth about the fighting, he would run the risk of being destroyed both himself and the whole army with him (for he thought they would all attack him once informed of what had happened), reflecting on this, had told nothing of it to the Phokians, and now to the Thessalians he said: “I, as you see, Thessalians, am eager to march by the shortest way to Thrace; I am in great haste, having been sent with these men on a certain business from the army. Mardonius himself and his army are to be expected here shortly, marching close after me. Give him entertainment and show yourselves serviceable, for you will not in the end repent having done so.” Having said this, he continued to march his army with haste through Thessaly and Macedonia straight for Thrace, truly eager to press on and going through the country by the shortest possible way. So he came to Byzantion, having left behind him great numbers of his army — either cut down on the way by the Thracians or overcome by hunger and fatigue — and from Byzantion he crossed over in ships. Thus he himself made his return to Asia.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Now on the same day on which the defeat took place at Plataea, another, as fortune would have it, took place at Mycale in Ionia. When the Greeks who had come in ships with Leotychides the Lacedaemonian were lying at Delos, there came to them as envoys from Samos Lampon son of Thrasycles, Athenagoras son of Archestratides, and Hegesistratos son of Aristagoras — who had been sent by the people of Samos without the knowledge either of the Persians or of the tyrant Theomestor son of Androdamas, whom the Persians had set up as tyrant of Samos. When these were brought before the commanders, Hegesistratos spoke at length using all kinds of arguments, saying that as soon as the Ionians saw them, they would at once revolt from the Persians, and that the barbarians would not await the attack; and if after all they did, the Greeks would take a prize such as they would never take again thereafter. Appealing to the gods worshipped in common, he tried to persuade them to rescue men who were Greeks from slavery and to drive the barbarian away. This was easy for them to do, he said, because the enemy's ships sailed badly and were no match for theirs in battle. Moreover, if the Greeks suspected they were trying to lead them on by fraud, the envoys were ready to be taken as hostages in their ships.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 91
paragraphs: Then, as the stranger of Samos pressed his plea, Leotychides inquired — either wishing to hear for the sake of the omen, or perhaps by a chance Providence brought about: “Stranger of Samos, what is your name?” He said, “Hegesistratos.” Leotychides cut short the rest of the speech, stopping all that Hegesistratos had intended to say further, and said: “I accept the omen given in the name Hegesistratos, stranger of Samos. For your part, see that you give us assurances — you and the men with you — that the Samians will be our zealous allies without fail; and after that, sail away home.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 92
paragraphs: Thus he spoke, and to his words he added the deed; for at once the Samians gave assurance and sworn pledges of alliance with the Greeks, and having done so, the others sailed away home. Hegesistratos, however, he bade sail with the Greeks, considering his name a good omen for success. The Greeks then, after staying still that day, offered sacrifices for success on the next day, their diviner being Deïphonos son of Euenios, an Apolloniate — from that Apollonia which lies on the Ionian gulf.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 93
paragraphs: To this man's father, Euenios, this happened. At Apollonia there are sheep sacred to the Sun which by day feed by a river running from Mount Lakmon through the land of Apollonia to the sea near the harbor of Oricos; by night they are watched by men chosen for the purpose, who are the most highly regarded citizens for wealth and noble birth, each man having charge of them for a year. For the people of Apollonia set great store by these sheep because of an oracle, and they are folded in a cave at some distance from the city. At the time of which I speak, this Euenios was keeping watch over them, having been chosen for the task. It happened one night that he fell asleep during his watch, and wolves came into the cave and killed about sixty of the sheep. When he noticed this, he kept it secret, telling no one, meaning to buy others and substitute them for those killed. It was discovered, however, by the people of Apollonia, and when they were informed they brought him to court and condemned him to be deprived of his eyesight for having fallen asleep on watch. But once they had blinded Euenios, their flocks immediately ceased to bring forth young and their land to bear crops as before. Prophecies were uttered to them both at Dodona and at Delphi, when they asked the prophets the cause of the evil they were suffering, and they told them they had acted unjustly in depriving Euenios the watcher of the sacred sheep of his sight — for the gods of whom they inquired had themselves sent the wolves to attack the sheep; and they would not cease to take vengeance for him until the men of Apollonia paid Euenios such satisfaction as he himself should choose and deem sufficient. This being fulfilled, the gods would give Euenios a gift of such a kind that many men would think him happy in possessing it.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 94
paragraphs: These oracles, then, were uttered to them, and the people of Apollonia, keeping it a secret, entrusted certain citizens to handle the matter; and they handled it for them thus. When Euenios was sitting on a seat in public, they came and sat beside him, and conversed about other matters, and at last they came to sympathizing with him in his misfortune; and leading him on in this way, they asked what satisfaction he would choose, if the people of Apollonia should undertake to give him satisfaction for what they had done. He, not having heard the oracle, made his choice and said that if there were given him the lands belonging to certain citizens — naming those he knew to own the two best plots of land in Apollonia — along with a house as well, which he knew to be the best in the city, if he became owner of these, he would have no anger against them in the future, and this satisfaction would be sufficient if given to him. While he was speaking thus, the men sitting beside him interrupted: “Euenios, this is the satisfaction the Apolloniates pay to you for your blinding, in accordance with the oracles given them.” At this he was angry, finding out the whole matter and considering that he had been deceived; but they bought the property from those who owned it and gave him what he had chosen. And immediately after this he had a natural gift of divination, so that he became very famous.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 95
paragraphs: Of this Euenios, I say, Deïphonos was the son, and he was acting as diviner for the army, having been brought by the Corinthians. I have heard, however, that Deïphonos was wrongly making use of Euenios's name and undertook work of this kind around Greece, not being really the son of Euenios.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 96
paragraphs: When the sacrifices were favorable to the Greeks, they put their ships to sea from Delos to go to Samos; and arriving off Calamisa in Samos, they moored their ships there opposite the temple of Hera at this place and made preparations for a sea-fight. But the Persians, informed that they were sailing there, also put out to sea and went over to the mainland with their remaining ships (the Phoenician ships having already been sent home). On deliberating, they had thought it good not to fight a battle at sea, since they did not think themselves a match for the enemy; and they sailed away to the mainland so as to be under the protection of their land-army at Mycale, a body that had stayed behind the rest of the army by Xerxes's command, keeping watch over Ionia. Its number was sixty thousand, and its commander was Tigranes, who in beauty and stature surpassed the other Persians. The fleet's commanders, then, had decided to take refuge under this army's protection, draw their ships up on shore, and build an enclosure around them as a protection for the ships and a refuge for themselves.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 97
paragraphs: Having so decided, they began to put out to sea. They came past the temple of the “Revered Goddesses” to the Gaison and to Scolopoeis in Mycale, where there is a temple of Eleusinian Demeter, built by Philistos son of Pasicles when he accompanied Neileus son of Codros for the founding of Miletus. There they drew their ships up on shore and put an enclosure of stones and timber around them — cutting down fruit trees for the purpose — and fixed stakes around the enclosure, making preparations either to be besieged or to gain a victory; for in making their preparations they reckoned on both possibilities.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 98
paragraphs: The Greeks, however, when informed that the barbarians had gone off to the mainland, were vexed, thinking they had escaped, and were at a loss what to do — whether to go back home or to sail down toward the Hellespont. At last they resolved to do neither, but to sail on to the mainland. Having prepared for a sea-fight both boarding bridges and everything else required, they sailed toward Mycale; and when they came near the camp, no one was seen putting out against them, but they perceived ships drawn up within the wall and a large land-army ranged along the shore. Then first Leotychides, sailing along in his ship and coming as near the shore as he could, made proclamation by a herald to the Ionians, saying: “Ionians, those of you who chance to be within earshot, attend to what I say — for the Persians will understand nothing of what I enjoin to you. When we join battle, let every one of you remember first the freedom of all, and then the watchword ‘Hebe'; and let him who has not heard this learn it from him who has.” The intent of this act was the same as that of Themistocles at Artemisium: either the words uttered would escape the barbarians' notice and persuade the Ionians, or, if reported to the barbarians, would make them distrustful of the Greeks.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 99
paragraphs: After Leotychides had made this suggestion, the Greeks next brought their ships up to land and disembarked on the shore. They were ranging themselves for battle; and the Persians, seeing the Greeks preparing for battle and that they had exhorted the Ionians, first deprived the Samians of their arms, suspecting they inclined to the Greek side — for when Athenian prisoners whom Xerxes's army had found left behind in Attica had come in the barbarians' ships, the Samians had ransomed them and sent them back to Athens, supplying them with means for the journey; this is why they were especially suspected, since they had ransomed five hundred of Xerxes's enemies. Secondly, the Persians appointed the Milesians to guard the passes leading to the heights of Mycale, on the pretext that they knew the country best; but the real reason was to get them out of the camp. Against these Ionians, whom they suspected would make some hostile move if they found the chance, the Persians sought to secure themselves in the manner mentioned; and they themselves then brought together their wicker shields to serve as a fence.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 100
paragraphs: When the Greeks had completed all their preparations, they proceeded to attack the barbarians. As they went forward, a rumor came suddenly to their whole army, and at the same time a herald's staff was found lying on the beach; the rumor went through the army to this effect — that the Greeks were fighting in Boeotia and conquering the army of Mardonius. By many signs is the divine power seen in earthly things, and by this too: that now, when the day of the defeat at Plataea and of the one about to happen at Mycale chanced to be the same, a rumor came to the Greeks here, so that the army was much more encouraged and more eager to face the danger.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 101
paragraphs: Moreover, this other coincidence occurred besides: a sacred precinct of Eleusinian Demeter stood close beside both battlefields. Not only in the Plataean land did the fight take place close beside the temple of Demeter, as I have said, but in Mycale too it was to be the same. And the rumor that reached them — that a victory had already been won by the Greeks with Pausanias — proved to be a true report; for what happened at Plataea came about while it was still early morning, but the fighting at Mycale took place in the afternoon. That it happened on the same day of the same month as the other became evident to them not long afterwards, when they inquired into the matter. Before the rumor arrived, they had been afraid — not so much for themselves as for the Greeks in general, lest Greece should stumble and fall over Mardonius. But when this report came suddenly to them, they advanced on the enemy much more vigorously and swiftly than before. Both Greeks and barbarians were going eagerly into the battle, since the islands and the Hellespont were placed before them as prizes of the contest.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 102
paragraphs: For the Athenians and those ranged next to them, numbering perhaps half the whole army, the route lay along the sea-beach and over level ground, while the Lacedaemonians and those ranged with them were compelled to go through a ravine and along the mountainside. So while the Lacedaemonians were still going around, those on the other wing were already beginning the fight. As long as the Persians' wicker shields still remained upright, they continued to defend themselves and rather had the advantage in the fight; but when the Athenians and those ranged next to them, wanting the achievement to belong to them and not to the Lacedaemonians, with exhortations to one another set themselves more vigorously to the work, then from that point the fortune of the fight changed. They pushed aside the wicker shields and fell upon the Persians in a single rush; the Persians sustained their first attack and continued to defend themselves for a long time, but at last fled to the wall. The Athenians, Corinthians, Sikyonians, and Troizenians — for that was the order of their ranks — followed close after them and rushed in together with them into the space within the wall. When the wall too was captured, the barbarians no longer turned to resistance but began to take flight — all except the Persians, who formed into small groups and continued to fight the Greeks as they rushed in within the wall. Of the Persian commanders, two escaped and two were slain: Artaÿntes and Ithamitres, commanders of the fleet, escaped, while Mardontes and the land-army commander Tigranes were slain.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Now while the Persians were still fighting, the Lacedaemonians and those with them arrived and joined in carrying through the rest of the work. Many of the Greeks themselves fell there, especially many of the Sikyonians, along with their commander Perilaos. The Samians serving in the army — in the Median camp and having been stripped of their arms — when they saw that the battle was going against the Persians from the very first, did as much as they could to help the Greeks. The other Ionians, seeing that the Samians had set the example, themselves revolted from the Persians and attacked the barbarians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 104
paragraphs: The Milesians, too, had been appointed to guard the passes for the Persians, in order to secure their safety, so that if what actually came to pass should happen after all, they might have guides and so get safely away to the heights of Mycale. The Milesians, I say, had been appointed to do this, not only for that end but also from fear that, if they were present in the camp, they might make some hostile move. But they did in fact the opposite of what they were appointed to do; they not only directed the Persians in flight by wrong paths — by paths that led toward the enemy — but also at last themselves became their worst foes and began to slay them. Thus for the second time Ionia revolted from the Persians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 105
paragraphs: In this battle, of the Greeks, the Athenians were the best men, and of the Athenians, Hermolycos son of Euthoinos, a man who had trained for the pancration. This Hermolycos, after these events, when there was war between the Athenians and the Carystians, was killed in battle at Kyrnos in the Carystian land near Geraistos, and was buried there. After the Athenians, the Corinthians, Troizenians, and Sikyonians were the best.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 106
paragraphs: When the Greeks had slain most of the barbarians — some in battle, others in their flight — they set fire to the ships and the whole wall, having first brought out the spoils onto the shore; and among the rest they found some stores of money. Having set fire to the wall and the ships, they sailed away; and when they came to Samos, the Greeks deliberated about removing the inhabitants of Ionia, and considered where they ought to settle them in those parts of Greece under their control, leaving Ionia to the barbarians. For it was clear to them that, on the one hand, it was impossible for them always to be stationed as guards to protect the Ionians; and on the other, if they were not so stationed, they had no hope that the Ionians would escape unpunished from the Persians. The Peloponnesians in authority thought it good to remove the inhabitants of the trading ports belonging to those peoples of Greece who had sided with the Medes, and to give that land to the Ionians to dwell in. But the Athenians did not think it good for the inhabitants of Ionia to be removed at all, nor that the Peloponnesians should deliberate about Athenian colonies. As these resisted the proposal vehemently, the Peloponnesians gave way. So the outcome was that they joined as allies to their league the Samians, Chians, Lesbians, and the other islanders who happened to be serving with the Greeks, binding them by pledges and oaths to remain faithful and not withdraw from the league. Having bound them by oaths, they sailed to break up the bridges, for they supposed they would find them still stretched across the straits.
These, then, were sailing toward the Hellespont.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 107
paragraphs: Meanwhile, those barbarians who had escaped and been driven to the heights of Mycale — being not many in number — were making their way to Sardis. As they went, Masistes son of Darius, who had been present at the disaster that befell them, was saying many harsh things of the commander Artaÿntes — among others, that he had shown himself worse than a woman in his generalship, and deserved every kind of evil for having brought evil on the king's house. Now for Persians, to be called worse than a woman is the greatest possible reproach. So Artaÿntes, after much reviling, at length grew angry and drew his sword on Masistes, meaning to kill him. As he was running at him, Xeinagoras son of Prexilaos, a man of Halicarnassus, who was standing just behind Artaÿntes, perceived it; he seized him round the waist and, lifting him up, dashed him to the ground, and meanwhile Masistes's spearmen came in front to protect him. Thus did Xeinagoras, and thus he laid up thanks for himself both with Masistes and with Xerxes for saving the life of his brother; for this deed Xeinagoras became ruler of all Cilicia by the king's gift. Nothing further happened on the way, and they reached Sardis.
Now at Sardis, as it happened, King Xerxes had been staying ever since the time he came there in flight from Athens, after his defeat in the sea-fight.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 108
paragraphs: During that time, while he was in Sardis, he conceived a passionate desire, it seems, for the wife of Masistes, who was also there. Since she could not be bent to his will by his messages, and he did not wish to use force — out of regard for his brother Masistes, and the same consideration also restrained the woman, for she well knew that force would not be used against her — Xerxes then gave up on all else and set about bringing about the marriage of his own son Darius to the daughter of this woman and Masistes, supposing that if he did so he would obtain her more easily. Having made the betrothal and performed all the customary rites, he went away to Susa; and when he had arrived there and brought the woman into his own house for Darius, then he ceased trying to gain the wife of Masistes, and changing his inclination, conceived a desire for the wife of Darius (who was the daughter of Masistes) and obtained her. The name of this woman was Artaÿnte.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 109
paragraphs: As time went on, however, the matter became known in the following way. Amestris, Xerxes's wife, had woven a mantle — large, of various workmanship, and a sight worth seeing — and she gave it to Xerxes. Greatly pleased, he put it on and went to Artaÿnte. Being greatly pleased with her too, he bade her ask whatever she wanted to be given in return for the favors she had granted him, for she would obtain, he said, whatever she asked. Since it was destined that she should perish miserably along with her whole house, she said to Xerxes: “Will you give me whatever I ask?” He, supposing she would ask anything rather than what she did, promised this and swore to it. Then when he had sworn, she boldly asked for the mantle. Xerxes tried every means of persuasion, not wanting to give it to her — and for no other reason than that he feared Amestris, lest by her (who even before this had some inkling of the truth) he should thus be caught out. He offered her cities and gold in any quantity, and an army that no one else should command except herself — this last being a thoroughly Persian gift. When, however, he could not persuade her, he gave her the mantle; and she, overjoyed by the gift, wore it and prided herself on it.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 110
paragraphs: And Amestris was informed that she had it. Having learned what was going on, she was not angry with the young woman but, supposing that her mother was the cause and that she was bringing this about, she planned destruction for the wife of Masistes. She waited until her husband Xerxes had a royal feast set before him — this feast is served up once a year, on the day the king was born, and the name of it in Persian is tycta, which in Greek means “complete”; on this occasion alone the king washes his head, and he then makes gifts to the Persians. Amestris, I say, waited for this day, and then asked Xerxes that the wife of Masistes might be given to her. He considered it a strange and untoward thing to hand his brother's wife over to her — especially since she was innocent of this matter, for he understood why she was making the request.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 111
paragraphs: At last, however, as she continued to beg urgently and he was compelled by the rule — namely, that among them it is impossible for anyone who makes a request when a royal feast is laid before the king to fail to obtain it — he at last, very much against his will, consented. In handing her over, he told Amestris to do as she wished; meanwhile, he sent for his brother and said these words: “Masistes, you are the son of Darius and my brother, and in addition you are a man of worth. I tell you: live no longer with this wife you now live with. I give you instead my daughter; live with her as your wife, but do not keep the wife you now have — for it does not seem good to me that you should keep her.” Masistes, astonished at what was said, answered: “Master, how unprofitable is the speech you utter to me, in bidding me send away a wife by whom I have sons who are grown young men, and daughters — one of whom even you yourself took as wife for your son — and who is herself, as it happens, very much to my liking; that you bid me send her away and take to wife your daughter! I, O king, consider it a very great matter to be judged worthy of your daughter, but nevertheless I will do neither of these things. Do not compel me by force to do such a thing. For your daughter another husband will be found, in no way inferior to me; and let me, I beg you, still live with my own wife.” He answered with words something like these; and Xerxes, moved with anger, said: “This then, Masistes, is your case: I will not give you my daughter for your wife, nor shall you live any longer with that one — so that you may learn to accept what is offered to you.” On hearing this, he went out, saying first these words: “Master, surely you have not yet brought ruin upon me?”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 112
paragraphs: During this interval of time, while Xerxes was conversing with his brother, Amestris had sent Xerxes's spearmen to bring the wife of Masistes, and she was inflicting shameful outrage on her: she cut away her breasts and threw them to the dogs, and she cut off her nose, ears, lips, and tongue, and sent her home so mutilated.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Then Masistes, not yet having heard any of these things but supposing that some evil had fallen on him, came running to his house; and seeing his wife thus mutilated, at once he took counsel with his sons and set out to go to Bactria together with them — and doubtless some others as well — intending to make the province of Bactria revolt and to do the greatest possible injury to the king. This in fact would have come to pass, I believe, if he had reached the land of the Bactrians and Sacans before he was overtaken, for they were much attached to him and he was moreover governor of the Bactrians. But Xerxes, informed that he was doing this, sent an army after him on his way and killed him, his sons, and his army. So much for what happened about Xerxes's passion and the death of Masistes.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 114
paragraphs: Now the Greeks who had set out from Mycale to the Hellespont first moored their ships about Lecton, being stopped from their voyage by winds; and from there they came to Abydos and found the bridges broken up, which they had thought to find still stretched across, and for the sake of which especially they had come to the Hellespont. So the Peloponnesians with Leotychides resolved to sail back to Greece, while the Athenians and their commander Xanthippos determined to stay behind there and make an attempt on the Chersonese. So the Peloponnesians sailed away, while the Athenians crossed from Abydos to the Chersonese and began to besiege Sestos.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 115
paragraphs: To this town of Sestos — since it was the greatest stronghold in that region — men had gathered from the cities around when they heard that the Greeks had arrived at the Hellespont; especially Oiobazos, a Persian, had come from the city of Cardia, bringing to Sestos the ropes of the bridges. The inhabitants of the city were Aiolians, natives of the country, but there were also living with them a great number of Persians and their allies.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 116
paragraphs: The tyrant of the province was Artaÿctes, a governor under Xerxes — a Persian, but a man of desperate and reckless character — who had also practiced deception on the king on his march against Athens, by taking away from Elaius the things belonging to Protesilaos son of Iphiclos. For at Elaius in the Chersonese there is the tomb of Protesilaos with a sacred precinct around it, where there were many treasures — gold and silver cups, bronze, robes, and other offerings — all of which Artaÿctes carried off as plunder, the king having granted them to him. He deceived Xerxes by saying to him something like this: “Master, here there is the house of a man, a Greek, who made an expedition against your land, met with his deserts, and was killed. I ask you to give me this man's house, so that everyone may learn not to make expeditions against your land.” By saying this, it was likely enough that he would persuade Xerxes to give him a man's house, not suspecting what was in his mind. When he said that Protesilaos had made an expedition against the king's land — understand that the Persians consider all Asia theirs and belonging to their reigning king.
